title: FlowPAC: Flow-Guided Visual Pruning and Action Caching for Efficient VLA Inference
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for embodied AI, yet their high inference latency and memory footprint remain major barriers to edge deployment. Existing training-free acceleration techniques, such as visual token pruning and action caching, typically rely on static resource allocation. This mismatch with dynamic robotic interactions not only degrades control performance but also causes severe hardware inefficiencies, including fragmented KV-cache layouts and wasted compute on non-critical regions. To address this, we propose FlowPAC, a locality-aware framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to jointly optimize visual and action computation. Specifically, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP) and Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT) to jointly handle visual token dynamics and enforce spatial locality, reducing memory fragmentation and enabling efficient KV-cache compression. This is complemented by Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR) for adaptive action computation based on motion dynamics. Extensive closed-loop evaluations on LIBERO demonstrate that FlowPAC achieves a 2.13$\times$ end-to-end speedup over the dense baseline while essentially maintaining the success rate with 30% visual-token retention. These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems.

These results validate that aligning computation allocation with both physical dynamics and hardware constraints is essential for efficient VLA deployment on edge systems. vision-language-action models, robotic manipulation, token pruning, diffusion caching, inference acceleration Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising solution to enhance generalization of robotic control in embodied intelligence~ brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt,team2024octo,kim2024openvla . The mainstream VLA architecture pairs a pretrained VLM backbone with a dedicated action expert to unify visual, textual, and action information within a token-domain framework~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi05 . While implementations like the series demonstrate strong generalization, they suffer from prohibitive end-to-end latency on device deployment. Recent work on model efficiency spans quantization of VLA policies~ zhang2026quantvla and visual geometry transformers~ zhang2026fgq , layer skipping~ zhang2026mole , knowledge distillation~ dong2025vitavla , visual token pruning~ cheng2026vla , and action-head feature caching~ yang2026efficientvla . Efficient multimodal inference has also been explored in robotic perception, including training-free visual place recognition~ cheng2025scale . Among these, visual token pruning and action caching have emerged as effective techniques for improving VLA inference efficiency, as they offer the distinct advantage of significantly reducing computational and memory overheads without requiring costly model retraining or architectural modifications~ liu2025vla,xu2026vla,oi2026training . Visual token pruning reduces spatial redundancy by scoring patches with instruction-conditioned attention, action-decoding relevance, or recent action dynamics and retaining a compact token set under a prescribed budget, thereby reducing subsequent token processing and KV-cache storage~ pei2026action,liu2025vla . Caching-based methods reduce temporal redundancy either by reusing visual-token KV states across adjacent observations~ xu2026vla or by retrieving intermediate action trajectories from similar multimodal contexts to warm-start iterative action generation~ oi2026training . However, the holistic impact of these disjointed optimizations on the end-to-end VLA pipeline remains under-explored. Crucially, adapting these isolated optimizations to resource-constrained robotic platforms is non-trivial~ kwon2023mobile,lee2024vit,fan2026sata . First, existing pruning methods typically decide which visual tokens to keep based on their importance in the current frame~ pei2026action,liu2025vla . However, a region that is unimportant in the current frame may become critical in the next few frames, for example, when the gripper moves toward it or approaches a contact boundary. Pruning decisions must be made before this future importance becomes directly observable. Premature pruning can therefore discard future-critical information and misallocate the compute budget, degrading control accuracy. Second, existing action-side caching methods typically use a fixed refresh rule, such as recomputing the action expert every few steps or when a predefined threshold is reached~ chen2026real,oi2026training . Yet recomputation needs vary throughout an interaction: frequent refreshes during smooth phases waste computation by repeating similar work, whereas infrequent refreshes during rapid or contact-rich transitions can reuse outdated action updates and introduce control lag. Fixed refresh rules thus fail to adapt computation to changing interaction dynamics. Both problems arise from the same limitation: the computational value of visual tokens and the freshness of cached action updates change with the interaction dynamics. This motivates a shared dynamic signal that can capture both where visual information is likely to become important and when cached action updates need to be refreshed. To tackle these bottlenecks, we present FlowPAC, a training-free framework that leverages task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to restore the temporal and spatial continuity overlooked by existing acceleration methods. We design this framework to directly address the aforementioned bottlenecks. First, to mitigate the compute budget misallocation caused by current-frame-only pruning, we introduce Direction-Aware Trajectory Propagation (DATP). DATP exploits the fact that optical flow is a pixel-wise temporal derivative to propagate token importance along the signed flow field, explicitly preserving tokens in future interaction regions regardless of their current redundancy. Second, we introduce Flow-Conditioned Action-Block Refresh (FCAR), which adapts cache refreshes to optical-flow dynamics, reducing updates during stable phases and increasing them during transients to match computation with task demands. Furthermore, to ensure these optimizations yield genuine end-to-end speedups on resource-constrained robotic platforms instead of being negated by fragmented masking, we incorporate Locality-Aware Contiguous Token Selection (LACT). By leveraging the inherent spatial locality of optical flow, LACT enforces contiguous block selection after a dense warm-up phase, reducing memory fragmentation while preserving physically meaningful token groups, thereby making the above dynamic scheduling practically deployable. To summarize, this work makes the following contributions: We propose DATP, which combines instruction-conditioned semantic relevance with signed optical flow to propagate semantic relevance toward future interaction regions and allocate visual tokens along predicted trajectories. We introduce FCAR, which maps semantic-weighted dual-view motion to a causal, episode-calibrated refresh budget. FCAR selectively reuses action-expert residuals during stable solver steps without shortening the original flow-matching trajectory. We develop LACT with deferred physical packing. LACT constructs an exact-budget, spatially coherent token mask, while deferred packing preserves early cross-token interaction and physically shortens the position-preserving visual prefix and its KV cache for subsequent layers. Profiling and Motivation sec:profiling_motivation As illustrated in the introduction, VLA systems typically consist of a VLM backbone and an action expert. To gain deeper insights into their execution efficiency, we profile as our representative model. Profiling Setup subsec:profiling_setup To identify the computational and memory bottlenecks of flow-matching VLA inference, we profile the complete policy inference under the same closed-loop rollout protocol used for evaluation. Our analysis targets three questions: (1) where execution time concentrates, (2) how the visual-prefix KV state scales with token count, and (3) whether optical-flow magnitude between consecutive observations varies across task phases. All measurements are taken on a single NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB GPU with BF16 precision and batch size one. The live tensor allocation of the visual-prefix KV state is captured at each retention setting. To construct the optical-flow magnitude trace, we compute dense optical flow between each pair of consecutive rollout frames and average the magnitudes of the top 15 of pixels within each frame pair. Here, the magnitude of a flow vector denotes its Euclidean norm, consistent with Sec.~ subsec:fcar . We show the raw trace together with an offline centered moving-average trace to suppress frame-level noise and apply within-rollout percentile normalization for visualization. Bottleneck Analysis subsec:motivations Panel~I of Fig.~ fig:overview (a) reveals two distinct resource imbalances between the sources of latency and persistent memory in dense inference: action denoising dominates runtime (77.6 ), while visual tokens dominate the prefix KV state (79.3 ). As shown in panel~II of Fig.~ fig:overview (a), visual tokens account for 768 of the 968 prefix tokens (79.3 ) and occupy 13.50 of the 17.02\,MiB live KV state. Across the evaluated retention settings, physical packing reduces the prefix KV state from 17.02\,MiB to 9.81, 8.02, and 6.19\,MiB, showing that physically shortening the prefix substantially reduces persistent KV storage. However, vision encoding and prefix computation together account for only 22.2 of policy-core latency, so even their idealized removal yields a visual-only speedup ceiling of . Visual pruning alone is therefore insufficient; repeated action denoising, the dominant latency component, must also be addressed. At each control query, the action expert performs ten flow-matching denoising steps, consuming 236.3\,ms, or 77.6 of the 304.6\,ms policy-core latency. However, the action expert does not need to be recomputed at every step. When the interaction changes slowly, consecutive observations are similar, so the previous action update can be reused. During more dynamic interactions, such as grasping or contact, the scene changes more quickly and the cached update may no longer be accurate, requiring more frequent recomputation. Therefore, the key is to decide when the cached update can be reused and when it should be refreshed. As shown in the rightmost panel (III) of Fig.~ fig:overview (a), the optical-flow magnitude also changes across different interaction phases, with larger values during more active interactions. This suggests that optical flow can provide a simple observable signal for deciding when to reuse the cached update and when to recompute the action expert. Method Overview sec:overview jointly optimizes visual and action computation by using task-aware optical flow as a shared physical signal to coordinate two complementary axes: where visual computation is preserved and when action-expert computation is refreshed. As summarized in Fig.~ fig:overview (b), the spatial branch comprises DATP, which predicts future-critical tokens using instruction-conditioned relevance and signed motion, and LACT, which converts the spatial score into an exact-budget, spatially coherent mask followed by deferred physical packing. The temporal branch, FCAR, aggregates the same task-aware motion evidence into a causal refresh signal that adapts action-expert recomputation to the current dynamics of the interaction. title: Intervention-Robust VLA: Diverse Demonstrations for Robot Deployment with Safety Filters
summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to 90% from 0% for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have shown strong potential for learning complex robotic behaviors from demonstrations. However, learning safe behavior directly from data requires extensive coverage of safety-critical situations, which is often impractical in real-world settings. Test-time safety filters provide an alternative by correcting unsafe actions during deployment, but these interventions can drive the robot into states poorly covered by the training data, thereby degrading task performance. We introduce InteR-VLA, an intervention-robust framework for VLAs that leverages diverse task-completing demonstrations to broaden task-relevant state coverage and maintain competence under safety interventions. By better aligning the training distribution with safety-filtered deployment under the same data budget, our approach mitigates intervention-induced distribution shift while preserving task performance. Real-world experiments across in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings show that InteR-VLA maintains safety, increases Safe Success Rate up to from for nominal policies, and consistently outperforms nominal-data training on both evaluated VLAs. Introduction Vision--language--action models (VLAs)~ rt2,bjorck2025gr00t,intelligence2025pi have emerged as a promising direction toward generalist robot policies capable of performing diverse tasks from multimodal instructions. Building on vision--language foundation models, VLAs map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions within an end-to-end framework. Through imitation learning on expert demonstrations collected via robot teleoperation~ fu2024mobile or portable interfaces such as UMI~ chi2024universal , these models can acquire complex manipulation behaviors without manually designing task-dependent controllers. Recent VLAs have demonstrated increasingly broad capabilities across objects, tasks, and environments, highlighting the potential of large-scale demonstration learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation. Despite this progress, deploying VLAs in real-world environments introduces a critical requirement beyond task completion: safety. In particular, robots must avoid collisions even when deployment conditions differ from those represented during training. Recent approaches~ liu2025evovla,honari2024safety address this challenge by broadening the training distribution with diverse safety-critical scenarios and incorporating safety objectives through safe reinforcement learning (SafeRL). This includes incorporating multiple unsafe and safety-critical behaviors during training~ zhang2026safevla and providing safety-critical benchmark environments and datasets for learning safe behaviors~ baisafelab . Such approaches improve safety by increasing exposure to risky situations, but their effectiveness depends on how well these scenarios cover deployment conditions and may be further limited by sim-to-real gaps. This motivates complementary test-time safety enforcement. Safety filters~ wabersich2023data,hsu2023safety provide such test-time enforcement by modifying policy actions when necessary to satisfy safety constraints. Control barrier functions (CBFs)~ CBF_Ames,huang2024learning are a widely used realization, enabling real-time safety correction without retraining the policy. This principle has been applied to generative robot policies~ xiao2023safediffuser,huang2025sad and extended to VLA deployment using vision--language reasoning and perception to derive safety constraints directly from the scene~ hu2025vlsa . However, these test-time corrections can alter the policy's behavior and drive the robot toward out-of-distribution states, as shown in , thereby substantially degrading task performance~ romer2025demonstrations . Path-consistent intervention can reduce this mismatch by keeping execution close to the nominal trajectory~ romer2025demonstrations , but becomes restrictive when safe task completion requires deviating from the nominal path. Thus, existing inference-time safety mechanisms alone do not ensure task completion after intervention. This limitation motivates our key insight that intervention robustness can be improved by broadening the distribution of task-relevant behaviors represented in the demonstrations, as shown in . We introduce InteR-VLA (Intervention Robustness for VLA), a framework for successful task completion which accounts for deviations induced by safety-filter interventions. InteR-VLA combines complementary roles: diverse demonstrations preserve task competence under intervention, while a safety filter enforces safety at deployment. We propose and analyze two offline collection strategies: diverse demonstrations, which complete tasks in different ways without obstacles to broaden task-relevant coverage, and multimodal avoidance demonstrations, which use path-blocking obstacles to provide direct intervention coverage when hazards are known during collection. Our main contributions are: [leftmargin=*] Analysis of intervention-induced covariate shift. We analyze how demonstration coverage affects VLA robustness to safety-filter interventions and characterize the shift between training and safety-filtered deployment. Intervention-robust data collection. We propose InteR-VLA, using diverse task-completing offline demonstrations to broaden task-relevant coverage at a fixed data budget. By increasing behavioral modes rather than data quantity, our strategy better covers states induced by safety-filter interventions without policy rollouts or filter-specific tuning. Real-world validation. We validate InteR-VLA across in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings on two VLA models, achieving Safe Success Rate up to and consistently outperforming nominal-data baselines. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models and Safety Learning VLAs~ rt2,bjorck2025gr00t,intelligence2025pi leverage pretrained vision--language representations and large-scale robot demonstrations~ o2024open,khazatsky2024droid to learn multimodal policies for diverse manipulation tasks. These demonstrations naturally capture variations across tasks, environments, embodiments, and task-completing behaviors~ chi2025diffusion,huang2024toward , from which VLAs acquire broad capabilities such as cross-embodiment transfer~ gupta2025umi and dexterous manipulation~ zhong2026dexgraspvla . However, since most VLAs are trained through imitation learning, their performance remains strongly dependent on the state--action coverage of the demonstration data. To facilitate VLA deployment in safety-critical scenarios, several works introduce safety objectives during training~ liu2025evovla and optimize them through SafeRL, commonly formulated as constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs)~ altman2021constrained . SafeVLA~ zhang2026safevla , for example, models safety requirements and generates diverse unsafe and safety-critical behaviors for SafeRL, while SafeLab~ baisafelab provides safety-critical environments and safety learning frameworks. These methods broaden safety-relevant training coverage, but provide no hard constraint when deployment conditions fall outside their training scenarios. Unlike these approaches, InteR-VLA leaves safety to a test-time filter and uses demonstrations to maintain competence under safety interventions. Safety Filtering for Learned Robot Policies Safety filters~ wabersich2023data,hsu2023safety enforce constraints at deployment by modifying nominal policy actions, often through online optimization. Predictive safety filters~ tearle2021predictive explicitly optimize for safe actions, while control barrier functions (CBFs)~ CBF_Ames provide safety conditions enforceable through lightweight optimization. When applied to collision avoidance, CBFs are commonly constructed from differentiable distances between geometric approximations such as spheres~ singletary2021safety and ellipsoids~ dai2023safe , while recent work learns barrier functions from high-dimensional latent representations~ nakamura2025train . CBF constraints have been integrated into generative robot policies~ xiao2023safediffuser,huang2025sad , and VLSA~ hu2025vlsa uses vision--language reasoning and perception to construct explicit geometric constraints for VLA filtering. However, safety interventions can deviate from demonstrated actions and drive the system toward underrepresented states. Path-consistent braking mitigates this shift by preserving the nominal trajectory~ romer2025demonstrations , but cannot provide alternative task-completing motions when the nominal path must be bypassed. Unlike path-consistent braking, InteR-VLA lets the filter deviate from the nominal path and maintains competence under safety interventions by training on demonstrations that complete the task along different task-space paths. Preliminaries and Problem Setting Imitation Learning with Vision-Language-Action Models VLAs learn to execute language-specified tasks from a demonstration dataset . It encodes the desired behavior for the task and contains~ episodes with state and action sequence of length . Each state belongs to the VLA state space and contains the language instruction and current observation , typically comprising camera images and robot proprioception, e.g., joint angles. The action belongs to the action space and typically specifies a high-level command such as the relative Cartesian displacement. Given an expert dataset , a VLA policy parameterized by is trained through imitation learning to model the conditional action distribution represented by the demonstrations: Modern VLAs often predict actions in chunks of horizon ~ chi2025diffusion , executing the first actions before replanning from the latest state, resulting in receding-horizon closed-loop execution. However, imitation learning only reproduces behaviors represented in and does not explicitly enforce safety at test time. Thus, even a well-trained VLA policy cannot guarantee safe execution. Safety Filter for Vision-Language-Action Models To ensure safety during deployment, a common approach is to integrate a safety filter wabersich2023data into the VLA inference pipeline. The safety filter can be interpreted as an operator that modifies the action proposed by VLA: such that executing the corrected action satisfies the safety requirements while deviating minimally from the originally proposed VLA action. The filter is applied at each time step before the action is executed. If the robot state remains in the safe set , i.e., for all whenever , then the set is forward invariant, ensuring collision-free execution throughout the task. title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 9 tables: a 4-page paper with appendices. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.

Introduction sec:intro On meal assembly lines, a robot station picks an ingredient from a pan with a utensil and places it into a tray. Every pick must deliver a target weight, such as 167\,g of rice, within a tolerance that customers set in percent. A heavy portion gives food away, and a light one fails the meal specification. The pan changes under the robot. Each pick leaves a crater, food slides into it, and the next pick meets a different surface (Fig.~ fig:front ). Foods also differ: rice holds a crater, beans in sauce flow back, and broccoli pieces roll and fall. Production controllers convert the target weight into a volume with a density from recent scale readings, then choose the depth where the heightmap says the utensil captures that volume. The density times the volume at that depth is the controller's internal estimate. Picked masses stay near the commanded target. Learning a policy by trial and error in production is slow and costly. Granular and compliant food is hard to model analytically or simulate~ clarke2019thesis,shi2022robocraft . A world model~ ha2018worldmodels , a learned model of what an action does to the environment, offers another route. Every production pick is a free training example~ pinto2016supersizing,levine2018handeye : a camera sees the surface before and after the pick, and a scale under the pan weighs the removed food. Such a model could estimate each portion before the scale settles and later help choose the pick, if it is accurate and responds to the action. We built such a model (Fig.~ fig:front ) and evaluated its prediction of the picked mass with robot inputs against the commanded target and three other baselines. Our contributions are: A food world model learned from production data: to our knowledge, the first for food picking. From the pre-pick heightmap, it predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty for nine foods with nonlinear, hard-to-model dynamics. An evaluation on real production data against four baselines: 9 lower mass root-mean-square error (RMSE) than the commanded target or the mean of each food, and 24 lower than the controller's internal estimate. Gradient-boosted trees have a 0.2\,g lower RMSE but predict only the mass, not the next state. A simple, efficient architecture for deployment: a 2.3\,M-parameter U-Net that also estimates the uncertainty of each prediction, trained with a faithful heteroscedastic loss. Related Work sec:related World models. Learned models of how the environment responds to an action are used to plan or to train policies~ ha2018worldmodels,hafner2019planet,hafner2025dreamerv3,wu2023daydreamer , mostly in latent or image space. Our model predicts height in millimeters and mass in grams. Granular material and food. Graph networks learn granular and deformable dynamics~ sanchezgonzalez2020gns,shi2022robocraft , and image-space models suit piles~ suh2021linear . Schenck~ ~ schenck2017granular predicted the heightmap of granular media after a scoop, Zhu~ ~ zhu2023fewshot the scooped volume, and Clarke~ clarke2019thesis the scooped mass and the heightmap change. Clarke also chose scoops for a target mass. Takahashi~ ~ takahashi2021targetmass,takahashi2022entangled predicted the mass of a food grasp with uncertainty, and Mori~ ~ mori2025ros2 the grasped weight of granular food. SCOOP'D~ wang2025scoopd learns scooping in simulation. Industrial portioning measures a volume and assumes a density~ thongprasith2025portioning , as the production controller does. These works use lab setups, simulation or a fixed density. Uncertainty and declining. Deep ensembles~ lakshminarayanan2017ensembles,chua2018pets and mean-and-variance networks~ nix1994meanvariance,kendall2017uncertainty,stirn2023faithful give predictive uncertainty. At a fixed reject rate~ chow1970reject , the optimal regression rule declines the inputs with the largest conditional variance~ zaoui2020reject . Learning from production data. Machine learning in production fails in ways that benchmarks hide~ sculley2015debt : inputs that exist only after the decision leak the outcome~ kaufman2012leakage,kapoor2023leakage , networks learn shortcuts in their data~ geirhos2020shortcut , and label errors in test sets reorder models~ northcutt2021labelerrors . Production pipelines guard against such defects by validating their data~ breck2017mltestscore,breck2019datavalidation . Methodology sec:method Data and Training Pairs sec:data Each station has a UR5e arm, an Intel RealSense D415 depth camera about 0.8\,m above two pans, and scales under the pans. Our records hold 133,340 picks of nine foods (Table~ tab:food ) from 43 robots at customer sites and our own facility over 19 months. A session is one production run of one robot on one food. We split sessions at random into training and test sessions. A training pair holds the heightmaps before and after the pick and the picked mass, the drop in the scale reading. The pre-pick frame is the last depth frame with the arm clear of the pan. The post-pick frame is the first one after the scale settles. The data export had paired many frames with a neighboring pick's record. We re-pair each pick by the record shift that puts its crater nearest the commanded pick point on the food surface. We drop the pick if that crater lies more than 4\,cm away or if its weight is impossible. The checked records form 1,012 training sessions (61,773 picks) and 440 test sessions (15,598 picks). All results use checked picks. Model and Training At pick , the state is the pan surface , a heightmap of grid squares of \,mm over a \,mm pan. The mask if square has a depth reading before the pick, and 0 otherwise. The action is the commanded pick location and the scalars the controller sets; is the food and the utensil. Our model learns , the distribution of the surface change and the picked mass , with for each grid square and . The network is a U-Net~ ronneberger2015unet with a surface head and a mass head. Its residual layers are modulated (FiLM~ perez2018film ) by learned food and utensil embeddings and the pick position (Fig.~ fig:arch ). The surface head predicts and per square. Self-attention at the coarsest levels adds context from the whole pan. The mass head pools the bottleneck features globally, over the pan, and locally, around the pick. The mass head also takes the pick scalars and the removed volume of the predicted surface change. In this way, the surface head feeds the mass head. Each output needs an accurate mean and a spread that says how far off the mean usually is. The usual Gaussian likelihood divides the gradient of the mean by , so a model can predict a large on hard picks instead of fitting them~ seitzer2022pitfalls ; our mass head did this and stopped learning. The faithful heteroscedastic loss~ stirn2023faithful separates the two tasks. For a residual and a predicted spread , where stops the gradient: the first term trains the mean as a plain squared error, and the last two train to match the size of the residual without changing the mean. The total loss is where is the mean of~( eq:faithful ) over the squares measured both before and after the pick, and is~( eq:faithful ) on the standardized mass. The last term ties the picked mass to the removed volume through a density. In this term, is one density per food (g/cm ), learned with the network, and is the standard deviation of the training masses. The weights , and are hyperparameters chosen by a parameter sweep. We train five models with different seeds (AdamW~ loshchilov2019adamw , one-cycle cosine schedule, 40 epochs), each in about 2.6\,h on one GPU; Appendix~ app:network gives all settings. A crater square often loses its reading after the pick, so the gaps of this mask mark the coming crater and leak part of the outcome. Model Inference sec:robot Inputs. title: MAWAM: Joint Imagination for Collaborative Robot Manipulation with a Multi-Agent World Action Model
summary: World action models (WAMs) excel at robot manipulation by imagining future observations and decoding actions from them, yet remain confined to a single embodied agent. In practice, manipulation often requires multiple robots to collaborate across disjoint workspaces, coupled timing, and heterogeneous embodiments. Such coordination demands both spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions and awareness of individual embodiment and role identities, whereas existing decentralized per-robot policies, flat centralized models, and multi-robot VLAs fail to unite both. To bridge this gap, we present MAWAM, a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation. Through an agent-axis curriculum, MAWAM expands a single-agent WAM along an agent dimension to coordinate teams under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, joint self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment. We further formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation along three axes (why, when, and who) and develop MA-Task Harness, a coding-agent pipeline where mutually constraining generators and evaluators co-evolve customizable simulation-data and evaluation packages. Using this pipeline, we build MA-Bench across all axes with seven tasks, pairing joint success rate with role and collaboration scores for fine-grained analysis. On MA-Bench, MAWAM reaches 82.7% mean joint success, 30.7% above the strongest baseline, and achieves real-time closed-loop collaboration on a real heterogeneous robot team.

Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs)~ kim2026cosmospolicy,li2026lingbotva,ye2026wamzero,yuan2026fastwam,bi2026motus2,yu2026openwam advance robot manipulation by coupling control with future visual modeling, imagining how observations evolve to ground actions in physical foresight. Yet existing WAMs remain confined to a single embodied agent, whereas real-world manipulation often requires multiple robots collaborating beyond one agent's limits. These limits stem from what one agent can observe, where it can reach, what it can actuate and so on, often under tight temporal coupling ( four-arm tray transport) and across heterogeneous embodiments. Thus, the future is no longer rolled out by one agent against a passive scene, but co-authored across space, time, and distinct embodied agents with specialized views, kinematics, and roles. Existing multi-robot methods fall into three categories, yet none unites spatiotemporal alignment of future interactions with awareness of individual embodiment and role identities. First, LLM planners~ mandi2023roco,liu2024coherent,chen2024emos,tan2025roboos negotiate subtasks while delegating physical coupling to motion planners, struggling with closed-loop contacts. Second, decentralized policies~ qin2025robofactory,dong2025mimicd,doshi2026chorus condition each robot on local views, leaving partner cues invisible and failing to align coupled futures across agents. Third, centralized or coupled multi-robot VLAs~ zhang2026mavla,zhang2026vlafabric,xu2026coopmavla map observations reactively to actions via multi-arm prompting, peer feature exchange, or pooled views, lacking visual foresight while blurring agent, role, and embodiment identities. Our key insight is straightforward: let a team imagine together, then act individually ( ). We present , a multi-agent world action model that jointly predicts the future observations of multiple embodiments and decodes each agent's actions from them for collaborative manipulation ( ). Through an agent-axis curriculum, expands a foundational single-agent WAM along an agent dimension from single-role trajectories to synchronized multi-robot episodes under shared weights. Within one unified causal sequence, self-attention spans all agents to spatiotemporally align their imagined futures, while hierarchical language, Fourier identity encodings, and embodiment masks bind each stream to its role, identity, and embodiment across homogeneous and heterogeneous teams. Studying such collaboration also exposes a benchmark gap: most manipulation suites focus on a single embodied agent ( RoboTwin~ mu2025robotwin,chen2025robotwin2 and RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2024robocasa,nasiriany2026robocasa365 ), whereas multi-robot suites~ mandi2023roco,qin2025robofactory design collaborative tasks case by case: they neither verify that a task is beyond any single agent, nor systematically cover why collaboration is needed, how tightly agents couple in time, and which embodiments take part, while success-rate scoring cannot separate individual role competence from genuine collaboration. We therefore formalize multi-agent-necessary manipulation ( ) along three tested axes: why collaboration is needed (information, spatial, or capability complementarity), when intervals couple (asynchronous, partially synchronous, or synchronous), and who executes each role (homogeneous or heterogeneous embodiments), paired with milestone metrics separating Role and Collaboration Scores from Success Rate. Building on this formalism and capable coding agents, we build ( ) to co-evolve simulation generators and deterministic evaluators into customizable data-synthesis and evaluation packages, upon which we propose ( ) with seven tasks (700 certified pairs) across all axes. title: ProMix: Efficient Data Mixture Optimization for Robotic Imitation via Proxy-Reference DRO
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. We further provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model's role in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy, low-quality domains (-3.8% average and -14.3% worst-domain success rate), and that entropy regularization is needed to prevent weight collapse. Evaluated on 9500 real-world episodes from the Open-X Embodiment dataset, ProMix improves the average success rate over uniform mixing from 68.4% to 76.2%, matching Re-Mix within evaluation noise while reducing mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours - versus 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B for full-scale searches - with a +17.1% absolute gain on the worst-case domain.
full_text: ProMix: Efficient Data Mixture Optimization for Robotic Imitation via Proxy-Reference DRO Qie Sima , Wei Xue, Yike Guo Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models excel in open-world manipulation, yet their performance often saturates when training data are naively pooled across heterogeneous robots, tasks, and environments. Distributionally robust data mixture optimization, exemplified by Re-Mix, can recover much of this performance, but its weight search requires training full-scale policies twice on the entire corpus, placing it out of reach for most laboratories. We present ProMix, a compute-efficient instantiation of the proxy-reference DRO recipe for robotic imitation learning: a 15M-parameter proxy learns per-domain sampling weights by minimizing worst-case excess loss against a frozen reference model, and the learned weights transfer, without re-tuning, to VLA backbones up to 7B parameters. We further provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model's role in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy, low-quality domains ( average and worst-domain success rate), and that entropy regularization is needed to prevent weight collapse. Evaluated on 9500 real-world episodes from the Open-X Embodiment dataset, ProMix improves the average success rate over uniform mixing from 68.4 to 76.2 , matching Re-Mix within evaluation noise while reducing mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours---versus 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at 7B for full-scale searches---with a absolute gain on the worst-case domain. Vision-Language-Action model, data mixture optimization, distributionally robust optimization, data curation, imitation learning Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are rapidly transforming the robotics landscape, enabling agents to execute complex, open-world tasks from natural language instructions. The impressive generalization capabilities of these foundation models, such as RT-1 RT1 , are a direct result of pre-training on massive, diverse multimodal datasets. Recently, the field has gravitated toward ``general-purpose physical intelligence'' with the emergence of the model family black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_ , which achieves state-of-the-art control through sophisticated data curation and distillation. Beyond proprietary efforts, open datasets such as Open-X openx202 and DROID khazatsky2024droid and open models such as OpenVLA kim2025openvla and GR00T N1 bjorck2025gr00t have made large-scale pre-training broadly accessible. However, a critical bottleneck is shifting from architecture to data: effectively blending heterogeneous data collected from disparate robots, platforms, and tasks. Naively pooling these domains causes performance saturation, and the curation recipes used by industrial labs are neither public nor reproducible. Recent research has started to bridge LLM data optimization and robotics. DoReMi xie2023doremi showed that in LLM pre-training, domain weights can be learned cheaply by a small proxy model trained against a frozen reference model, so that the expensive weight search never touches the final large model. Re-Mix remix ported this distributionally robust optimization (DRO) objective to large-scale imitation learning and demonstrated substantial gains over uniform and hand-tuned mixtures on Open-X Embodiment. However, Re-Mix's instantiation retains a prohibitive cost structure: both the reference model and the robust proxy are trained on the full corpus at (near-)final policy scale, so the weight search roughly doubles the training budget before the final policy is even trained---a limitation the authors themselves highlight. Moreover, two questions that determine whether such methods are practical at the scale of modern VLA training remain unquantified. First, is the reference model actually load-bearing in robotics, where continuous action spaces and heteroscedastic demonstration noise dominate the loss? Without it, a standalone proxy may become overly pessimistic, disproportionately assigning weights to inherently chaotic or noisy trajectories rather than to domains with the most headroom for cross-domain generalization. Second, do weights learned at a small proxy scale transfer to the large backbones where the savings matter most? This transfer is asserted in prior work but has not been systematically measured for robotic policies. This paper introduces ProMix, a framework that makes proxy-reference data mixture optimization practical for robotic imitation learning. ProMix learns mixture weights with a 15M-parameter proxy guided by a frozen, standardly-trained reference model, at a cost of 11 GPU-hours that is fixed regardless of the final backbone---under matched accounting, a full-scale search in our reimplementation of Re-Mix costs 16 GPU-hours at the 50M comparison scale and 192 GPU-hours at the 7B scale---and transfers the learned weights, without re-tuning, to 50M and 7B VLA backbones. Beyond efficiency, we use ProMix as an experimental probe of the proxy-reference design itself: we provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled ablation of the reference model in robotic DRO, showing that removing it induces over-pessimism toward noisy domains ( average and worst-domain success rate), and that an entropy regularizer on the weight simplex is essential to prevent weight collapse. This offers a practical path for researchers to achieve competitive performance without industrial-scale computing clusters, aligning with the industry trend toward compact yet capable models like intelligence2025pi_ . Our key contributions are as follows: We present ProMix, a compute-efficient proxy-reference framework for data mixture optimization in robotic imitation learning, which reduces mixture-optimization cost to a backbone-independent 11 GPU-hours---versus 16 GPU-hours at 50M and 192 GPU-hours at 7B ( ) for full-scale searches---by performing the entire search with a 15M proxy rather than full-scale policies. We provide, to our knowledge, the first controlled analysis of the reference model in robotic DRO, demonstrating that the excess-loss objective is essential for mitigating over-pessimism on noisy, heterogeneous robotic data, and we identify entropy regularization as the stabilizer that prevents weight collapse. We quantify cross-scale transferability on the Open-X Embodiment dataset: weights learned by the 15M proxy consistently improve 50M and 7B VLA models, lifting the average success rate from 68.4 to 76.2 and the worst-domain rate from 51.4 to 68.5 . Related Work sec:related work Robotics Foundation Models and Data Efficiency Foundation models have enabled general-purpose agents to acquire complex skills from large-scale datasets. RT-1 RT1 demonstrated the potential of transformer-backed Visual-Language-Action (VLA) architectures, and the model family (e.g., black2024pi_0 and intelligence2025pi_ ) shows that sophisticated data curation yields capable policies with a fraction of the parameters. Open models such as OpenVLA kim2025openvla and GR00T N1 bjorck2025gr00t , together with open corpora such as Open-X openx202 and DROID khazatsky2024droid , have made large-scale pre-training broadly accessible. The success of these models remains tied to how well heterogeneous data sources are combined. Beyond large teleoperation corpora such as BridgeData walke2023bridgedata , existing data-efficiency efforts---synthetic data generation, distillation, and demonstration filtering---typically improve training efficacy while still treating all real-world data equally, overlooking the core challenge: how to optimally combine heterogeneous data from disparate sources. ProMix addresses this by automating the discovery of the most informative data blend. Distributionally Robust Learning Alternative approaches select training data online---via curriculum sequencing or active human-in-the-loop queries---but require interaction or iterative labeling that does not scale to large-scale pre-training. Theoretically, our approach is grounded in Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO), which minimizes worst-case loss over an uncertainty set to guard against distribution shift, here applied in its group-level form over predefined training domains. Recent work on distributionally robust imitation learning tasil_2025 has highlighted the necessity of DRO to handle data heterogeneity-induced shifts. ProMix operationalizes these insights through a scalable proxy-reference framework. In noisy robotics environments, the reference model converts the objective from absolute worst-case loss to an excess loss, which we show empirically is the difference between robust optimization and over-pessimistic weight collapse. Data Pruning and Demonstration-Level Curation To handle the scale of robotics datasets, researchers have explored selection and pruning to improve efficiency. At the demonstration level, DemInf hejna2025deminf ranks individual trajectories by mutual-information estimates and achieves consistent gains, while quality filtering and subsetting have been used to reduce training costs. Such methods may, however, discard data from minority domains or outlier tasks, potentially harming out-of-distribution robustness. Domain-level mixing and demonstration-level pruning are orthogonal: ProMix retains the entire dataset but dynamically re-weights domains, ensuring that high-variance minority domains contribute appropriately to generalization, and is complementary to trajectory-level curation. Data Mixture Optimization (DMO) The concept of learning an optimal data mixture (DMO) originated in LLM pre-training. DoReMi xie2023doremi introduced the canonical recipe: a lightweight proxy model is trained with group DRO against a frozen reference model trained on a uniform mixture, minimizing worst-case excess loss, and the resulting weights transfer to much larger models. Follow-up LLM work refined this recipe: Data Mixing Laws ye2025data fits parametric scaling laws that predict the loss of unseen mixtures, and RegMix liu2025regmix fits a regression over small-scale runs to predict large-model performance under unseen mixtures. These alternatives require training multiple candidate mixtures to fit the mixture--performance model; ProMix instead requires a single proxy--reference pair whose search cost is independent of the final backbone. In robotics, Re-Mix remix successfully ported DoReMi's excess-loss DRO to imitation learning, showing large gains over uniform and human-selected weights on Open-X. However, its instantiation leaves two gaps that matter for VLA-scale training. First, the reference model and the robust proxy are trained on the full corpus at (near)final policy scale, so computing the weights roughly doubles the total training budget -- the authors themselves flag this two-pass cost as a key limitation and call for cheaper alternatives. Second, the paper asserts but does not measure transfer of weights across model scales, and provides no ablation isolating the reference model's contribution in the robotic setting. ProMix closes both gaps: it performs the entire search with a 15M proxy and frozen reference (11 GPU-hours, versus 16--192 GPU-hours for full-scale searches at 50M--7B under matched conventions), provides to our knowledge the first controlled study of the reference model's role in robotic DRO, and quantifies cross-scale transfer up to a 7B backbone. We additionally identify entropy regularization on the weight simplex as a practical necessity---without it, the weights collapse onto a few noisy domains, a failure mode we characterize empirically. title: WorldWeave: Rethinking Embodied Navigation through Cross-Task World Modeling
summary: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.
full_text: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose , a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines. Introduction sec:intro A mobile robot's observations are inherently shaped by its own actions: each movement changes what the agent perceives and alters its spatial relationship with the environment and task goal. This creates a continuous perception--action loop, in which current decisions shape future observations, which in turn inform subsequent decisions. Effective mobile decision making therefore requires not only understanding the current interaction state, but also anticipating how that state may evolve as the agent acts. The dynamics underlying this evolution can vary substantially with the task goal and interaction setting. While an agent's own motion continuously changes its visual observations and spatial relationships with the environment, a moving target introduces an additional source of state variation. Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN)~ Visionandlanguagenavigation,Beyondthenavgraph and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT)~ zhong2019ad,trackvla represent two complementary settings that capture these different aspects of mobile embodied interaction. In VLN, an agent grounds natural-language instructions in visual observations and navigates toward an instruction-specified goal that remains fixed within an episode. Its state evolution is primarily driven by the agent's own motion as it progresses through environmental structures over extended trajectories. EVT, in contrast, requires a mobile agent to actively follow a moving target through continuous perception and control, where the evolving interaction state is jointly shaped by the agent's movement and the target's independent motion. Although VLN and EVT differ in task objectives and interaction patterns, both involve mobile agent-environment interaction. In VLN, state evolution primarily reflects the agent's progression through environmental structures over extended trajectories~ navmorph,zhang2026futurenav , whereas in EVT, it additionally involves the continuously changing agent--target relationship shaped by both agent and target motion~ uss . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:intro \,(a), the two tasks offer complementary perspectives on embodied state evolution. Together, they provide an opportunity to study world modeling beyond the dynamics of either task alone. Despite their distinct goals and action spaces, can these related interaction patterns be leveraged to learn shared predictive dynamics? A natural framework for modeling such predictive dynamics is a world model~ worldmodels , which learns how latent states evolve through interaction. Conventional world models typically model state transitions conditioned on predefined actions, i.e., ~ learning,dream . While well suited to individual tasks, extending it across heterogeneous tasks introduces additional challenges, as the actions conditioning state transitions may differ across task settings~ zhang2026mixture . In our setting, directly conditioning a shared world model on the heterogeneous actions of VLN and EVT would tie its learned dynamics to task-specific action definitions. Latent-action learning provides an alternative by inferring latent transition variables from state changes encoded in consecutive observations, rather than relying on predefined action labels~ genie,gao2026dreamdojo . This motivates a shared transition representation across heterogeneous embodied tasks. Establishing such a transition representation, however, does not determine how the shared dynamics should support each task. VLN and EVT rely on predictive dynamics differently for downstream decision making, while naive sharing across heterogeneous tasks can introduce interference and negative transfer~ jeong2024quantifying,jeong2025selective . Our preliminary experiments make this issue explicit. As shown in Fig.~ fig:intro \,(b) , using a single shared adapter preserves VLN performance but yields little effective tracking capability for EVT. Introducing task-specific adapters substantially recovers EVT performance, whereas directly incorporating the shared world representation into VLN's decision pathway degrades navigation performance. These observations suggest that effective dynamics sharing requires not only a common transition representation, but also task-specific adaptation of the shared predictions to the distinct representations and decision processes of each task. Motivated by these observations, we propose , a cross-task world-modeling framework that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation for VLN and EVT. During pretraining, learns state transitions through inverse--forward dynamics: latent actions are inferred from state changes encoded in consecutive observations and used to predict subsequent states. Because these latent actions characterize observed state transitions rather than task-specific physical actions, the learned dynamics are not tied to either task's action definition and can be pretrained from videos without action annotations. To enable prediction without access to future observations at inference time, the model further learns to infer these latent actions from current interaction context. The resulting future-state predictions are then adaptively integrated into each task's representation, allowing shared predictive dynamics to support distinct downstream decision processes. In this way, shares how state transitions are modeled while preserving how predictive information is used for task-specific decision making. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We investigate cross-task dynamics sharing in embodied navigation, focusing on Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) as two complementary interaction settings with distinct forms of state evolution and decision making. We propose , which couples shared latent dynamics with task-specific predictive adaptation. It learns latent transitions from state changes in consecutive observations without relying on task-specific action definitions, while adapting shared future-state predictions to distinct task representations and decision processes. Extensive experiments across VLN and EVT benchmarks show consistent improvements over task-specific baselines, supporting the effectiveness of cross-task dynamics learning across complementary embodied interactions. Predictive modeling has also been explored, e.g., NavMorph~ navmorph learns latent state transitions to anticipate future navigation states. Visual Tracking. Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) extends active visual tracking to embodied agents that actively follow moving targets through egocentric perception and closed-loop control~ zhong2019ad,zhong2019ad+,trackvla . title: FlexWAM: Learning Flexible Visual Routing for World Action Models
summary: Humans dynamically adjust their reliance on sensory modalities across manipulation stages. Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. For action prediction, View-Routed Action Attention uses an observation-conditioned router to prioritize relevant views. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view's contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/.

Although existing World Action Models (WAMs) fuse multi-camera observations, they struggle to adapt their reliance on individual views based on the current observations. This raises a central question: how can the action expert integrate complementary visual evidence while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action? FlexWAM addresses this challenge through three modules. First, we alternate within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and complementary cues. To calibrate routing, we train a critic using counterfactual view credit, estimated from action loss sensitivity upon suppressing each view’s contribution to action attention. We evaluate FlexWAM with two video backbones on five challenging real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. The two variants improve mean task success by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points over the strongest baseline. Project website: https://flexwam.github.io/ . Introduction sec:introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ pi0,pi05,openvla and World Action Models (WAMs)~ ye2026dreamzero,yuan2026fast,lingbotva commonly use multi-camera observations for robotic manipulation. External cameras provide global workspace context, while wrist cameras capture local gripper--object relationships. In Fig.~ fig:teaser (a), the robot arm occludes the placement area in the external view, and the area lies outside the right wrist camera's field of view. Only the left wrist view reveals the local geometry needed for placement. Several WAMs tile camera images onto a fixed canvas, allocating fewer pixels and visual tokens to wrist views and making these fine details harder to preserve~ ye2026dreamzero,motus,yuan2026fast,gigaworldpolicy05,wang2026openwam,flexpi . For video prediction, these models mix tokens from different cameras at every layer. When other views offer little relevant evidence, repeated mixing may interfere with modeling the local structure and motion in the left wrist view. (1)Does predicting each view's future require cross-view interaction at every layer? For action generation, standard action--video cross-attention assigns weights at the token level, leaving each camera's contribution implicit as observations and control demands change. (2)How can the action expert integrate complementary information while prioritizing views most relevant to the current action? Human perception dynamically prioritizes task-relevant sensory cues while integrating complementary evidence across modalities ~ rohe2015cortical . At different manipulation stages, people adjust their reliance on sensory cues as control demands change~ purdy1999manipulation,johansson2009coding . When plugging in an Ethernet cable, for example, vision guides the approach and initial alignment of the connector. Once the connector touches the port, touch and force provide a more direct cue for detecting misalignment and making fine adjustments~ park2026force . Inspired by this flexibility, we propose FlexWAM to address both questions(Fig.~ fig:teaser (b)) . (1) For video prediction, FlexWAM encodes each view independently and integrates complementary context through cross-view attention at alternating layers, with within-view attention modeling view-specific structure. (2) For action generation, an observation-conditioned router assigns per-view weights, and View-Routed Action Attention uses these weights to combine complementary cues while prioritizing the views most relevant to the current action. When trained end to end with the action prediction loss alone, the action expert can improve by adapting to a nearly fixed mixture of views, leaving the routing weights close to their uniform initialization. To address this limitation, we introduce counterfactual view credit. We estimate each view's contribution by how much masking that view alone increases the action prediction loss. A larger increase indicates greater view importance. A view critic uses these credits to provide stable supervision for the router, enabling it to learn observation-dependent view weights without predefined task stages or view-importance annotations. Our contributions are threefold: We explore an effective multi-view modeling strategy alternating within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and cross-view complementarity. We introduce flexible view routing to estimate view relative importance and View-Routed Action Attention to flexibly regulate visual attention during action generation. We propose counterfactual view credit assignment to estimate each view's relative contribution to action. A critic network uses these estimates to calibrate the router, mitigating shortcuts from action-loss-only training. Experiments on five challenging real-world tasks using two robot platforms and two video-generation backbones demonstrate FlexWAM’s effectiveness. With Wan2.2-TI2V-5B~ wan2025 and LingBot-Video-Dense (1.3B)~ ma2026lingbotvideo,robbyant2026lingbotdense , FlexWAM achieves mean task success rates of 77.2 and 83.8 , exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 16.4 and 23.0 percentage points, respectively. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models Generalist robot policies learn language-conditioned manipulation across diverse tasks through large-scale multitask training~ rt1,octo .Vision-language-action (VLA) policies build on pretrained vision-language models to leverage visual and linguistic knowledge for robot action prediction~ rt2,openvla . For continuous action prediction, diffusion and flow-matching policies model conditional action distributions from multimodal observations~ pi0,pi05,grootn1,rdt1b,smolvla,dexvla . Beyond action modeling, recent work incorporates video prediction into policy to capture visual dynamics for robotic manipulation~ vpp,gr1 . FlexWAM follows this direction by learning to use predictive visual representations from multiple cameras for action generation. World Action Models World action models (WAMs) combine visual dynamics prediction with action learning. Prior work recovers actions from generated visual trajectories~ unipi,vidar,robodreamer , conditions action decoders on predictive video features~ vpp,mimicvideo,dit4dit , or jointly models video and actions~ gr1,uwm,uva,ye2026dreamzero,cosmospolicy . Other studies explore causal temporal modeling~ lingbotva and latent action representations~ motus . To reduce inference cost, Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fast and related methods~ gigaworldpolicy05,dit4dit retain future-video prediction as training supervision and predict actions without completing future-video generation at deployment. Multi-camera WAMs often combine views in a fixed spatial layout by concatenating images~ ye2026dreamzero,motus,yuan2026fast,gigaworldpolicy05,wang2026openwam,flexpi or latent features~ lingbotva,tau0wm . Other methods maintain separate latent streams and exchange information through cross-view attention~ genieenvisioner,wallwm,geact2 . For video prediction, FlexWAM encodes each view separately and alternates within-view and cross-view attention to capture view-specific dynamics and cross-view complementarity. Adaptive Visual Perception for Robot Control The relevance of each camera view to action prediction varies across manipulation stages. Active perception methods adjust viewpoints or observation regions~ tvve,activevla,maeselect , and visual token selection aims to retain task-relevant tokens from available observations~ lightvla,vlapruner,specprunevla,efficientvla . Prior work also adapts sensory inputs through stage-dependent masking~ longvla , multisensory weighting~ playtothescore , or target-region highlighting in selected views~ hint . BFA~ bfa and Selective Perception~ selectiveperception learn camera or modality weights from VLM-assisted importance annotations, while FocusVLA~ focusvla guides view routing with future interaction intent learned from rule-based trajectory labels. For action prediction, FlexWAM’s Action Expert uses an observation-conditioned router to dynamically adjust its reliance on each camera view. To calibrate the router, FlexWAM estimates counterfactual view credit by measuring changes in action loss when each view branch is masked, without additional task-stage or view-importance annotations. title: Spiking World-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
summary: World action models (WAMs) predict how the world responds to actions and offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence, but they are large and run the network many times per plan, so they are hard to deploy on robots. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) compute with sparse binary spikes and use additions instead of multiplications, which saves power. However, existing WAMs use dense videos as the world state, so a spiking version would spend most of its computation on the background. We therefore introduce SpikingWAM, the first spiking WAM, which uses a sparse task skeleton as the world state. Inspired by biological motor control, which attends only to the key positions of a task, the Task Skeleton State (TSS) keeps the keypoints of the arm and the task objects, and a small spiking front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA) keep millimetre precision, and the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR) runs the network once per plan. On the simulated benchmarks LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, SpikingWAM achieves competitive success rates with far less energy than ANN methods and surpasses all compared methods on LIBERO-Plus. Real robot experiments further confirm its effectiveness. These results show that a task skeleton lets spiking networks implement WAMs at very low energy, offering a new solution for low power embodied intelligence. Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam/
