Project page: https://wxqnl.github.io/spikingwam Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs)~ dreamzero,fastwam,kim2026cosmos,sheng2026skelewam,geact let a robot learn in one model how to act and how the world changes in response. They offer a promising path toward general embodied intelligence. However, most existing WAMs use videos or visual latents as the world state~ dreamzero,fastwam,kim2026cosmos,geact . These models are large and hard to run on robots with limited resources. To this end, recent work skips future generation at inference~ fastwam,sheng2026skelewam , which reduces computation. These models still rely on dense multiply and accumulate operations, and each plan runs the network several times for multistep sampling. A robot in closed loop control plans again and again, so this cost adds up. Lowering the energy of each plan is therefore key to deploying WAMs on board. Neurons in spiking neural networks (SNNs) communicate with discrete spikes and fire only when the membrane potential crosses a threshold. On neuromorphic hardware, this event-driven computation replaces multiply and accumulate with accumulate, so its energy grows with the number of events~ roy2019towards . SNNs have recently moved from visual perception~ yao2025scaling to embodied control. Spiking vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ song2026spikevla,wang2026spikedriven and spiking diffusion policies~ hou2024sdp,wang2024stmdp generate actions, and a spiking world model~ sun2025spiking predicts the next state after an action. However, WAMs are hard to implement directly with SNNs. Mainstream WAMs are built on large video generation models~ dreamzero,fastwam,kim2026cosmos,geact , and there is still no mature way to turn such models into SNNs. Even if this were done, dense video representations would still spend most events on a background unrelated to the task. Small jitter in the image would also keep triggering new events. Running the network several times per plan further cancels the savings from sparsity. Existing approaches therefore cannot exploit the sparse and event-driven nature of SNNs. Integer spikes also struggle to keep the millimetre precision of fine manipulation. In contrast, biological motor control attends to the key positions of a task and represents space relative to the body. When people manipulate objects, their gaze falls almost only on grasp points and targets~ johansson2001eye . The premotor and posterior parietal cortices represent targets relative to the arm or the hand~ graziano1994coding,buneo2002direct . Grid cells encode position with periodic firing~ hafting2005microstructure , and cortical neurons can detect spikes that arrive at the same time~ konig1996integrator . This suggests that the world state only needs the key positions of the arm and the task objects. Once coordinates are written into spikes relative to the body, the positions of hand and object can be compared by spike coincidence. Following the event-driven principle, only changes pass between consecutive plans. Based on these ideas, we propose a sparse and event-driven paradigm for spiking WAMs and build SpikingWAM on it. To our knowledge, SpikingWAM is the first spiking world action model. A single spiking network trained from scratch learns future skeletons and action chunks together, and it generates only the action chunks at inference ( ). First, we propose the Task Skeleton State (TSS), which uses only the keypoints of the arm and the task objects as the world state. A small spiking perception front end estimates the object keypoints from images. Next, we propose Body Frame Spike Coding (BFSC) and Grid Coincidence Attention (GCA). BFSC encodes coordinates relative to the body and GCA compares positions by spike coincidence, so the geometry keeps millimetre precision. Finally, we propose the Persistent Single Step Readout (PSR). It runs the network once per plan and passes only the changes between consecutive plans. On LIBERO~ liu2023libero and LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026liberoplus , SpikingWAM reaches success rates comparable to state-of-the-art (SOTA) artificial neural network (ANN) methods. On bimanual manipulation in RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , it reaches a mean success rate of 80.20 without pretraining on robot data. On LIBERO, it needs only 1.467\,mJ per plan including the perception front end, which is more than an order of magnitude below every compared method ( ). On a real robot arm, SpikingWAM completes a pick and place task given by a language instruction, with a success rate comparable to ANN VLAs and only 3.07\,mJ per plan. Our main contributions are as follows. We design TSS and a small spiking perception front end that estimates its object keypoints from images. They focus the events and attention of the policy on the parts that matter for the task, which lowers the energy of each plan. We propose BFSC and GCA to recover the millimetre precision that integer spikes lose. We propose PSR and an offline check that tells when it applies, so the network runs only once per plan. We propose a sparse and event-driven paradigm for spiking WAMs and build on it SpikingWAM, the first spiking world action model. It reaches 98.25 , 88.76 and 80.20 on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0. On LIBERO-Plus, it exceeds all compared methods. Related Work sec:related World Action Models and Fast Sampling VLA models generate actions directly from camera images and language instructions~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05 , and compact designs further reduce the inference cost~ xie2026turbovla . World action models build on this by adding future prediction, so that the model also learns how the scene evolves. Mainstream approaches build on pretrained video models and generate future frames together with actions~ dreamzero,kim2026cosmos,geact , which makes them large. Recent work steadily reduces the cost of the world state. VLA-JEPA~ sun2026vlajepa replaces pixel reconstruction with visual latents. Fast-WAM~ fastwam shows that the benefit of future prediction comes mainly from joint training, so future generation can be skipped at inference. SkeleWAM~ sheng2026skelewam represents the world state as a 3D skeleton and compresses the scene into a few keypoints. In parallel, policy distillation~ prasad2024consistency,wang2024onedp and mean flows~ sheng2026mp1,geng2025meanflow compress action generation into one or a few steps. However, while these works shrink the model and the sampling steps, the computation itself still consists of dense multiply and accumulate operations. Repeated planning in closed loop control thus still costs too much energy on board. SNNs and Spiking Embodied Models Spiking Transformers allow SNNs to handle vision tasks at a large scale. Spiking self-attention~ zhou2023spikformer , spike-driven attention~ yao2023spikedriven,yao2024spike and integer training~ yao2025scaling have steadily improved their scale and accuracy. This progress has carried SNNs into embodied control along two lines. One line generates actions. Spiking VLAs~ song2026spikevla,wang2026spikedriven and spiking diffusion policies~ hou2024sdp,wang2024stmdp have been applied to navigation and manipulation. The other line predicts states. A spiking world model~ sun2025spiking learns the next state after a given action for model-based reinforcement learning. A separate network produces the actions. However, the two lines have developed separately. Action generation and scene prediction have not been unified in one spiking network, so world action models do not yet use event-driven computation. title: SemGuard: Semantics-Decoupled Watermarking for Gaussian Splatting
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Multimedia (under review)
summary: Gaussian Splatting provides an efficient representation for high-fidelity rendering of static and dynamic 3D scenes, motivating the copyright protection of Gaussian assets. In CLIP-guided Gaussian watermarking, a universal message decoder pretrained on textual watermark representations is subsequently applied to visual features containing both watermark information and scene-dependent semantics. However, text-only pretraining does not explicitly account for the semantic interference encountered during watermark extraction. To address this challenge, we propose SemGuard, a simple yet effective semantics-decoupled watermarking framework that learns to suppress scene-dependent semantic interference during universal message decoder pretraining. Specifically, SemGuard combines message-related CLIP text features with message-independent visual features extracted from unwatermarked scene images, constructing training representations with controllable semantic interference relevant to the target Gaussian assets. A progressive semantic interference curriculum gradually increases the contribution of visual features, allowing the decoder to first learn reliable message representations and then adapt to increasingly strong scene-dependent semantic interference. After pretraining for a given message length and semantic image pool, the decoder is frozen and reused across multiple Gaussian assets whose visual semantics are covered by the pretraining data. Experiments on static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting assets demonstrate improved rendering fidelity alongside reliable watermark extraction, while evaluations on static assets further show enhanced robustness against image-space distortions.

Introduction sec:introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as an efficient representation for high-fidelity novel-view synthesis and real-time rendering~ kerbl20233d . Extensions of Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes, including 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS), further enable the modeling and rendering of time-varying content~ luiten2024dynamic,wu20244d,yang2024deformable . As Gaussian assets become increasingly accessible and widely shared, protecting their intellectual property and verifying ownership have become important concerns. Digital watermarking provides a practical solution by embedding imperceptible binary messages into digital content~ cox1997secure,zhu2018hidden,tancik2020stegastamp . Unlike watermarking individual images, protecting a Gaussian asset requires the embedded message to remain recoverable from different rendered observations of the same underlying representation. An effective Gaussian watermarking framework should therefore maintain reliable watermark extraction under varying viewpoints and temporal conditions while minimizing watermark-induced rendering distortions. Recent studies have explored watermarking techniques for Gaussian Splatting assets~ huang2024gaussianmarker,jang20253d,chen2025guardsplat . Among them, GuardSplat~ chen2025guardsplat introduces an efficient CLIP-guided watermarking framework by pretraining a universal message decoder in the shared vision-language embedding space of CLIP~ radford2021learning . Specifically, binary messages are converted into CLIP textual representations, from which a lightweight decoder learns to recover the corresponding message bits. After pretraining, the decoder is frozen and reused to extract watermark messages from CLIP visual features of rendered Gaussian views. However, a discrepancy remains between decoder pretraining and actual watermark extraction. During pretraining, the decoder learns message recovery solely from CLIP text features, whereas during extraction, it receives CLIP visual features containing both watermark-related information and scene-dependent semantics. Although both stages operate in CLIP's shared vision-language embedding space, text-only pretraining does not explicitly expose the decoder to the visual semantic interference encountered during watermark extraction. We refer to this discrepancy between watermark-centric textual training features and semantics-entangled visual extraction features as the semantic entanglement gap, which can hinder reliable watermark recovery when appearance modifications are constrained to preserve rendering fidelity, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Addressing semantic interference while retaining decoder reusability remains an important challenge. Guard4D~ shiguard4d improves watermark extraction from dynamic Gaussian assets by introducing a temporal modeling and semantic decoupling (TMSD) module, which aggregates temporal information and suppresses scene-dependent semantic interference using control clips. Although its pretrained message decoder remains frozen, the TMSD module requires asset-specific optimization, introducing additional overhead into the complete watermark extraction pipeline. This motivates a complementary approach to handling semantic interference: instead of learning an additional semantic correction module during asset-specific watermark optimization, can a message decoder learn to suppress the influence of scene-relevant visual semantics during pretraining and subsequently be reused across multiple Gaussian assets? Such a design shifts semantic-interference handling toward a shared pretraining stage, allowing the same frozen decoder to guide watermark embedding in different assets whose visual semantics are represented by the training image pool. To this end, we propose SemGuard, a simple yet effective semantics-decoupled watermarking framework that incorporates visual semantic interference directly into universal decoder pretraining. Instead of learning message recovery solely from textual watermark representations, SemGuard constructs semantics-entangled training features by combining message-related CLIP text features with message-independent visual features extracted from unwatermarked images. The auxiliary visual features provide visual semantics relevant to the target Gaussian assets, while the binary message remains the supervision target. By supervising message recovery from these mixed representations, the decoder is encouraged to rely on watermark-related information while reducing its sensitivity to scene-dependent semantic interference, thereby learning to recover watermark messages in the presence of visual semantics represented during pretraining. Furthermore, we introduce a progressive semantic interference curriculum that gradually increases the contribution of visual features during pretraining, allowing the decoder to first establish a reliable message representation and then adapt to increasingly challenging semantic interference. For each message length and semantic image pool, SemGuard trains a single reusable message decoder, which is then frozen and shared by multiple Gaussian assets without further decoder adaptation. Each target asset is watermarked independently by optimizing only its spherical-harmonic appearance offsets, while the pretrained CLIP encoders and message decoder remain fixed. In this way, semantic-interference learning is performed jointly across a collection of scene semantics during decoder pretraining, whereas watermark embedding remains asset-specific and explicitly constrained to preserve the original rendered appearance. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in rendering fidelity while maintaining reliable watermark extraction, together with enhanced robustness against image-space distortions on static Gaussian assets. In particular, for 16-bit watermarking of static Gaussian assets, SemGuard improves PSNR from 41.55 dB to 50.29 dB and reduces LPIPS from 0.0017 to 0.0004 compared with GuardSplat, while maintaining a near-perfect Bit Acc. of 99.97 . Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We identify the lack of scene-dependent visual semantics during text-only decoder pretraining as a key challenge in CLIP-guided Gaussian watermarking, particularly when reliable watermark recovery must be achieved under rendering fidelity constraints. We propose SemGuard, a simple yet effective semantics-decoupled watermarking framework that combines message-related CLIP text features with scene-relevant visual features under a progressive mixing curriculum. By learning message recovery in the presence of visual semantics covered by the pretraining pool, a single frozen decoder can be reused across multiple Gaussian assets without asset-specific decoder adaptation. We evaluate SemGuard on static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting assets, demonstrating substantial improvements in rendering fidelity while maintaining reliable watermark recovery, together with enhanced robustness against image-space distortions on static assets. Related Work sec:related_work Watermarking across Visual and Neural Representations Digital watermarking has been extensively studied across different visual representations to protect content ownership while balancing imperceptibility and robustness. Classical image watermarking methods typically embed information in spatial or transform domains~ cox1997secure,navas2008dwt , while learning-based approaches employ trainable embedding and extraction networks to improve robustness against image distortions and post-processing operations~ fang2022end,wu2025robust,tancik2020stegastamp,fernandez2022watermarking,ma2022towards . Watermarking and information-hiding techniques have also been developed for generative visual content~ fernandez2023stable,wen2023tree and geometric representations, including meshes and point clouds~ praun1999robust,ohbuchi2002frequency,zhu2021gaussian,zhang2023adaptive,zhu2024rethinking,yoo2022deep,zaman2025deep . With the development of neural rendering~ barron2021mip,barron2022mip,muller2022instant , watermarking has further expanded to implicit scene representations, where messages are embedded into neural radiance fields and recovered from synthesized views~ luo2023copyrnerf,jang2024waterf . ZeroW-NeRF~ zhu2026zerow further explores neural scene copyright protection through an uncertainty-driven zero-watermarking strategy without modifying the original model parameters. These studies demonstrate the applicability of watermarking and information hiding across visual, geometric, and neural scene representations, motivating further research on protecting explicit Gaussian assets. title: MotionServe: Efficient Multi-Robot Serving by Exploiting Robot Execution Slack
summary: As robotic arms undertake diverse manipulation tasks, a deployment may need to serve many task-specific vision-language-action (VLA) policies concurrently. Dedicating a GPU to each robot is costly, motivating shared-GPU inference. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone with lightweight policy-specific adapters, reducing model-weight memory and enabling cross-policy batching. However, robot inference must keep pace with physical execution. With action chunking, robots continue executing buffered actions while awaiting new predictions, and the remaining buffered time provides each robot's execution slack for serving its next request. Once this slack is exhausted, the robot stalls until new actions arrive, interrupting task progress. Observing earlier preserves more slack but can lead to disruptive replanning and lower task success, whereas delaying dispatch to form larger batches can improve GPU efficiency but consumes slack and risks stalls. To balance these competing demands, we present MotionServe, a shared-GPU serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with server-side batch formation. MotionExec selects observation triggers based on motion structure in predicted action chunks, allowing inference to overlap with remaining buffered execution. SlackBatch combines the resulting per-robot execution budgets with estimated outstanding GPU work to determine when to wait, which requests to batch, and when to dispatch them. We evaluate X-VLA on LIBERO and SimplerEnv's WidowX tasks and OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO, with up to 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU. At 96 robots, MotionServe reduces mean stall per episode by 43.4% and 32.6% and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points, respectively, over each model's lowest-stall baseline. Backbone sharing also reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 97.6% and 91.1%.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Robotic arms are widely deployed across automotive, electronics, and general manufacturing to perform diverse manipulation tasks~ Keshvarparast2024 . A single automotive spot-welding operation can involve 42 robots across 13 workstations~ LOPES20171033 . Vision--language--action (VLA) models offer a common foundation for manipulation, mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions and supporting adaptation to new robot settings through fine-tuning~ pmlr-v270-kim25c,KimM1-RSS-25 . A fleet performing different tasks may therefore require multiple fine-tuned variants of a common VLA. As the fleet grows, serving these variants with a dedicated GPU for each robot becomes increasingly costly, motivating centralized inference on a shared GPU server. On a shared server, however, hosting each variant as a separate model instance duplicates backbone weights and splits requests across instances that cannot be batched together~ MLSYS2024_906419cd . Because these variants originate from the same VLA, fine-tuning them with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) resolves both issues. Each variant then becomes a lightweight adapter over one shared frozen backbone, which reduces model-weight memory and allows requests for different policies to be batched together~ hu2022lora,pmlr-v270-kim25c . A growing body of multi-LoRA serving work provides the machinery for this sharing. S-LoRA and Punica batch requests that target different adapters over a common language-model backbone~ MLSYS2024_906419cd,MLSYS2024_054de805 , and dLoRA further improves efficiency through dynamic adapter merging and request placement~ 298762 . Batching nevertheless trades latency for throughput. Larger batches amortize computation, yet accumulating requests and executing larger batches both lengthen response latency~ 201468 . For robots, this latency carries a direct physical cost. A robot whose action buffer runs out before new actions arrive must pause, interrupting task progress~ NEURIPS2025_300ccb21 . Robot serving thus cannot trade latency for throughput freely. The time remaining in each robot's buffer defines a time budget for serving its next request. This budget differs across robots and shrinks as execution proceeds. Existing multi-LoRA serving systems do not consider such execution-dependent budgets when deciding which requests to batch and when to dispatch them. Unlike application-defined latency targets in conventional model serving, the time available for robot inference depends on ongoing physical execution and observation timing. With action chunking, each inference produces a sequence of future actions, allowing a robot to observe and request its next chunk before completing the current one while continuing to execute buffered actions~ NEURIPS2025_300ccb21 . We term the remaining buffered execution time at request generation execution slack. This slack defines the time available for communication, queueing, inference, and result delivery before the robot stalls. Observing earlier leaves more slack for serving, but replanning from an intermediate motion state can disrupt execution and reduce task success~ NEURIPS2025_300ccb21,nie2026pace . Observing later reduces the risk of premature replanning but leaves less time for batching. Efficient multi-robot VLA serving therefore requires coordinating two coupled decisions: when each robot observes and how the server batches requests within the resulting execution budgets. To balance timely robot updates with efficient GPU batching, we propose MotionServe, a multi-LoRA VLA serving system that coordinates robot observation timing with batch formation through execution slack. Its Motion-Guided Pipelined Action Execution (MotionExec) selects observation triggers from predicted motion structure, allowing robots to request new actions while they continue executing buffered actions. Its Slack-Driven Asynchronous Batching (SlackBatch) combines each robot's remaining slack with estimated outstanding GPU work to decide how long to defer dispatch and which requests to include. Together, these mechanisms enable independent robot updates and cross-policy batching on a shared backbone. With 96 simulated robots sharing one NVIDIA H200 GPU, MotionServe reduces mean stall by 43.4 on X-VLA and 32.6 on OpenVLA-OFT and improves task success by 8.98 and 2.30 percentage points over each model's lowest-stall baseline. MotionServe also achieves the highest throughput at every fleet size, and backbone sharing reduces weight memory for 96 policies by 91.1--97.6 . Our contributions are: We propose MotionServe, a framework that brings multi-LoRA serving to multi-robot VLA deployment while exploiting robot execution slack to coordinate observation timing with batch formation. It hosts each robot's policy as an adapter over one shared VLA backbone and batches action-chunk requests across adapters. We develop MotionExec, a motion-guided Pipelined action execution mechanism that selects observation triggers from predicted action chunks while overlapping inference with buffered execution. We develop SlackBatch, a slack-driven scheduler that uses each robot's execution slack and outstanding GPU work to adapt batch dispatch timing and request selection. Related Work and Motivations sec:background Multi-Robot VLA Serving sec:bg-adapters Multi-robot deployments require distinct VLA policies adapted to different robot embodiments and manipulation tasks~ pmlr-v270-kim25c,KimM1-RSS-25 . Deploying each policy as an independent model instance duplicates backbone weights and separates requests across instances, limiting cross-policy batching. Keeping fewer checkpoints resident reduces memory use but incurs loading overhead for nonresident policies. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) instead allows compatible policies to share a frozen backbone through lightweight policy-specific updates~ hu2022lora . At an adapted layer with frozen weight , policy uses , where is a scaling factor and the adaptation rank is much smaller than the weight dimensions. For policies adapted from the same frozen backbone, a multi-LoRA runtime stores the backbone once and applies the corresponding adapter to each request within a batch, enabling cross-policy inference. Let denote the backbone's weight memory, the adapter and other policy-specific weight memory (including action heads where applicable), and the memory of a complete policy checkpoint. For resident policies, the model-weight footprints are Multi-LoRA serving systems enable heterogeneous-adapter batching over a shared language-model backbone. S-LoRA and Punica batch requests using different adapters~ MLSYS2024_906419cd,MLSYS2024_054de805 , while dLoRA further improves efficiency through dynamic adapter merging and request placement~ 298762 . These systems focus on autoregressive language-model serving rather than action-chunk inference constrained by robot execution. In robotics, CORAL trains task-specific LoRA experts on a frozen VLA backbone and provides inference-time expert routing~ luo2026coralscalablemultitaskrobot , but does not address cross-robot batch scheduling. Robion supports multi-robot, multi-model VLA serving through stage co-execution, model placement, and traffic control~ adamopoulos2026efficientvisionlanguageactionmanagementserving , but uses model-homogeneous batches within each stage. These approaches do not bring multi-LoRA serving to multi-robot VLA deployment, nor do they coordinate observation timing with batch formation through each robot's execution slack. 1. Shared VLA serving should support independent robot update schedules while pooling requests across policies. This motivates an architecture in which robot-side execution determines request generation and a common multi-LoRA runtime combines the resulting requests into cross-policy batches. Pipelined Action Execution and Observation Timing sec:bg-refresh Action chunking allows a VLA policy to predict a sequence of future actions in a single inference request~ KimM1-RSS-25 , so a robot can continue moving while it awaits the next prediction. Pipelined action execution exploits this buffer by letting the robot capture a new observation and request its next chunk before exhausting the current one~ NEURIPS2025_300ccb21 . As Figure~ fig:bg-async-overlap illustrates, the robot keeps executing buffered actions while the request is served, and the remaining buffered execution time forms its execution slack. When the result arrives, the robot skips the new chunk's first actions, where counts the policy actions completed since observation capture, and executes the remaining suffix. This handoff aligns the new chunk with completed execution and avoids idle waiting whenever the result arrives before the buffer is depleted. Because each robot follows its own execution progress, requests from different robots arrive independently at the shared server~ bansal2026actionchunkschedulingbatched , each carrying a different amount of slack. Observation timing determines how much slack remains for serving. Earlier observation provides more slack but may trigger replanning before a coherent motion segment finishes, disrupting execution and reducing task success~ NEURIPS2025_300ccb21,nie2026pace . Table~ tab:bg-refresh-quality examines this tradeoff on LIBERO-10 across five VLA policies with different action-generation designs: TurboVLA~ xie2026turbovlarealtimevisionlanguageactionmodel , OpenVLA-OFT~ KimM1-RSS-25 , X-VLA~ ICLR2026_630d2938 , TBD-VLA~ lee2026tbdvlatemporalblockdiffusion , and ActionCodec-AR~ dong2026actioncodecmakesgoodaction . Full observes after completing the chunk, while Short prefix and Long prefix use fixed observation triggers. Sweet spot selects the earliest suitable observation point under a motion-derived progress criterion (Section~ sec:sweet-spot-execution ). The latter three use the same overlap-and-skip protocol. Short prefix reduces success by 1.4--29.0 percentage points relative to Full, while Long prefix improves success over Short prefix for every policy but exceeds Full only for X-VLA and ActionCodec-AR. Sweet spot exceeds Full by 0.6--5.0 percentage points across all five policies, showing that well-placed early observation can preserve or improve task success. Real-Time Chunking (RTC) overlaps execution with flow-policy inference using inpainting to improve continuity~ NEURIPS2025_300ccb21 . Adaptive execution-horizon methods select replanning points using motion transitions (PACE)~ nie2026pace , action uncertainty (AAC)~ Liang_2026_CVPR , or self-attention (AutoHorizon)~ 10.1007/978-3-032-37196-6_33 . However, these methods do not coordinate observation timing with slack-aware batch formation across multiple robots. 2. Observation timing should balance task progress, timely feedback, and the execution slack available for serving. This motivates selecting the earliest suitable observation point based on predicted motion structure, allowing robots to avoid premature replanning while retaining buffered actions for shared inference. Execution Slack for Asynchronous Batching sec:bg-async Asynchronous robot execution produces independently arriving requests with different execution slack. Batching these requests can improve shared-GPU efficiency, but waiting to accumulate requests consumes the time available before robots run out of actions. Immediate dispatch avoids this delay, yet may occupy the GPU with less urgent requests and delay later arrivals whose buffers deplete sooner. Figure~ fig:bg-execution-slack illustrates this tradeoff. Robot A requests inference first while the GPU is idle, so first-come-first-served (FCFS), earliest-deadline-first (EDF), and any other work-conserving scheduler dispatch it immediately. When B arrives with less slack remaining, it must wait behind A and stalls. title: S-Mind: Internalizing Multi-View Geometry for Spatial Intelligence
summary: Spatial intelligence, the ability to reason about 3D space from visual observations, becomes essential as multimodal large language models (MLLMs) move into the physical world. Beyond perceiving each view, it rests on two cornerstones of human cognition: fusing multiple views into one coherent 3D scene and mentally transforming that scene to new viewpoints as reasoning unfolds. Yet our spatial probes reveal that MLLMs largely lack both capabilities, even after spatial fine-tuning. We therefore present S-Mind, which internalizes multi-view geometry within the MLLM through a compact set of spatial tokens. It supervises these tokens to hold the fused 3D scene and re-emits them to re-express this scene from every viewpoint the reasoning adopts. Across four spatial benchmarks, S-Mind improves its Qwen3.5 backbones by up to 22.26 points and surpasses frontier general models such as GPT-6-Astra (+0.45), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (+1.97), and GLM-5.3-Flash (+7.80) in average accuracy. Moreover, the same probes confirm that it acquires both capabilities, reaching fusion and transformation accuracies of 65.11% and 82.17%, against at most 16.02% and 37.28% for the baselines. At inference, S-Mind also runs about 100x faster than a tool-based agent on the same backbone. Instilled through these spatial tokens during training, spatial capability becomes intrinsic to the backbone and persists even when the tokens are withheld, offering a promising path toward spatial intelligence in MLLMs.

Behind this lie two operations: assembling the snapshots into one model of the room, and mentally rotating that model to the new standpoint~ shepard1971mental . As multimodal large language models (MLLMs)~ step3vl,phi4reasoningvision,qwen35 advance rapidly in visual understanding and reasoning, real-world tasks such as embodied AI~ pragmaticvla,threedthinkvla , autonomous driving~ lastvla,nureasoning , and extended reality~ egocopilot,openglass increasingly hinge on such spatial intelligence. Despite its importance, spatial intelligence remains a major bottleneck for MLLMs~ mindcube,easi,theoryofspace , requiring the model to mentally construct a coherent 3D scene rather than merely recognize 2D visual patterns. As a illustrates, existing approaches generally fall into two paradigms: (i)~External-geometry methods construct the scene outside the model, via 3D reconstruction and rendering~ think3d,mindjourney,spatialclaw or an attached geometry encoder~ spatialmllm,vlm3r,spacemind . While providing explicit geometry, they fail to internalize spatial capability and incur high inference latency~ spatialopsd,gpd . (ii)~Spatial fine-tuning methods aim to train the MLLM to construct the scene internally, with supervision progressing from the output text alone~ spatialladder,vst,prosr to latent states aligned with 3D geometry~ threedthinker,threedthinkvla,geovr,hatch,geoanchor . This paradigm has drawn growing attention for its promise of internalizing spatial capability within the model itself. However, the evidence for this promise rests largely on end-task accuracy. We therefore introduce spatial probes, extending recent analyses of the spatial representations inside MLLMs~ sspace , to decode the scene a model holds internally. Our probes reveal that, despite substantial gains in accuracy, spatially fine-tuned models retain two persistent deficiencies in spatial capability, as illustrated in b. (i)~Limited multi-view fusion: these models encode each view well but in isolation, and the views are barely fused into a coherent scene. (ii)~Incomplete perspective transformation: as in base models~ sspace , their internal representation still largely fails to follow when the reasoning shifts to a new viewpoint. This mismatch raises a natural question: Research Question How can an MLLM truly internalize spatial capability, assembling its views\\ into one scene and rotating that scene to a new viewpoint, as humans do? To address this question, we introduce , a framework that endows an MLLM with an internal scene representation, built from its input views and transformed as its reasoning unfolds. (I) Multi-view fusion. introduces a compact set of whose hidden states consolidate the views into a unified 3D scene, encoding both the geometry each image observes and the pose of each camera in a shared coordinate frame. (II) Perspective transformation. With the views fused into one scene, adopting a new viewpoint reduces to re-expressing that scene in a different frame of reference. Whenever the reasoning shifts to a new viewpoint, the model therefore re-emits the , which now encode the fused scene as observed from that viewpoint, and conditions its subsequent reasoning on them. By training the model to construct and manipulate an entire 3D scene, internalizes genuine spatial capability rather than superficial heuristics. Tool-based designs invoke specialist modules at inference: some build and operate on an explicit scene representation, such as a 3D reconstruction, an object-level abstraction, or a vector sketch~ think3d,spatialclaw,mentalimagery,mentalthink ; others synthesize views from new standpoints using generative models~ mindjourney,camcue or warp visual tokens toward them~ tokenwarping . title: RoboThink: Let the Agent Think, Let the Policy Act
summary: Robot policies act in real time but fail without knowing why, whereas a reasoning agent that watches the robot can often tell what went wrong. Existing systems either hand the agent control, which takes minutes per episode, or let it send instructions. Yet a policy follows a new instruction only from a fresh start, since a half-finished task leaves it in states outside its training data. Nor can an instruction fix how the robot moves. If a drift keeps pulling the hand to the left, "push right, slightly" is not a task the policy has learned. We propose RoboThink, in which the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent's guidance. An instruction channel tells the policy what to do. When the user says "the milk, not the butter" after the robot has started, the agent rewrites the instruction and the robot undoes its own motion, with no training. A feedback channel tells it how to move. It is taught from the agent alone with agent-labelled DAgger, role tokens and counterfactual feedback, and is read only by the policy's action module. On LIBERO, RoboThink with Claude Opus 5.5 raises success from 0.09 to 0.87 under an unknown constant drift and from 0.42 to 0.84 under a random one. It also completes misheard and changed requests in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. Acting alone, GPT-6 Astra needs 2.1 min per success and over a million tokens per episode, whereas RoboThink needs 55 s and 8k tokens. The same recipe works across policies, for both vision-language-action models and world action models, and across robots, from one arm to two arms and a mobile manipulator. On all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with two arms, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 under the constant drift and from 0.31 to 0.56 under the random one. Finally, the agent is a plug-in. A policy taught by one agent works with other agents, including open-weight ones, and grows stronger with a stronger agent, without retraining.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,pi2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00t and world action models (WAMs)~ du2023unipi,li2025uva,zhu2025uwm,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero,yuan2026fastwam map camera images and an instruction to chunks of actions in real time. However, outside their training conditions they fail without knowing why. At deployment, two things can go wrong. The execution can drift away from a correct plan. Asked to pick up the orange juice, the policy plans the right motion, yet a small unknown drift on every motion command, which we call a drift, keeps pushing the hand away from the bottle ( a). The policy can also pursue the wrong goal, because the instruction it acts on is not what the user wants. The user’s request may be worded unlike any training instruction, such as ``the stove needs to be on now'' for ``turn on the stove'', and the policy often misunderstands it. It may be misheard, so that the robot fetches the cream cheese when the user wanted the milk ( b). Or the user may change their mind after the robot has started (``the milk, not the butter''). In both cases, a reasoning agent that watches the robot, such as a vision-language model (VLM), can detect the failure and explain its cause~ duan2025aha,huang2022innermonologue,geminiroboticsteam2025geminirobotics15pushing ( ). How should a robot policy and a reasoning agent work together? Existing systems take one of three routes. The agent can take over and control the robot through code or tool calls~ liang2023cap,chen2026show,jia2026agp . This can handle both a wrong execution and a wrong goal, but at a high cost. In our experiments, GPT-6 Astra acting alone needs \ per success and over a million tokens per episode. On RoboDojo, it spends 8.6 minutes per episode~ jia2026agp . The agent can instead instruct the policy~ ahn2022saycan,huang2022innermonologue,shi2025hirobot . A new instruction fixes a wrong goal, but the policy can follow it only from familiar states, not from the middle of the wrong task. Given the corrected task after three chunks, a trained WAM completes it in only 0.07 of the episodes. Moreover, a wrong execution cannot be fixed this way at all, because ``push right, slightly'' is not a task. Appending such a correction to the prompt of a strong WAM~ yuan2026fastwam even lowers its success under a random drift from 0.42 to 0.16. Finally, reasoning can be trained into the policy~ zhao2025cotvla,liu2026agenticwam , but this locks it into the weights, preventing the policy from correcting a drift it has not seen ( ) or improving with a stronger agent. In short, each route either gives up the policy's speed or cannot pass the agent's understanding of what went wrong to the policy. Our key insight is that the agent and the policy complement each other. The policy knows how to act but cannot see why it fails, whereas the agent sees why but acts too slowly. Existing routes do not play to these strengths. They either make the agent act or the policy reason, or they let the agent speak to the policy in words the policy cannot act on. The difficulty lies in the policy, not the agent. A policy is trained only to follow task instructions. It therefore cannot follow feedback on how to correct its motion, since it has never learned what such feedback means. What is missing is a channel through which the policy learns to understand what the agent tells it. To this end, we propose , where the agent thinks and the policy learns to act on the agent's guidance ( ). The agent is called only every few chunks, as a bias on the motion commands or the user's request usually persists from one chunk to the next, and between calls the policy acts in real time on the agent's latest guidance. This guidance reaches the policy through two channels, one for a wrong goal and one for a wrong execution. The instruction channel [INST] fixes a wrong goal by telling the policy what to do. The agent knows the user's request and checks whether the instruction that the policy acts on aligns with it. If the request is worded unclearly, the agent rewrites it as a plain instruction, such as ``turn on the stove'' for ``the stove needs to be on now''. If the request was misheard or changed, the agent writes the correct one, such as ``put the milk in the basket'' when the robot was told the cream cheese. A corrected instruction alone is not enough once the robot has started on the wrong task, since the policy can follow it only from familiar states. The robot therefore first retraces its own motion back to such a state and then acts on the new instruction, which we call undo before redo. This channel needs no training and works with any policy. The feedback channel [FB] fixes a wrong execution by telling the policy how to move. It carries the agent's estimate of the drift, such as ``push right, slightly''. Unlike the instruction channel, it must be learned, since the policy has never seen such feedback, and we teach the policy to read it from the agent alone ( ). With agent-labelled DAgger~ ross2011dagger , we run the policy on training tasks under drift. The robot executes the policy’s plan, corrected by the agent for the drift it estimates, and these corrected plans become the training targets, so the true drift is never needed. Learned role tokens keep the feedback separate from the instruction. Counterfactual feedback pairs the same state with different feedback and different corrected plans, so that the policy cannot guess the plan from the state and must learn to read the feedback. Finally, only the policy's action module reads the feedback, while its world module keeps reading the task alone. The world module imagines how the scene will unfold from the task, and feedback there distorts what it imagines. The action module turns this imagined future into motion, so it is where a correction belongs. We evaluate with two WAMs and a VLA, and with ten proprietary and open-weight agents, in three simulators. On LIBERO~ liu2023libero , we test unknown drifts, reworded, misheard and changed requests, and perturbed scenes~ fei2025liberoplus,kim2026liberopara,zhang2026liberomax . On RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 , the policy controls two arms in joint space, and on RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa , a mobile manipulator works in unseen kitchens. Our contributions are threefold: , a way for a robot policy and a reasoning agent to work together, in which the agent thinks and the policy acts. The agent's guidance reaches the policy through an instruction channel, which fixes a wrong goal with undo before redo and needs no training, and a feedback channel, which fixes a wrong execution. A recipe that teaches the feedback channel from the agent alone, and the finding that the feedback must reach the action module, not the world module. The recipe needs neither the true drift nor human labels, works from about a hundred agent-labelled episodes, and carries over to a VLA, a second WAM, two arms and a mobile manipulator. Evidence across three policies, three simulators and ten agents. On LIBERO, success rises from \ to \ under a constant drift and from \ to \ under a random one, and misheard or changed requests are completed in 0.91 to 1.00 of the episodes. On all 50 RoboTwin~2.0 tasks, success rises from 0.12 to 0.74 and from 0.31 to 0.56. succeeds at least as often as the strongest agent acting alone, in \ instead of \ per success. Its success grows with the accuracy of the agent, so a policy trained once improves as reasoning agents improve. Related work sec:related Reasoning agents for robots. Language models plan for robots by choosing skills~ ahn2022saycan , by re-planning from feedback in text~ huang2022innermonologue , or by writing control code~ liang2023cap . VLM agents now act as the policy themselves through tool calls and scripts~ chen2026show,jia2026agp,zhang2026astrarobodojo . Hierarchical and dual-system policies pair a high-level model that emits language with a low-level policy~ shi2025hirobot,zhang2024hirt,pi2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00t , and the high level speaks to the low level only through instructions that the low level was trained to follow. In contrast, keeps the agent out of the control loop and gives it a channel for conclusions that are not instructions, so that the agent is called only every few chunks and can be replaced without retraining. Corrections and reasoning inside policies. Language corrections steer VLAs after training on corrections~ shi2024yay,belkhale2024rth,liu2023olaf,dai2024racer,xia2025phoenix or as motion offsets~ kwon2026correctvla , and VLMs explain robot failures~ duan2025aha . Reasoning has also been trained into policies, as chains of thought before the actions~ zhao2025cotvla or, in AW-0~ liu2026agenticwam , as code generated with video and actions. Unlike these methods, which put corrections into the instruction of the policy or fix the reasoning in its weights, gives the agent's feedback a channel of its own, read by the action module only, and learns this channel from an off-the-shelf agent alone. World action models and robustness. WAMs build policies on video generators, decoding actions from predicted frames~ du2023unipi,tian2024seer,hu2024vpp or modelling video and actions jointly~ li2025uva,zhu2025uwm,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamze

title: SWAM: State-aware World Action Model for Multi-Agent 3D Environments
summary: Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches.

Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches. Introduction sec:intro Most existing generative world models rely on autoregressive prediction, where previously generated frames provide the context for generating future observations. While effective at maintaining short-term visual continuity, this paradigm faces challenges in multi-agent environments, where independently acting players and non-player characters (NPCs) move, interact, and change states inside and outside the ego player's field of view. Such changes cannot be reliably inferred from the ego player's action and visual history alone, leading to inconsistencies when characters reappear after prolonged absence or occlusion. Recent work has addressed multi-agent consistency through two broad directions. The first jointly models multiple player perspectives, as in Solaris savva2026solaris and MultiWorld wu2026multiworld , enabling synchronized multi-view generation through coordinated training and shared multi-agent representations. The second introduces persistent state representations to decouple world evolution from visual generation, like in MultiGen po2026multigen , where an explicit map of the game is used to express game state and perform visibility tests. Despite these advances, existing approaches employ different forms of explicit state representations, distributed coordination, or scene-level structure to maintain consistency. This motivates a complementary approach that propagates the dynamics of independently acting agents while retaining autoregressive visual history for high-fidelity generation. By asking whether an explicit scene representation is necessary for consistent multiplayer generation, we present , a State-aware World Action Model that combines action-driven agent-state propagation with history-conditioned visual generation. maintains a lightweight representation of character states that evolves independently of the generated video. A small state model combines simple motion priors with learned corrections to predict character positions, orientations, and interaction states directly from actions, without rendered observations or external scene geometry. Consequently, characters can continue evolving even when they remain outside the ego player's view, and their states can be shared across independently generated viewpoints. A diffusion world model then generates the ego frames from the state using a novel FOV conditioning: predicted character states are projected into spatial indicators that encode their possible appearance in a player's ego frame. Unlike conventional geometry-based rendering, these indicator masks do not require explicit visibility tests. The diffusion world model learns to use the mask together with previously generated visual latents to synthesize temporally coherent observations and learn scene-dependent player occlusion. In this way, visual history preserves appearance and scene continuity, while explicit agent states provide information about character dynamics that cannot be recovered from visual history alone. Removing the explicit map and explicit visibility maps changes what the system can do. The approach applies to full 3D environments with free 6-DoF camera motion, which a 2D layout does not capture. Characters are simulated by the state model alone and incur no generation cost, while each human player only needs to run one instance of the same lightweight world model. Because character identity and location come from the propagated state rather than from past frames, we show that characters remain consistent across occlusions, long absences from the view, and respawns. We evaluate the approach in a custom-designed 3D first-person shooter. Our model sustains consistent gameplay even over long-horizon rollouts of 10 minutes with the player's own actions as the only external input where comparison method fail to render other characters consistently. In summary, our contributions include: A factorized multiplayer world model that requires no explicit scene representation: the actions of the characters are the only explicit input, and scene geometry is learned implicitly. A lightweight state model that propagates the state of all characters from actions alone, without rendered observations, so that bots and unseen players are simulated at negligible cost. An FOV conditioning scheme based on box indicators whose size does not grow with the number of characters and which keeps other players and NPCs consistent. Related Work sec:related_work Action-Conditioned Interactive World Models Latent world models learn predictive dynamics for planning and control~ hafner2019planet,hafner2025dreamer . More recently, Genie ~ bruce2024genie learns controllable environments from video, and DIAMOND ~ alonso2024diamond and GameNGen ~ valevski2025gamengen demonstrate diffusion-based game simulation. GameFactory ~ yu2025gamefactory extends generation to novel game scenes, while Vid2World ~ huang2026vid2world adapts video diffusion to causal, action-conditioned prediction. Real-time and streaming generation has been explored by Matrix-Game 2.0 ~ he2025matrixgame2 , Self Forcing ~ huang2025selfforcing , and WorldPlay ~ sun2026worldplay . In first-person 3D games, WorldCam ~ nam2026worldcam uses camera poses to connect action control with geometrical consistency. However, these advances primarily address the controllability, visual quality, or geometric consistency of generated views; plausible ego-view prediction alone does not ensure that independently acting characters continue to evolve correctly while unseen. This motivates explicitly propagating agent dynamics outside the visual generation loop. Long-Horizon Memory and Multi-Agent Generation Long-range coherence is a central limitation of autoregressive visual simulation. Long-Context State-Space Video World Models ~ po2025longcontext extend temporal memory through state-space modeling; ReWorld ~ chen2026reworld uses pose-indexed retrieval and bounded memory, while ActWorld ~ xiong2026actworld retains action-relevant object and interaction events. PERSIST ~ garcin2026persist instead maintains a latent 3D scene to improve spatial consistency. These methods address remembering previously observed locations or events, whereas multi-agent gameplay additionally requires predicting changes to entities that are not currently observed. WRBench ~ lu2026persistent directly studies failures in persistent state evolution. World Observer ~ choi2026worldobserver maintains out-of-view dynamics by jointly generating an actor view and additional observer views, an alternative that incurs visual generation for the observer streams. Multi-agent world models increasingly coordinate multiple viewpoints and actions. Solaris ~ savva2026solaris generates synchronized player views in Minecraft; MultiWorld ~ wu2026multiworld incorporates global state into multi-agent video prediction; and -World ~ liu2026gammaworld develops permutation-aware mechanisms for multi-agent generation. Prisma-World ~ sun2026prismaworld couples viewpoints through geometry-aware generation, PAWA ~ yang2026pawa models panoramic and first-person streams, and ME-World ~ chung2026meworld jointly denoises egocentric videos conditioned on fine-grained actions and shared environment memory. WorldWeaver ~ mo2026worldweaver augments multi-agent generation with persistent world-state registers. Although these approaches improve multi-view consistency, jointly generating player views incurs visual synthesis for streams that need not be displayed, while visual memory alone cannot determine unobserved actions and state changes. This motivates a world model that maintains NPC and off-screen player states without rendering their views. Shared State and Spatial Conditioning Explicit or factored state is increasingly used to separate world evolution from appearance generation. MultiGen ~ po2026multigen factorizes multiplayer diffusion game engines into memory, observation, and dynamics components, using a specified 2D level map and observation-derived features. WorldCast ~ ye2026worldcast supports distributed players with camera-aligned, fixed-resolution state conditioning and estimates geometry-related signals from generated observations. MASS ~ cai2026mass uses authoritative shared state to drive action-dependent updates separately from visual synthesis. Particularly close to our approach, Programmable World Model ~ huang2026programmable evolves a persistent global entity state through executable, user-specified rules and projects state-augmented 3D oriented boxes into pixel-aligned video conditions. Thus, neither separating state updates from rendering nor using projected boxes is new in isolation. Instead, we target a first-person 3D multiplayer setting with action-driven state propagation: motion priors and learned residuals update agent states without consuming generated observations, and fixed-resolution field-of-view box indicators mark possible agent locations without performing geometric visibility tests. Existing approaches variously depend on supplied level layouts, rendering-derived state updates, or externally specified entity dynamics; they leave open how to combine low-cost autonomous agent simulation with occlusion-aware ego-view generation in a 3D multiplayer game. SWAM addresses this gap by learning the scene-dependent corrections to agent dynamics and letting the video generator resolve visibility from simple state-projected box indicators. title: ViewAgent3D: A Training-Free Multi-View Pipeline for 3D Scene Understanding
summary: 3D scene understanding tasks are often approached by building explicit 3D scene representations or by training specialized multi-modal models over point clouds, voxels, or scene graphs. We take a complementary view: for many queries, the main bottleneck is not the absence of a stronger 3D representation but the selection of a small subset of multi-view RGB views that actually makes the query answerable. We present a training-free, query-conditioned multi-view pipeline that performs diverse tasks using only 2D images and a set of tools used purely for inference. Our method first decomposes each query into a set of concepts that identify unique attributes that assist with reasoning. This drives a coarse-to-fine evidence selection process: a coarse retrieval selects and scores all views, a diversity-aware selector reduces redundancy, and a reranking stage helps shortlist views by target visibility or answerability. The resulting evidence is optionally grounded for queries that benefit from explicit localization, and a self-verification step helps refine the final response, especially for open-ended cases. Despite using no task-specific training and no explicit 3D representations at inference time, our approach provides approximately 10% gain on 3D VQA and 5% gain on dense captioning and Embodied QA while being applicable across different scenarios. We further propose a unique judge-based evaluation system, motivating a judge who takes into account many semantically correct or partially correct answers, thereby improving holistic scene understanding.
full_text: ViewAgent3D sec:method An illustration of is shown in . Our method treats language-driven 3D scene understanding as a test-time reasoning problem over RGB views: instead of utilizing an explicit 3D scene representation, it reasons about which informative subset of observations makes the query answerable. To this end, Sec.~ sec:routing abstracts the query into a compact semantic decomposition that exposes the entities, relations, and cues the system should reason over; Sec.~ sec:view_selection uses this structure to retrieve candidate views, remove redundancy, and allow the VLM to observe and reason over views that are actually answerable; Sec.~ sec:grounding invokes 2D grounding only when explicit localization is likely to sharpen the evidence; and Sec.~ sec:answering produces the final response from the selected evidence. This enables the VLM to not only answer but also reason and decide which evidence can be useful before generating a response. Formally, we represent the 3D scene as a set of multi-view RGB images \( =\ _i\ _ i=1 ^ N \), where \( _i ^ H W 3 \) denotes the \(i\)-th RGB image. Given a query \( \) and optional context \( \), the goal is to predict a textual output from the VLM \( ( )\), The remainder of the method specifies how reasons over through tool-based evidence selection and uses the resulting information to generate the final response. Semantic Concept Decomposition sec:routing Inspired by semantic parsing and symbolic visual reasoning techniques~ johnson2017inferring, yi2018neural , we first extract the relevant set of concepts from the query into a compact set , where denotes the question type, the target concept, an optional reference concept, an optional relation, an attribute cue, a grounding flag, and a parse confidence score. The role of is to extract only the semantic factors that later stages need to reason over: what the query is about, whether disambiguation requires a reference object, and whether explicit grounding is likely to help. This structured set is particularly useful for compositional queries, where retrieval over raw text can drift toward incidental nouns or views with similar salient features. For example, in “What shape is the refrigerator on the left of a kitchen counter?”, isolates the target (refrigerator), reference (kitchen counter), and relation (left of), yielding a cleaner interface for evidence acquisition. Multi-view Evidence Selection sec:view_selection We formulate the retrieval query with a view budget augmented with the obtained semantic decomposition~set~ ~ prasad2023rephrase , where denotes the evidence budget, with as the shortlist size and as the final number of views passed to the answering model . Thus, the query encodes a structured relationship between the target, reference, and relation given in rather than directly processing open-ended queries with an adaptive budget for selecting views (i.e. smaller for attribute/object-centric queries and larger for location or referential, and general queries). Coarse candidate view retrieval. We begin with a fast, high-recall retrieval stage that reduces multi-view images to a smaller candidate pool. Specifically, we encode the structured query ( ) and each image ( ) into a shared embedding space, using a SigLIP2 retriever~ tschannen2025siglip , and score every view by, Here, denotes the inner product with -normalized embeddings, and corresponds to the cosine similarity score between the query and view representations. We then retain the top- scored views as the initial candidate pool. This formulation intentionally selects relevant frames within the broader scene context while removing undesirable frames; however, it is still insufficient to determine whether the selected views contain sufficient visual evidence to answer the query. Because the image embeddings depend only on the scene, they can be computed once and reused across multiple queries. The retrieval of views from the previous step is often coarse and leads to clustering around the same object or viewpoint. This leads to redundancy in the selected views, which hinders effective reasoning: overlapping frames increase the cost without contributing any new information. Therefore, DAS reduces the retrieved views into a refined set of views that is both relevant to the query and reduces overlap across viewpoints. To measure redundancy between two candidate views \(i\) and \(j\), we combine a unit-scale viewpoint distance with the appearance similarity represented by the image embeddings, where \( \) balances the viewpoint-level and appearance-level redundancy, and \( \) is a decay constant. Intuitively, \( (i,j)\) is large when two views contain near-duplicate target concepts or appearances. Using this redundancy score together with retrieval relevance, we greedily build the set \( \) with Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR)~ carbonell1998use . Let \( _i= u_i- _ j (u_j) _ j (u_j)- _ j (u_j) \) denote the normalized retrieval score for the candidate set. At each step, DAS selects the next view \(i^ \) by, where \( \) controls the trade-off between retrieval relevance and diversity. The first term preserves semantic compatibility with the query, whereas the second suppresses views that duplicate information already present in \( \). Balancing between the full set of views and retrieved views allows DAS to account for moderately relevant views whose information complements the retrieved ones, especially where naive top-\(M\) retrieval tends to cluster. After DAS, the candidate set is diverse and semantically relevant; however, some views may still be visually insufficient: the target can be occluded, too small, or not jointly visible with the reference target. We pass this compact set to the VLM and use it to assess which views provide the strongest evidence for answering a query. Given \(( , )\), the semantic decomposition \( \), and the candidate views \( \), the VLM ranks them by answerability rather than by semantic similarity alone. We present the views in \( \) as a numbered set and prompt the VLM to return an ordered list \( =(i_1, ,i_L)\) of the most-answerable candidates. We convert this ordering into a score, Therefore, higher-ranked views receive larger values. We then fuse this answerability score with the normalized retrieval prior \( _i\), where \( _r\) controls the trade-off between semantic relevance and answerability. This step on \( _i\) yields the selected set of views \( ^ \) of size \(K_ \). Thus, V-Rank is the main reasoning step in . Instead of passing all retrieved views to the VLM, we first use it to identify the few observations that actually support the query. For relation-heavy questions, for example, only a subset of views may jointly expose the target, the reference, and their spatial relation clearly enough to justify an answer. Conditional 2D Grounding sec:grounding Grounding is useful when explicit localization is likely to sharpen the evidence in views, primarily for counting, existence, and broad object-centric queries. Therefore, it acts as a tool for V-Rank, as it decides which views are trustworthy, while grounding identifies where within those views the target concept lies. When the grounding flag in \( \) is active, we form an open-vocabulary detector prompt from the extracted target and reference concepts and apply GroundingDINO~ liu2024grounding to each selected view in \( ^ \), where \(b_ ij \) is a bounding box, \( _ ij \) is its label, and \(s_ ij \) is its confidence. The answer model then receives the selected views, together with optional box overlays and a compact detection summary . To resolve ambiguity with the same information, we allot an iterative budget \((k )\), where \( \) controls the maximum number of alternative candidates considered during the verification. We then ask the VLM to compare and verify this bounded candidate set under fixed information, where \(s( )\) is a scalar verification score produced by the same VLM from a single verification prompt over the bounded candidate set under the fixed selected evidence \( ^ \), and higher values indicate stronger support from the available observations. For example, the same evidence may support both window and the more specific glass. The model compares a small set of evidence-compatible candidates and commits to the one that is better supported by the selected observations. This enables adherence to the query more accurately and generates the final response .

title: Quantizing in the Loop: Drift-Aware Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models

summary: Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths ($\le$ 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, $π_{0.5}$ still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit $π_{0.5}$ runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1$\times$ smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ
