We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present , an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, achieves a 60.4 success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T~N1.7, close to the 61.8 of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, still completes 80.0 of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1 smaller weights and 44 less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at ~ github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ . Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t have become the standard recipe for generalist robot policies: a pretrained vision-language backbone, a flow-matching or diffusion transformer action head~ lipman2022flow,chi2025diffusion , and several billion parameters evaluated many times per second on onboard hardware. While language models of this scale are routinely compressed to 2 bits per weight with modest loss~ tseng2024quip,egiazarian2024extreme,tseng2024qtip , VLAs resist such extreme compression. Existing VLA quantizers stop at 4 bits or keep the action head in higher precision~ xu2026qvla,zhang2026quantvla,akbari2026actquant ; applying the strongest 2-bit quantizers across an entire VLA drops perturbed success by 4 to 62 points. a illustrates this failure: from the same initial state and noise, the full-precision policy opens the drawer, whereas its 2-bit counterpart reaches for the upper drawer and stalls. Why does a recipe that works for language models break a policy? Because a policy acts in closed loop: its outputs determine its next inputs. This single fact invalidates two core assumptions behind standard post-training quantizers, explaining both why they fail and how to fix them. Quantization drift. Layer-wise quantizers minimize output error on static calibration data (human demonstration frames), pushing the unavoidable ultra-low-bit error into input directions that those frames never excite. While a language model rarely encounters this hidden error because its test and calibration distributions align, a closed-loop robot inevitably does: a 2-bit policy acts slightly differently from full precision, enters an unseen state, triggers the error hidden there, and deviates further. We term this self-reinforcing divergence quantization drift. b traces it in a real episode, where the 2-bit end-effector leaves the reference path and never recovers. Across every VLA module, policy-induced states dominate the input distribution shift at deployment, accounting for 45 in the language model and up to 83 in the action head. Readout corruption. Because the action head interacts with the backbone solely through attention readouts over backbone tokens, action generation depends not on raw weights, but on what the head reads. Ultra-low-bit quantization systematically displaces this interface, shifting the readout by a nearly constant offset at every step of an episode ( c). The head is not reading a noisier copy of the same content; it is reading something else. translates both diagnoses into two steps atop a trellis-coded format~ marcellin1990trellis,tseng2024qtip . Closed-loop calibration quantizes every layer on the states the quantized policy itself visits, so the quantizer can no longer hide error where the policy will go; it requires a few hundred rollouts and no training. Readout-aligned fine-tuning then updates only a 512-entry lookup table and a scale vector per layer around the frozen codes, aligning the action head's readouts with the full-precision model. Neither step alters the storage format, bit budget, or decoder. The result is a VLA quantized end to end, across both backbone and action head, that behaves like the original ( d). Without any training, closed-loop calibration alone outperforms the strongest post-training quantizer on LIBERO-Plus, reaching 73.4 vs.\ 72.6 on and 57.5 vs.\ 55.9 on GR00T~N1.7. Adding readout alignment brings the 2-bit policies to 74.9 and 60.4 , within 1.6 and 1.4 points of full precision, recovering three quarters of the degradation incurred by the best existing 2-bit quantizer on GR00T. Nor does our approach stop at 2 bits: at 1 bit per weight, still completes 80.0 of LIBERO, far surpassing the 48.0 reported for 2-bit backbone-only quantization~ akbari2026actquant . Finally, the compressed policy is directly deployable: with 8-bit activations, the 2-bit executes on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor with smaller weights and 44 less memory ( e). On a real AgileX Piper arm, the 2-bit policy succeeds in 58 of 75 trials, against 59 for full precision. Our contributions are: A closed-loop diagnosis. We show that ultra-low-bit VLAs fail due to two phenomena rooted in closed-loop execution: quantization drift, caused by calibration statistics that miss policy-induced states, and readout corruption, a systematic displacement of the representations consumed by the action head under layer-wise objectives. . We propose closed-loop calibration to align calibration statistics with the policy's own state distribution, outperforming the strongest post-training quantizers on two VLAs without any training, followed by readout-aligned fine-tuning, which optimizes only per-layer lookup tables and scales while keeping all stored codes and the decoder untouched. End-to-end VLAs at 2 bits and below. We present the first VLAs with both backbone and action head quantized entirely to 2 bits that stay within two points of full precision under perturbation, while remaining functional policies even at 1 bit. Furthermore, we deploy the 2-bit policy on a physical AgileX Piper arm, demonstrating reliable closed-loop execution across three real-world manipulation tasks: precision stacking, two-stage lidded-bin lemon placement, and multi-object grasping in clutter, each within one success of full precision. Related Work sec:related Vision-language-action models. RT-2~ brohan2023rt and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla cast actions as tokens of a vision-language model; and ~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_ and the GR00T family~ bjorck2025gr00t attach a flow-matching action head that reads the backbone through attention and denoises an action chunk in a few steps. We study the latter family, where the interface between backbone and head is an attention readout. Low-bit quantization of large models. GPTQ~ frantar2022gptq and AWQ~ lin2024awq quantize layer by layer using second-order statistics of the layer inputs, following the optimal-brain line of work~ hassibi1992second . At two bits, scalar quantizers collapse and vector formats take over: QuIP and QuIP ~ chee2023quip,tseng2024quip combine incoherence processing with lattice codebooks, AQLM~ egiazarian2024extreme and VPTQ~ liu2024vptq learn additive and vector codebooks, and QTIP~ tseng2024qtip uses trellis-coded quantization~ marcellin1990trellis to approach the rate--distortion limit with a decoder that needs only a small lookup table. Rotations reshape weight and activation statistics before quantization~ ashkboos2024quarot,liu2025spinquant,chen2026prismquant , and fine-tuning or distillation repairs the continuous parameters afterwards~ tseng2024quip,egiazarian2024extreme,malinovskii2024pv,chen2026gated . We adopt the trellis-coded format and contribute what is specific to policies: the calibration statistics and the fine-tuning objective. Quantizing VLAs. QVLA~ xu2026qvla , QuantVLA~ zhang2026quantvla , ActQuant~ akbari2026actquant , and DA-PTQ~ xu2026ptq adapt bit allocation, scaling, or calibration to action sensitivity, mostly at four bits or with parts of the action pathway kept in higher precision. BitVLA~ wang2025bitvla instead train the policy with quantization in the loop. VLAQuantBench~ xu2026vlaquantbench shows that a single action-interface layer can dominate the loss. These works calibrate on demonstrations; we quantize every linear layer to two bits and identify the closed loop as the root cause of failure. Calibration data and distribution shift. Post-training quantization is sensitive to its calibration set~ williams2024impact . In imitation learning, DAgger~ ross2011reduction corrects the mismatch between demonstrations and learner-induced states by querying an expert and retraining. Closed-loop calibration needs neither labels nor training: it re-estimates layer statistics on the states the quantized policy itself visits. title: Calibrating World Action Models: From Adaptive System 2 Takeover to Self-Evolution
summary: World action models (WAMs) deliver fast visuomotor control, yet degrade sharply in challenging scenes and act blindly when about to fail; conversely, foundation-model-based agents generalize and recover reliably, but incur prohibitive latency and cost when queried at every step. To achieve both WAM (System 1)-level speed and agent (System 2)-level reliability--- we propose \textbf{\oursfull (\ours)}, a framework that calibrates WAMs' confidence--- adaptively triggering System~2 only when necessary, and distilling System~2's knowledge to form an evolving System~1. First, \ours equips a frozen WAM with \textbf{calibrated self-assessment}: a single lightweight judgment token reading internal video--action features is trained via our proposed \textbf{cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning} using only binary rollout success/failure signals. It can predict a \textbf{calibrated success probability} at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions. Second, this calibrated success probability schedules control chunk by chunk---invoking System~2 to resolve bottlenecks when confidence drops, and handing control back to the WAM once confidence recovers, preserving WAM-like speed while approaching System~2 reliability. Third, as System~2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, its takeover trajectories directly capture the WAM's capability gaps. JiL distills these takeovers into the WAM to repair those gaps so System~1 can operate standalone without System~2 at test time, while our mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating prevent degrading existing capabilities.

Introduction sec:intro Generalist robotic manipulation has recently advanced rapidly along two complementary paradigms. On the reactive side, World action models (WAMs)~ unipi,uva,cosmospolicy,lingbotva,fastwam,wang2026openwam,kairos couple action generation with world modeling for fast visuomotor control~ robotwin2,libero , yet degrade sharply in challenging OOD scenes and lack self-assessment---blindly executing erroneous actions even in scenarios beyond their capability~ robotwinplus,liberoplus . On the deliberative side, manipulation agents built on frontier foundation models such as GPT-6-Astra~ jia2026agp,zhang2026astra,he2026astra,liu2026roboicl,galbot2026astra offer high task capability, broad generalization, and reliable error recovery, but incur high latency and token cost when queried at every step. Bridging a fast WAM (System~1) with a foundation-model-based agent (System~2) ( ) promises the best of both worlds, yet faces two fundamental bottlenecks: (1)~the Scheduling Gap and (2)~the Consolidation Gap. The Scheduling Gap lies in knowing when to invoke System~2: calling a slow agent only on impending failures requires a fast, calibrated estimate of System~1's success probability before executing each chunk. Some existing methods achieve this estimation by querying external VLMs~ grislain2026ifailsense,spotter , but incur heavy latency and miss System~1's internal action intent. Others compute multi-sample consistency~ sentinel,vlacalib,vgps or simulate world-model rollouts ~ foresight,geotts,fare,favor , which require repeated forward passes or future generation, sacrificing reactive speed. Single-pass feature and conformal detectors~ knowno,conformal,safe,vlaconf,seligmann2026vlafail instead output uncalibrated anomaly alarms~ knowno,conformal,safe,seligmann2026vlafail or action-agnostic observation scores~ vlaconf , rather than calibrated task-success probabilities. Meanwhile, the Consolidation Gap lies in turning System~2's help into permanent System~1 capability: existing dual-system frameworks~ zhang2026harness,spotter,callastra,galbot2026astra treat System 2 as a permanent runtime dependency, repeatedly paying its high latency and cost without internalizing its experience into System 1. To bridge both gaps, we propose ( ), a self-evolving System~1 2 framework that equips the WAM with calibrated self-assessment---enabling adaptive System~2 takeover at runtime and continual skill consolidation into System~1. To resolve the Scheduling Gap, appends a lightweight judgment token to the frozen WAM's final denoising step via a causal mask and token-gated adapters~ lora , reading internal video--action features without affecting action predictions. Trained solely on binary rollout success/failure signals via our cross-fitted temporal-difference (TD) learning, which propagates multi-step value estimates without self-bootstrapping bias, this token outputs a calibrated success probability in only \,ms per chunk. Guided by this probability, runs the WAM by default, invokes System~2 below a confidence threshold, and returns control to the WAM once confidence recovers. To resolve the Consolidation Gap, progressively distills knowledge from System~2's takeovers into System~1, turning runtime rescues into permanent skills and eliminating the need to call System~2 at test time. Because System~2 intervenes only when the WAM lacks confidence, these takeover trajectories automatically pinpoint System~1's capability gaps without manual labeling. However, we prove via a competence shrinkage law ( ) that directly fine-tuning the base WAM on off-distribution recovery data pulls it away from its original behavior, fixing those gaps at the cost of hurting mastered skills. Guided by this law, keeps the base WAM frozen, trains a separate repaired action expert on System~2 takeovers mixed with mastered-skill anchor data (own successes and pre-training replay), and reuses the base WAM's calibrated confidence to switch to the repaired expert only on low-confidence states---preserving mastered skills while achieving multi-round self-evolution. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose ( ), a two-system framework uniting WAM speed with agent reliability---slashing agent calls via on-demand takeover and evolving System~1 to run standalone. We design a non-invasive judgment token trained via cross-fitted TD learning on binary outcomes alone, predicting unbiased, calibrated success probabilities in \,ms per chunk without altering actions. We prove a competence shrinkage law revealing the repair--erosion trade-off, guiding mastered-skill anchoring and dynamic confidence gating for erosion-free gap repair and self-evolution. Across Fast-WAM, LingBot-VA, and Kairos on RoboTwin~2.0, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world tasks, beats all -call baselines and boosts standalone WAM success by to with zero agent calls. Related Work sec:related World action models. WAMs couple video diffusion backbones~ wan,unipi with action generation to model physical dynamics and future world states: UVA and Cosmos Policy jointly predict future video and actions~ uva,cosmospolicy , LingBot-VA unifies autoregressive video dynamics and causal action generation in a mixture-of-transformers~ lingbotva,mot , OpenWAM systematizes modular world--action pretraining~ wang2026openwam , and Fast-WAM bypasses test-time video imagination for low-latency control~ fastwam . By leveraging world modeling and future prediction, WAMs achieve strong dexterous manipulation performance~ robotwin2,libero , yet remain fragile in challenging out-of-distribution scenes~ robotwinplus,liberoplus . Confidence prediction in embodied models. Runtime success prediction for embodied policies follows four main paradigms: (i)~external VLM failure judges~ grislain2026ifailsense,spotter , which incur high latency and miss internal action intent; (ii)~multi-sample consistency, prompt ensembling, and candidate scoring~ sentinel,vlacalib,vgps , which require multiple forward passes or discrete action-token logits; (iii)~world-model rollout verification~ foresight,geotts,fare,favor , which sacrifices reactive speed by generating future latents or videos at test time; and (iv)~internal-feature and conformal detectors~ knowno,conformal,safe,vlaconf,seligmann2026vlafail , which either output uncalibrated anomaly alarms and abstention sets~ knowno,conformal,safe,seligmann2026vlafail or post-hoc calibrate action-agnostic observation features~ vlaconf . In contrast, our proposed cross-fitted TD judgment token calibrates to the accurate task-success probability at negligible overhead without affecting action predictions, enabling both on-demand System~2 takeover and erosion-free self-evolution. Foundation-model-based embodied control agents. Foundation-model-based manipulation agents divide into two tracks. Pure foundation-model-based agents drive robots directly without learned visuomotor policies, spanning programmatic and constraint-synthesis agents~ rekep,liu2026guava,chen2026gap , zero-shot direct and tool-mediated controllers powered by GPT-6-Astra~ jia2026agp,zhang2026astra,he2026astra,zhou2026gptgear , and in-context memory-augmented agents~ cheng2026gptpolicy,guo2026robodawn,liu2026roboicl , all of which face high per-step latency and token cost~ galbot2026astra,zhou2026gptgear . Dual-system frameworks pair foundation-model-based agents with embodied policies via memory-guided primitive orchestration~ zhang2026harness , parallel VLM screening and primitive-based failure repair~ spotter , learned post-hoc assistance heads or proposal-review gates for selective agent hand-offs~ callastra,galbot2026astra , or agent-guided policy distillation that replaces the base model wholesale~ liu2026guava . However, keeping the agent permanently in the runtime loop perpetuates high invocation costs, while wholesale replacement causes negative flips and degrades already-learned skills~ bct,pct,wiseft,biderman2024lora . bridges both tracks by invoking System~2 adaptively only when the WAM lacks confidence and consolidating those takeover trajectories into a standalone WAM without degrading existing capabilities. title: Counterfactual Velocity Steering for World Action Models
summary: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field, so test-time bias correction seems simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic condition and subtract that velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show this is often wrong. On Fast-WAM across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, mean-instruction predictions align strongly with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately 0.94-0.95). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: their mean norm is 98.3% of the mean individual norm. References thus contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages generation. We propose a same-state diagnostic and shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing, which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small task-dependent scale from instruction geometry. In controlled RoboTwin experiments, corrupting instructions still permits 25.1% success (50 tasks, 20 episodes), whereas dynamic visual corruption nearly eliminates success. A fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches 92.7% versus a 92.1% baseline in one randomized 1000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within run-to-run variation. An angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated bound of 94.5%; its best learned online realization reaches 92.5%. These results identify shared flow and train-serve mismatch as central obstacles and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction.
full_text: Flow-based robot policies generate actions by repeatedly evaluating a conditional velocity field. This makes test-time bias correction appear deceptively simple: query the action expert under a task-agnostic or nominally stationary condition, then subtract the resulting velocity from the task-conditioned prediction. We show that this interpretation is often wrong. On Fast-WAM evaluated over 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, predictions obtained from a mean instruction are highly aligned with task-conditioned velocities (cosine approximately -- ). Averaging eight completed-state references barely cancels this direction: the norm of their mean is of the mean individual norm. Thus, reference branches contain a large shared transport component, not only harmful bias, and aggressive subtraction damages the generative trajectory. We develop a same-state diagnostic framework and a shrinkage analysis showing that the optimal correction scale depends on reference signal-to-noise. This motivates geometry-calibrated action debiasing ( ), which removes only the component orthogonal to the task velocity and predicts a small, task-dependent scale from within-task and cross-task instruction geometry. Controlled RoboTwin experiments reveal three findings: corrupting the instruction still permits success on a complete 50-task, 20-episode study, whereas dynamic corruption of visual observations nearly eliminates success; a fixed centered orthogonal correction reaches versus a baseline in one randomized 1,000-trial sweep, but gains are non-monotonic and within observed run-to-run variation; and an angular scale pilot has an offline oracle-gated upper bound of , while its best learned online realization reaches . Our results identify shared flow and train--serve mismatch as central obstacles, and provide a reproducible foundation for conditional correction rather than claiming that reference subtraction is universally beneficial. Introduction World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising framework for embodied intelligence by jointly modeling visual dynamics and robot actions. Unlike conventional vision-language-action policies that directly map observations and instructions to actions, WAMs also learn how the observed world changes during interaction. This additional objective can encourage representations of object motion, contact dynamics, spatial relations, and task progression. It may also broaden the sources of supervision available for robot learning. Videos collected from humans, other robots, or passive observations can reveal how objects move and how manipulation unfolds, even when action labels for the target robot are unavailable. Recent WAMs have demonstrated promising transfer across tasks, environments, and robot embodiments, while large-scale video representation models have shown that visual pretraining can support physical reasoning and downstream robot planning~ ye2026worldactionmodels,assran2025vjepa2 . In parallel, the broader AI Flow perspective emphasizes that capable generative models must be coordinated across heterogeneous models, devices, and interaction contexts rather than treated as isolated predictors~ an2025aiflow,shao2025aiflowedge . These results suggest that video modeling can provide useful knowledge beyond what is available from narrowly collected robot demonstrations, making it an increasingly important component of general-purpose robot learning. However, learning to predict visual futures and learning to select an appropriate action are not equivalent objectives. A video model must account for many changes in the visual input, including object appearance, texture, lighting, camera motion, and background structure. A control policy, in contrast, should preserve the information that determines the correct action under the current task and environment while ignoring changes that are irrelevant to control. Consequently, visually accurate prediction does not necessarily imply reliable action selection, causal physical understanding, or robust adaptation to changes in the robot and its surroundings. Recent evaluations show that video generation models can produce plausible visual futures while failing to extrapolate physical rules beyond familiar cases~ kang2025physical,motamed2025physicsiq . Fast-WAM further demonstrates that much of the benefit of video modeling may come from shaping the learned representation during training, since competitive action performance can be retained after explicit future-video generation is removed at inference~ yuan2026fastwam . These findings leave open a broader question about conditional control: after video and action learning are combined, does the policy adapt its action to the full conditioning state—including task intent, visual observations, robot proprioception, and interaction context—or does it primarily reproduce a behavior associated with the current observation? This question is closely related to a broader concern in generative-model post-training: optimizing a convenient surrogate, whether a likelihood term or a learned reward, can improve the measured objective while failing to preserve intended semantics, controllability, or robustness~ liang2025rlvisual,liang2026teleboost . A potential failure mode is that WAM predictions become dominated by the current visual observation. When similar visual scenes repeatedly co-occur with particular actions in the training data, the policy may learn to reproduce the visually associated behavior while paying insufficient attention to the task instruction and robot state. Recent VLA studies report related modality imbalance, in which strong visual-action priors weaken the influence of language and proprioception~ fei2025liberoplus,xu2025bayesvla . This is also analogous to the non-visual statistical shortcuts exposed in visual-relationship recognition, where models can exploit predictable relationships without using the image evidence intended to support the decision~ liang2019vrr . We observe a similar asymmetry in Fast-WAM: replacing the instruction with one sampled from another task still yields success on randomized RoboTwin episodes, whereas dynamically replacing the visual observation reduces success to on the same condition. These results are consistent with the possibility that Fast-WAM relies strongly on visual observations and may not always respond adequately to non-visual conditioning. In this paper, we propose a counterfactual velocity-steering framework for diagnosing and mitigating conditioning imbalance in WAMs. Our starting point is to query the action expert under alternative instruction contexts while holding the visual observation, proprioception, noisy action, and flow time fixed. A mean context constructed from training instructions serves as a task-agnostic reference, allowing us to examine which components of the action prediction persist when task-specific language is attenuated. This reference is a probe, not a ground-truth estimate of bias: neither averaging embeddings nor removing task intent guarantees that the resulting prediction should correspond to a stationary robot. The main challenge is to distinguish an unwanted action tendency from the transport required by the generative process itself. Even a stationary action endpoint generally requires a nonzero velocity at an intermediate noisy state. Consistent with this distinction, our diagnostics reveal strong alignment between task-conditioned velocities and both mean-instruction and completed-state reference velocities. Directly subtracting a reference can therefore remove useful transport together with any unwanted component. We address this ambiguity by constructing centered residuals and retaining their components orthogonal to the task velocity. This preserves the instantaneous projection along the original prediction, while allowing a controlled change in direction; it does not assume that the original prediction is always correct or that the residual is purely harmful. We instantiate this framework as geometry-calibrated action debiasing ( ). A noisy-reference analysis motivates shrinking the correction according to its signal-to-noise ratio rather than applying a uniform, large scale. We use within-task and cross-task instruction geometry as observable proxies for this calibration, separating the correction amplitude from a gate that estimates whether an intervention is beneficial. The same residual also provides a training-time signal: we use it to define two detached sample-weighting rules based on angular displacement and relative correction norm. These objectives test whether reference information can be incorporated during learning without requiring an auxiliary branch at deployment. Our RoboTwin study combines input interventions, same-state velocity diagnostics, and controlled correction sweeps. The results show that reference geometry is informative but does not make debiasing automatic: small corrections help some tasks, while stronger corrections can hurt, and offline scale-selection gains need not transfer to online rollouts. We therefore distinguish evidence of conditional dependence, the quality of a candidate bias estimate, and the downstream utility of applying it. Our contributions are: A controlled diagnostic framework that probes conditioning dependence in Fast-WAM and distinguishes action-space stationarity from shared transport in velocity space. A geometry-aware correction formulation combining centered residuals, orthogonal projection, and calibrated scales, together with training-time extensions based on corrected supervision and detached loss weighting. An empirical analysis of reference selection and correction strength on RoboTwin, identifying task-dependent benefits, failure modes of naive subtraction, and the gap between offline calibration and deployed control. Related Work Generative robot policies. Imitation-learning policies have progressed from direct action regression to expressive sequence generators. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) models temporally coherent action chunks for precise bimanual manipulation zhao2023act , while Diffusion Policy represents multimodal visuomotor behavior through iterative action generation chi2023diffusionpolicy . Recent extensions incorporate explicit spatial structure, including 3D Diffusion Policy and 3D Diffuser Actor, which combine action generation with point-cloud or 3D scene representations and language or proprioceptive conditioning ze2024dp3,ke2024diffuseractor . These works motivate our use of a conditional action field, but do not study how counterfactual conditioning signals should be used to debias that field during fine-tuning. Generalist vision-language-action policies. Large-scale robot datasets and multimodal pretraining have enabled policies that transfer across tasks, embodiments, and environments. RT-1 studies scaling a robotics transformer across diverse real-world data brohan2022rt1 ; RT-2 transfers web-scale vision-language knowledge into robotic control by representing actions in the same sequence model brohan2023rt2 . Open X-Embodiment and RT-X further investigate cross-robot data and positive transfer openx2023 , while Octo provides an open generalist policy intended for efficient downstream adaptation octo2024 . OpenVLA uses an open vision-language backbone for instruction-conditioned manipulation kim2024openvla , and uses a flow-based action expert for general robot control black2024pi0 . Our focus is complementary: given a WAM action expert that already receives vision, language, and proprioception, we construct a same-state reference and use its geometry to shape fine-tuning. title: RoboAda: Adapting Frozen Robot Policies at Test Time to Physics They Cannot See
summary: Pretrained robot policies decide what to do from camera images, yet some of the physics that decides whether their plans succeed is not visible. An object may look light but be 100 times heavier, and a weakened joint or a lagging controller leaves no trace in the image. When the physics at deployment differs from training, the plan is often still right but is executed as if nothing had changed. Training on such variations in advance cannot handle unseen changes, while adapting once deployed either changes the plan, leaving the miscalibrated commands in place, or updates a robot model by gradient steps that do not know how reliable they are and can make the robot worse even when nothing has changed. We propose RoboAda, which keeps the policy and its plan unchanged and corrects the commands that carry it out by inferring at test time how the robot turns commands into motion. The key observation is that the robot's own motion reveals the change: after each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model of the original robot converts the observed motion into the commands it would have needed, yielding free labels at every step. Competing hypotheses of how the robot responds, including that nothing has changed, are weighted by how well they predict these labels, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under them. RoboAda needs no reward, no gradient step and no data from the changed robot. We evaluate RoboAda with five frozen policies on LIBERO, two world action models and three vision-language-action models. Under eleven physical shifts, it more than doubles their average success, from 27.8% to 62.9%. It beats the best of seven test-time adaptation methods by 17.3 points on Cosmos Policy, and largely preserves the policies' success when nothing has changed. On bimanual RoboTwin 2.0 in joint space, it raises success under joint-target offsets from 24.9% to 78.8%.

Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs) and vision-language-action models (VLAs) have made pretrained robot policies broadly capable. A WAM predicts how the scene will evolve and decodes the actions that produce this future, either from predicted frames~ du2023unipi,ko2023avdc,tian2024seer,hu2024vpp or by denoising video and actions jointly~ li2025uva,zhu2025uwm,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero . A VLA maps observations to actions directly~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,pi2025pi05 . We call the chunk of actions that either kind of policy outputs its plan. Both kinds learn to plan under the physics of their training data, and their plans are executed as if that physics still held. Yet some of the physics that decides whether a plan succeeds is not visible. A full mug looks like an empty one, a block that looks wooden may be made of iron, and a worn joint or a lagging controller looks the same as a healthy one. In each case, the physics at deployment differs from that of the training data, and the camera cannot reveal the difference. Such hidden physical shifts are common once robots leave the lab, where actuators wear, controllers are tuned differently from robot to robot, and the objects to be handled vary in weight. They are also costly. In Fig.~ fig:method , a hidden 35\,N payload acts on the robot while it carries a cream cheese box. The policy plans the same motion as on the training robot and sends the same commands, and the box falls short of the basket. On RoboTwin-Phys, randomizing physical conditions, together with table geometry and camera pose, lowers the success of Fast-WAM from 91.8 to 44.2 and of from 76.8 to 31.6 , whereas visual and layout randomization alone costs at most 6 points~ zhang2026robotwinphys . Existing remedies fall into two groups ( ). The first prepares the policy in advance, either by training on randomized dynamics~ peng2018sim,robustvla2026 or by inferring a latent physical context from recent interaction~ yu2017preparing,zhou2019epi,lee2020cadm,kumar2021rma,zhang2026selfadaptivevla . Both handle only variations seen during training. The second adapts at deployment. Some of these methods change what the robot plans or predicts, by adapting the world model to the observed outcome~ yuan2026adaworldpolicy,wan2026worldagen,park2026t3vf,zhang2026jepattt or by sampling several plans and keeping the one a verifier prefers~ qi2025gpc,zhang2026wap,zhang2026wcd , and the plan is still executed with the same miscalibrated commands. Others update a dynamics model~ nagabandi2019grbal,sun2024tttlayer or a residual on the commands~ alra2026,sandwich2026 by gradient steps. These updates carry no estimate of how reliable they are, so they also move when nothing has changed and can make an unchanged robot worse. We argue that under such shifts the plan is usually still right, and only the commands that carry it out are wrong. If the robot executes only half of every command, it reaches only half of the motion that Cosmos Policy imagines for it ( ). We therefore treat test-time adaptation as inferring how the robot turns commands into motion and correcting the commands accordingly. We refer to the actuators, the controller and any load the robot carries, which together turn commands into motion, as the robot's body. This is hard because the shift cannot be seen, no reward or label is available at test time, and a correction that chases execution noise can make an unchanged robot worse. We introduce to address this ( ). After each action chunk, an inverse-dynamics model trained on the nominal robot, the one the policy was trained on, returns the command the nominal robot would have needed for the motion that actually happened, as in hindsight relabeling~ andrychowicz2017her,ghosh2019gcsl . If the robot executes only half of every command, this label is half the command sent, so every step yields a free label of how the robot responds. Per action axis, fits three competing hypotheses to these labels, namely that the robot is unchanged, that it scales and offsets every command, or that its response depends on its state, as when a payload appears at the grasp. Each hypothesis is weighted by how well it predicted each new label, and the next chunk is sent with the commands that best realize the plan under these weights. A systematic shift moves the weight away from the unchanged hypothesis within a few chunks, while pure noise leaves the weights spread, so the commands do not chase it. Only the priors and features of the hypotheses are learned in advance, from the nominal robot alone. The fitting and weighting follow multiple-model adaptive control~ magill1965optimal,narendra1997adaptive , which we apply around a frozen foundation policy with its own plan as the target and no robot model or reward. We evaluate with five frozen policies on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , two WAMs and three VLAs from 2B to 7B parameters, and with Fast-WAM on the bimanual RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 . With the same settings for every policy, it more than doubles their average success under eleven physical shifts, from 27.8 to 62.9 ( ). Our contributions are threefold: Test-time adaptation as inferring the body. We reframe adapting a frozen robot policy to unseen physics as inferring a posterior over explicit hypotheses of the robot's body, in the policy's own action space, from hindsight labels of the robot's own motion. It needs no reward, no retraining and no data from the changed robot. . We weigh body hypotheses by their predictive evidence and command under the posterior, with priors meta-learned on synthetic changes of the nominal robot. Unlike latent-context inference, which recognizes variations seen in training, fits the body at hand from the robot's own motion and needs no data from the changed robot. Unlike world-model adaptation and verifier-based steering, it changes how a plan is executed rather than which plan is chosen. Evidence on five policies and two simulators. more than doubles the average success under eleven physical shifts, recovers much of the success lost to objects 100 times heavier than they look, keeps its gains under perception, language and world changes, outperforms seven test-time adaptation methods, and transfers to a bimanual robot commanded in joint space. Its posterior recovers the true command gain within four to six chunks. Related Work sec:related World action models and inference-time steering. Video-based policies plan in pixel space and recover actions with inverse dynamics or tracking~ du2023unipi,ko2023avdc,du2023vlp,tian2024seer,hu2024vpp . Joint models denoise video and actions in one network~ guo2024pad,li2025uva,zhu2025uwm,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva , and hybrid VLAs add foresight to action prediction~ zhao2025cotvla,zhang2025dreamvla,zheng2025flare . Several works use such models to construct behavior at inference time. They rank policy proposals in a predictive world model~ qi2025gpc , search end-effector goals with a vision-language model as proposer and judge~ zhang2026wap , infer a setup's action-to-pixel mapping from a calibration episode~ yang2026syncworld , refine a latent physical embedding after failures~ ko2025relic , verify a world model with an inverse model~ liu2026wav , or learn an internal model of external forces online~ gao2026impact . Test-time selection for WAMs scores imagined futures with a verifier, by surprisal, geometry or inverse consistency~ zhang2026wcd,zhao2026geobon,ruan2026compatible,seo2026acid . Unlike these methods, which choose or refine what is planned, infers the body that executes the plan and can complement any of them. Test-time adaptation and physical inference. Test-time adaptation updates a model from unlabeled test data~ sun2020ttt,wang2021tent,niu2022eata . For VLAs and WAMs it has been driven by future-prediction losses~ park2026t3vf,ji2026vane,zhu2026juno,wan2026worldagen,feng2026wamttt and by test-time reinforcement learning~ liu2026ttvla,bai2025evolvevla . Robustness benchmarks change what a policy sees and is told~ fei2025liberoplus,zhou2025liberopro , change the world while it acts~ zhang2026liberomax , or vary the physical conditions~ zhang2026robotwinphys,lee2026selfcomp , and of these changes only the physical ones are not visually apparent. Hidden physical parameters have been inferred from interaction by online system identification~ yu2017preparing , probing interactions~ zhou2019epi and context-aware dynamics models~ lee2020cadm , and RMA, its version for manipulator arms and Self-Adaptive VLA infer a latent context from recent history~ kumar2021rma,liang2024rapid,zhang2026selfadaptivevla . title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design
summary: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.
full_text: Native Model-Agent Co-Design sec:introduction The physical world is open-ended, partially observable, and dynamically evolving, where actions have uncertain consequences and failures may incur irreversible costs. While foundation models have substantially advanced embodied intelligence, standalone foundation models still struggle to sustain reliable behavior over long horizons, particularly when execution requires self-correction and adaptation. Extending their capability boundaries therefore requires coupling native model capabilities with persistent agentic reasoning~ yao2023react,schick2023toolformer , memory~ nvidia2026gr00t2,lu2026aspire , and interaction~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,gemini2025robotics . However, simply integrating models and agents may not fully realize their combined potential. Inconsistencies between planning and control may lead to unreliable physical execution and limited adaptation from accumulated experience. This motivates a shift from a standalone embodied model toward a native embodied world system. To this end, we characterize native through three core capabilities: Plan lays the foundation for the system to accomplish long-horizon tasks by coordinating model execution across subtasks; Recover further bolsters the system, enabling it to handle uncertainties and recover from unexpected failures during real-world execution; and Evolve extends the system to continuously adapt to new environments and scenarios through accumulated experience. To jointly realize these capabilities, we introduce Innata-0, a model-agent co-designed system that advances native embodied intelligence. As illustrated in , our co-design establishes complementary roles for the embodied model and agent, allowing the model to fully leverage its native capabilities while the agent extends its effective operating scope. On the model side, Innata-0-WAM serves as the physical execution foundation of the system. We adopt a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture~ liang2024mixture0of0transformers0 , which provides understanding, prediction, and action generation capabilities. The model is conditioned on the complete instruction, active subtask, and verified task history. By incorporating current- and history-plan annotations during training, Innata-0-WAM aligns its learned conditioning interface with the agent's evolving representation of task progress. On the agent side, Innata-0-Agent serves as the system coordinator, supporting long-horizon planning, failure recovery, and continual evolution. It orchestrates model execution across subtasks while maintaining hierarchical memory. Grounded in observations and execution feedback, the agent verifies against intended physical outcomes and invokes tool-based recovery upon deviations. Verified interactions and experiences are consolidated into reusable skills that refine subsequent decisions and recovery strategies. Innata-0-Agent aligns its execution logic with the model's capabilities, enabling coordinated execution, outcome verification, and experience-driven adaptation. Realizing Plan, Recover, and Evolve requires the model and agent to work together and play complementary roles. We therefore establish a co-design protocol that enables them to operate in concert, leveraging their respective strengths while guiding their subsequent design. Crucially, this protocol operates in both directions: the model's execution capabilities shape how the agent organizes and delegates tasks, while the agent's requirements for planning, recovery, and adaptation guide model design and training. Our protocol aligns the model's training data with the agent's task instructions, subtask plans, and recovery commands, allowing complex tasks to be carried out through coordinated execution. The agent, in turn, validates execution outcomes and consolidates experiences to refine its task commands and reusable recovery strategies. It also feeds successful rollout segments, including corrective actions and post-recovery continuations, into the shared data pipeline for subsequent policy training. These principles guide our data construction, model training, and agent design, laying the foundation of native embodied intelligence. We evaluate the physical capabilities underlying Innata-0 and their use in closed-loop task execution. Among the compared models, the understanding tower ranks first on nine benchmarks and within the top two on fourteen. On WorldArena~2.0 Track~1~ li2026worldarena2 , Innata-0 achieves an EWM score of 67.63, the highest among the open-source models. Policy evaluations on RoboCasa365~ robocasa365 and RoboDojo-Sim~ chen2026robodojo examine manipulation and task completion. On RoboCasa365, Innata-0 achieves 60.2 overall success and ranks first on Atomic-Seen tasks with an 88.4 success rate. These evaluations characterize the model's grounding, prediction, and control capabilities, as well as its use within an agent-guided execution loop. To conclude, we propose Innata-0, a native embodied world system that extends physical intelligence beyond individual task execution. Our approach jointly designs the embodied model and agent to leverage their complementary strengths. A shared interaction protocol aligns model capabilities with agent requirements and guides data construction, model training, and agent design. Together, these designs enable long-horizon planning, failure recovery, and continual evolution. Our system co-design establishes a basis for studying how aligned task context, physical-outcome verification, and validated experience contribute to reliable open-world interaction. Embodied Data Construction Overview Raw visual, linguistic, action, and tactile data contain rich knowledge about objects, interactions, and physical processes, yet their existing annotations make only part of this knowledge explicit. Following the co-design protocol, we make task goals, subtask relationships, and completion evidence explicit, while preserving the links between corrective behavior and subsequent task execution. We therefore develop Task-Oriented Knowledge Refinement, a unified data construction pipeline that extracts shared annotations from heterogeneous sources and prepares supervision tailored to each learning objective and training stage. Each source can support multiple training tasks wherever the necessary observations and annotations are available. The resulting task annotations align the model's training context with the agent's subtask objectives for Plan. Corrective trajectories and task continuations provide supervision for Recover, while validated rollout segments enter the same pipeline for subsequent policy training, supporting Evolve through experience reuse. We assemble our initial source pool mainly from open-source datasets and web-accessible corpora, including image--text pairs and other vision--language corpora, general videos, egocentric human videos, real-robot recordings, and robot simulation data. Video provides the main source of physical experience, complemented by image--text supervision, native state and action channels, and tactile observations. Together, these sources cover diverse scenes, objects, embodiments, and manipulation tasks. The knowledge available in a source can exceed the supervision made explicit by its original annotations. A video may record objects, spatial relationships, intermediate goals, and state changes while its caption names only the overall activity. Relevant evidence may also occupy only a brief interval within a longer recording. Each learning objective requires a different view of this information. For example, the same video of putting a cup into a cabinet can support a grounding question about the cup, an instruction-conditioned prediction of its placement, and an action-learning example when corresponding recorded or reconstructed trajectories are available. When synchronized tactile observations are available, the same interaction can also support prediction of contact and loading during grasping or placement. Constructing these views requires us to locate the event, identify its participants and task structure, and align the context and target at the appropriate granularity. A frame may suffice for a spatial question, whereas visual prediction requires a coherent transition and action prediction additionally requires aligned motion supervision. We therefore make the relevant knowledge explicit in the form each objective needs, while retaining the context needed to interpret it. This lets one experience contribute to several learning tasks, with each example focusing on a specific capability. Figure~ fig:embodied_data_pipeline summarizes Task-Oriented Knowledge Refinement in three stages: source acquisition, unified annotation, and task-specific data preparation. The unified annotation stage performs semantic interpretation once per sample to create a shared record of hierarchical task labels, event boundaries, and scene and action descriptions. It preserves the original observations and available state, action, and tactile streams, together with spatial, contact, and quality information, without filtering samples. The vision--language pipeline uses shared spatial and task annotations to select observations and construct instruction--target pairs through task-specific rewriting, followed by validation and distribution balancing. Existing public QA is validated and reformatted without regeneration. The video-generation pipeline uses shared temporal annotations for clip construction, applies frame- and clip-level quality criteria for each training stage, and assembles descriptive or instructional prompts from shared scene and action descriptions. The policy pipeline pairs native or reconstructed motion with shared instructions and task intervals, unifies action semantics, and uses task, outcome, and quality annotations for trajectory filtering and multi-view assembly. For eligible human videos, this includes hand reconstruction and camera-aware motion alignment. The tactile pipeline combines sensor observations with shared contact, coverage, and validity records, followed by sensor-to-MANO alignment, regional proxy construction, and temporal alignment with visual and motion streams. One source can thus yield multiple training forms, depending on its available observations and supervision. Unified Information Extraction and Annotation We attach a shared annotation record to each source, preserving its original timestamps, camera views, source metadata, native state and action channels, and tactile observations where available. The record combines source-level context with frame-level and interval-level annotations. We prompt Qwen3.8-Flash-Next~ qwen3.8flashnext once per sample to produce the applicable semantic, relational, temporal, and perceptual-quality fields in a single structured response. Specialized perception models add dense masks to this record, alongside source-provided depth and camera calibration. Thus, one VLM pass supplies a broad description of the experience, while dedicated visual modules recover spatial measurements and available tactile observations provide contact evidence for downstream tasks. and Geometric Annotation. We combine specialized perception models with source-provided depth and camera calibration to obtain object localization and spatial information. Detection, segmentation, and tracking. We use Grounding DINO~ liu2024groundingdino for object detection and SAM~3.1~ carion2025sam3,meta2026sam31 for instance segmentation and video tracking. VLMs provide additional object detection and localization for data requiring further annotation. We retain boxes, masks, prediction scores where available, and cross-frame object identities linked to the shared entity record. Depth and 3D structure. We use source-provided depth-camera measurements, together with available camera intrinsics and extrinsics, to obtain spatial inputs and supervision signals

title: AERIN: Aerial Instance Navigation with a Visual World Model
summary: Searching from high altitude and navigating to a target instance specified by a reference image is a common application for UAVs. In such tasks, high-altitude observations provide broad ground coverage for efficient search, but targets occupy fewer pixels, making instance verification and action selection more difficult. We present AERIN, a visual world model that uses action-conditioned prediction to guide the UAV toward the target while adjusting its viewpoint to obtain higherquality observations for subsequent instance verification. Highaltitude navigation requires fine-grained target details and scene context relevant to visibility, but repeatedly predicting dense visual representations of this information is computationally expensive. AERIN addresses this challenge with a compact, fixedsize, target-conditioned latent state that separately represents both for efficient action evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that AERIN outperforms the evaluated baselines in target approach and observation quality, while requiring substantially less decision time than similar world models.
full_text: Searching from high altitude and navigating to a target instance specified by a reference image is a common application for UAVs. In such tasks, high-altitude observations provide broad ground coverage for efficient search, but targets occupy fewer pixels, making instance verification and action selection more difficult. We present AERIN, a visual world model that uses action-conditioned prediction to guide the UAV toward the target while adjusting its viewpoint to obtain higher-quality observations for subsequent instance verification. High-altitude navigation requires fine-grained target details and scene context relevant to visibility, but repeatedly predicting dense visual representations of this information is computationally expensive. AERIN addresses this challenge with a compact, fixed-size, target-conditioned latent state that separately represents both for efficient action evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that AERIN outperforms the evaluated baselines in target approach and observation quality, while requiring substantially less decision time than similar world models. Introduction Instance ImageGoal Navigation (IIN) requires an agent to navigate to a specific object instance depicted in a reference image ref1 . Existing UAV-based IIN work ref2 has investigated near-ground navigation in indoor environments, where exploration and collision avoidance are important challenges. In this work, we consider Aerial Instance ImageGoal Navigation (AIIN) in high-altitude patrol settings, where predefined patrol routes can organize regional coverage and broad aerial observations help locate potential targets efficiently. However, targets often occupy few pixels in the high-altitude aerial images and may be partially occluded, providing insufficient evidence for reliable instance verification. Therefore, observation improvement while approaching becomes a key issue in such task, i.e., navigate the UAV toward the target while selecting viewpoints that reveal useful visual details. Guiding such an approach requires anticipating how UAV motion changes the available visual evidence. Moving closer or descending may enlarge the target in the image, but can also increase its occlusion by surrounding structures, such as a tree canopy. Actions must therefore be evaluated according to their effects on both target detail and visibility. A useful viewpoint may require several moves to reach, even when the first move provides little immediate observation gain. An action-conditioned world model supports such lookahead by recursively predicting how the visual state changes under successive actions, allowing candidate sequences to be evaluated before execution. However, applying world models to AIIN places particular demands on the predictive representation. First, high-altitude views cover larger areas, facilitating target search, but also contain substantial amounts of task-irrelevant background content, while targets may occupy relatively few informative pixels. Moreover, background changes during flight are often more pronounced than those encountered in near-ground and indoor environments. Second, in near-ground IIN settings, user-provided reference images are often captured from near-horizontal viewpoints similar to those encountered during navigation. In AIIN, however, UAVs typically observe the target from above, making target details more difficult to identify. Meeting these observational requirements calls for retaining fine-grained target cues alongside scene context relevant to occlusion. Dense, multiscale feature maps offer one way to preserve both types of information. However, directly using these maps as the predictive state incurs substantial computation, as they must be processed repeatedly across candidate action sequences and rollout steps. This cost can increase planning latency and limit how frequently the UAV replans from new observations. Even with the latest latent-space prediction methods, such as JEPA, this overhead, although reduced, remains substantial. Compressing the state reduces this cost, but may suppress small-target cues, obscure local appearance differences, or discard context relevant to visibility. Therefore, the key challenge is to construct a compact predictive state that preserves the information needed to distinguish the outcomes of different actions while remaining efficient for repeated prediction. To address this challenge, we present AERIN, a visual world model that guides UAVs toward target while improving observation quality through efficient action-conditioned prediction. Its core is a fixed-size, target-conditioned latent state that allocates representational capacity according to the roles of target details and scene context. Guided by the reference image, the state separately represents local appearance differences within the target region and surrounding information relevant to its visibility. This organization decouples perception resolution from predictive state size: high-resolution visual features inform state construction, while repeated prediction operates on the resulting compact state. AERIN uses action-conditioned predictions of this state to evaluate the observation outcomes of candidate action sequences. Guided by these predictions, the UAV approaches the target while acquiring clearer, less occluded observations for subsequent instance verification. Experiments show that AERIN improves observation quality and the success rate of acquiring high-quality observations over the compared methods, while requiring substantially less decision time than the evaluated dense-state world models. Related Work Visual navigation and active perception. Image-goal navigation specifies destinations or instances through reference images ref1,ref3,ref4,ref5 , using feature matching, cross-view learning ref4,ref5 , or explicit scene representations ref6,ref7,ref8 . Active perception acquires additional evidence through movement ref9,ref10,ref11,ref12 , including candidate approach and verification in IEVE ref13 . Active tracking combines target appearance, observation history, and scene context ref14,ref15,ref16,ref17 ; OA-VAT ref18 integrates instance association with occlusion recovery. Geometric approaches jointly consider visibility, kinematics, and collision avoidance ref19,ref20,ref21,ref22,ref23,ref24 . Recent aerial approaches include altitude-aware embodied tracking with AaDWorlds ref55 and JEPA-based active object detection ref56 . Our focus is reference-guided target approach and observation improvement after candidate discovery. Visual world models for planning. Action-conditioned world models support planning through video prediction ref25 , latent-state prediction ref26,ref27,ref28 , and policy learning from imagined trajectories ref29 . Pretrained visual features enable prediction and goal-directed action optimization in feature space ref30 . In navigation, predicted ref31 or rendered ref32 views support trajectory evaluation, while navigation policies provide candidate actions ref33,ref34 . WoMAP ref35 and CST-WM ref36 couple future prediction with task-related readouts for active localization and tracking, respectively. UA-NWM ref57 uses uncertainty-aware predictions to score trajectories toward a goal view. However, preserving decision-relevant evidence through these predictive pipelines remains a distinct challenge when the target occupies only a small fraction of the image. Compact representations for visual prediction. Visual computation can be reduced through spatially selective detection ref37,ref38 , latent bottlenecks ref39 , and token aggregation ref40 . Object-centric learning organizes image and video observations into object-level representations ref41,ref42,ref43 , while object-centric world models capture object dynamics and interactions for prediction ref44,ref45,ref46 and planning ref44,ref45 . Causal-JEPA ref47 combines compact object states with masked latent prediction and efficient planning, while Sparse Imagination ref48 reduces rollout cost using sparse patch subsets. While object-centric models typically assign slots to different objects, we explore compact, task-relevant representations that allocate capacity across target regions to better capture local details in small-target observation tasks. Task Definition sec:task We study Aerial Instance ImageGoal Navigation (AIIN) in high-altitude patrol settings, where a UAV navigates to a specific object instance depicted in a reference image. Given an available map, a geometric coverage planner can generate predefined patrol routes for surveying the search region. Broad aerial views support the discovery of potential targets along these routes, but the observed objects may occupy few pixels or be partially occluded, providing insufficient visual evidence for reliable instance verification. This creates a need to approach candidate objects while actively selecting viewpoints that reveal useful target details. This patrol-based organization motivates our focus on target approach and active observation. title: Beyond Which: Where, How, and When in Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically rely on vision-language model (VLM) features as the primary perceptual source for action prediction, showing strong generalization across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. Although VLM features can identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, precise manipulation also requires understanding where task-relevant entities are located within the spatial layout, how their geometric structure constrains physical interaction, and when spatial or geometric information should make a greater contribution to action prediction. To this end, we introduce {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA to organize VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. Specifically, {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA retains VLM-based semantic entity perception which and further introduces spatial distance perception where and geometric structure perception how with adaptive spatial-geometric guidance when to enrich the perceptual information available for action prediction. Experiments across real-world settings and simulation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of {\mathcal{W}^{3}\mathcal{H}}-VLA.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically rely on vision-language model (VLM) features as the primary perceptual source for action prediction, showing strong generalization across diverse robotic manipulation tasks. Although VLM features can identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, precise manipulation also requires understanding where task-relevant entities are located within the spatial layout, how their geometric structure constrains physical interaction, and when spatial or geometric information should make a greater contribution to action prediction. To this end, we introduce to organize VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. Specifically, retains VLM-based semantic entity perception (which) and further introduces spatial distance perception (where) and geometric structure perception (how) with adaptive spatial-geometric guidance (when) to enrich the perceptual information available for action prediction. Experiments across real-world settings and simulation benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superior performance of . Introduction sec:introduction Robot policies optimized for specific tasks often suffer from limited generalization~ kim2024openvla . Meanwhile, recent advances in large-scale vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-modal learning and reasoning~ achiam2023gpt, beyer2024paligemma . The advances provide a strong basis for visual perception and language understanding, enabling robot policies to leverage broad vision-language knowledge for interpreting visual observations and language instructions across the physical world. Building upon these, vision-language-action (VLA) models combine a pre-trained VLM for perceptual and semantic understanding with an action prediction module that maps observations and instructions to robot actions, enabling robot policies to generalize across diverse tasks~ zitkovich2023rt, kim2024openvla, black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_, zheng2026x, luo2026simvla . Despite the strong generalization, most VLA models still rely on the VLM-based 2D visual perception, resulting in a primary focus on the semantic information about the entities relevant to the action prediction. Recent efforts have begun to enrich perception with spatial depth information~ qu2025spatialvla and 3D scene representations~ zhen20243d . Although these advances show the benefits of richer perception, they also motivate a broader question: Consider the task of placing a blue cube surrounded by other cubes onto a cube tower. Given 2D visual observations and a language instruction, the VLM provides semantic information for identifying cube to manipulate. Semantic information therefore remains essential throughout the manipulation process to ensure that action prediction remains grounded in relevant entities. Beyond this, precise action prediction also depends on knowing the cube, the tower, and the end effector are located relative to one another. Furthermore, the model must also account for the shapes and local geometric details of the entities constrain grasping, alignment, and placement. During manipulation, it is also required to decide action prediction should emphasize spatial relationships for localization or prioritize geometric constraints for grasping, alignment, and placement. Accordingly, we argue that precise action prediction requires not only VLM-based semantic entity perception but also spatial distance perception, geometric structure perception, and adaptive spatial-geometric guidance, which together advance VLA perception beyond with the consideration of , , and . As shown in~ , we introduce , a novel framework that organizes VLA perception and action prediction around which, where, how, and when. For which, follows the standard VLA paradigm, using a VLM to derive semantic entity perception from 2D visual observations and language instructions, thereby preserving the full semantic information as the primary task-relevant context throughout action prediction. In terms of where, introduces spatial distance perception by incorporating task-relevant distance relationships and spatial layout features derived from a pre-trained depth estimation model yang2024depth . About how, enables geometric structure perception by capturing task-relevant geometric structure features from a pre-trained visual geometry model wang2026vggt . For when, integrates adaptive spatial-geometric guidance into action prediction by coordinating the contributions of spatial distance perception and geometric structure perception, conditioned on the current task semantic context and evolving action state. By unifying which, where, how, and when, complements semantic entity perception with spatial distance perception, geometric structure perception, and adaptive spatial-geometric guidance to support precise action prediction in the complex physical world. To validate the effectiveness of , we conduct extensive experiments on 4 benchmarks, LIBERO~ liu2023libero , LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero , CALVIN~ mees2022calvin , LIBERO-PRO~ zhou2025libero , and 4 real-world manipulation tasks. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows. We formulate VLA perception and action prediction in terms of which, where, how, and when, extending VLM-based semantic entity perception with spatial distance perception, geometric structure perception, and adaptive spatial-geometric guidance. Building on the formulation and the corresponding perceptual design, we propose , a novel VLA framework that incorporates a broader range of perceptual information into action prediction. We evaluate on 4 benchmarks and 4 real-world manipulation tasks, showing its effectiveness and superior performance in simulated and physical settings. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models VLA models build upon pre-trained VLMs to map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions~ black2024pi_0, qu2025spatialvla, zheng2026x, luo2026simvla . One line of research advances VLA models by scaling robot interaction data and vision-language pre-training. RT-1~ brohan2022rt demonstrates the benefits of large and diverse real-world robot data, and RT-2~ zitkovich2023rt transfers web-scale vision-language knowledge to action prediction. Open X-Embodiment~ o2024open aggregates cross-embodiment robot data, enabling the training of generalist policies~ team2024octo, kim2024openvla . More recently, ~ intelligence2025pi_ integrates heterogeneous robot and web data to improve open-world generalization. Another line of research improves VLA action prediction through specialized policy architectures. RDT-1B~ liu2025rdt employs the diffusion model for continuous action prediction. Within the flow matching paradigm, ~ black2024pi_0 introduces an action expert for continuous action chunks, X-VLA~ zheng2026x incorporates soft prompts for cross-embodiment learning, and SimVLA~ luo2026simvla adopts a lightweight action transformer. Perception for Robotic Manipulation Research on robotic perception has progressively expanded from 2D semantic perception to spatial and geometric representations, and more recently to adaptive perceptual guidance. Early methods primarily extract semantic features from 2D visual observations. CLIPort~ shridhar2022cliport combines VLM-derived semantic features with spatially precise action prediction, and RoboGround~ huang2025roboground predicts masks for relevant entities and placement regions to guide manipulation. Beyond 2D semantics, subsequent methods incorporate depth and 3D representations to capture physical structure features. PerAct~ shridhar2023perceiver encodes depth observations into a voxel grid, Act3D~ gervet2023act3d uses depth observations to lift pre-trained 2D features into a 3D field, and RVT~ goyal2023rvt aggregates features across virtual views for 3D-aware action prediction. Recent studies further explore adaptive perceptual guidance conditioned on task demands and action execution context. HyperTASR~ sun2025hypertasr adaptively modulates scene features according to task and execution progress, and ActiveVLA~ liu2026activevla dynamically selects 3D regions, viewpoints, and spatial resolutions for precise manipulation. In contrast, unifies VLM-based semantic entity perception to identify which entities are relevant to action prediction, spatial distance perception to establish where relevant entities are located, geometric structure perception to capture how the geometric details constrain physical interaction, and adaptive spatial-geometric guidance to determine when the spatial distance or geometric structure perception should make a greater contribution to precise action prediction.
