title: ConsisX: Cross-View Consistency Thinking in 3D for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding from vision-language models (VLMs) with action prediction for robotic manipulation. Although multi-view observations provide complementary scene information, VLMs model cross-view interactions based on 2D feature similarity, which can lead to physical inconsistency in the form of cross-view incorrect association between distinct entities and cross-view information fragmentation about the same entity. To address these challenges, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for physically consistent robotic manipulation. Specifically, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to introduce cross-view spatial proximity constraints in a shared 3D space to reduce cross-view incorrect association. Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) is designed to organize cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thereby addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) is introduced to condition action prediction on task-relevant 3D entity evidence for cross-view consistent action execution. Experiments on 3 real-world manipulation tasks and 4 simulation benchmarks establish ConsisX as an effective and competitive framework for robotic manipulation. Introduction sec:intro In modern embodied intelligence systems, robots take natural language instructions and multi-view visual observations as input to predict actions for task execution. Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation by extending the visual and language understanding of pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) achiam2023gpt, beyer2024paligemma to robot control through an action prediction module optimized via demonstration learning wang2026vla, zheng2026x . RT-2 and OpenVLA adapt VLMs into robotic policies to predict actions as discrete tokens zitkovich2023rt, kim2024openvla . Subsequently, introduces an action expert to predict continuous action sequences black2024pi_0 . Building upon the , combines diverse robot and vision-language data during training for enhanced generalization to unseen environments intelligence2025pi_ . A common setup for robotic policies incorporates multi-view visual inputs from environment and wrist cameras to provide complementary observations of the current scene for reliable action prediction. To integrate these observations, VLA models enable interactions between visual features from different views through jointly processing within the VLM. However, the joint processing can introduce cross-view ambiguity. As shown in (a), both cups appear in the environment view but only one is visible in the wrist view, and feature interactions may link the front one to the rear one. In (b), the two cameras capture different faces of the same triangular prism, and 2D feature similarity alone may fail to link the local observations. The above cases highlight a challenge: cross-view interactions in VLMs rely on learned similarities between 2D features and can therefore lead to physically inconsistent action execution. Specifically, the challenge involves two forms of cross-view ambiguity. (Q1) Visually similar observations may be incorrectly associated despite corresponding to distinct physical entities. (Q2) Cross-view information remains fragmented despite coming from the same physical entity. Do visually similar observations across views actually refer to the same physical entity? How should fragmented information from different views of the same physical entity be organized? We regard these ambiguities as a 3D cross-view consistency problem and argue that cross-view thinking should jointly consider cross-view association and entity coherence in 3D. Specifically, visual similarity alone is insufficient to establish physical identity, and cross-view association is therefore needed to provide 3D spatial constraints. The fragmented information from the same entity also requires entity coherence to guide its organization into physically consistent evidence. The above considerations lead to the central question: How to think about cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency in 3D? To answer this question, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that combines cross-view association and entity coherence for cross-view consistency thinking in 3D. Specifically, the consistency thinking follows a progressive process. Firstly, Cross-View Association Modeling (CAM) is proposed to organize 3D features from each view in a shared 3D coordinate system and infer cross-view association with spatial proximity constraints and feature similarity. (A1) CAM provides cross-view correspondences under 3D spatial constraint, thereby reducing cross-view incorrect association. Secondly, Entity Coherence Organization (ECO) groups fragmented local 3D feature within each view into entity candidates through spatial affinity and feature compatibility before organizing cross-view entity pairs according to the cross-view association from CAM. (A2) ECO organizes cross-view local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, thus addressing cross-view information fragmentation. Finally, Consistent Action Conditioning (CAC) retrieves candidate entity pairs from ECO according to task relevance, providing the corresponding 3D entity features for cross-view consistent action prediction. ConsisX thus jointly considers cross-view association and entity coherence, enabling cross-view consistency thinking in 3D for reliable robotic manipulation. The main contributions of this work can be summarized as follows. To address the challenge of cross-view physical inconsistency, we propose ConsisX, a novel VLA framework that integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D. We design CAM to reduce cross-view incorrect associations through 3D spatial constraint, ECO to organize fragmented local information into coherent 3D entity evidence, and CAC to provide task relevant 3D entity features for cross-view consistent action prediction. We evaluate ConsisX on 4 simulation benchmarks and conduct real-world experiments on 3 manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness and competitive performance of the proposed framework. Related Work sec:formatting Vision-Language-Action Models VLA models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action prediction for robotic manipulation kim2024openvla, black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_ . Recent progress builds on scalable robot learning and pre-trained vision language knowledge. RT-1 brohan2022rt and Octo team2024octo learn from diverse robot demonstrations, while RT-2 zitkovich2023rt and OpenVLA kim2024openvla adapt pre-trained VLMs. To further advance VLA models, some studies explore ways to improve policy adaptation and generalization. OpenVLA-OFT kim2025fine improves adaptation with optimized fine-tuning, and intelligence2025pi_ enhances generalization through more diverse data. For action prediction, FAST pertsch2025fast compresses action sequences into discrete tokens, and black2024pi_0 introduces flow matching for continuous action prediction. Beyond direct action prediction, some methods integrate intermediate reasoning to improve action prediction zawalski2024robotic, zhao2025cot, zhong2026acot . Cross-View Association Learning Cross-view association learning establishes correspondences between different views for consistent scene understanding. In computer vision, SuperGlue sarlin2020superglue relies on cross-view feature similarity, and CCMP yan2026learning identifies corresponding object instances. Most VLA policies integrate multiple views through joint feature interactions within the VLM black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_ . StereoVLA deng2025stereovla further integrates cross-view information through stereo matching, and ConsisVLA-4D li2026consisvla enhances task-relevant cross-view features with geometric priors. Moreover, XVR jeong2026learning optimizes VLMs to improve cross-view understanding in VLA policies. 3D-Aware Policy Learning 3D-aware learning improves spatial understanding in robotic policies for reliable action execution in the physical world. Some approaches incorporate additional spatial information into policy learning. PerAct shridhar2023perceiver predicts actions from voxelized RGB-D observations, and RVT goyal2023rvt aggregates point cloud-based virtual views. For VLA models, 4D-VLA zhang20264d augments visual feature with 3D position encoding, and PointACT chen2026pointact introduces point cloud feature for action prediction. Researchers further explore 3D object keypoint constraints li20253ds and 3D-consistent waypoints huang20263dway for robot control. Other VLA methods leverage pre-trained 3D vision models to refine visual features feng2026spatial, li2026spatial . In contrast, ConsisX integrates cross-view association and entity coherence to enable cross-view consistency thinking in 3D. Through spatially constrained cross-view association and coherent entity organization, ConsisX leverages cross-view 3D entity evidence for physically consistent action prediction. title: Seeing Together, Acting Apart: Shared Environmental Understanding for Multi-Robot Navigation
summary: Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment? We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context. To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.
full_text: Experiments Experimental Setup We evaluate SEER in both simulated VLN environments and real-world robot deployments. The simulated evaluation contains three parts: standard single-robot VLN, multi-robot VLN constructed from paired R2R trajectories, and downstream integration with different navigation agents. Detailed construction of multi-robot episodes are provided in Appendix~ app:multi_robot_episode_construction . For standard VLN, we follow the continuous VLN-CE setting and report results on the Val-Unseen splits of R2R-CE~ anderson2018vision,krantz2020beyond and RxR-CE~ ku2020rxr in the Habitat simulator~ savva2019habitat . We use standard VLN metrics, including Navigation Error (NE), Success Rate (SR), Oracle Success Rate (OSR), Success weighted by Path Length (SPL), and normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW)~ anderson2018vision,ilharco2019dtw . These single-robot evaluations test whether adding SEER preserves the original navigation ability of downstream agents. For multi-robot evaluation, we use the paired R2R episodes constructed by ourself. The evaluation set is divided into four subsets according to the spatial relationship between the two robots: different-scene, same-scene non-intersecting, same-scene intersecting, and same/sub-trajectory. These subsets allow us to test whether shared environmental understanding helps under different levels of shared context, from no shared scene to highly overlapping trajectories. Following the spirit of collaborative navigation evaluation~ wang2026conavbench , we report both individual and collaborative success. For a paired episode , let denote whether robot A and robot B successfully reach their respective goals. We define Individual Success Rate (ISR) and Collaborative Success Rate (CSR) as ISR measures whether each robot can still complete its own task, while CSR measures whether both robots succeed in the paired episode. We emphasize that our paired-R2R evaluation is not intended to model full physical multi-robot coordination; instead, it provides a controlled abstraction for isolating SEER’s core question: whether independently collected egocentric observations can be transformed into reusable shared environmental context for decentralized navigation. We instantiate downstream navigation with two agents: a specialized StreamVLN agent~ wei2025streamvln and a general Qwen3.5-based agent~ yang2025qwen3 , testing whether SEER is reusable rather than model-specific. We further conduct real-world indoor experiments on two embodiments, AgileX LiMO Pro and Unitree Go2, which performs inference and returns actions to robot-specific low-level controllers via ROS~2. Details on splits, evaluation, deployment, and implementation are in Appendix~ app:experimental_setup . Task-Level Validation: Shared Environmental Understanding for Navigation Single-agent preservation. A key requirement of SEER is that it should not degrade ordinary single-agent navigation. In this sense, single-agent navigation can be viewed as a special case of our setting, where the robot mainly relies on its own observation context and receives no useful cross-robot information. Table~ tab:comp-vlnce evaluates this property, when SEER is added to StreamVLN, the resulting agent preserves the strong performance of the original navigation model and improves the main success-oriented metrics. These results show that SEER tokens provide useful environmental context while preserving the downstream action space and output format. SEER-World is trained independently of downstream navigation policies and frozen during downstream adaptation, while the projector and downstream navigation agent are optimized. Here, policy-agnosticism refers to reusing the same shared world model across downstream navigation policies. Multi-robot navigation improvement. Table~ tab:multi_agent_performance evaluates SEER in paired multi-robot episodes under varying shared environmental context. Across all subsets, SEER improves both ISR and CSR. ISR gains show that each robot benefits from shared environmental context while solving its own task, whereas CSR gains indicate that both robots are more likely to succeed in the same paired episode. SEER achieves stronger gains in same-scene and overlapped-trajectory settings, where cross-robot observations are more relevant. Compatibility with different downstream agents. We evaluate SEER with both a specialized VLN agent (StreamVLN) and a general VLM-based navigation agent (Qwen 3.5), using the same integration strategy. Results show that SEER improves StreamVLN and brings even larger gains to the Qwen 3.5 agent. This supports that SEER is not a model-specific trick, but a reusable environmental understanding layer for different downstream navigation agents. It enables collaborative navigation by sharing latent world understanding, without sharing actions, histories, or a centralized policy. Representation-Level Validation: Action-Relevant Latent Dynamics We introduce a representation-level inverse dynamics probe to test whether SEER encodes action-relevant environmental structure. Since the latent state is not directly interpretable, we freeze the learned forward latent dynamics and, for each transition, enumerate candidate actions. The action whose predicted next latent is closest to the true next latent is selected. High recovery accuracy therefore indicates that the latent space preserves how different navigation actions transform the world state, rather than merely encoding static appearance. Table~ tab:inverse_dynamics_analysis shows that the probe is non-trivial: V-JEPA2 achieves reasonable accuracy, indicating that generic predictive video features capture motion cues, but still lags behind SEER. Ours w/o Retrieval ( replaced by uniform random sampling ) already performs well, suggesting that SEER-World learns discriminative latent dynamics via multi-view prediction. SEER Retrieval further improves both single- and dual-agent settings, isolating the benefit of shared retrieval: relevant observations from the anonymous SEER Pool provide cleaner cross-robot context than the world model alone. Importantly, LIDA is a held-out counterfactual action recovery test across diverse spatial configurations, not a direct training-loss measure, making high scores unlikely to stem only from action bias, visual repetition, or retrieval leakage. What Should Robots Share: World Understanding vs. Agent-Centric Traces Table~ tab:share_what compares SEER with several sharing strategies. We position these baselines as controlled comparisons against representative agent-centric sharing strategies, while leaving stronger learned communication, map-sharing, and centralized multi-agent architectures as complementary directions for future work rather than direct targets of this representation-layer study. Sharing actions only reveals what another robot did, without explaining the environmental structure that made the action useful. Sharing spatial structure improves over these simple signals by providing explicit geometric context, but it requires an additional 3D expert and mainly captures static layout, without modeling how actions change the world state. SEER showing that collaboration benefits more from shared world understanding than from sharing raw histories, actions, or hand-crafted maps. Notably, semantic or topological maps are not mutually exclusive with SEER; they can be viewed as complementary external structures, while SEER provides a learned, action-aware representation layer.

title: SOAR: temporal Structure-guided One-step Action generation for Robotic manipulation
summary: Efficient robotic manipulation requires temporally coordinated actions with low inference latency. Multi-step diffusion and flow policies progressively refine action trajectories but require costly iterative inference, whereas one-step policies eliminate iterative trajectory refinement to reduce inference cost. We introduce **SOAR**, a structure-guided one-step generative policy that improves action quality while preserving one-step efficiency. SOAR predicts an observation-conditioned discrete cosine transform (DCT) representation of future actions, capturing temporal variations across multiple frequency bands to provide explicit guidance from key temporal structural information. Unlike velocity-parameterized one-step flow policies that recover clean actions indirectly from a predicted velocity field, SOAR directly generates clean action trajectories in action space. This aligns the model output with the executable control target and provides a direct interface for structural calibration. The predicted structure further corrects the generated trajectory according to their spectral discrepancy, without requiring an additional evaluation of the generative backbone. During training, the corresponding MeanFlow velocity is derived from the calibrated clean action and used for consistency learning, while an endpoint objective aligns training with the pure-noise condition used for one-step inference. Across 53 Adroit and Meta-World tasks, SOAR achieves 83.9% overall success with only 8.7 ms inference latency. When applied to the VLA model, π0.5, SOAR further achieves 97.2% on LIBERO and 71.7% on RoboTwin 2.0. Real-world experiments and extensive ablations further validate its effectiveness and efficiency.
full_text: Introduction Learning visuomotor policies from expert demonstrations enables robots to acquire complex manipulation skills without manually designing task-specific controllers. However, given the same observation and task goal, multiple action trajectories may succeed while differing in approach direction, motion timing, or contact strategy. Unlike deterministic behavior cloning, which can average across distinct action modes, diffusion- and flow-based policies address this ambiguity by modeling the action distribution itself and have shown strong performance in robotic manipulation~ chi2023diffusion,zhang2025flowpolicy . Despite their effectiveness, generative policies often rely on iterative inference. Diffusion policies progressively denoise action trajectories, while flow-based policies typically integrate learned velocity fields over multiple steps. Such interactive strategy repeats network evaluations, introducing substantial inference latency that reduces responsiveness to dynamics and can leave predicted actions stale as the scene evolves~ black2025realtimechunking . Some recent efforts seek to reduce inference steps through accelerated sampling, distillation, consistency learning, or shortened flow trajectories~ song2021ddim,salimans2022progressive,prasad2024consistencypolicy,hu2024adaflow,su2025freqpolicy , even pushing them to a single network evaluation~ geng2025meanflow,sheng2026mp1,fang2026omp . However, such efficiency comes at the cost of iterative refinement. Multi-step generation repeatedly revisits the action trajectory, progressively correcting its temporal organization; a one-step policy must instead determine the entire trajectory structure at once, with no subsequent opportunity for correction. To provide explicit temporal structure guidance without relying on iterative refinement, we propose SOAR, a temporal Structure-guided One-step Action generation framework for Robot manipulation, as shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser . Unlike velocity-parameterized one-step flow policies that recover clean actions indirectly, SOAR directly generates clean action trajectories in action space, aligning the model output with the executable control target and enabling direct structural calibration. Given the current observation, SOAR predicts a multi-band discrete cosine transform (DCT) representation of future actions to provide temporal structure guidance~ ahmed1974dct,zhong2025freqautoregressive . The predicted structure is incorporated into the observation condition to guide base action generation and is subsequently used to calibrate the generated trajectory according to their spectral discrepancy, without additional evaluation of the generative backbone. During training, the calibrated action is mapped to the corresponding MeanFlow velocity for consistency and endpoint supervision. SOAR thus improves action quality while retaining inference and millisecond-scale latency. Our contributions are: We propose SOAR, a direct one-step action generation policy that generates clean action trajectories in action space with and millisecond-scale inference. SOAR consistently outperforms compared one-step policies on Adroit and Meta-World while retaining , and further demonstrates competitive performance in the VLA setting on LIBERO and RoboTwin2.0. Related Work Inputs for Robot Learning. Visuomotor policies commonly operate on either image observations or explicit 3D scene representations. Image-based methods such as Behavior Transformer, ACT, and RT-1 use learned visual representations for multimodal action prediction, action chunking, and large-scale robot control~ shafiullah2022bet,zhao2023act,brohan2023rt1 . Because images encode geometry only through projection, several works instead reason explicitly in 3D. PerAct, Act3D, RVT, and GNFactor represent scenes using voxelized features, continuous 3D features, virtual views, or neural feature fields~ gervet2023act3d,goyal2023rvt,ze2023gnfactor . Explicit 3D representations have also been combined with generative action models, including 3D Diffuser Actor, DP3, and EquiBot~ ke2024diffuseractor,ze2024dp3,yang2025equibot . These studies highlight the value of 3D geometry for precise and data-efficient manipulation, although observation modality alone does not determine action-generation cost. -based Visuomotor Policies. Diffusion policies represent multimodal action distributions through progressive denoising~ ho2020ddpm . Diffusion Policy and subsequent methods such as ChainedDiffuser and HDP use iterative refinement to generate structured action trajectories~ chi2023diffusion,xian2023chaineddiffuser,ma2024hdp . Reducing this inference cost has motivated accelerated samplers and distillation. DDIM shortens the sampling trajectory, while progressive distillation compresses multiple denoising steps into fewer evaluations~ song2021ddim,salimans2022progressive . Consistency Models further enable one- or few-step sampling by enforcing consistency along the generative trajectory~ song2023consistency,song2024improvedconsistency . In robot learning, Consistency Policy, ManiCM, SDM Policy, and OneDP apply related consistency, distribution-matching, or distillation objectives to accelerate action generation~ prasad2024consistencypolicy,gao2026manicm,jia2024sdm,wang2024onedp . These methods reduce the cost of iterative denoising, while many one-step variants obtain their one-step mapping by compressing or distilling a multi-step generative process. -based Visuomotor Policies. Flow Matching models generation as transport under a learned time-dependent velocity field~ lipman2023flowmatching . Standard flow inference numerically integrates this field and therefore requires repeated network evaluations. Rectified Flow reduces integration difficulty by encouraging straighter transport paths, while AdaFlow adaptively determines the number of integration steps~ liu2023rectifiedflow,hu2024adaflow . Consistency Flow Matching instead imposes consistency along flow trajectories to support efficient generation~ yang2024consistencyfm . For robotic manipulation, FlowPolicy applies consistency-based flow generation to point-cloud-conditioned control, and FreqPolicy introduces frequency-domain constraints for action-sequence consistency~ zhang2025flowpolicy,su2025freqpolicy . MeanFlow removes numerical integration at inference by directly predicting interval-averaged velocity~ geng2025meanflow , providing the basis for native one-step policies such as MP1, OMP, and OFP~ sheng2026mp1,fang2026omp,li2026ofp . SOAR builds on this one-step formulation but introduces explicit trajectory-structure conditioning and direct action-space correction to improve the generated trajectory without additional sampling iterations. title: AgentMoT: An Agentic Mixture-of-Transformers for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
summary: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. The relative-capability principle guides these choices by relating the benefit of additional computation or intervention to its cost. After open-loop initialization, dual-loop evolution trains the Router, agent, and self-scheduler from closed-loop experience while failure-driven updates refine skills and execution feedback. AgentMoT achieves state-of-the-art results on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4, with 94.48/92.33 driving score and 85.45/82.73% success rate, respectively. With skills disabled, learned routing improves over the strongest fixed pathway by 1.79 driving-score points and 4.09 percentage points of success rate on v0.0.3. Ablation studies further show gains from closed-loop agent learning, two-view queries, and event-triggered wake-up.

Introduction sec:intro End-to-end driving connects sensor observations to motion through learned perception and planning~ uniad,vad . Vision-language reasoning enriches scene interpretation~ simlingo,automot , while world prediction anticipates traffic evolution~ occwam,interact . Their value in a particular scene depends on which capabilities the model chooses to use and when it revisits that choice. Using these capabilities requires choosing a native pathway, deciding whether to delegate to a skill, and determining when to reconsider (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Each choice depends on context. Repeated confirmation wastes agent calls, while new interactions demand attention. We present , which embeds agent capabilities into a driving Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT, Fig.~ fig:overview ). The model learns to select native computation, delegate tasks, and reconsider decisions in response to execution feedback. (2) We develop dual-loop evolution that connects scheduling learned from closed-loop experience with failure-driven refinement of skills and execution feedback. (3) We achieve state-of-the-art performance on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4. Ablation studies demonstrate the benefits of learned routing, agent learning, and execution feedback. title: OVOGO: Offline Value-Guided On-Policy Generative Optimization for Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Flow-based vision-language-action models can benefit from robot experience collected during deployment, but repeatedly acquiring new physical interactions for policy improvement is costly. Offline reinforcement learning provides a natural way to reuse collected experience, while flow-based policies offer an additional opportunity because fresh generation trajectories can be cheaply resampled from the current policy at replay observations. This motivates separating offline value learning from on-policy optimization of the generative process. We propose OVOGO, an offline reinforcement learning framework that realizes this separation for flow-based VLAs. A central challenge in this formulation is to learn a critic that remains grounded in logged robot experience while providing useful value signals for newly generated actions. OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic that combines in-sample distributional value learning with guarded local ranking, improving discrimination among generated actions without assigning them artificial return targets. The frozen critic then provides group-relative value signals for selected-transition optimization of fresh action candidates sampled from the current flow policy. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, DexJoCo, and LIBERO, as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task, show that OVOGO improves the initial VLA across all four settings and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated offline adaptation and value-guided baselines. These results suggest that offline robot experience can be repeatedly reused for value learning while inexpensive generative sampling supports policy optimization, providing an effective approach to experience-based post-training of flow-based VLAs.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities and generalization by combining large-scale, cross-task robot data with pretrained vision-language representations~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . However, further improving these models still relies heavily on collecting high-quality demonstrations, whose acquisition is expensive and difficult to scale. In contrast, deployment and autonomous execution naturally produce large amounts of experience spanning successful, failed, and suboptimal behaviors, together with task-outcome signals that behavior cloning cannot fully exploit. Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a natural mechanism for learning from such experience, and offline RL is particularly attractive for robotics because it can repeatedly reuse previously collected interactions and their reward feedback without requiring new physical interaction for every policy update~ kostrikov2022iql,physicalintelligence2025recap,wang2026lwd . As VLA training moves beyond imitation pretraining toward experience-based post-training, offline RL is emerging as a promising approach for improving large generative VLAs from accumulated robot experience. Applying offline RL to flow-based VLAs, however, is not straightforward. Because actions are produced through a multi-step flow process, a central question is how value information should be translated into updates of the generative policy. Existing approaches adopt different value-to-policy interfaces. RECAP converts estimated advantages into conditioning variables and extracts an improved policy through supervised training on collected experience~ physicalintelligence2025recap . This design is simple and scalable, but its improvement supervision is attached to replayed actions rather than actions freshly sampled from the current policy. Other approaches, such as LWD and Q-VGM, use the critic's action gradient to construct improvement targets for the flow dynamics~ wang2026lwd,wang2026qvgm . These methods enable more direct value-based policy improvement, but make the update depend on reliable action-gradient information from the critic around policy-generated actions. Flow policies offer a complementary opportunity because physical interactions are expensive and should be reused extensively, whereas generation trajectories are inexpensive computational samples that can be repeatedly resampled from the current policy at the same replay observation. This asymmetry suggests that physical experience and generation trajectories need not be consumed at the same rate during policy improvement. Motivated by this observation, we decouple flow-based VLA reinforcement learning by separating offline value learning from on-policy generative policy optimization. The former learns long-horizon values from a fixed robot dataset, while the latter repeatedly samples fresh actions from the current flow policy at replay observations. The critic serves as the key interface between these two processes. Directly incorporating policy-generated actions into Bellman updates would make temporal targets depend on value estimates for actions without observed environment outcomes. Errors in these estimates, especially overestimation, can then propagate through bootstrapping and be further exploited during policy improvement. Keeping Bellman value propagation in-sample provides a more stable foundation for learning long-horizon returns because temporal targets remain grounded in replayed experience. However, restricting all critic supervision to replayed actions would leave the critic unable to reliably distinguish fresh candidates sampled from the evolving policy. The key challenge is therefore to preserve in-sample temporal value propagation while extending the critic's discriminative ability beyond replayed actions, without compromising the return-grounded value estimates on which offline learning relies. In this paper, we propose OVOGO (Offline Value-Guided On-Policy Generative Optimization), an offline RL framework for flow-based VLAs that combines stable offline value learning with fresh on-policy optimization of the generative process. For offline value learning, OVOGO introduces a Return-Anchored Ranking Critic (RARC) that separates long-horizon return propagation from local action discrimination. RARC uses in-sample distributional value learning to propagate long-horizon values through real replay transitions without bootstrapping through policy-generated actions, and augments this return-grounded objective with local ranking supervision around replayed actions. Synthetic actions receive only relative preference supervision rather than artificial Bellman targets, while a guarded ranking objective combines temperature-dependent gradient decay with a gap cutoff to control ranking pressure, helping preserve the return scale established by real experience. With RARC frozen, OVOGO repeatedly samples groups of fresh action candidates from the current flow policy at replay observations and constructs group-relative improvement signals directly from their scalar critic values, without differentiating through the critic. We further adopt a selected-transition flow update inspired by Flash-GRPO~ he2026flashgrpo , making on-policy generative optimization tractable for large flow-based VLAs. In our experiments, we evaluate OVOGO on RoboTwin~2.0~ chen2025robotwin , DexJoCo~ wang2026dexjoco , and LIBERO~ liu2023libero , as well as a real-robot dexterous manipulation task. The results demonstrate that OVOGO more effectively improves flow-based VLAs from collected robot experience than existing offline adaptation and value-guided methods, while additional comparisons and ablations analyze the contributions of its critic design and generative policy optimization. Related Work Reinforcement Learning for VLA Post-Training Recent studies have explored reinforcement learning (RL) as a post-training paradigm for improving pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs). One line of work directly applies on-policy RL to VLAs by repeatedly collecting trajectories from the current policy and optimizing them with PPO~ schulman2017ppo , GRPO~ shao2024deepseekmath , or related objectives~ tan2025ript,li2025simplevla,chen2025pirl . While effective, such approaches require repeated environment rollouts, which are expensive for robotic systems; consequently, many studies rely primarily on simulated environments for RL training. Another line of work seeks to better reuse previously collected robot experience. RECAP~ physicalintelligence2025recap converts learned value information into advantage conditioning and improves the policy through supervised learning, preserving the scalability of imitation-style training but deriving its policy-improvement signal primarily from actions already contained in the collected experience. More recent approaches such as LWD~ wang2026lwd and Q-VGM~ wang2026qvgm learn explicit critics and use action gradients of the critic to guide flow-policy updates, enabling more direct value-based improvement but placing stronger requirements on the local first-order accuracy of the critic around policy-generated actions. In contrast, our method resamples candidate actions from the current flow-based VLA and uses only scalar critic values to construct relative policy-improvement signals, directly optimizing the current generative policy without differentiating through the critic. Policy Optimization for Diffusion and Flow Policies RL for diffusion and flow policies has been studied primarily in generic continuous-control settings. One class of methods treats the denoising or flow-generation process itself as a sequential policy and directly optimizes the generative trajectory with reinforcement learning~ ren2025dppo,hu2025decisionflow ; another class avoids direct optimization of the full iterative generation process and instead transfers value information through one-step surrogate actors, value-weighted behavior learning, or regularized policy extraction~ park2025fql,tiofack2025guidedflow,liang2026dipole . Most of these approaches are developed for conventional diffusion/flow control policies rather than large-scale VLAs with pretrained vision-language backbones. OGPO~ patil2026ogpo combines an off-policy critic for reusing expensive environment transitions with freshly sampled trajectories from the current generative policy, and our separation between offline value learning and on-policy generative optimization is inspired by this principle. OGPO, however, focuses on online fine-tuning of relatively lightweight generative control policies, where the replay buffer is continually refreshed through environment interaction, whereas we study offline post-training of large pretrained VLAs and explicitly address how an offline-trained critic can reliably evaluate actions generated by the evolving policy. Finally, recent work has shown that single-step policy optimization can substantially reduce the cost of reinforcement learning for large diffusion models~ he2026flashgrpo ; we adopt this idea to make on-policy generative optimization practical for large flow-based VLAs. title: EgoStudy: How Does Scaling Egocentric Data Affect VLA and WAM Pretraining?
summary: Egocentric human manipulation data offer a scalable resource for training dexterous robot policies. However, how effectively robots can learn and benefit from these data remains unclear due to the embodiment gap between humans and robots. We present EgoStudy, a systematic, controlled study of egocentric data for robot learning. Holding the robot dataset fixed, we vary the scale and diversity of egocentric data, data processing strategies, and co-training configurations. We investigate three questions: (1) Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? (2) Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? (3) How do scaling effects differ between vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs)? Our experiments yield three main findings. First, data diversity, alignment between trajectories, and detailed language annotations are key factors in effective transfer. Second, scaling egocentric data yields larger gains in predicting end-effector translation than in predicting fine-grained finger movements. Third, WAMs perform better when egocentric data are limited, whereas VLAs exhibit greater gains as the amount of egocentric data increases. Together, these findings provide practical guidance on processing and using egocentric data to train VLAs and WAMs, while clarifying the benefits and limitations of scaling these data.

Introduction sec:intro Learning general-purpose dexterous manipulation requires experience spanning diverse objects, environments, and interaction patterns. Robot demonstrations provide direct supervision for control, but collecting them at scale requires substantial hardware resources and effort for operation and maintenance. Egocentric human videos offer an attractive source of manipulation experience: people perform a broad range of everyday activities, exposing models to interactions that are expensive to reproduce through robot data collection. Recent efforts have made this experience increasingly accessible through hand-motion annotations~ yu2025dyn,potamias2025wilor,hoque2026egodex , creating opportunities to pretrain Vision--Language--Action Models (VLAs)~ kim2024openvla,physicalintelligence2025pi05,pmlr-v229-zitkovich23a and World--Action Models (WAMs)~ ye2026dreamzero,guo2026videopredictionpolicy2 with growing amounts of human experience. However, limited attention~ li2025vitra,guo2026videopredictionpolicy2,zhu2026harp has been given to the fundamental questions about scaling egocentric data for robot foundation model pretraining: Which data processing and pretraining choices most effectively exploit egocentric data? Which components of robot action prediction benefit most from scaling these data? How do egocentric scaling effects differ between VLAs and WAMs? Answering these questions requires examining more than data volume alone. Existing studies have shown that egocentric human videos can improve robot policy learning, but their conclusions are difficult to compare. Different studies typically use different robot datasets, action representations, model architectures, optimization budgets, and evaluation protocols. Consequently, it remains unclear whether an observed improvement comes from additional human experience, a particular data-processing choice, or a model-specific training recipe. Moreover, most evaluations report an aggregate action loss, leaving open which components of dexterous control actually benefit from egocentric pretraining and whether these offline gains translate to closed-loop control. Studying VLAs and WAMs together is particularly informative because they learn from different pretrained priors and objectives. Representative VLAs adapt vision-language representations for action prediction~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,kareer2025emergence,zhu2026harp,liu2026gala,chen2026villax , while video-based WAMs combine action learning with future visual prediction~ yuan2026fastwam,hu2024video,guo2026videopredictionpolicy2,guo2024pad . These differences suggest that the same egocentric experience may benefit the two model families in different ways. To investigate these questions, we conduct a systematic empirical study named , a unified pretraining and evaluation protocol for VLAs and WAMs. combines egocentric human demonstrations and bimanual robot data through a shared dexterous action interface describing wrist motion and fingertip poses, providing common action targets across embodiments and supporting comparisons between model families. We vary only the scale and construction of the egocentric human data, including episode curation, source diversity, caption detail, and temporal sampling, while holding robot training data and exposure fixed. We assess human-to-robot transfer using a common evaluation protocol with held-out samples, component-wise action metrics, and validation loss on robot data. Finally, standardized robot posttraining and evaluation on target robot domain ensure that pretraining improvements translate into better deployment outcomes. The results reveal that the benefits of egocentric pretraining are selective rather than uniform. Controlled comparisons in show that VLAs show larger gains from scaling egocentric data, and WAMs generally attain lower robot-domain validation loss. Semantically complete episodes, detailed language captions, diverse egocentric data, fixed-step sampling for VLA and event-level sampling for WAM pretraining all contribute to lower robot validation loss and stronger human-to-robot transfer. Scaling egocentric data improves wrist-motion prediction more than finger-motion prediction. Furthermore, we compare how the visual representations of VLAs and WAMs evolve as egocentric data increases and how their gains vary with backbone capacity, providing a basis for explaining why the two model families scale differently. Together, these findings provide practical guidance and empirical insights for training VLAs and WAMs with human videos, while revealing the capability gains and limitations of scaling egocentric data. Our contributions are as follows: Pretraining protocol. We introduce , which includes a unified pretraining and evaluation protocol to support systematic study of egocentric human-to-robot transfer across VLAs and WAMs. Comprehensive study. We conduct comprehensive experiments of data scale, semantic completeness, caption detail, source diversity, temporal sampling, action components and backbone capability, identifying how these choices affect robot foundation model pretraining. Practical guidance. We derive practical recommendations for improving human-to-robot transfer, outline expected limitations, and offer insights into the performance discrepancies between VLA and WAM scaling. Related Work Robot Foundation Models sec:foundation_models Vision--language--action models adapt pretrained vision--language backbones to predict robot actions from observations and language instructions~ zhang2026vlm4vla,guo2025irevla,guo2026vlaw,huang2026breakinglockin . RT-2~ pmlr-v229-zitkovich23a and OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla predict discrete action tokens, while GR00T N1~ gr00tn1_2025 and ~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 use an action expert to generate continuous action sequences. Recent work also explores how to connect perception and control, either by separating high-level visual reasoning from low-level action generation~ cui2025openhelix,zhang2025hirt or by training a shared model for multimodal understanding and future prediction~ zhang2025upvla,hu2026bagelvla . Video-based policies also learn from how a scene changes during manipulation. The VPP family~ hu2024video,guo2026videopredictionpolicy2 and GE-Act~ agibot2025genie use predictive video features to generate actions. DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero , Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam , OpenWAM~ wang2026openwam , and LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva couple video and action prediction during training, with different choices about how the two streams interact and whether to generate future frames at inference. We use StarVLA~ community2026starvla and Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam to compare these two model families in the same dexterous action space. Learning from Egocentric Videos sec:learn_from_ego Egocentric demonstrations provide two forms of supervision for robot manipulation. First, tracked human hand motion supplies action targets for dexterous imitation~ wang2024dexcap,yang2025egovla and for co-training on human and robot demonstrations~ kareer2024egomimic,li2026aceego . VITRA~ li2025vitra and EgoScale~ zheng2026egoscale pair egocentric observations with hand trajectories for policy pretraining and report improved downstream manipulation as the amount of human data increases. Kareer et al.~ kareer2025emergence find that diverse robot pretraining improves transfer from human video, while HumanScale~ ma2026humanscale shows that curated human demonstrations can outperform an equal amount of robot pretraining data. Even with accurate hand tracks, differences in how humans and robots move can limit transfer~ li2026everyday,wu2026atomego,zhang2026egoforesight . Second, video records the effects of an action on the scene, such as an object moving as a hand grasps it. OpenWAM~ wang2026openwam , Open-HumanWAM~ ma2026openhumanwam , and GE-Act 2.0~ agibot2026geact use human manipulation footage to train visual prediction alongside or before action learning. In a comparison of prediction targets, EgoWAM~ li2026egowam reports stronger transfer on bimanual tasks when predicting visual features or 3D motion instead of pixels. Ego4WAM~ sun2026ego4wam studies how human--robot alignment, task diversity, and action supervision affect transfer within a fixed WAM. We compare VLAs and WAMs at fixed robot exposure and measure how scaling human data affects wrist translation, wrist rotation, and fingertip pose. Study Design sec:study_design provides a shared pretraining pipeline and matched evaluation protocols to enable controlled comparisons of egocentric human-to-robot transfer in VLAs and WAMs. The study examines which data choices improve robot action prediction, how the gains differ between wrist and finger motion, and the scaling difference between VLAs and WAMs. Model Architecture sec:study_models The VLA pairs a pretrained Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct vision--language backbone with a GR00T-style action expert~ community2026starvla,gr00tn1_2025 . The backbone encodes the current camera views and instruction. Given these features and the current geometric state, the action expert predicts continuous actions. The WAM pairs a pretrained video backbone Wan2.1-I2V-14B-480P with an action diffusion transformer for joint video--action prediction~ yuan2026fastwam . Action tokens attend to video latents as the model jointly predicts future video and actions from the initial observation, instruction, and state. During pretraining, both models predict 32-step chunks in the same 108-dimensional action space. title: ArgsWorld: Unifying 3DGS Scene Reconstruction, Generation and Extrapolation with Autoregressive Diffusion Transformer
summary: Autoregressive diffusion world models deliver strong video generation performance, yet they typically output only RGB frames rather than explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representations, creating a gap between learned visual world dynamics and usable 3D assets for downstream robotics, simulation and rendering. To bridge this gap, we introduce ArgsWorld, an autoregressive diffusion model that also produces an explicit 3DGS scene. For each generation chunk, the diffusion transformer jointly processes clean historical image latents and noisy latents for new views. It keeps the historical image latents fixed and refreshes the scene features so that the Gaussian representation can be revised as new regions come into view. Our 3D Self-Forcing Distillation trains the model on its own generated histories using a mixture of single-view and multi-view data. Distribution matching supervises direct image latents and latents of Gaussian renderings at both generation and additional cameras. ArgsWorld unifies 3D scene reconstruction from posed images, scene generation from image or text prompts, and scene extrapolation across camera segments with disconnected endpoints. Experimental results demonstrate that ArgsWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D scene modeling tasks. Project page: https://m4a1tastegood.github.io/ArgsWorld/

Our 3D Self-Forcing Distillation trains the model on its own generated histories using a mixture of single-view and multi-view data. Project page: Introduction sec:intro Video diffusion models provide strong priors for visual synthesis~ wan2025wan . Autoregressive generation extends these models beyond a single sampling window~ huang2026self,rui2026biwm , and camera conditioning lets users specify where to look next~ rui2026biwm . These models describe a scene through the RGB frames they generate along a trajectory. An explicit scene representation would also allow users to render the same world from additional cameras and reuse it as a 3D asset. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) represents a scene with explicit primitives and supports differentiable rendering~ kerbl2023gaussians . Feed-forward methods such as pixelSplat~ charatan2024pixelsplat , MVSplat~ chen2024mvsplat , and AnySplat~ jiang2025anysplat recover Gaussian scenes from observed images. FlashWorld~ flashworld2025 extends this capability to scene generation by coupling a video diffusion backbone with a Gaussian decoder, and PixWorld~ gao2026pixworld unifies reconstruction and generation in pixel space. Building on these approaches, we ask how a generative model can revise and extend an explicit Gaussian scene as new camera queries arrive. Three challenges arise when generating a Gaussian scene over successive chunks of camera views. Plausible image predictions provide only an indirect constraint on the geometry needed to render them. As the trajectory reveals new regions, newly predicted geometry must agree with the already generated appearance in overlapping views. Finally, a model trained with ground-truth histories encounters a different distribution of contexts when it must condition on its own predictions at inference time~ huang2026self . We introduce ArgsWorld, an Autoregressive 3DGS World Model for reconstruction, generation, and spatial extrapolation. In , ArgsWorld reconstructs a 3D Gaussian scene from three posed images, generates views along the initial trajectory, and extends the scene along vertical and aerial camera paths. We build on the camera-conditioned, 3D-adapted Wan backbone of FlashWorld~ wan2025wan,flashworld2025 . At each chunk, its diffusion transformer attends jointly to clean historical image latents and noisy new-view latents. The historical image latents anchor the appearance, and the model refreshes scene features across the active views to decode an updated set of Gaussians ( ). This lets ArgsWorld continue the same scene on a new camera orbit without generating bridging views. Our 3D Self-Forcing Distillation trains the model in the same autoregressive setting used for inference ( ). Completing all four denoising steps supplies the clean history for the next chunk. During training, we replay a randomly selected denoising step with gradients and apply distribution-matching distillation~ yin2024dmd,yin2024dmd2 to the direct image predictions and to renderings of the updated Gaussian scene at both generation and additional cameras. The training mixture includes single-view images and posed multi-view sequences. Our contributions are threefold: A unified 3DGS world model. ArgsWorld uses one camera-conditioned autoregressive diffusion 3DGS model to reconstruct scenes from posed images, generate scenes from image or text prompts, and extrapolate scenes along an extended trajectory. Consistent autoregressive scene expansion. ArgsWorld grows a Gaussian world one chunk at a time, using completed generations as fixed visual context. Joint scene decoding and rendering consistency supervision encourage consistent renderings at historical viewpoints while allowing the scene representation to evolve as new regions are generated. 3D Self-Forcing Distillation. Training on self-generated histories and matching distributions in both the image and rendering branches yields a four-step autoregressive sampler with explicit 3DGS output. Related Work sec:RelatedWork Video generation and autoregressive world models. Video foundation models such as Wan~ wan2025wan supply visual priors for controllable world generation. Existing approaches condition generation on actions~ bruce2024genie or camera trajectories~ he2025cameractrl,wang2024motionctrl,wang2026taming . Training autoregressive video diffusion on ground-truth histories can lead to error accumulation on generated histories at inference. Self Forcing~ huang2026self addresses this mismatch by training on self-generated rollouts with sequence-level supervision. BiWM~ rui2026biwm retains bidirectional attention and combines camera-control adaptation with few-step distillation. CausVid and LongLive accelerate causal rollouts~ yin2025causvid,yang2026longlive , while WorldMem retrieves past views for consistency~ xiao2025worldmem . SolarWM~ huang2026solarwm scales long-horizon video training, and InSpatio-World~ inspatio2026world uses state-anchored autoregression for interactive 4D simulation. ArgsWorld uses self-generated histories to condition a bidirectional generator that jointly predicts images and updates an explicit Gaussian scene. Gaussian scene reconstruction and generation. NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf and 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl2023gaussians enable differentiable rendering, with 3DGS providing explicit primitives. Feed-forward models estimate multiview geometry~ wang2024dust3r,wang2025vggt or synthesize novel views~ wang2021ibrnet,jin2025lvsm . pixelSplat, MVSplat, and DepthSplat reconstruct Gaussians from posed images~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,xu2025depthsplat . AnySplat~ jiang2025anysplat handles uncalibrated image collections by predicting Gaussian primitives and camera parameters jointly. Diffusion priors support novel-view synthesis~ liu2023zero123,gao2024cat3d,yu2025viewcrafter and text-driven 3D generation~ poole2023dreamfusion,hollein2023text2room . FlashWorld~ flashworld2025 integrates Gaussian decoding into video diffusion for image- or text-conditioned generation. For extrapolation, WonderWorld~ yu2025wonderworld constructs Gaussian surfels from outpainted views, and LucidDreamer~ chung2025luciddreamer uses diffusion-guided completion and alignment. WonderTurbo~ ni2025wonderturbo combines image inpainting and depth completion with incremental fusion of newly predicted 3D Gaussians. ArgsWorld revises the scene jointly across historical and new views within a single autoregressive generator. Distribution-matching distillation. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD)~ yin2024dmd trains a fast generator using the difference between the scores of a pretrained teacher and an online model of the generated distribution. DMD2~ yin2024dmd2 improves score estimation through a two-time-scale update rule and adds adversarial supervision. FlashWorld~ flashworld2025 uses distribution matching to transfer its multi-view image prior to Gaussian renderings. BiWM~ rui2026biwm distills bidirectional video generation from self-generated histories. ArgsWorld applies distribution matching to the direct image sequence and to renderings of the updated scene at two sets of cameras. This supplies training signals for both image synthesis and geometry through the same rollout. title: JEPA-ICL: Progress-Aligned Latent Plans for In-Context Robotic Manipulation
summary: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.
full_text: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot’s current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot’s own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0 seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1 to 97.6 on LIBERO and from 62.9 to 73.2 on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2 to 75.2 . Introduction sec:intro Demonstrations provide more than examples of successful actions: they reveal how a task progresses toward completion. To use this experience, a robot must relate the demonstrated process to what remains to be accomplished in its own execution, even when embodiment, appearance, and execution speed differ. This calls for a representation that supports both anticipating task progress and identifying relevant guidance. Joint embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) offer a natural basis for learning such representations through future feature prediction without requiring image reconstruction. Recent work has advanced both predictive control and demonstration learning. JEPA-WAM~ jepawam uses latent transition supervision for action generation, while HOST~ host connects demonstration localization with future observation prediction. JEDI~ jedi learns predictive representations for demonstration compression, and MUTEX~ mutex demonstrates the benefits of learning from complementary task specifications. These advances motivate a more specific question: how can the plan that guides a robot's own actions also organize its use of demonstration experience? Future prediction alone does not establish correspondence across executions, while access to relevant context does not by itself ensure better planning. We study it through the state changes that remain before subtask completion. We introduce , a vision-language-action framework that connects predictive planning and demonstration learning through progress-aligned latent plans. Our central idea is to describe an execution stage by the ordered state changes that remain before the current subtask is complete ( ). We learn this representation through a plan-conditioned Markov predictor, a latent world model that forecasts future states in JEPA feature space. The resulting plans support action generation and provide progress keys for locating relevant stages in demonstrations. Prediction and demonstration alignment jointly supervise these plans, connecting the ability to anticipate an execution with the ability to learn from another. Specifically, plan queries from the VLA backbone condition this world model, which starts from the current JEPA state and predicts four ordered checkpoints in the remaining subtask, one shared Markov transition at a time; supervising the intermediate checkpoints as well as completion makes the plan retain the remaining process, not only the endpoint. For demonstration use, the same backbone produces plans for robot observations and demonstration frames, and a learned indexer associates their stages under stage and temporal-consistency supervision. The policy then reads JEPA-supervised content features from a short window around the aligned stage through memory tokens, and the retrieved context is updated during execution so that guidance stays tied to the robot's observed progress. We evaluate these capabilities separately and in combination. On LIBERO~ libero and LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus , JEPA-ICL achieves 97.6 and 73.2 success without contextual demonstrations, respectively; demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at test time further raise LIBERO-Plus success to 75.2 . On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0 seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM~ zerowam (68.0 ) by 12.0 percentage points. Under C45 pretraining, it reaches 85.5 unseen-task success after fine-tuning on 10 robot demonstrations per task. Real-robot gear assembly further demonstrates the use of recorded experience: JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0 success with a deployment-setup demonstration, compared with 40.0 for the kai0 (\( _ 0.5 \)) baseline. Controlled comparisons separate the contributions of latent planning, of progress-aligned retrieval, and of context at test time. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Markov-supervised latent planning. We learn progress-aware plans through recurrent prediction of ordered future JEPA states within the remaining subtask, supervised at intermediate checkpoints and at subtask completion. Progress-aligned demonstration context. We use latent plans to locate relevant demonstration stages and read separate JEPA-supervised content features through memory tokens, which separates progress correspondence from content retrieval and updates guidance as execution progresses. Joint planning and demonstration learning. We combine future prediction, demonstration alignment, and action supervision to train one shared policy that runs both with and without contextual demonstrations. Related work sec:related Predictive planning in VLAs. VLA models map observations and an instruction to action chunks with a pretrained vision-language backbone~ rt2,openvla,octo,pi0,pi05,groot . To give them foresight, recent work adds a model of the future: generated frames~ vpp,worldvla,genieenvisioner,dreamvla,dreamzero , latent actions~ lapa,univla , or predicted features~ flare,vlajepa,jepawam,juno . VLA-JEPA~ vlajepa and JEPA-WAM~ jepawam are closest to ours, since both supervise a latent plan with frozen V-JEPA features~ vjepa,vjepa2 . Their plan predicts a fixed number of steps ahead, so it says what comes next but not how much of the task remains; progress is instead estimated by a separate model~ gvl or given to the policy as sub-goals~ stellavla,tpfm,seetraceact . JEPA-ICL instead predicts ordered future states up to subtask completion. Its latent plan provides a shared interface for action generation and demonstration matching, connecting prediction of the remaining subtask with reuse of demonstrated experience. Demonstrations as context. In-context imitation conditions the policy on a demonstration at test time~ icrt,hist,instantpolicy,synthicl,matchingpolicy,perceiver,vid2robot,contextflow,vivla,ricl,recap,iclrvr,mapvla,zerowam,simpleicl,mimicdroid . The difficulty is to decide which part of the demonstration matters now. Policies that read it by time index tend to copy or ignore it~ icivla,ravla,stellavla,instantpolicy , because a long demonstration and a short action chunk rarely advance in step; policies that align by similarity need a hand-crafted metric, such as DTW over actions~ icivla,ravla or DINO features~ ricl,recap,xicm ; HOST~ host and Demo-JEPA~ demojepa learn a dedicated correspondence between demonstration and robot. In these methods the representation used for matching is built apart from the one the policy acts with. aligns by progress with the plan it already computes for control, so it needs no hand-crafted metric and no separate correspondence model, only a small projection of the plan, and the stage it reads is the one that fits what remains to be done. From context back to the plan. When the matching representation is fixed, learning to use demonstrations does not change how the policy plans. MUTEX~ mutex shows that training one policy on several task modalities improves each of them alone, and memory of the policy's own history~ robottt,reflectivevla improves it within an episode. extends this across executions: the action loss under aligned context also updates the backbone that produces the plan. Method sec:method is a latent-world-model VLA~ vlajepa whose plan predicts the states that remain until the current subtask is complete. Such a plan describes an execution stage by what is left to do, so it serves two purposes at once: it conditions the robot's actions, and it locates the same stage in a demonstration, whose content is then read back into action generation. shows the three parts. We first describe the shared policy and its query tokens ( ), then how the plan is supervised ( ), how it retrieves demonstration context ( ), and how the whole is trained and run ( ). Overview sec:overview At time the policy observes camera images , an instruction and the proprioceptive state , and outputs a chunk of actions . As in VLA-JEPA~ vlajepa , a vision-language model (Qwen3-VL~ qwen3vl ) encodes and , and learnable query tokens appended to this sequence carry the outputs of the model ( a). The plan queries yield the latent plan ; the future queries yield the content features ; the action queries yield the features that, together with , condition a flow-matching action head~ flowmatching,dit . When a demonstration is available, memory tokens computed from it join the same sequence. World states are described by a frozen V-JEPA~2.1 encoder~ vjepa21 , and we write for the patch features of an image . The attention mask fixes who may read whom. The plan queries read only the observation and the instruction, so depends on nothing but the current input. The future and action queries read and , and the action queries do not read the future queries. Every action is thus generated with access to the plan and, when present, to the demonstration context, while the plan is never altered by the context it retrieves. The queries only add tokens to the VLM and read its outputs, so they are not tied to one backbone; instantiates them on a second one, ~ pi05 . Markov supervision for latent plans sec:latent_plans Checkpoints in the remaining subtask. A target placed a fixed number of steps ahead is tied to time rather than to the task: at the same offset, a slow execution may still be approaching an object that a fast one has already grasped. We therefore define the targets of the plan by the progress that remains in the current subtask. Training episodes are segmented into subtasks, and denotes the end of the subtask that contains . We place checkpoints at , , and of the remaining interval, so the last target is always the completion of the subtask and the others are the ordered states that lead to it. Markov prediction. A latent world model predicts the checkpoints one after another. It starts from the current state and, at every step, sees only the preceding state and the plan, One transition model serves all four steps, and the gradient is stopped between steps so that each transition is trained as a one-step prediction. The plan and the world model are trained to match the checkpoints in feature space, where weights the patches that move within transition above the static ones (see the appendix). What the plan carries. Because sees only the current state and , whatever the current frame does not reveal about the rest of the subtask must be carried by the plan, and supervising every checkpoint rather than the endpoint alone asks it to carry the order of the remaining changes, which is what the action head needs to decide the next chunk. title: DelayOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation from a Synchronous Teacher for Real-time Asynchronous Policies
summary: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur substantial inference latency due to their large vision-language backbones and iterative denoising. Asynchronous execution reduces this latency by generating the next action chunk while executing the current one, but the new chunk is conditioned on a stale observation, degrading performance as the delay increases. We investigate this mismatch by comparing actions predicted from observations at planning and execution times. We find that these predictions differ little on expert demonstrations but diverge substantially on the policy's own delayed rollouts, particularly in failed episodes. Motivated by this observation, we propose DelayOPSD, which trains an asynchronous policy to imitate its synchronous counterpart on the policy's own rollouts. Specifically, a synchronous teacher, obtained from the same policy using the observation at execution time, supervises a delayed student that observes only the earlier frame and the actions still being executed. The student learns to match the teacher throughout its own denoising process. Under a 10-step delay, training SmolVLA on demonstrations achieves only 70.2% success, comparable to naive asynchronous execution (70.4%), whereas training on its own rollouts improves success to 78.7%. Across LIBERO and Kinetix, DelayOPSD achieves the highest average success among the compared methods, without introducing additional modules at deployment. On a real robot, it further improves success from 46% to 62%.
