Generating each action chunk requires a forward pass of a large vision-language backbone and multiple denoising steps, taking tens to hundreds of milliseconds on a desktop GPU and even longer on edge or networked hardware~ agouzoul2026async,eaglevla . Under synchronous execution the robot stops while each chunk is generated, increasing task completion time and preventing the robot from reacting during generation~ rtc,vlash . Asynchronous execution~ rtc removes these pauses by generating the next chunk while the current chunk is being executed, making it essential for VLA deployment~ rtc,smolvla . However, asynchronous execution introduces a mismatch between the observation used for action generation and the state at which the generated actions are executed. While a new chunk is generated, the robot continues executing the committed actions of the current chunk for control steps (the delay). Consequently, the new chunk generated from observation is executed from step , when the environment has already evolved to , which was unseen by the policy during generation ( a). Since flow-based policies trained with behavior cloning do not account for this mismatch, executing them asynchronously leads to a drop in task success rate, which becomes more pronounced as the delay increases ( ). Existing remedies keep the new chunk consistent with the committed actions at inference time~ rtc,bid , predict the missing observation with an added module~ futurertc , or fine-tune the policy on demonstrations~ trainingtimertc,legato,softrtc,remac,deflect,rfd . While these approaches mitigate the effects of execution delay, our goal is to directly improve the delayed policy under its own execution dynamics. In particular, the observation-action mismatch can lead the delayed policy to visit states different from those in demonstrations, where the policy may require different actions to recover. In our measurements, the delay barely changes the policy's actions on demonstration states but changes them substantially on its own delayed rollouts, especially in failed episodes ( ). This motivates on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), which trains the student on its own rollouts rather than relying solely on demonstration states. Here, we introduce DelayOPSD, an on-policy self-distillation framework for asynchronous VLA execution. Our key insight is to construct an asymmetric teacher-student pair from the same policy through different conditioning. Specifically, the synchronous teacher obtains the execution-time observation , while the asynchronous student conditions on and the committed actions. By querying the teacher along the student's delayed rollouts, we obtain improved supervision even at states where the student fails, without an external teacher model or ground-truth action annotations. We then distill the teacher into the student by matching their velocity fields along the student's own denoising trajectory, providing dense supervision beyond matching the final actions. In practice, repeatedly collecting student rollouts online during training is expensive, since it requires interaction with the environment. We therefore collect delayed rollouts once before training and perform distillation offline, as in offline on-policy distillation~ lightningopd,semiopd . In our experiments, the evaluated online collection variants give no significant gain over this one-time collection. DelayOPSD requires no external expert or additional inference-time module, preserving the original policy architecture and sampler at deployment. Our contributions can be summarized as: Asynchronous execution as on-policy self-distillation from the synchronous policy. We train the policy on its own delayed rollouts, and its teacher is the same policy run synchronously on the execution-time observation. SmolVLA then reaches 78.7 at , against 70.2 when trained on demonstrations. Distillation on the student's own states in physical and denoising time. On the student's rollouts, using the student's own samples in denoising time instead of re-noised teacher samples adds 3.4 points of success on average over delays ( ). Highest average success with no module added at deployment. DelayOPSD has the highest average success of all compared methods on LIBERO (SmolVLA, ) and Kinetix, without an inference-time module or simulator lookahead at deployment, and raises real-robot success from 46 to 62 . It needs no rollouts interleaved with training, which makes training on a real robot practical. Related Work sec:related Asynchronous and real-time chunk execution. VLAs~ pi0,pi05,smolvla denoise chunks of actions~ act , and streaming decoding~ flashvla lowers per-step decoding latency. Asynchronous methods are compared in a controlled study~ agouzoul2026async . Inference-time methods leave the policy unchanged: guided inpainting of the committed actions (real-time chunking, RTC~ rtc ), initial-noise inversion toward them (PAINT~ paint ), or selection among sampled chunks by coherence with the previous chunk and contrast with an early checkpoint (BID~ bid ). Training-time RTC~ trainingtimertc fine-tunes the policy to continue a ground-truth prefix. Legato~ legato and Soft RTC~ softrtc replace the hard prefix with soft weights and blend the previous chunk into every denoising step, and REMAC~ remac adds a delay-conditioned LoRA adapter. VLASH~ vlash fine-tunes on time-shifted samples to take as input the robot state at execution time, rolled forward through the committed actions. FutureRTC~ futurertc keeps the policy frozen and adds modules that predict the execution-time latent of its vision encoder and correct the rolled-forward robot state, and EagleVLA~ eaglevla predicts the compressed future VLM (vision-language model) output. A2C2~ a2c2 reads the latest observation at every step (not compared), and DREAM-Chunk~ dreamchunk selects among sampled chunks at each step by matching the observed state to a latent world model's predictions. teachers and interactive imitation. DAgger~ dagger and its delayed-RL variant DIDA~ dida query an expert on the states the learner visits. Students without privileged information are also supervised on their own states, with the waypoints of a privileged agent~ lbc or a latent of privileged environment factors~ rma . Such a student learns a version of the teacher's policy with the privileged information marginalized out~ advisor . Off-policy imitation with unobserved context can latch onto past actions~ swamy2022 . -policy and self-distillation. On-policy distillation evaluates a teacher on student-generated sequences and minimizes a divergence between their next-token distributions, such as forward KL, reverse KL or the Jensen--Shannon divergence~ gkd . On-policy self-distillation uses one model as student and teacher, with only the teacher given privileged information~ sdr,pidistill,dopsd . For diffusion and flow models, DiffusionOPD~ diffusionopd matches the student's and teacher's one-step transition means along the student's own denoising path, and Flow-OPD~ flowopd reduces a reverse KL on the student's own samples to a time-weighted squared error between student and teacher velocities. Contemporaneous work applies on-policy distillation to VLAs, to consolidate domain specialists into one policy~ mtopdvla or to compress a large VLA into a few-step student~ fastopd . Both distill from separate teacher policies. Here the teacher is the same policy given the execution-time observation, and the student is its delayed version. -conditioned teachers. DEFLECT~ deflect queries a frozen reference policy with the current and the future observation at demonstration timesteps, and trains the delayed policy with a flow-matching direct preference optimization (DPO) loss on the two chunks, anchored by flow matching on demonstrations. Contemporaneous with and independent of our work, RFD~ rfd regresses the delayed policy's velocities onto those of a frozen policy given the later observation, on noised samples of that policy's chunks at demonstrated transitions, and pairs it with a resolver that selects among proposed chunks once the later observation arrives. Both train on demonstration states, where the delay barely changes the policy's actions ( ). In contrast, DelayOPSD trains on the delayed policy's own rollouts, where the delay changes these actions most, and on its own samples in denoising time ( ). title: NavDecision: Parallel Multi-Step Action Prediction with Persistent Self-Referential Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation
summary: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires timely decisions based on instructions and visual observations. However, autoregressive VLN models generate action descriptions token by token, introducing substantial inference overhead. Decision models offer an efficient alternative but face challenges in maintaining short-horizon action coherence and long-horizon goal alignment. To address these challenges, we propose NavDecision, an efficient multi-step VLN decision model. We introduce parallel multi-step action prediction (PMAP) to predict multiple action distributions from a shared vision-language state, and memory-augmented self-referential policy optimization (M-SRPO) to learn from unsuccessful trajectories using successful trajectories as references. A cross-iteration success memory further accumulates historical successful trajectories to provide informative training feedback. NavDecision achieves success rates of 64.60% on R2R-CE and 64.57% on RxR-CE with a 4B backbone. Compared with existing autoregressive VLN methods, it delivers significant inference speedups of up to $22.28\times$ and $18.96\times$ while maintaining comparable navigation performance.
full_text: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires timely decisions based on instructions and visual observations. However, autoregressive VLN models generate action descriptions token by token, introducing substantial inference overhead. Decision models offer an efficient alternative but face challenges in maintaining short-horizon action coherence and long-horizon goal alignment. To address these challenges, we propose NavDecision, an efficient multi-step VLN decision model. We introduce parallel multi-step action prediction (PMAP) to predict multiple action distributions from a shared vision-language state, and memory-augmented self-referential policy optimization (M-SRPO) to learn from unsuccessful trajectories using successful trajectories as references. A cross-iteration success memory further accumulates historical successful trajectories to provide informative training feedback. NavDecision achieves success rates of 64.60 on R2R-CE and 64.57 on RxR-CE with a 4B backbone. Compared with existing autoregressive VLN methods, it delivers significant inference speedups of up to and while maintaining comparable navigation performance. Introduction sec:intro ; cite with . ; cite with . ; cite with . ; cite with . ; cite with . ; cite with . Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to reach goals using natural language instructions and visual observations~ anderson2018vln,krantz2020vlnce . Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) use pretrained cross-modal representations to ground instructions in visual scenes, improving navigation in unseen environments and sim-to-real transfer~ zhang2024navid,cheng2025navila . However, as shown in (a), autoregressive VLN models decode action descriptions such as ``move forward 75~cm'' token by token before converting them into executable actions~ cheng2025navila . Action latency thus depends on output length, while navigation requires timely responses to observations~ sheng2026navjev . In contrast, decision models directly predict distributions over candidate options~ almeida2026jev,li2026llmasjev , enabling low-latency execution in time-sensitive interactive tasks~ zhang2026jevmobile . We explore direct action prediction for VLN to reduce generation overhead while preserving vision-language understanding. However, directly applying decision models to VLN requires addressing both the temporal coherence of consecutive actions and long-horizon goal alignment. Although decision models reduce the overhead of autoregressive generation, designing an effective decision model for VLN remains challenging. First, single-step primitive-action selection avoids token-by-token decoding but requires one model call per action and does not explicitly model temporal dependencies across actions, making it difficult to maintain action coherence. Autoregressive multi-step policies generate several actions sequentially in one decoding run, conditioning on preceding outputs to capture temporal dependencies~ zhang2026activevln,hong2026simplevln . Alternatively, decision models can treat predefined fixed action chunks as candidate options, but this restricts action combinations to a fixed library, whose expansion increases the candidate space and decision complexity. Waypoint-based decision methods, in turn, depend on the quality and coverage of externally predicted candidates~ sheng2026navjev . We therefore seek to predict multi-step action distributions from a shared vision-language state, capturing short-horizon temporal dependencies for coherent execution at low inference cost. Second, agents must track task progress under changing observations to keep local actions aligned with long-horizon goals. Autoregressive policies can scale test-time computation through explicit reasoning or search to improve navigation success~ lin2025navcot,fried2018speaker . To retain low inference overhead, long-horizon exploration experience needs to be internalized in the local policy during training. Online reinforcement learning optimizes policies using task-level rewards from complete navigation trajectories, including terminal binary success rewards~ zhang2026activevln,hong2026simplevln . However, decision models lack explicit test-time computation scaling, making it difficult to consistently discover successful trajectories during long-horizon exploration. Consequently, successful trajectories may be scarce, and terminal binary success rewards provide identical feedback for unsuccessful trajectories despite differences in their progress toward the goal. This limitation highlights the need for more informative trajectory-level feedback to learn from unsuccessful trajectories and improve local action policies. We propose NavDecision, an efficient multi-step VLN decision model trained with cross-iteration self-referential reinforcement learning. As shown in (b), we predict multiple action distributions in parallel from a shared vision-language state. Temporally causal interactions among prediction features and joint multi-step supervision capture short-horizon temporal dependencies. Inspired by self-referential policy optimization (SRPO)~ fei2026srpo , we encode complete navigation trajectories with a frozen world model. Using environment-verified successful trajectories as references, we combine bounded similarity-based rewards for unsuccessful trajectories with terminal binary success rewards for online reinforcement learning. A cross-iteration success memory combines current-batch and historical successful trajectories, providing references when the current batch contains no successful trajectories and incorporating new successful trajectories as training proceeds. This internalizes long-horizon exploration experience during training while retaining fast action prediction at deployment. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We extend single-step option selection to parallel multi-step action prediction. Using a shared vision-language state representation, we learn short-horizon temporal dependencies through temporally causal interactions among prediction features and joint multi-step supervision. A single forward pass outputs action distributions for multiple steps, supporting coherent navigation actions and efficient decision-making. We design a reinforcement learning reward for decision models that uses current-batch and historical successful trajectories to provide more informative training feedback for unsuccessful trajectories. This internalizes long-horizon exploration experience in the decision policy. The world model and cross-iteration success memory are used only during training and do not participate in action inference at deployment. NavDecision achieves 64.60 and 64.57 SR on R2R-CE and RxR-CE with a 4B backbone. It features adjustable inference efficiency, enabling up to and speedups over autoregressive VLN baselines while maintaining competitive navigation performance. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-and-language navigation has progressed from R2R and RxR benchmarks to low-level action execution in continuous environments~ anderson2018vln,ku2020rxr,krantz2020vlnce . Prior work improves generalization through instruction synthesis, environment perturbations, and large-scale data augmentation~ fried2018speaker,tan2019envdrop,wang2023scalevln . Cross-modal pretraining and history encoding strengthen state representations~ hao2020prevalent,hong2021vlnbert,chen2021hamt ; topological planning supports global path reasoning~ chen2022duet , and waypoint prediction connects planning with local continuous control~ hong2022bridging,an2025etpnav . Navigation methods based on large models explore explicit reasoning and map-based planning~ zhou2024navgpt,chen2024mapgpt,zhou2025navgpt2,lin2025navcot , as well as video-to-action modeling and hierarchical control~ zhang2024navid,zhang2025uninavid,cheng2025navila,wei2026dualvln . Recent methods use action chunking to predict actions across multiple time steps~ zhu2026navida,hong2026simplevln , while dataset aggregation~ ross2011dagger , reinforcement fine-tuning with expert-action supervision~ qi2025vlnr1 , and multi-turn online reinforcement learning~ zhang2026activevln,hong2026simplevln improve policies. Sequential autoregressive decoding introduces additional action latency. Although NavJev directly selects candidate waypoints to avoid autoregressive action generation, it relies on an external waypoint predictor~ sheng2026navjev . In contrast, we introduce parallel multi-step action prediction over discrete primitive actions, eliminating sequential decoding and reducing model calls. Decision models predict probability distributions over candidate options, enabling structured decisions without autoregressive generation of action descriptions~ almeida2026jev . Recent studies explore candidate probability readout, decision-distribution distillation, and batched decisions to leverage the decision-making capabilities of pretrained models~ li2026llmasjev,geuter2026innerjev,duan2026generaldecision,yu2026visualjev . Such models have also been applied to GUI automation and navigation, where agents select or verify candidate actions or waypoints, or represent predefined mid-level actions as single tokens~ zhang2026jevmobile,sheng2026navjev,liu2026memvln,wang2026vernav . However, applying decision models to VLN requires more than single-step option selection: agents need to predict consecutive actions while maintaining short-horizon temporal dependencies. Existing robotic policies explore autoregressive action tokens and compressed action representations~ kim2025openvla,pertsch2025fast , as well as action chunking and parallel action prediction~ zhao2023act,kim2025openvlaoft . Diffusion and flow models further generate continuous action chunks, but their original implementations require iterative sampling~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2025pi0 . In contrast, we predict multiple primitive-action distributions in parallel from a shared vision-language state representation, using temporally causal interactions among prediction features to capture short-horizon dependencies. Our Approach sec:method ; cite with . ; cite with . ; cite with . ; cite with . ; cite with . ; cite with . As shown in , we propose a multi-step decision model for vision-and-language navigation and a cross-iteration self-referential policy optimization framework. From a shared vision-language state representation, the model predicts action distributions in parallel through temporally causal interactions among prediction features. During reinforcement learning, current and historical successful trajectories jointly define a trajectory-level reward for training the model, allowing long-horizon navigation experience to improve the local action policy. The two components support consecutive action execution over short horizons and alignment with long-horizon goals, respectively. defines the navigation task and the decision model. presents parallel multi-step action prediction and its supervised training, and introduces cross-iteration self-referential policy optimization. title: Body and Soul: Decoupling Robotic Brain and Policy with RoboHarness-Zero
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can execute individual skills but fail to complete tasks that require combining several of them. In our audit of Xiaomi-Robotics-1, an estimated 43\% of failures involve choosing the wrong target or losing track of task progress. Wrapping a frozen VLA in a vision-language model (VLM) harness is a natural remedy. Existing harnesses can gain substantially from task- and policy-specific preparation, raising the question of how much of that gain transfers to a new task or policy. An ideal harness should (i) need minimal preparation for a new task, (ii) need no redesign for a new policy, and (iii) preserve standalone capabilities the policy already has. To the best of our knowledge, our \ours{} is the first harness built this way. Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, \ours{} with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from \textbf{\color{blue}57.5\%} to \textbf{\color{blue}70.5\%} and preserves \textbf{\color{blue}90.4\%} of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy.

Its premise is that choosing targets and tracking progress are easy for a VLM such as GPT-6 without task preparation, while the frozen VLA already handles continuous, contact-rich motion. The frozen VLA therefore executes continuous control while the VLM plans zero-shot and monitors execution; when progress stalls or targets drift, the VLM first rephrases the instruction and, only as a fallback, executes short generated code over generic motion primitives before returning fine control to the VLA. The supervision rules stay fixed across policies, requiring only a thin interface adapter and an automatically profiled skill configuration per policy. On 200 RoboCasa365 scenes, with GPT-6 Astra raises the success rate of frozen Xiaomi-Robotics-1 from 57.5 to 70.5 and preserves 90.4 of its standalone successes (104/115) while rescuing 37 of 85 failures. On a shared 50-scene subset, the same rules add 8 to 10 percentage points to each of four other frozen policies, while existing preparation-based harness systems often fail to transfer to a new policy. title: HighwayVerse: A Chain-of-Inspection Benchmark for Highway Infrastructure Anomaly Understanding
summary: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. Meanwhile, current datasets focus primarily on highway pavement defects, falling short of real-world inspection across diverse infrastructure components such as highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, and introduce HighwayVerse. HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world Ground and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) inspection records spanning 100 and 17 anomaly categories, respectively, with 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs. We evaluate 12 open-source and closed-source MLLMs using the chained metric Final, which credits a correct maintenance decision only when all preceding diagnostic stages are completed correctly. Results show that although models achieve relatively high accuracy when initially judging whether an anomaly is present, their markedly lower Final scores expose struggles across downstream recognition, analysis, and decision-making. This discrepancy indicates that current MLLMs do not fully comprehend specific highway anomaly patterns beyond superficial initial judgments. Furthermore, we propose LaneRAG, a training-free retrieval-augmented framework that provides hierarchical reference guidance achieving consistent performance improvements across diverse MLLMs. Our dataset, evaluation benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
full_text: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. Meanwhile, current datasets focus primarily on highway pavement defects, falling short of real-world inspection across diverse infrastructure components such as highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, and introduce HighwayVerse. HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world Ground and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) inspection records spanning 100 and 17 anomaly categories, respectively, with 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs. We evaluate 12 open-source and closed-source MLLMs using the chained metric Final, which credits a correct maintenance decision only when all preceding diagnostic stages are completed correctly. Results show that although models achieve relatively high accuracy when initially judging whether an anomaly is present, their markedly lower Final scores expose struggles across downstream recognition, analysis, and decision-making. This discrepancy indicates that current MLLMs do not fully comprehend specific highway anomaly patterns beyond superficial initial judgments. Furthermore, we propose , a training-free retrieval-augmented framework that provides hierarchical reference guidance achieving consistent performance improvements across diverse MLLMs. Our dataset, evaluation benchmark, and source code will be publicly released. Introduction sec:intro Highway infrastructure, including highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems, is continuously exposed to heavy traffic loads and harsh environmental conditions. Timely and accurate anomaly inspection is essential for maintaining structural integrity, ensuring transportation safety, and reducing maintenance costs~ Spencer_2019_InfrastructureInspection,Zhu_2022_UAVPavement . Conventional automated inspection primarily relies on task-specific detectors and segmenters~ Maeda_2018_RoadDamage,Zhou_2024_CrackSeg , which focus on localized visual perception. In practice, highway infrastructure inspection involves a progressive diagnostic process in which inspectors verify anomalies, recognize and localize them, characterize their conditions, evaluate associated risks, and determine appropriate maintenance actions~ Spencer_2019_InfrastructureInspection . We formalize this progression of interdependent diagnostic judgments as the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), a structured framework linking visual anomaly understanding to maintenance-oriented decisions. Toward this goal, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer strong potential by integrating visual perception with domain-contextualized reasoning across all stages~ Bai_2025_Qwen3VL,Wang_2025_InternVL35 . However, existing benchmarks still fall short of this complete progression, where RoadBench covers road damage classification and defect description~ Xiao_2026_RoadBench , while DriveLM, RoadSocial, and RoadSceneBench focus on object perception, traffic event analysis, motion prediction, and driving action planning~ Sima_2024_DriveLM,Parikh_2025_RoadSocial,Liu_2026_RoadSceneBench . These benchmarks do not assess maintenance correctness under the diagnostic prerequisites of the HIIP-Chain, leaving a critical gap in highway infrastructure inspection evaluation. A further limitation lies in the restricted variety of infrastructure entities and anomaly categories covered by current datasets. Ground-level datasets, which capture fine-grained anomalies at close range, such as CrackSeg~ Zhou_2024_CrackSeg and RoadAnomaly~ Lis_2019_RoadAnomaly , focus on pavement cracks and unexpected roadway obstacles. Meanwhile, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) imagery covers long road segments efficiently, yet datasets incorporating this perspective, such as RDD2022~ Arya_2024_RDD2022 and UAPD~ Zhu_2022_UAVPavement , remain restricted to pavement distress, with RDD2022 covering only four damage types. In contrast, real-world highway infrastructure spans far more diverse entities, giving rise to a much broader and more complex spectrum of anomaly categories. Existing datasets therefore fall short of real-world inspection demands and cannot adequately evaluate MLLMs on practical inspection tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce HighwayVerse, a multi-view benchmark designed to evaluate MLLMs across the complete HIIP-Chain. In terms of scale, HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world inspection records, including 7,680 Ground records across 100 anomaly categories and 6,463 UAV records across 17 categories, as shown in Figure~ fig:highwayverse_overview . Furthermore, these records naturally preserve the long-tailed category distributions of field inspection depicted in Figure~ fig:highwayverse_overview . Specifically, each record contains six multiple-choice questions organized into four progressive stages, namely Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis covering parallel Anomaly Localization, Anomaly Description, and Risk Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:highwayverse_overview . Crucially, across these four stages, a correct answer in a later stage receives credit only when the preceding stages are completed correctly. In total, the dataset contains 84,858 question-answer pairs generated semi-automatically and reviewed by domain-trained annotators over 400 hours. Building upon HighwayVerse, we evaluate 12 representative open-source and closed-source MLLMs across Ground and UAV perspectives via Final, the overall chained accuracy requiring correct completion across all stages of the HIIP-Chain. Although evaluated models achieve high accuracy when initially determining whether an anomaly is present, their overall chained accuracy in Final drops substantially. On the UAV perspective, for instance, InternVL3.5-8B attains 72.48 when initially judging whether an anomaly exists yet reaches only 25.96 in Final. Because Final incorporates downstream recognition, condition analysis, and maintenance decisions, this sharp drop reveals widespread errors in anomaly-related analysis and decision-making, indicating that MLLMs likely fail to truly comprehend specific anomaly patterns and that their high initial scores largely stem from chance guessing. Compared with prior isolated task evaluations, our chain-structured HIIP-Chain protocol is therefore far more effective at assessing genuine MLLM understanding of highway infrastructure anomalies. To further strengthen highway infrastructure inspection along the HIIP-Chain, we introduce Local-and-Global Navigated Exemplar Retrieval-Augmented Guidance ( ), a training-free adaptation framework for frozen MLLMs. Built upon an offline hierarchical reference bank that organizes highway infrastructure anomalies from coarse-grained to fine-grained categories, performs route-guided complementary retrieval across Primary, Expanded, and Global Scopes, assembling retrieved reference images with their category labels into a reference-conditioned prompt for in-context visual guidance. Empirically, pairing with all 12 evaluated MLLMs yields consistent and substantial improvements across the chain. On the UAV perspective, raises Anomaly Recognition and Final by 12.35 and 6.75 on the open-source InternVL3.5-8B, and by 7.99 and 4.68 on the closed-source Gemini 2.5 Flash. Our main contributions are summarized below. [leftmargin=*,topsep=2pt,itemsep=1pt,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt] We construct HighwayVerse, a multi-view highway infrastructure dataset of 14,143 real-world inspection records and 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs, spanning 7,680 Ground records across 100 anomaly categories and 6,463 UAV records across 17 categories. We formulate the HIIP-Chain, a progressive evaluation protocol aligned with engineering inspection workflows, providing a faithful standard to assess genuine MLLM comprehension of highway infrastructure anomalies across 12 open-source and closed-source models. We propose , a companion retrieval-augmented framework that integrates reference images into a reference-conditioned prompt to substantially boost inspection performance across all evaluated MLLMs without updating any MLLM parameters. Related Work sec:related_work Road and Infrastructure Benchmarks Vision-based inspection supports civil infrastructure monitoring and maintenance planning~ Spencer_2019_InfrastructureInspection,Peraka_2020_PavementAsset,ElHakea_2023_PavementCV , yet conventional methods and datasets predominantly target localized perception of cracks, potholes, guardrails, bridges, or roadway obstacles~ Cha_2017_CrackDetection,Maeda_2018_RoadDamage,Fan_2020_PotholeSeg,Jin_2024_Guardrail,Zhang_2020_BridgeDamage,Zhou_2024_CrackSeg,Lis_2019_RoadAnomaly,Arya_2024_RDD2022,Zhu_2022_UAVPavement . Beyond pure perception, general multimodal benchmarks evaluate broad visual reasoning~ Liu_2024_MMBench,Yu_2024_MMVet,Yue_2024_MMMU,Fu_2025_VideoMME , whereas industrial benchmarks progress from unsupervised defect detection~ Bergmann_2019_MVTecAD,Zou_2022_VisA to independent multi-task question answering in MMAD~ Jiang_2025_MMAD . In road scenarios, RoadBench introduces synthetic road-damage image and text pairs~ Xiao_2026_RoadBench , and DriveLM links perception, prediction, and planning through graph-structured QA~ Sima_2024_DriveLM . RoadSocial and RoadSceneBench address traffic-event analysis and relational road semantics~ Parikh_2025_RoadSocial,Liu_2026_RoadSceneBench . As summarized in Table~ tab:comparison , these benchmarks have limited coverage of highway infrastructure across Ground and UAV views and do not assess maintenance correctness under the diagnostic prerequisites of the HIIP-Chain. HighwayVerse bridges this gap with the HIIP-Chain spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution. MLLMs for Anomaly Understanding Although general-purpose MLLMs couple visual encoders with language models for instruction following~ Li_2023_BLIP2,Liu_2023_VisualInstructionTuning,Bai_2025_Qwen3VL,Wang_2025_InternVL35 , they still struggle with fine-grained visual discrimination~ Tong_2024_MMVP,Xu_2025_AnomalyOV . Existing remedies incorporate language-guided visual refinement~ chen2024improving or specialist localization modules~ Gu_2024_AnomalyGPT,Li_2025_Myriad,Xu_2025_AnomalyOV , which require task-specific training, while small-and-large model collaboration routes queries via lightweight modules to assist large models~ chen2024data,chen2025improving . KKA~ chen2026kka uses language model knowledge to generate anomalous examples for training category-level visual detectors. VISPROG and ViperGPT compose external visual tools without task-specific training~ Gupta_2023_VisProg,Suris_2023_ViperGPT , while MMAD retrieves textual domain knowledge~ Jiang_2025_MMAD and MuRAG learns multimodal retrieval and generation~ Chen_2022_MuRAG . For in-context example selection, Flamingo uses visual similarity~ Alayrac_2022_Flamingo , whereas MMICES adds text-based reranking~ Chen_2025_MMICES . Rather than flat similarity matching, constructs an offline hierarchical reference bank from coarse-grained to fine-grained anomaly categories and combines DINOv2 and CLIP representations~ Oquab_2024_DINOv2,Radford_2021_CLIP for route-guided retrieval across Primary, Expanded, and Global Scopes, assembling retrieved references into a reference-conditioned prompt without updating any MLLM parameters. title: Not All Directions Are Flat: Decomposed-Gradient Flatness for Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Many applications of novel view synthesis, such as augmented reality and robotics, can afford only a few input views, since dense capture is costly. With such sparse views, however, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) overfits the training views and degrades at unseen viewpoints. Among the approaches to this problem, flat-minima optimization treats the Gaussians as trainable parameters and steers training toward flat minima, which generalize better, by perturbing the Gaussians with random noise or along the training gradient. However, these perturbations ignore their direction relative to the other training views. Interestingly, we find that the direction of the perturbation determines whether it improves generalization. Specifically, we decompose the gradient of each training view into a component parallel to the average gradient of all views, on which the views agree, and an orthogonal component, on which they disagree. Perturbing along the orthogonal component improves generalization, whereas perturbing along the parallel component does not. We further find that the flatness correction often opposes the reconstruction gradient, shrinking or even reversing the reconstruction step. Based on these findings, we propose DecoFlat, which perturbs each Gaussian along the orthogonal component together with random noise. Furthermore, we introduce a conflict-aware correction, which removes the part of the flatness correction that opposes the reconstruction gradient, and a rescheduling of the spherical-harmonics color, which suppresses the overfitting of view-dependent appearance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DecoFlat, as a plug-in optimizer, consistently improves vanilla 3DGS and a wide range of sparse-view 3DGS methods.

Neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2020nerf first achieved it from dense captures, and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussian has since become the mainstream representation because it renders in real time at comparable quality, representing a scene as a set of anisotropic Gaussians optimized by differentiable rasterization. Many applications, such as augmented reality and robotics, however, can afford only a few input views. With such sparse views, NeRF recovers wrong geometry~ niemeyer2022regnerf and 3DGS overfits the training views~ zhu2024fsgs . Sparse views thus produce floaters, spurious Gaussians in empty space, and distorted geometry at novel viewpoints. Two families of methods seek them. Random weight perturbation injects noise into the parameters during training~ li2024rwp , whereas sharpness-aware minimization (SAM)~ foret2021sam perturbs the parameters along the gradient and descends from the perturbed point. Both have counterparts in 3DGS. Noise injected into the Gaussian parameters appears in 3DGS-MCMC~ kheradmand2024mcmc for exploration and in SAP~ seo2026sap for flatness, while FASR~ yun2026flat adapts SAM to 3DGS by setting its radius and weight from the local image frequency. These methods thus decide how far to perturb and how much to correct, but not in which direction. In particular, they choose the perturbation without regard to the other training views, which under sparse supervision are the only evidence of what generalizes. summarizes this comparison. title: VeriTouch: Verified Visuo-Tactile World Models that Improve Robot Policy Learning
summary: Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning is constrained by the high cost of real-world data collection and the difficulty of building realistic simulations. Generative models offer a scalable source of training data, yet useful demonstrations require plausible tactile feedback, temporal alignment with visual contact, and accurate actions. To this end, we present VeriTouch, a framework for generating and verifying synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories for policy learning. Conditioned on initial images and task instructions, our world model, VeriGen, jointly generates high-fidelity dual-view videos and realistic tactile sequences over complete manipulation trajectories. By integrating a dedicated tactile expert with a pretrained video model, it captures realistic visual details and tactile deformation dynamics through joint visuo-tactile modeling. Our multimodal verifier VeriEval then checks visual quality while focusing on tactile reliability, assessing tactile realism, contact-force plausibility, and temporal alignment between visible contact and tactile signals, thereby directly filtering out unreliable sequences. Finally, our inverse dynamics model, VeriIDM, combines global scene information from both camera views with fine-grained gripper details and motion across neighboring frames to extract actions from verified videos. Experiments on five real-world tasks show that synthetic data improves all four evaluated policies, with further scaling synthetic trajectories substantially boosting policy performance without additional real-world data collection.

Introduction sec:intro Contact-rich manipulation requires robots to reason about physical contact, which is often difficult to infer from visual observations alone. By providing direct feedback on contact states, tactile sensing enables visuo-tactile policies to better handle contact-rich tasks~ neoteai2026n0vtla,yuan2026ftp,bi2026vla . However, collecting visuo-tactile data in the real world requires expensive tactile sensors~ do2022densetact and labor-intensive teleoperation~ dass2023pato,wu2023gello . Simulation reduces the need for real-world data collection but requires realistic environments and accurate modeling of objects' physical properties~ aljalbout2026reality,zhang2020contact,wang2022tacto . To reduce these costs, recent work synthesizes manipulation videos and extracts the corresponding actions for policy training~ jang2025dreamgen,he2026cosmossurgical . However, extending video-based synthesis to visuo-tactile demonstrations requires generating plausible tactile responses that are synchronized with visible contact. Existing approaches augment training with synthetic rollouts~ huang2026vitacworld or corrective segments for policy failures~ Liu_2026_TACO , with repeated rounds of data generation and policy retraining. Other approaches rely on simulation to generate or validate physically feasible trajectories~ jiang2026grounded,he2026vdreamer . Meanwhile, existing verification methods assess kinematic and tactile plausibility~ Liu_2026_TACO or score predicted tactile signals against task instructions~ Wu_2026_ViTaL . While these methods improve different aspects of data generation and quality control, several challenges remain. Iterative augmentation requires repeated data generation and policy retraining, while simulation-based approaches depend on additional environments, increasing the cost and complexity of generating training data. Existing verification methods can identify specific errors, but lack a joint assessment of tactile plausibility and temporal alignment with visual contact throughout complete demonstrations. These quality requirements, together with the costs of iterative augmentation and simulation, motivate a more efficient and comprehensive pipeline for generating reliable visuo-tactile training data. As shown in Fig.~ fig:teaser , we introduce , a framework that jointly generates visual and tactile observations, verifies the resulting sequences without iterative retraining and simulation replay, and extracts actions from the sequences that pass verification. Our world model, , extends a pretrained video backbone~ agarwal2026cosmos with a dedicated tactile expert. It uses cross-view attention to combine scene context with close-up contact details and jointly models visual and tactile dynamics. Alongside checks for physical plausibility and instruction following, our multimodal verifier, , assesses tactile reconstruction error and task-dependent contact forces, and checks the temporal alignment of visual and tactile contact intervals. By filtering out unreliable sequences before action extraction, produces higher-quality synthetic visuo-tactile training data. Finally, uses local gripper cues and temporal context to extract actions from the retained videos. We evaluate on five real-world contact-rich tasks using two vision-based and two visuo-tactile policies. Augmenting real demonstrations with our synthetic data improves all four policies, increasing the overall average success rate from 19.4 with real data alone to 33.8 . Moreover, policy performance continues to improve as the synthetic dataset scales without collecting additional real-world demonstrations, more than doubling the average success rate from 33.0 to 67.0 when the amount of synthetic data reaches four times that of real data. Ablations show that generated tactile signals improve policy performance and that training on data selected by our multimodal verifier yields higher success rates than training on synthetic data with visual-only filtering or no filtering. These results demonstrate that verified synthetic visuo-tactile trajectories improve policy performance on contact-rich manipulation tasks. Our main contributions are as follows: We introduce , a framework for synthesizing high-quality visuo-tactile training trajectories. Its world model jointly captures visual and tactile contact dynamics, while an IDM preserves fine motion details to recover precise actions. We develop a multimodal verifier that checks tactile plausibility and visual--tactile contact consistency alongside visual quality, filtering unreliable observations before extracting actions without physical or simulated replay. We improve all four policies and show that scaling synthetic data more than doubles average success rate over the real-data baseline without collecting additional real-world demonstrations. Related Work sec:related World Models for Robot Data Generation. Generative world models can synthesize videos of robot manipulation from initial images and task instructions. DreamGen~ jang2025dreamgen converts generated videos into robot demonstrations by recovering pseudo-actions, while RoboDream~ robodream2026 expands scene diversity through motion-conditioned generation. For contact-rich manipulation, visuo-tactile world models predict future visual and tactile observations to support planning and control, sometimes jointly predicting robot actions~ higuera2026visuo,zheng2026omnivta,team2026n_0,tian2026vt,lou2026dream , whereas Physical Canvas~ xing2026physicalcanvas uses a learned simulator for policy evaluation and optimization. Closer to our focus on visuo-tactile data synthesis, ViTacWorld~ huang2026vitacworld generates action-conditioned visuo-tactile rollouts, and TACO~ Liu_2026_TACO produces corrective segments near policy failures for iterative post-training. Sharing the goal of expanding visuo-tactile training data, jointly models visual scene evolution and tactile deformation dynamics to synthesize observation sequences covering the full manipulation process from initial images and task instructions, without conditioning on future robot actions. Verification of Synthetic Demonstrations. Visual verifiers use video-language models to judge whether generated videos follow the task instruction and depict physically plausible motion~ jang2025dreamgen,bansal2025videophy,bansal2026videophy . By contrast, tactile verifiers assess the physical contact directly. TACO filters corrective segments by checking predicted force and torque signals against task-specific bounds~ Liu_2026_TACO . ViTaL uses both modalities in policy steering: visual predictions guide long-horizon action selection, while predicted tactile features are scored against phase-specific contact descriptions to refine short-horizon actions~ Wu_2026_ViTaL . For data filtering, a plausible video and a plausible tactile sequence can still disagree on when contact occurs. therefore verifies visual quality, tactile plausibility, and cross-modal contact timing throughout each demonstration. title: GeoMerge-OPD: Balanced Skill Integration in Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: 29 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables. The first four authors contributed equally. Wenshuo Chen is the project leader. Yutao Yue and Xiaochun Cao are co-corresponding authors
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models excel at individual robotic skills, yet integrating heterogeneous skills into a single policy remains a key challenge for general-purpose robotic control, especially in whole-body tasks with differing manipulation and locomotion requirements. Common multi-skill integration strategies, such as joint fine-tuning and parameter merging, can induce unintended actions during closed-loop execution, severely degrading individual skills. Task-conditioned analysis of expert updates reveals response energy concentrated in a few dominant directions and opposing expert responses along high-energy directions within a shared, task-relevant response subspace. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, combining response-space regularization, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation. During independent expert fine-tuning, G-isometry constrains update-response gains within task-activation subspaces; the expert parameters are then statically merged into a student with preliminary multitask capabilities. Fine-tuned task experts serve as teachers, providing velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate action-flow states visited by the student to calibrate residual behavioral deviations. Experiments with two VLA backbones show strong, balanced humanoid skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, outperforming joint fine-tuning and multitask reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining robustness under perturbations.

Common multi-skill integration strategies, such as joint fine-tuning and parameter merging, can induce unintended actions during closed-loop execution, severely degrading individual skills. Task-conditioned analysis of expert updates reveals response energy concentrated in a few dominant directions and opposing expert responses along high-energy directions within a shared, task-relevant response subspace. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, combining response-space regularization, parameter merging, and on-policy distillation. During independent expert fine-tuning, G-isometry constrains update-response gains within task-activation subspaces; the expert parameters are then statically merged into a student with preliminary multitask capabilities. Fine-tuned task experts serve as teachers, providing velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate action-flow states visited by the student to calibrate residual behavioral deviations. Experiments with two VLA backbones show strong, balanced humanoid skill integration on SIMPLE and consistent performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, outperforming joint fine-tuning and multitask reinforcement-learning baselines while maintaining robustness under perturbations. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language models to robotic control using demonstration data, combining semantic understanding and referential grounding with strong performance on individual manipulation tasks knowledge_insulation,pi05,actions_as_language . Generalist robots, however, must integrate multiple skills within one policy; humanoids must additionally coordinate upper-body manipulation and lower-body locomotion wholebodyvla,psi0 . This makes reliable integration of heterogeneous skills a central challenge for VLA models. A common approach is joint fine-tuning on demonstrations pooled across skills. Although effective for homogeneous tasks, it can improve some skills at the expense of others when task demands differ openvla_oft,rethink_vla_scaling . These trade-offs also arise with a shared control interface: with a \( _ 0.5 \) backbone, joint training on a stream of real-robot tasks improved one normalized task score from 52 to 92 while reducing another from 100 to 33.3 continualvla . On whole-body tasks, jointly fine-tuned \( _0\) underperformed its single-task counterparts across all evaluated tasks, with some skills nearly lost psi0 . An alternative is to fine-tune experts separately and merge their parameters, an approach effective in language and vision models ties,regmeanpp,isoc . MergeVLA extends this approach to VLAs through task masks, dedicated action heads, and test-time routing mergevla . However, we find that directly merging whole-body VLA experts can severely degrade individual skills, even when the task-specific experts retain those skills. In our \( _0\) experiments, the merged policy issued unintended locomotion commands during BendPick, a task requiring bending and grasping in place, resulting in task failure. These failures motivate our central question: how can heterogeneous task behaviors be retained in shared parameters to form a balanced, robust policy without maintaining separate models for individual tasks? Prior work documents concentrated update spectra and interference arising from disagreements in parameter signs or singular directions ties,tsvmerge,isoc,dcmerge . It also shows that the functional effects of updates depend on inputs and may concentrate in low-dimensional activation or output-shift subspaces wudi,esm . Building on these findings, we analyze task-conditioned responses of \( _0\) experts, using task activation statistics to characterize the functional effects of their parameter updates. We observe opposing components within a shared task-relevant response subspace, concentrated along high-energy response directions. This structure co-occurs with unintended action shifts after merging, suggesting that energy concentration can amplify the impact of opposing responses. These observations motivate regularizing update responses before merging and calibrating the resulting policy afterward. We propose GeoMerge-OPD, which combines regularized expert fine-tuning, static parameter merging, and on-policy distillation (OPD). Starting from a common pretrained backbone, each expert is fine-tuned with G-isometry to constrain update-response gains in task-activation subspaces. This regularizer acts on responses induced by task inputs, reducing excessive dominance by a few directions. Static merging then establishes a balanced initialization with preliminary multitask competence. Inspired by multi-teacher OPD for integrating heterogeneous expert capabilities in language and text-to-image models mopd,flowopd , we use OPD to consolidate skills from task-specific VLA experts into a unified student policy. The student interacts with the environment in closed loop and generates its own action-flow trajectories. The corresponding task expert provides dense velocity-field supervision at the environment observations and intermediate flow states actually visited by the student. This supervision calibrates residual behavioral deviations under the student's own state and action-generation distributions, further coordinating multitask skills within the shared model. We evaluate GeoMerge-OPD on LIBERO libero , LIBERO-PRO liberopro , and SIMPLE simple , using \( _ 0.5 \) and \( _0\) as the two VLA backbones, covering tabletop manipulation, whole-body loco-manipulation, and generalization to perturbed evaluation conditions. Our main contributions are: Empirical diagnosis of multitask VLA integration. We characterize failures in merging task-specific VLA experts and identify concentrated update responses and opposing components in shared task-relevant subspaces, connecting these observations to unintended behavioral shifts in closed-loop execution. A framework for balanced skill consolidation. GeoMerge-OPD combines G-isometry regularization and static merging to establish a balanced initialization, followed by task-routed OPD to calibrate residual behavior on student-visited states and action-flow trajectories, consolidating heterogeneous skills in shared parameters. Skill consolidation and robustness across two backbones. GeoMerge-OPD achieves 26/30 whole-body successes on SIMPLE versus 22/30 for Joint FT from the same G-regularized merge, reaches 97.1 on LIBERO versus 96.2 for Joint FT from the pretrained base, and attains the highest average LIBERO-PRO success (67.3 ) across five perturbation axes among the evaluated policies. Related Work Model Merging and VLA Skill Integration Model merging research has expanded from parameter combination to conflict resolution, task-subspace modeling, and spectral regulation to improve the integration of expert capabilities ties,tsvmerge,isoc . Mergeability has also been incorporated into expert training and architectural design to prepare models for subsequent consolidation mergopt,mergevla . In parallel, studies of input-dependent update effects use input or feature subspaces to characterize how parameter updates influence task behavior wudi,esm . Together, these studies provide a basis for understanding post-merging capability retention through both expert-update structure and task-dependent functional responses, informing the analysis of behavioral degradation in heterogeneous robotic skill integration. Policy Distillation and Multi-Teacher Capability Integration Behavioral data generated by specialized experts can supervise generalist robotic policies, consolidating experience across tasks or manipulated objects within a single policy rldg,unigrasp_transformer . Applying teacher supervision to student-generated sequences or trajectories helps mitigate distribution mismatch between training and execution and correct errors induced by the student's behavior gkd,vlaopd . In large language models and text-to-image generation, multi-teacher OPD further integrates heterogeneous capabilities into a unified student through supervision from domain-specialized teachers on student-generated trajectories mopd,flowopd . To our knowledge, multi-teacher OPD for integrating heterogeneous skills across VLA tasks remains underexplored. Inspired by this capability integration paradigm, we use task-specific VLA teachers to provide dense velocity-field supervision along the student's own action-flow trajectories, conditioned on observations encountered during its environment rollouts, to coordinate multi-task skills after parameter merging. Why Multi-Task Integration Fails Capability collapse after integration We refer to severe degradation of individual skills after multitask integration as capability collapse. On the BendPick, CloseDoor, and OpenOven tasks with \( _0\), both joint fine-tuning and static parameter merging exhibited this phenomenon, with BendPick nearly failing completely. An examination of failed episodes showed that the merged policy continuously issued lower-body movement commands in BendPick scenes requiring bending and grasping in place, whereas the corresponding task-specific expert did not issue such commands. This unintended movement caused the merged policy to deviate from the control behavior required by the task. title: SWEEP-Bench: Do Embodied Policies Act on the Speed They See?
summary: Robot policies must adapt to the speed of moving objects, yet existing benchmarks rarely measure this ability across diverse tasks and speeds. We introduce SWEEP-Bench, a simulation benchmark with 80 conveyor-belt manipulation tasks spanning 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 belt speeds (0.10-0.40 m/s). Objects are transported through physical contact with a visibly moving belt. Each task has a static counterpart, and each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds. We fine-tune eight vision-language-action and world-action models on demonstrations spanning the full speed range, comparing observations from the current frame alone with those including two past frames. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds, and their failures indicate that they tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed rather than to the actual one. Past frames raise the success rate by 10-40 percentage points for three models, and linear probes show that the belt speed is also most linearly decodable from these three. Adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and a speed estimated from the images keeps most of this gain. These results show that SWEEP-Bench exposes speed-dependent failures and suggest that past frames help only policies from which the speed is most decodable, such as those pretrained on multiple frames. Project page: damin3927.github.io/SWEEP-Bench Introduction sec:intro Robot policies trained from demonstrations are largely evaluated on benchmarks in which objects remain stationary until robot contact~ liu2023libero,nasiriany2024robocasa . Manipulating a moving object requires the robot to adjust the timing and location of contact to the object's speed. Recent studies report that vision-language-action (VLA) models struggle with moving objects~ xie2026dynamicvla and examine temporal motion cues~ fang2026domino , inference latency~ wen2026vlalagbench , and physical prediction~ yun2026physmani . However, it remains unclear whether these policies adapt their actions to object speed when that speed can be inferred from past frames. Answering this question requires evaluating success rates across speeds to reveal speed-dependent failures and across diverse manipulation skills so that the findings are not tied to a few tasks. Each task must also be solvable at the tested speeds so that failures reflect policy limitations rather than task infeasibility. Existing moving-object benchmarks rarely provide all three. Those with larger task sets report success rates at no more than three speeds or provide no per-speed results; those reporting more speeds do so for at most four tasks. Few also check during task construction that an expert solves every task at several speeds. We introduce (Speed-Wise Evaluation of Embodied Policies), a simulation benchmark for moving-object manipulation on a conveyor belt. We use a conveyor because we can set its speed while keeping the rest of the scene fixed, it supports many manipulation skills, and its motion is visible in the camera images. The benchmark contains 80 conveyor-belt tasks in 16 skill categories, each evaluated at 13 speeds from 0.10 to 0.40~m/s, with constant speeds in the main protocol and within-episode speed changes in an acceleration setting. To isolate the effect of speed, each evaluation episode uses the same randomized scene at all 13 speeds, and the training demonstrations span the full speed range. To ensure that failures reflect the policy, a scripted expert solves every task at four speeds spanning the range, and each task has a static counterpart that checks whether it can be learned with a stationary object. We fine-tune six VLA models and two video-based world-action models~ kim2026cosmospolicy,fastwam2026 . For each model, we compare the current frame alone with the current frame plus two past frames and evaluate both policies on every task at every speed. For six models, the success rate peaks at intermediate speeds with or without past frames, as the policies tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed. Measuring success at 13 speeds makes this pattern visible, whereas averaging over speeds hides it. A small network on the optical flow between two frames 0.1~s apart estimates the belt speed with a mean absolute error of 0.010~m/s. Past frames, however, raise the mean success rate by 10--40 percentage points for three models and by at most one point for the other five. Linear probes on the fine-tuned policies show that the belt speed is most linearly decodable from these three ( -- at the action module), whereas the other five reach at most and gain little from past frames. The speed is useful once a policy has it: on a 20-task subset, adding ground-truth speed input to four of the models improves all of them, and an image-based speed adapter recovers most of this gain. In 720 real-conveyor trials, past frames raise Fast-WAM's score slightly more than 's, as in simulation, and adding belt speed input raises 's score from 31 to 80, and to 66 when the adapter estimates the speed. Our contributions are: We introduce , with 80 tasks across 16 skill categories and 13 speeds, paired evaluation scenes, an expert check of every task at four speeds, and a static counterpart for every task. We will release the code, demonstrations, and evaluation protocol. We evaluate eight VLA and world-action models with and without past frames on every task at every speed, showing that six of them peak at intermediate speeds and tend to produce actions suited to the average demonstration speed. Using linear probes and speed-conditioned policies, we find that past frames help only the three models from which the belt speed is most linearly decodable, and that a speed estimated from the images keeps most of the gain from ground-truth speed input. Related Work sec:relatedwork Benchmarks for moving-object manipulation. Dynamic grasping benchmarks such as DGBench~ burgesslimerick2022dgbench and DQ-Bench~ liang2026dqbench vary target speed for a single manipulation skill. Larger suites broaden task coverage: DOMINO~ fang2026domino includes 35 dynamic tasks and static counterparts, DynaGrasp-32~ chang2026dynawm contains 25 moving-object tasks, LIBERO-Industry~ liberoindustry2026 covers industrial transfer workflows, and LIBERO-Dynamic~ ren2026liberodynamic evaluates 40 LIBERO tasks at three speeds. These studies do not report dense speed-wise success-rate curves across their full task sets. Benchmarks with more speed levels use them on few tasks and to study other factors: VLALagBench~ wen2026vlalagbench uses nine speeds on four tasks to study inference latency, and AHEAD~ syed2026ahead uses four speeds in one conveyor scenario to evaluate its predictive world model. In contrast, measures how the success rate itself changes with speed, at 13 belt speeds across 80 tasks in 16 skill categories ( ). Visual history and motion representations. In behavior cloning, observation history can lower performance because the policy learns to copy its own past actions from it~ dehaan2019causal,wen2020copycat,chuang2022copycat , and recent VLA methods add dedicated history mechanisms~ liu2026ttfvla,koo2025hamlet,lin2026hifvla . MoveBench~ zhang2026ppc argues that VLAs trained on single frames are structurally blind to temporal dynamics. For moving objects, DynamicVLA~ xie2026dynamicvla succeeds more often with an earlier frame, whereas DOMINO finds little benefit from raw-frame history on a 10-task subset and instead combines optical flow with future-state prediction. DynaWM uses observation history in a world model that regenerates VLA action chunks. Motion can also be given to a policy explicitly, as frame differences~ wang2016tsn , optical flow~ simonyan2014twostream , or point traces~ zheng2025tracevla . Another route to motion is video pretraining~ wu2024gr1,hu2025vpp : Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmospolicy and Fast-WAM~ fastwam2026 adapt pretrained video generation models for control, and Fast-WAM retains video prediction during training without generating future frames at test time. These studies examine history within their own methods. We instead compare VLA and world-action models using the current frame alone or the current frame plus two past frames, and measure the effect at each belt speed. As DynamicVLA does, we feed past frames through each model's own image input, without past actions, so measures what standard fine-tuning extracts from visible motion. Probing and speed conditioning. Linear probes test whether a variable can be decoded from intermediate features~ alain2017probe . However, decodability alone does not show that a model uses that information~ elazar2021amnesic,hermann2020texture,fu2025hidden , so we relate speed probes to changes in success rate caused by visual history and explicit speed input. Conditioning a policy on physical parameters estimated from recent observations has precedents in online system identification~ yu2017uposi and rapid motor adaptation~ kumar2021rma , and DynamicWAM~ lou2026dynamicwam conditions a world-action model on image-plane velocity from optical flow. Our image-based speed adapter follows this pattern and measures how much of the gain from ground-truth speed remains when speed must be estimated. sec:benchmark evaluates manipulation success rates on 80 conveyor-belt tasks in 16 skill categories at 13 constant belt speeds (0.10--0.40~m/s). We use ManiSkill~3~ tao2024maniskill3 with a Franka Panda arm beside the conveyor. Further benchmark details are provided in the supplementary material. Task Suites and Demonstrations sec:tasks Task design. shows one representative task from each of the 16 skill categories. Categories group tasks by the main action their instruction asks for, inspired by DROID~ khazatsky2024droid , which measures task diversity by instruction verbs. Each task has a language instruction, a simulator-defined success condition, and a scripted expert that uses the object's pose and velocity to generate demonstrations. To ensure that each task is solvable at the tested speeds, we include a task only if its expert succeeds in at least 80 of evaluation episodes at each of four representative speeds: 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, and 0.40~m/s. Static counterpart. Every task also has a static counterpart with the belt stopped and the object initially within reach. We treat it as a separate task that checks whether a policy can learn the manipulation with a stationary object, since its initial object pose and success condition may differ. Environment. Demonstrations and evaluation episodes draw from 185 backgrounds, including indoor scenes from ReplicaCAD~ szot2021habitat2 , ArchitecTHOR~ deitke2022procthor , and RoboCasa~ nasiriany2024robocasa , as well as a plain table. We also randomize the platform material (39 options), lighting, the object (668 across all task sets), belt direction, the entry point (within 0.10~m), and exterior camera positions (up to 5~cm per axis). The policy receives a image tiling three exterior cameras and a wrist image at 20~Hz. Episodes last at most 15~s. Demonstrations. title: Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary:

However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation.
