full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models benefit from strong semantic representations that support object recognition and instruction understanding. However, precise manipulation also depends on resolving object locations and workspace relations, and on selecting actions with an estimate of how the scene will evolve. Existing geometry-aware methods make the current scene more explicit, while predictive methods model future observations or representations. Yet future information is often neither grounded in a control-relevant spatial state nor directly used to guide action generation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), which uses the grounded present as the reference for predicting an actionable near-future representation. A frozen spatial teacher first distills geometric priors into policy-connected spatial tokens. A current-conditioned bottleneck then learns a compact latent that captures future information relative to the present scene. This latent is predicted from the current policy context and initial Action Expert features, without access to future observations or the spatial teacher. Finally, zero-initialized residual fusion incorporates the predicted latent into the Action Expert to refine action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and three real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate improvements over in both simulation and real-robot settings. https://github.com/Cqhddyb/SG-LL Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified policy that maps visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. Large-scale pretraining and robot data have produced increasingly capable generalist policies, including the RT, OpenVLA, and \( \) families brohan2022rt,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . These models execute diverse manipulation instructions and transfer across task conditions, yet strong task performance leaves open whether their internal representations explicitly expose the scene geometry needed for control and whether action generation anticipates how the interaction is likely to evolve. This distinction matters under variations in viewpoint, robot state, object configuration, and observation noise, where a semantically competent policy must still resolve precise spatial relations fei2025libero . Reliable manipulation calls for both spatial grounding and predictive lookahead. Semantic visual features can identify an object without making its location, robot--object relation, or local configuration readily available to the Action Expert. Conversely, directly mapping the current context to an Action Chunk does not explicitly represent the near-future scene evolution implied by the current task and policy context. This motivates the central question of this work: Can a VLA ground the present scene with control-relevant spatial structure, anticipate where the interaction is heading, and use that lookahead to refine control? Spatially aware robot policies address the first requirement through depth, point clouds, explicit 3D representations, or geometry-aligned features shridhar2021cliport,pmlr-v205-shridhar23a,ze20243d,li2025spatial,qu2025spatialvla . Such representations can make scene structure more accessible, but they are often introduced through an additional online modality or a specialized spatial architecture. Our objective is instead to use a frozen visual geometry model solely as a training-time supervisory reference while retaining the standard RGB policy interface. Its geometric priors are distilled into a policy-connected current-state representation, while the teacher itself is absent from the deployed policy. Predictive representations address the second requirement from another direction. Prior work predicts images, videos, latent futures, or world-action features for representation learning, visual subgoals, action conditioning, or rollout-based control du2023learning,black2024zero,zheng2025flare,su2026world,fang2026privileged,zhao2026frappe,zhang2026dreamvla,miao2026jepa . These studies establish future-oriented representation learning as a promising direction for robot control. This raises a key interface challenge: how can a compact, future-informative representation be integrated into an existing flow-matching VLA such that prediction directly informs action generation? In SG-LL, lookahead takes the form of a compact near-future latent predicted once from the current policy context and directly used to refine the inherited action computation. We introduce Spatially Grounded Latent Lookahead (SG-LL), summarized in Figure~ fig:teaser . SG-LL first maps VLM Backbone features into Grounded Spatial State Tokens under supervision from a Frozen VGGT wang2025vggt Spatial Teacher. It then predicts compact, current-conditioned Future Latent Tokens from the grounded state, instruction, robot state, horizon, and an Action Intent Representation derived from initial Action Expert hidden states. Finally, zero-initialized Spatial Grounding Residual Injection and Future-Latent Residual Fusion connect these representations to the inherited policy. Together, these components implement a simple principle: ground the present, look ahead in latent space, and refine the action. Because both residual pathways are zero-initialized, SG-LL preserves the pretrained policy computation at initialization while requiring no future observations, no online geometry model, and no additional 3D sensors at deployment. We evaluate SG-LL at both the system and mechanism levels. SG-LL outperforms the official -LIBERO baseline across 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes and an original-architecture baseline under matched CALVIN D-to-D adaptation. Targeted interventions and trained controls examine whether the policy behaviorally uses episode-matched future latents and policy-derived action context, while distinguishing behavioral reliance from architectural contribution. We further evaluate SG-LL on three real-robot manipulation tasks. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce a spatial grounding interface that distills geometric priors from a frozen spatial teacher into policy-connected Grounded Spatial State Tokens, enabling control-relevant spatial grounding while retaining RGB-only deployment. We propose a decodable latent lookahead mechanism that predicts a compact, current-conditioned near-future representation from policy-available context and directly couples it to action generation through zero-initialized residual refinement. We validate SG-LL through paired simulation evaluations, targeted mechanism interventions, and real-robot experiments, demonstrating improved end-to-end control performance and showing that the trained policy makes functional use of its predicted future latent. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Control VLA policies combine pretrained vision-language representations with diverse action-generation mechanisms, ranging from autoregressive action tokenization to diffusion and flow matching for continuous control brohan2022rt,zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla,team2024octo, chi2025diffusion,liu2025rdt,black2024pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . Large-scale robot datasets and multimodal backbones further support transfer across tasks and embodiments, while recent work improves action representations and adaptation efficiency through latent actions, efficient tokenization, or specialized policy heads collaboration2023open,bousmalis2023robocat,li2024cogact, bu2025univla,pertsch2025fast,kim2025fine . SG-LL targets a different axis: rather than redesigning the base VLA or its action parameterization, it augments the inherited policy with control-relevant spatial grounding and near-future predictive information that directly participate in action generation. Spatial Representations and Geometric Grounding Spatial structure has been incorporated into robot policies through factorized what/where pathways, volumetric representations, point-cloud inputs, and explicit 3D feature encoders shridhar2021cliport,pmlr-v205-shridhar23a,ze20243d . Recent VLA methods bring similar spatial inductive biases into pretrained vision-language policies through 3D positional encoding, representation alignment, or geometry-aware supervision qu2025spatialvla,li2025spatial,wu2026pragmatic . SG-LL instead uses spatial grounding as part of a predictive control interface: frozen geometric priors supervise a policy-connected current spatial state that both feeds into the inherited action pathway and supports near-future latent prediction. Spatial grounding is therefore coupled with predictive lookahead and action refinement rather than introduced only as an additional spatial representation. Predictive Representations and World Models Predictive representation learning captures temporal structure by predicting future information in representation space rather than reconstructing every image pixel assran2023self,bardes2024revisiting . In robotics, future observations, visual subgoals, latent actions, and predictive features have been used for representation learning, action conditioning, and goal-directed control lynch2020learning,du2023learning,black2024zero,ye2025latent,zhao2025cot . More recent VLA-oriented methods align policy representations with future visual features or latent futures, or generate future-oriented conditions and imagined observations to guide action generation zheng2025flare,su2026world,fang2026privileged,zhao2026frappe, hu2024video,tian2025predictive,zhang2026dreamvla,sun2026vla,miao2026jepa, li2026fomovla,xie2026forediffusion,yuan2026fast . Related world-model approaches learn action-conditioned dynamics for prediction, rollout, and planning hafner2019learning,hansen2022temporal,zhou2024dino,assran2025v , including spatially structured models that connect geometric scene representations to predictive robot control zhen20243d,qiu2026making . SG-LL brings spatial grounding and predictive representation learning together through a decodable, current-conditioned near-future latent. Rather than using future prediction only as a pretraining signal or externally generated subgoal, SG-LL directly integrates the predicted latent into Action Expert hidden states through residual fusion, making near-future information actionable within the pretrained VLA pathway. Methodology Overview Let \(o_t\) denote the current multi-view RGB observation, \( \) the language instruction, \(s_t\) the robot state, and \(A_t=a_ t:t+K-1 \) the action chunk. The base VLA encodes the current multimodal context into a policy prefix, while the inherited flow-matching Action Expert predicts a velocity field over the noisy action suffix that is integrated to obtain \(A_t\). SG-LL augments this computation by forming Grounded Spatial State Tokens \(S_t\), predicting a current-conditioned near-future representation as Predicted Future Latent Tokens \( Z_t\), and using both representations to refine the inherited action-generation pathway. Figure~ fig:architecture organizes SG-LL into two stages. Stage I, the Decodable Future Abstraction Stage, establishes a compact, decodable future latent space from paired Current and Future Spatial Target Tokens. Stage II, the Spatial Grounding and Future Planning Stage, learns the policy-connected grounding, lookahead, and residual refinement pathways. It forms \(S_t\), derives an Action Intent Representation \(I_t^ \) from initial Action Expert hidden states, predicts \( Z_t\) from the current policy context, and injects the grounded present and predicted future into the inherited policy through residual interfaces. In SG-LL, planning is realized as a single near-future latent prediction that directly informs action generation. title: LLM-Guided Compositional Continual Learning for Robot Manipulation with Gated Low-Rank Experts
summary: General-purpose manipulation robots must acquire new skills over time without forgetting prior ones or retraining from scratch. We present a continual learning framework that represents each skill as a dedicated expert sub- network in a Progressive Neural Network (PNN). New tasks reuse prior knowledge through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on lateral connections controlled by learnable per-parent gates, enabling explicit attenuation of individual transfer paths while reducing the parameter cost of dense PNN laterals. For long-horizon deployment, a frozen local large language model decomposes natural-language instructions into sub-tasks, routes them to suitable experts, and requests a new expert only when the library is insufficient. Using a shared task-space action interface, we evaluate the framework on twelve MetaWorld tasks and in a Sawyer-to-Panda-to-UR5e cross-embodiment transfer experiment, showing improved task success relative to learning from scratch when demonstrations are limited. Real-robot manipulation experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework supports compositional execution and expert orchestration.
full_text: General-purpose manipulation robots must acquire new skills over time without forgetting prior ones or retraining from scratch. We present a continual learning framework that represents each skill as a dedicated expert sub-network in a Progressive Neural Network (PNN). New tasks reuse prior knowledge through low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules on lateral connections controlled by learnable per-parent gates, enabling explicit attenuation of individual transfer paths while reducing the parameter cost of dense PNN laterals. For long-horizon deployment, a frozen local large language model decomposes natural-language instructions into sub-tasks, routes them to suitable experts, and requests a new expert only when the library is insufficient. Using a shared task-space action interface, we evaluate the framework on twelve MetaWorld tasks and in a Sawyer-to-Panda-to-UR5e cross-embodiment transfer experiment, showing improved task success relative to learning from scratch when demonstrations are limited. Real-robot manipulation experiments further demonstrate that the proposed framework supports compositional execution and expert orchestration. Introduction Robots operating in unstructured environments must acquire new manipulation skills throughout their lifetime without losing previously learned ones. This requirement is difficult to satisfy with the dominant paradigm of training a single monolithic policy across all tasks. When new tasks are added, previously acquired knowledge can be partially or completely overwritten, leading to catastrophic forgetting~ ewc . Continual learning (CL) addresses this problem by enabling incremental skill acquisition while preserving earlier capabilities. However, forgetting is not the only limitation of monolithic policies kushawaha2024synapnet . Because different skills are entangled within the same set of parameters, it is difficult to identify which part of the network is responsible for a particular behavior or to quantify how much a new skill reuses prior knowledge. In safety-critical robotics~ binny2026safe , this lack of transparency limits inspection, verification, and selective deployment of individual competencies. We address these issues by learning each skill as a dedicated expert that is preserved after training and composed only when needed, as shown in Fig. fig:abs_achitecture . Our architecture is based on a Progressive Neural Network (PNN)~ pnn , where every task is assigned a new column, or sub-network, that is frozen once learned. This prevents parameter overwriting in previously learned columns. To enable forward knowledge transfer with a lower per-connection parameter cost than dense lateral connections, prior knowledge is reused through LoRA-style low-rank lateral adapters ~ lora . Each adapter is modulated by a learnable per-parent gate, allowing the new column to draw selectively from relevant prior experts while suppressing unhelpful ones. This design reduces the quadratic parameter growth of vanilla PNNs, mitigates negative knowledge transfer, and exposes transfer as a measurable quantity. Depending on the experiment, experts are trained either with soft actor-critic (SAC) augmented by behavior cloning or from demonstrations using conditional flow matching ~ sac . A library of reusable experts becomes most useful when paired with a planner that can decide which skill to invoke. We therefore integrate a frozen, locally served large language model (LLM) as a high-level supervisor. Given a natural-language instruction, the LLM decomposes it into an ordered sequence of sub-tasks, selects the appropriate expert for each step, and requests that a new expert be trained only when the current library is insufficient. The LLM operates purely at the symbolic planning level and is never fine-tuned, keeping task reasoning separate from low-level control and making the high-level task decomposition and routing explicit. Using shared task-space action conventions, we also evaluate the gated transfer mechanism across robot embodiments. We study transfer from a Sawyer arm in MetaWorld~ mclean2025metaworld to Panda and UR5e arms in Robosuite~ robosuite2020 , and finally to a real Franka Research~3 (FR3) arm performing a long-horizon manipulation task. In the simulated cross-embodiment experiments, the framework achieves higher mean task success than learning from scratch at every tested demonstration budget. The main contributions of this article are summarized as follows: We introduce a continual reinforcement learning (CRL) framework that combines frozen PNN columns with LoRA lateral adapters and learnable per-parent gates, enabling selective and parameter-efficient forward transfer. We develop a frozen local LLM planner that decomposes long-horizon instructions, routes sub-tasks to learned expert policies, and requests a new expert when the library cannot solve the task, while remaining separate from low-level control. We evaluate the framework against representative CL methods in the MetaWorld simulator, and demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer to the Robosuite simulator and then to an FR3 robot. We demonstrate a six-stage real-world manipulation sequence on the FR3, where the LLM planner coordinates dedicated expert policies across all the sub-tasks. Related Work sec:related Continual Learning for Robot Manipulation CL methods are commonly grouped into three categories: Regularization methods preserve previous knowledge by penalizing changes to parameters that are important for past tasks~ ewc . Rehearsal methods revisit stored samples from earlier tasks, or generate synthetic ones, to reduce forgetting~ er . Architectural methods allocate separate capacity to new tasks, either by expanding the network with task-specific modules~ den,pnn or by partitioning a fixed-size model through pruning or masking~ packnet . In robotic manipulation, CL is often studied with reinforcement learning (RL) or imitation learning (IL). Li et al.~ li2024continual study dexterous manipulation in simulation using an offline CRL student--teacher framework with replay. LEGION~ legion accumulates knowledge from a continuous task stream through a Bayesian nonparametric knowledge space, a SAC policy, and experience replay, while using language embeddings to infer tasks in long-horizon settings. CLARE~ clare adds encoder-decoder adapters to a frozen flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) model, expanding only when a feature-novelty score indicates a new task and routes without task IDs. SPECI~ speci builds a self-evolving skill codebook with frozen prior entries and decomposes shared and task-specific parameters. COLADA~ colada freezes an action-chunking transformer backbone, learns one LoRA adapter per skill from teleoperated demonstrations, and acquires missing skills through grounded human dialogue. While these methods are effective, many rely on large frozen VLA backbones that are costly to train, store, and deploy. In contrast, we use a PNN composed of compact task-specific expert policies, connected through LoRA-style low-rank lateral adapters~ lora . This design emphasizes selective forward transfer across both tasks and robot embodiments, a setting not addressed by the above methods. LLMs as High-Level Planners for Long-Horizon Manipulation Recent work increasingly uses LLMs to decompose natural-language commands into sub-goals rather than to generate low-level robot actions directly. Huang et al.~ huang2022language prompt a frozen LLM to map household goals to mid-level actions from a fixed vocabulary. LEAGUE++~ leaguepp combines task-and-motion planning with SAC, using an LLM to produce symbolic operators and design dense rewards, while warm-starting each new policy from the embedding-nearest prior skill. CLIMB~ climb constructs a symbolic PDDL world model and introduces new predicates after execution failures. LRLL~ lrll grows a library of LLM-written code skills through a gradient-free wake--sleep procedure. Tan~et al.~ mmllm_longhorizon decompose long-horizon tasks over a tree-structured skill library with GPT-4V perception, querying a human when a skill is unavailable. LCB~ lcb represents sub-goals as learnable latent tokens, but fine-tunes the LLM end-to-end and couples it to a single monolithic policy. These approaches similarly use LLMs primarily for high-level planning rather than direct control. Our framework differs by using a frozen local LLM to decompose tasks, select among learned expert policies, and request that a new expert be trained when no suitable expert is available. Problem Statement sec:problem We study lifelong manipulation, where a robot must acquire skills sequentially, reuse prior knowledge across tasks and embodiments, and compose learned skills from language. We separate this setting into two layers: a low-level control layer, in which each skill is represented by a state-feedback policy, and a high-level planning layer, in which language selects and orders those skills. Language is therefore used only for planning and never as an input to the control policy. This formulation leads to three requirements. (P1) Incremental skill acquisition. Skills arrive sequentially as tasks , with unknown in advance. Each task is an MDP , sharing the state space and task-space action space with all other tasks. The action is an end-effector command , while the dynamics , reward , and initial distribution may differ across tasks. At stage , the learner can interact only with and has access to a small demonstration set ; previous environments and data are unavailable. For each task, we learn a dedicated expert policy that maximizes The lifelong learner must satisfy two constraints: (R1) no forgetting, so learning a new task does not degrade previously learned experts, and (R2) selective forward transfer, so useful prior experts improve learning while unhelpful lateral connections are suppressed. (P2) Compositional orchestration. The learned experts form a library , where each policy is paired with a language descriptor . Given a long-horizon instruction that cannot be solved by a single policy, the planner decomposes it into sub-task descriptions and assigns each one to an expert, Here, returns an ordered list of sub-tasks, and routes each to a matching expert in the library. If no expert applies, , triggering acquisition of a new expert under (P1). The selected expert is then executed closed-loop on the robot state. We require both and to be implemented by a frozen, general-purpose planner rather than a task-specific trained module. (P3) Cross-embodiment reuse. The same library should support transfer across robot embodiments. Given experts learned on a source robot, such as a Sawyer in MetaWorld or a Panda in Robosuite, the learner should acquire a new skill on a target embodiment, such as a UR5e or a real FR3, from only a few target demonstrations. Since all policies share the same task-space action interface, prior experts can be reused when learning downstream skills on new robots. Methodology PNN-LoRA: Gated Low-Rank Lateral Transfer sec:pnnlora A PNN represents each task with a dedicated network column whose parameters are frozen after training~ pnn . When task arrives, a new column is appended while all previous columns remain fixed as shown in Fig. fig:lora_architec . Transfer to the new task occurs only through lateral connections from these frozen columns. Each column consists of blocks of width . Block has its own affine map and, for , receives one lateral adapter from every previous column . With , the activations are where is a ReLU nonlinearity for the hidden blocks, are the frozen features of parent column , and is a per-parent gate. The final block outputs the mean and log-standard-deviation over the action space , which together give the sampled action and its associated uncertainty. title: MQCODet: Modality Quality-Guided Collaborative Optimization for UAV-Based RGB-T Tiny Pedestrian Detection
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based RGB-thermal (RGB-T) remote sensing provides complementary visual and thermal information for pedestrian perception under complex aerial observation conditions. However, detecting tiny pedestrians in UAV-based RGB-T imagery remains challenging due to cross-modal spatial heterogeneity, manifested as modality quality imbalance and spatial position misalignment. Existing RGB-T detectors primarily address these challenges at the feature fusion stage, without establishing an effective coupling between feature fusion and object localization, potentially resulting in suboptimal detection performance. To address this limitation, we introduce a Modality Quality-Guided Collaborative Optimization Detector (MQCODet), which extends modality quality from a fusion prior to a localization supervision cue. Specifically, we propose a Dynamic Calibration and Region-Aware Fusion (DCRF) module that progressively refines cross-modal spatial alignment and performs region-aware fusion to generate reliable multi-scale features and a scene-level modality quality prior. We further design an Efficient Contextual Interaction (ECI) encoder to enhance multi-scale feature interaction while preserving fine-grained spatial details. Moreover, we propose a Modality-Aware Adaptive (MAA) loss that incorporates the modality prior and object scale to adaptively balance spatial consistency and geometric similarity for localization supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MQCODet surpasses state-of-the-art methods on two UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection benchmarks while achieving real-time inference on the edge platform.

UAV-based RGB-T tiny object detection modality awareness region-aware fusion bounding-box regression Introduction sec:intro Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based RGB-T pedestrian detection has emerged as an important remote sensing task. UAV-based sensing systems provide flexible observation perspectives and broad spatial coverage, while RGB and thermal modalities offer complementary visual information. These advantages enable reliable pedestrian perception across diverse scenarios, including disaster rescue~ zhang2025aerial , traffic monitoring~ sun2022dronevehicle,ma2025multi , and public surveillance~ du2018uav,zhu2018visdrone . Despite its practical value and potential for all-day perception, UAV-based RGB-T pedestrian detection remains challenging under complex imaging conditions, where modality quality exhibits substantial variation across scenes and spatial regions. These variations stem from the distinct motion patterns of UAV platforms~ ma2026tracking and the different imaging mechanisms of RGB and thermal sensors~ hwang2015multispectral , resulting in pronounced cross-modal spatial heterogeneity that hinders reliable tiny pedestrian detection. Specifically, this heterogeneity mainly exhibits two aspects: modality quality imbalance and spatial position misalignment. Modality quality imbalance refers to the spatial heterogeneity of modality quality. For example, the visible modality degrades in low-light regions, whereas the thermal modality becomes unreliable in areas with high background radiation (see Fig.~ fig:motivation (a)). Such spatially varying modality quality complicates cross-modal feature fusion, as unreliable responses may impair object representations. Furthermore, inherent viewpoint differences between RGB and thermal sensors lead to spatial misalignment of the same object across the paired images, which is particularly detrimental to tiny pedestrians with limited spatial details and high sensitivity to slight spatial displacement (see Fig.~ fig:motivation (b)). Consequently, effectively mitigating cross-modal spatial heterogeneity is essential for UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection under complex aerial conditions. Existing RGB-T detection methods have explored different strategies to mitigate cross-modal spatial heterogeneity. Illumination-aware fusion methods~ tinet,hu2025ei2det,Zhao_2025_ICCV exploit environmental conditions to adaptively adjust the contributions of RGB and thermal modalities during fusion, improving robustness to global or local illumination changes. However, illumination cues alone cannot capture cross-modal spatial correspondence, potentially resulting in suboptimal fusion under spatial position misalignment. Alignment-aware fusion paradigms~ yuan2024c2former,guo2024damsdet,peng2025coxnet establish cross-modal spatial correspondence before or during feature interaction, mitigating the adverse effects of spatial position misalignment. Nevertheless, these paradigms focus on spatial correspondence without explicitly modeling spatially varying modality reliability, potentially limiting adaptive modality fusion. Recently, some works~ zhang2023rgbtdroneperson,zhang2025c2dff have explored quality-aware fusion strategies that incorporate regional modality quality to guide spatially adaptive fusion, enabling dynamic weighting of modality contributions. However, these methods primarily use modality quality to guide feature fusion, without propagating this reliability information to subsequent localization. This separation between quality-aware feature construction and quality-agnostic localization is particularly problematic for UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection, where localization is sensitive to local modality reliability. Building on this insight, we propose a Modality Quality-Guided Collaborative Optimization Detector (MQCODet) for UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection. MQCODet is a unified detection framework that propagates modality quality from cross-modal feature fusion to localization supervision, while jointly enhancing cross-modal alignment and contextual feature interaction. First, we propose a Dynamic Calibration and Region-Aware Fusion (DCRF) module to address modality quality imbalance and spatial position misalignment. DCRF progressively refines cross-modal spatial alignment and performs region-aware fusion to generate reliable multi-scale fused features and a scene-level modality prior. Second, we introduce an Efficient Contextual Interaction (ECI) encoder that enhances multi-scale feature interaction while preserving fine-grained spatial details through lightweight channel recalibration. Third, we introduce a Modality-Aware Adaptive (MAA) loss that leverages a scene-level modality prior to adaptively balance spatial consistency and geometric similarity for localization supervision. As shown in Fig.~ fig:bubble , MQCODet achieves a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off on RGBTDronePerson, demonstrating its effectiveness while maintaining computational efficiency. The main contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose a modality quality-guided collaborative optimization paradigm that extends modality quality from a fusion prior to a localization supervision cue, unifying quality-aware feature fusion and reliability-aware localization for UAV-based RGB-T tiny pedestrian detection. We develop a Dynamic Calibration and Region-Aware Fusion module with an Efficient Contextual Interaction encoder to refine cross-modal spatial alignment, enhance regional feature fusion, and preserve fine-grained details in multi-scale representations. We introduce a modality-aware adaptive loss that leverages scene-level modality prior and object scale to adaptively balance spatial consistency and geometric similarity for accurate pedestrian localization. Recent UAV detectors exploit RGB and thermal observations to improve all-day perception. COXNet~ peng2025coxnet couples adaptive alignment with cross-level scale integration. IM-CMDet~ luo2025imcmdet combines intramodal enhancement and cross-modal fusion. Dynamic gated fusion~ gu2025uav,li2025elnet adjusts multimodal feature aggregation, while LF-DETR~ qi2026lfdetr strengthens frequency cues within a DETR detector. title: Object Count Generalization Is an Interface Problem: Warping a Frozen Skill Instead of Retraining It
comment: 37 pages, 15 figures, 15 tables. Submitted to International Conference on Learning Representations 2027. Code, videos and full results are available at https://hhi-robot-learning.github.io/wave-website/
summary: Reinforcement learning policies for robot manipulation degrade when the number of objects N in the scene grows beyond the training range. This is a covariate shift that also changes the dimension of the state. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which extends a pretrained single-object skill to many objects without updating its weights. WAVE has three parts. First, a selection policy picks the one object the robot works on next. Second, a warping policy reads a local view of the scene around that object, whose size does not depend on N. It emits a multiplier and an offset for every quantity the skill reads and every action it outputs. Third, the skill acts under this affine warp. It is shown a scene that holds a single object, while the warp steers it around the objects it is not shown and edits the actions that are sent to the robot. Both the selection and warping policies are trained with PPO on the multi-object reward and use the skill as a black box, so WAVE is task-general and skill-agnostic. It requires only that the skill was trained on the same embodiment and that every object has a goal pose. We also bound the number of attempts needed to place all N objects, assuming positive expected net progress per attempt, and measure this progress for each object count. We evaluate WAVE on cube arrangement tasks with a gantry robot and with a Franka Panda arm. Trained with at most nine cubes, it generalizes zero-shot to several times its training count, on the gantry to scenes of up to thirty cubes. Published methods that learn multi-object manipulation show count generalization up to six objects. Fine-tuning the skill, learning from the same local view without it, and an entity transformer, even when distilled from the pretrained skill, all collapse within their training counts under the same training budget.

Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) learns a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward of an agent interacting with an environment~ sutton2018 . Policies trained this way for robot manipulation solve the scene they were trained in and often degrade when that scene changes~ kirk2023 . This work addresses a covariate shift~ shimodaira2000 , a change of the state distribution under unchanged dynamics. In our case the number of objects in the scene changes, so a policy trained with a few objects is deployed with many. Such a shift also changes the dimension of the state, and appears for example when a robot that has learned to manipulate a few plates is asked to fill a dishwasher. This work asks what can be learned around a frozen pretrained skill to enable zero-shot generalization to object counts unseen during training. Two families of prior work address this shift. Set and relational architectures let a policy act at any object count~ zaheer2017,zambaldi2018 . Robot policies built this way learn the manipulation behavior itself~ li2020,haramati2024,lanier2019,li2022 . That is, a learned policy issues the robot command at every control step, and no primitive, planner or model supplies the motion. Such policies report whole-task success of at most at six objects~ li2020 and at most at eight~ park2025a,li2025dqc on their respective benchmarks. Further, the theory of size extrapolation shows that networks which pool over every entity can fail to generalize to sets larger than those seen in training~ xu2021a,velikovi2025,haramati2024 . Works that keep a trained skill frozen and learn a correction around it~ silver2018,johannink2019,yuan2024,wagenmaker2025, hirschowitz2026,zhang2023b,dcadand,policynda absorb dynamics shifts, sensor changes and task mismatch, but none edits both the input and the output interface of a frozen skill to generalize across the object count. We propose WAVE (Warping Actions and Views of an Expert), which learns a warping policy around a frozen skill. Because the skill can already place one object, training only has to learn the corrections needed for many. Figure~ fig:architecture gives an overview, and our contributions are as follows. We propose WAVE, which composes a frozen single-object skill with a learned warping policy. The policy applies an affine edit to every input and output channel of the skill and is trained with PPO. It uses the skill as a black box, so it applies to any goal-conditioned skill trained on the same robot and to any task that gives every object a goal pose. We show which shifts such a warp can absorb (Section~ sec:absorb ). We train WAVE on six cube arrangement tasks, on a gantry robot and on a Franka Panda arm with a gripper and with a pusher, with at most nine objects and evaluate it zero-shot on up to thirty. On the gantry, this is two to five times the largest count to which published methods that learn the manipulation itself generalize. We compare WAVE with ten baselines spanning skill fine-tuning, distillation, subgoal control, scratch-trained entity transformers~ haramati2024 , and a fixed-per-episode input edit~ zhang2023b . They either fail beyond six cubes, even with a non-learned scripted selection of fulfillable goals, or learn their training counts but extrapolate worse. We also ablate the parts of WAVE's architecture. Related Work sec:related A large body of work builds policies that are defined for any object count by making the network permutation invariant over a set of object entities~ zaheer2017,zambaldi2018 . Entity-centric RL (ECRL)~ haramati2024 learns per-object latent particles from pixels and trains an Entity Interaction Transformer with three objects that generalizes to six objects. EC-Diffuser~ ecdiffuser2025 replaces RL by behavior cloning with an entity-centric diffusion Transformer. li2020 stack blocks with an attention-based graph network trained by a curriculum that adds blocks, and their reported success declines beyond the counts the curriculum visited. Relational, curriculum and slot-based variants~ mambelli2022,lanier2019,li2022,locatello2020,zadaianchuk2021 and the successors of ECRL~ ecdiffuser2025,haramati2026 report whole-task success at up to six objects. li2020 show up to nine blocks as a figure without values, haramati2024 show a twelve-object sort qualitatively, and the stacking variant of that line is evaluated at two to four objects~ haramati2026 . FIOC-WM~ feng2025fiocwm learns an object-centric world model from pixels and generalizes over object attributes and skill compositions; its count test, three to eight objects, covers pushing and toggling but no stacking or other precise placement. janisch2020 reach thirty blocks in a symbolic block world without physics simulation. Slot models expose the count through their number of slots~ zimmermann2023,krimmel2024 . Theoretical work on size extrapolation shows that networks which pool over every entity can fail on larger sets~ yehudai2021,velikovi2025 , and that they can generalize when the local structure they see does not change with the count~ yehudai2021,ouellette2024 . Large-scale RL learns stacking at a fixed small count~ lampe2024,macaluso2026 . On the offline cube benchmarks, which train one policy per count, the best published baseline completes the stacking goal in of episodes with two cubes and in none with three or four~ ogbench2024 . The hierarchical methods evaluated at eight cubes reach at most averaged over five goals, from success on the rearrangement goals and almost none on the two stacking goals~ park2025a,li2025dqc . In task and motion planning, count generalization is easy, because a discrete search over a known symbolic model scales to any number of objects and motion primitives supply the manipulation~ garrett2020,chitnis2022 . The same holds when a network selects scripted primitives~ zeng2020,lin2021 . Neither applies here, since we have no model and no primitives, so the learned manipulation itself must generalize to more objects. Methods that pass arguments to a frozen executor~ riedmiller2023 assume that the executor works for every argument. Language and vision-language models can decompose a task into steps and call a skill for each step~ ahn2022,liang2023 . In our setting, such a planner would replace the selection policy, while each step would still be executed by the skill. This execution is the limiting part, since with a scripted order over fulfillable goals the unchanged skill completes no episode with three cubes (Table~ tab:exp-baselines ). A language-based planner could therefore be combined with the warp, which we leave for future work. A single-object skill can also be reused without freezing it. Kickstarting distills a teacher policy into a new student while the student learns the task reward~ schmitt2018 , and jump-start RL rolls a guide policy for the first part of every episode and hands the rest to an exploration policy, moving the switch point earlier as the exploration policy improves~ uchendu2022 . Both leave the multi-object behavior to a network trained on the new task. Another line of work keeps a trained policy or controller fixed and learns an edit of its interface. Most improve the policy on its own task and distribution, by an action residual~ silver2018,johannink2019,yuan2024,ankile2024 , steered diffusion noise~ wagenmaker2025 , or inserted latents and gated activations~ yu2026,miao2026 . Others address a shift, such as changed dynamics~ hirschowitz2026 , heterogeneous or missing sensors~ dcadand , a task mismatch around a shared backbone~ policynda , a new behavior mode~ das2026 , or out-of-distribution scenes~ liu2026 , but never a change in the number of objects. Closest to our approach, zhang2023b learn diagonal projections of the state and the action of a frozen pivoting skill with a policy gradient to transfer it to objects of other shapes and sizes. Their state projection depends on a learned descriptor of the manipulated object and is constant over an episode, while their action projection also depends on the current state. WAVE keeps the frozen skill and the per-channel edits, adds an offset on every channel, and conditions both edits at every step on the multi-object scene observation. Appendix~ sec:app-positioning compares these methods with ours. Methodology sec:method sec:intuition WAVE takes a skill that can move a single object to its goal and uses it, without changing its weights, to arrange many objects. A selection policy picks one object at a time, and is shown a scene in which this object is the only one. The other objects are still there, so a warping policy reads the neighborhood of the object and bends the inputs and actions of where needed, for example to steer the robot around a stack or to let go of a cube on top of another (Figure~ fig:architecture ). Where nothing is in the way, acts unchanged. Warping the skill is necessary because, with many objects, the behavior of itself has to change. Choosing the next object or sending to intermediate subgoals, as in hierarchical RL, leaves this behavior unchanged. For example, a subgoal can bring a cube above a stack, but it does not change how releases the cube there. A policy that adds a correction to the action of does change the behavior. However, still sees the unedited scene and moves along paths that collide with objects it is not shown, so the correction has to cancel part of 's action at every step. The warp edits both what sees and what it outputs. Editing the input makes itself compute a corrected action, and editing the output produces behavior never learned, such as the release onto a stack. First, can already place a single object, so it is a strong exploration prior that makes multi-object tasks learnable and training only learns the corrections needed with many objects. title: KineState-SWAM: A Surgical World Action Model with Explicit Kinematics and Causal Interaction Dynamics
summary: Existing surgical world models often leave implicit how instrument motion drives localized tissue responses and how interaction history informs subsequent actions. We introduce KineState-SWAM, a surgical world-action model coupling action prediction and video generation through a persistent interaction state, separating kinematically determined instrument motion from learned scene evolution. A flow-matching policy predicts joint trajectories conditioned on interaction state, robot configuration, and task instruction. Kinematic Geometry Conditioning converts these trajectories into surface-motion tokens and spatially aligned instrument renderings using calibrated URDF kinematics. Causal Interaction Dynamics recurrently updates the state through geometry-guided attention and motion-aligned feature transport, carrying interaction history into subsequent action predictions without intermediate video synthesis. The State-Geometry Adapter combines state-dependent spatial modulation with localized geometric residuals to guide video generation. Interaction-aware supervision emphasizes tissue responses near instrument working regions. We introduce dVRK-Chole5.2k, comprising 5,255 videos spanning 17 surgical tasks. Experiments demonstrate improved action accuracy and video fidelity over evaluated baselines within matched action-conditioning settings. Ablations support preserving and transporting interaction states for long-horizon prediction.

Introduction sec:introduction Learning to anticipate the consequences of robot actions is an important step toward surgical world models that support simulation and policy learning~ he2025cosmos,tejero2026nvidia . Such models must account for both articulated instrument motion and the evolution of deformable tissue. In manipulation tasks such as grasping, retracting, and dissecting, the visual consequences of an action depend on the ongoing instrument--tissue interaction. These consequences also shape the context in which subsequent actions are selected. A useful surgical world--action model should therefore connect action prediction to scene evolution while retaining interaction history, providing a consistent description of what the robot does and how the scene responds. Recent video foundation models, including CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo-1.5, and Wan, provide rich visual and motion priors for text- and image-conditioned video synthesis (Figure~ fig:overview (a))~ yang2025cogvideox,wu2025hunyuanvideo,wan2025wan . Building on such priors, embodied world models connect visual prediction with robot actions. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:overview (b), Ctrl-World supports action-conditioned rollouts through frame-level conditioning and pose-conditioned memory retrieval~ guo2026ctrl . World--action models further integrate action generation (Figure~ fig:overview (c)): DreamZero jointly models future videos and actions, OpenWAM investigates modular world--action pretraining, and X-WAM extends joint prediction to RGB-D observations with asynchronous denoising~ ye2026world,wang2026openwam,guo2026unified . In the surgical domain, Endora explores generative endoscopy simulation, while Surgical Vision World Model learns latent actions from unlabeled surgical videos~ li2024endora,koju2025surgical . Cosmos-H-Surgical uses generated videos and inferred pseudokinematics to support policy learning, whereas Cosmos-H-Dreams enables real-time, kinematics-driven streaming simulation~ he2025cosmos,tejero2026nvidia . SurgVista further addresses tissue-deformation consistency and long-horizon prediction drift through deformation regularization and drift-adaptation training~ pan2026surgvista . Collectively, these advances extend video generation toward action-aware world modeling, motivating more explicit representations of robot motion and its influence on scene evolution. A complementary line of research introduces spatially aligned visual and geometric conditions to control world-model predictions (Figure~ fig:overview (d)). DWM conditions interaction videos on scene and hand-mesh renderings, while GigaWorld-1 combines spatially aligned controls with hierarchical visual history for robot-policy evaluation~ kim2026dexterous,team2026gigaworld . Robot kinematics provides a direct route from joint trajectories to such visual conditions. BridgeV2W renders pixel-aligned embodiment masks from URDF models and camera parameters, Kinema4D projects kinematic robot trajectories into spatiotemporal pointmaps, and GeniWorld uses URDF-rendered visual actions to condition environmental dynamics~ chen2026bridgev2w,xu2026kinema4d,gu2026geniworld . Surgical methods develop related control interfaces tailored to instrument structure and scene appearance. Surg-UniWorld integrates edge, depth, and optical-flow conditions through modality experts anchored to first-frame appearance and hierarchical semantic masks~ zhou2026surg . SurgCast predicts future instrument skeletons from current structure, robot state, and prospective actions, then injects the predicted geometry and derived motion descriptors through geometric residuals and conditioning modulation~ liu2026surgcast . KVLR lifts articulated kinematics into image-aligned semantic, depth, orientation, velocity, and acceleration fields, routing these conditions across modalities and motion scales~ li2026articulated . These approaches establish explicit geometric interfaces for controllable surgical video generation. For surgical world--action modeling, we focus on a persistent interaction state that evolves under kinematic motion and provides shared context for both subsequent action prediction and video synthesis. In surgical videos, instrument appearance and motion often occupy larger image regions than the localized tissue responses induced by robot actions. This spatial imbalance can bias global video reconstruction toward instrument fidelity, leaving interaction-induced tissue deformation underemphasized. Yet these local responses are important for understanding how the scene evolves under robot motion and for informing subsequent actions. Given joint trajectories and calibration, URDF kinematics can determine instrument geometry and motion analytically, whereas tissue responses must be inferred from the current scene and its interaction history. This distinction motivates using kinematically determined instrument motion as an explicit driver of learned scene evolution, allowing the model to focus on interaction-dependent tissue changes. A persistent interaction state, recurrently updated under this driver, retains the effects of preceding manipulations and provides shared, history-aware context for subsequent action prediction and scene evolution. We propose KineState-SWAM, a surgical world--action model centered on a persistent interaction state shared by action prediction and video generation. The flow-matching Action Policy predicts an action chunk from this state, the current robot configuration, and the task instruction. Kinematic Geometry Conditioning uses calibrated URDF kinematics to embed joint trajectories into sparse motion tokens that retain surface correspondences and dense, spatially aligned features from instrument renderings. Causal Interaction Dynamics recurrently evolves the state through geometry-guided attention, motion-aligned feature transport, and gated residual updates, linking instrument motion to interaction-dependent scene changes. During training, ground-truth trajectories condition state evolution and video generation while the policy learns future action prediction. At inference, predicted instrument motion drives state updates within each action chunk, whose terminal state and final predicted joint configuration then condition the next policy call. This action--state recurrence preserves interaction history without requiring intermediate video synthesis. To generate video, the State--Geometry Adapter translates the evolving interaction context into spatial feature modulation, while localized geometric residuals guide instrument synthesis. To facilitate systematic evaluation of action and video prediction, we further introduce dVRK-Chole5.2k, comprising 5,255 videos spanning 17 surgical subtasks of robotic cholecystectomy. title: DexLatentWorld: 3D Cross-Embodiment Latent Action World Models for Zero-Shot Robotic Manipulation
summary: World models facilitate planning and control in robotic manipulation by enabling agents to anticipate the consequences of their actions. However, they typically rely on action-labelled interaction data that is costly to acquire and difficult to scale. These models are also often tied to the specific embodiment they were trained on, limiting transferability to previously unseen robot morphologies. We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90%, 92%, and 60% success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72%, 58%, and 28%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86% success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available at https://vinaymohan0409.github.io/DexLatentWorld/.

We introduce a 3D latent-action world model that learns continuous action representations directly from point-cloud observations of retargeted human manipulation demonstrations. A contrastive objective is used to encourage consistent representations of motion across embodiments. The resulting unified latent action space serves directly as the search space for model-predictive control, where sampled latent actions condition particle-based future predictions. Executable robot commands are then recovered from the predicted geometric motion without requiring an embodiment-specific action decoder. Through extensive evaluations, we demonstrate that the learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, transfer to unseen robot embodiments, and support zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries. Following task-agnostic adaptation, our model achieves 90 , 92 , and 60 success on reaching, grasping, and placing, respectively, compared with DexWM's reported 72 , 58 , and 28 . Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot real-world manipulation with an unseen dexterous hand, achieving an 86 success rate across 50 trials on five diverse tasks involving pushing, grasping, and lifting everyday objects. These results highlight the potential of geometry-grounded latent actions as a unified, transferable interface for world-model-based robotic manipulation. Project materials, including demonstration videos and source code, are available on our project page. Introduction sec:intro Developing world models that generalise across diverse robot embodiments remains a central challenge in robotic manipulation. Embodiments differ substantially in their morphologies, kinematics, and action spaces, making it difficult to learn predictive dynamics that transfer across platforms. This motivates learning a unified action representation that enables a world model to capture reusable interaction dynamics across different embodiments, including those unseen during training. A promising direction is to learn action representations directly from observed manipulation, without relying on embodiment-specific action labels Ye_2025_ICLR . Human manipulation videos provide a rich source of such observations, but representations learned from human motion alone may not generalise across robot morphologies. Retargeting these demonstrations to different robot embodiments produces corresponding manipulation trajectories that preserve the underlying interaction despite differences in morphology Zhang_2026_CVPR . These correspondences provide a natural basis for learning a shared latent action space that captures motion rather than embodiment-specific variation. Manipulation involves physical interactions that evolve over space and time. Explicit 3D geometry provides a natural way to represent this evolution, capturing the spatial relationships and contact geometry between interacting entities huang2026pointworld,Ai_2025_SciRob . Representing scene evolution through particle displacements provides direct supervision of physical motion, allowing predictive dynamics to focus on how the scene evolves rather than its visual appearance. We therefore seek to ground both latent action inference and predictive dynamics in a common geometric representation, enabling actions to be learned and their consequences to be predicted in the same physical space. In this work, we introduce DexLatentWorld, a unified 3D latent-action world model for prediction and control, learning continuous action representations directly from action-unlabelled manipulation observations (Fig. fig:overview ). We represent these observations as temporally corresponding 3D scene particles derived from tracked hand–object trajectories, with human manipulation trajectories retargeted to different robot embodiments. A cross-embodiment contrastive objective aligns corresponding human and robot transitions within a shared latent action space, while a forward dynamics model uses these representations to predict scene evolution in 3D particle space. At deployment, we perform closed-loop model-predictive control (MPC) directly in the learned latent action space, evaluating candidate latent-action sequences through their predicted geometric consequences. We then recover executable robot commands from predicted motion using known robot geometry and kinematics, without additional action-labelled demonstrations for training an embodiment-specific latent-to-action decoder. The learned latent actions exhibit controllable and compositional motion, enabling consistent geometric predictions across unseen robot embodiments. To evaluate the effectiveness of these capabilities in robotic manipulation, we employ MPC in both simulation and real-world deployment. We further demonstrate zero-shot manipulation with unseen gripper geometries without embodiment-specific adaptation. Extending to dexterous manipulation, our framework achieves 90 , 92 , and 60 success on reaching, grasping, and placing following task-agnostic domain adaptation, compared with DexWM goswami2026dexwm 's 72 , 58 , and 28 . In real-world deployment, the original pretrained model achieves 86 success on five manipulation tasks with an unseen dexterous hand, without any fine-tuning. Our contributions include: A unified 3D latent-action world model. We introduce a self-supervised framework that combines particle-based scene dynamics with a shared continuous latent action representation, enabling cross-embodiment world modelling and direct latent-space planning and control. A geometry-based prediction-to-control framework. We plan directly in the learned latent action space and recover executable robot targets from predicted 3D motion, avoiding the need for a learned embodiment-specific latent-to-action decoder. Cross-embodiment generalisation and dexterous manipulation. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to held-out end effectors, including real-world dexterous manipulation without world-model adaptation, and task generalisation following task-agnostic domain adaptation. Related Work sec:related_work Action Models. Learning latent actions from observations has emerged as a promising approach to leveraging large-scale, unlabelled interaction data. Typically, an inverse dynamics model encodes changes between observations into a latent action, which is then used to condition a forward dynamics model to predict the resulting scene evolution~ Schmidt_2024_ICLR,Ye_2025_ICLR . However, the learned representation does not necessarily isolate the underlying physical motion. When inferred from images, latent actions may become entangled with viewpoint changes, camera motion, background appearance, and other visual variations. Reconstruction-based objectives can also encourage shortcut learning, allowing latent representations to encode information about future observations rather than meaningful action-like transformations. To address these challenges, prior work has explored approaches including action-category-guided contrastive learning~ Dai_2026_arXiv , early temporal differencing and temporal contrastive learning~ Yang_2026_CVPR , cross-viewpoint reconstruction~ Lee_2026_ICML , and contrastive alignment of video-derived latent actions with executable action tokens learned from robot trajectories~ Zhang_2026_arXiv . We pursue a complementary direction by inferring latent actions directly from 3D point representations of the scene and aligning matched manipulation transitions across embodiments, encouraging shared motion representations across different morphologies. Models for Robotic Manipulation. Learning predictive dynamics has become an important direction in robotic manipulation, supporting model-based planning and control~ Hou_2026_IJRR . Much of this research has explored video-based world models, with more recent approaches investigating explicit 3D representations to model spatial interactions and scene evolution. PointWorld~ huang2026pointworld scales particle-based world modelling to diverse manipulation settings, predicting full-scene 3D point displacements through a shared geometric state and action representation. 3DPWM~ peri2026pwm addresses partial observability through point-cloud completion, enabling dynamics prediction over temporally corresponding 3D geometry. Exploring this direction in dexterous manipulation, He et al.~ he2026scaling train a graph-based particle dynamics model across different hand embodiments, demonstrating generalisation to unseen morphologies. These works demonstrate the effectiveness of explicit 3D representations for predictive modelling in robotic manipulation. Action World Models. Early work demonstrated that latent actions inferred from unlabelled videos could provide a conditioning interface for interactive world modelling~ Bruce_2024_ICML,Gao_2025_ICML . These approaches typically learn the latent action representation separately from the predictive model, limiting their ability to adapt jointly. This motivates joint training to better align action representations with predictive dynamics~ Wang_2026_ICML,Garrido_2026_ICML,Ayalew_2026_arXiv . More recently, LAC-WM~ huang2026lacwm extends latent-action world modelling across human and robot embodiments, learning a unified action representation using action-labelled motion supervision during training. Adapting the model to unseen robots additionally requires labelled robot interactions to train an action-to-latent projector. LAWM-3D~ Yang_2026_arXiv_a introduces geometric constraints and multi-view consistency to learn 3D-aware latent actions; however, its world model remains video-based. Despite these advances, planning for dexterous manipulation remains challenging, with existing approaches employing large sampling budgets and task-specific initialisation~ goswami2026dexwm , manually designed motion primitives~ he2026scaling , or learned motion priors~ Yamada_2025_CoRL,yang2026lamp to facilitate planning and control. In contrast, we optimise directly in the latent action space, recovering executable robot targets from predicted particle motion through known geometry and kinematics. title: Foresight Forcing: Learning Spatial Foresight for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing ($\mathcal{F}^{2}$), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, $\mathcal{F}^{2}$ achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Robotic manipulation has progressed from task-specific systems designed for controlled environments towards generalist policies that operate across diverse objects, instructions, and settings. A general-purpose robot must interpret task instructions, perceive objects in its surroundings, and execute precise actions under varying conditions. Recent advances in large-scale robot learning and pretrained vision-language models have enabled Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla,24pi0,intelligence2025pi05,kim2025openvlaoft . However, action labels do not directly supervise the visual outcomes of those actions. To incorporate this information into policy learning, World Action Models (WAMs) build on visual generative models and couple action learning with world modeling objectives~ imagewam,cen2025worldvla,bi2026motus,yuan2026fastwam . The resulting visual prediction task provides an additional training signal alongside action supervision and enables robot policies to benefit from pretrained generative representations. Most WAMs learn how a scene evolves by predicting future RGB observations or visual latents. These objectives encode task-relevant spatial relationships alongside object appearance, background, and viewpoint, leaving the geometric transitions that matter for control implicit. Geometry Forcing shows that pretrained 3D features can improve the geometric consistency of video generation~ wu2025geometryforcing , and geometry-aware WAMs have explored geometric supervision for manipulation~ ma2026geosemwam,zhang2026mecowam,li2026wam4d . For robot control, the 3D changes needed to advance the task provide a natural target for this supervision. Placing an object requires changing its pose relative to a target, while opening a drawer requires changing the configuration of an articulated object. Modeling such transitions gives the policy a way to anticipate how the scene needs to change when generating actions. Therefore, we introduce Foresight Forcing ( ), a WAM that fuses correspondence-aligned transitions in 3D geometry feature space of foundation models into spatial transition queries for action generation, rather than directly predicting explicit 3D motions (Figure~ fig:teaser ). During training, a frozen VGGT teacher~ wang2025vggt extracts patch features from an aligned observation pair, and their temporal differences serve as dense targets for the queries. A shared updater progressively refines the queries after each double block of the visual backbone using information from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state. We supervise the queries to match the direction and scale of the teacher targets and feed the refined queries directly to the action expert. At inference, the policy predicts the queries from its current inputs without access to future observations or the teacher. We evaluate on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin~2.0, and real-world manipulation tasks to assess manipulation performance, robustness, and inference efficiency. achieves state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real robot. 0pt Our contributions are summarized as follows: [topsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt,parsep=0pt] Transition-centric geometric supervision. During training, we align the refined queries with the frozen 3D teacher targets in direction and scale. The queries directly condition the action expert. Manipulation performance and robustness. Evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, with state-of-the-art average success rates on RoboTwin~2.0 Full and Clean-to-Random. On six real-world tasks, achieves a mean task score of 85.8 , exceeding ImageWAM and by 15.6 and 2.3 percentage points, respectively. Related Work sec:related World Action Models. World Action Models (WAMs) jointly learn action generation and future visual prediction through autoregressive video-action modeling, shared latent representations, compact future conditions, or image-based prediction~ cen2025worldvla,bi2026motus,lingbotva,su2026worldguidance,yuan2026fastwam,imagewam . Visual prediction provides supervision for control, even when future images are not generated during execution. Building on ImageWAM, we study a complementary signal: the spatial transition between current and future observations. 3D Representations for Visual Generation. Feed-forward 3D models recover spatial structure and dense features from images. DUSt3R and MASt3R establish pairwise geometry and correspondences~ wang2024dust3r,leroy2024mast3r ; subsequent models extend inference to multiple views and image streams~ yang2025fast3r,wang2025cut3r,wang2025vggt,wang2025pi3,lin2025da3,wang2026vggtomega . REPA aligns diffusion representations with pretrained visual features~ yu2025repa , while geometric features guide consistent video generation and image editing~ wu2025geometryforcing,liu2026camgeo,ma2026groupediting . We use a frozen VGGT to encode paired observations and supervise the policy with correspondence-aligned differences between its current and future features. Geometry in Action Learning. Existing action models incorporate geometry either as an observation or predicted spatial representation, or as supervision for learned features. The former includes geometric inputs, point flow, trajectories, future pointmaps, and spatially structured actions~ huang2026pointworld,park2026pointwam,wang2026unitas,chen2026mvgwam,yan2026flexpi,guo2026xwam,zhang2026mecowam . The latter uses geometric objectives or distilled priors to shape policy representations~ li2026spatial,ma2026geosemwam,li2026wam4d . Foresight Forcing instead supervises dedicated spatial queries with correspondence-aligned temporal differences in 3D teacher features. The queries are predicted from current inputs and directly condition the action expert. Method sec:method World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions. title: WorldLeague: Benchmarking Physical Agency
summary: AI systems can now operate Blender, follow instructions in complex video games, and manipulate objects with robot arms. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Answering this question requires testing systems on tasks that demand different combinations of perception, memory, planning, and action. We introduce \textbf{WorldLeague}, a benchmark that compares AI systems on a common set of \textbf{60 simulated robot tasks} by measuring progress toward each task's physical goal from the robot's trajectory. Robots explore scenes to gather evidence in \textbf{WorldSeek}, rearrange objects in \textbf{WorldShape}, and adapt to changes in \textbf{WorldShift}. Tying these goals to a single control interface limits which AI systems can be compared. In WorldLeague, vision-language models (VLMs) choose targets and motions, while vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs) use their native controls. For each of six capability dimensions, we measure how much progress a system makes toward its goals (Interactive Score) and how often it achieves them (physical success rate). Together, these measures form the system's \emph{Physical Agency Profile}. Among 13 representative AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 achieves 13 of the 60 goals and earns the highest mean Interactive Score (28.58/100). Fable leads in four dimensions, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra tie for first on rule-following tasks. Even when VLMs answer every final question correctly, they receive an Interactive Score of zero in 71.8\% of those episodes. WorldLeague gives Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI a shared basis for comparing what AI systems achieve autonomously, from partial progress toward a physical goal to full goal completion. Project Webpage: https://xyangzhou.github.io/WorldLeague
