Example tasks across six dimensions in WorldSeek (blue, right), WorldShape (green, left), and WorldShift (red, below). fig:worldleague_overview 0.62 Introduction sec:introduction Foundation models have recently become a promising direction for building general-purpose robots~ team2024octo . In digital environments, agents built on frontier models can follow instructions in open-world video games~ bolton2025sima and turn visual references into editable 3D scenes in Blender~ fang2026blenderworld . The range of tasks that physical robots can perform has also grown~ han2026video2sim2real,liu2026egoengine . Robots have performed long-horizon household tasks, such as cleaning a kitchen or bedroom, in homes they had never seen during training~ intelligence2025pi . To clean an unfamiliar kitchen, a robot must use what it sees to decide what to do next. Embodied AI systems connect perception to action in different ways~ huang2026best . A vision-language model (VLM) can identify an object from a spatial description~ chen2026behavior and estimate its distance from other objects~ chen2024spatialvlm . With a robot interface, it can use such judgments to choose where to move or grasp~ chen2026show . Vision-language-action (VLA) models produce robot actions directly from instructions and visual observations~ kim2024openvla . For example, Gemini Robotics 1.5 interleaves reasoning and action during multi-step manipulation~ team2025gemini . World-action models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and robot actions~ li2026causal,shen2026world,wang2026openwam,li2026badwam . This approach has enabled closed-loop manipulation on new tasks and in new environments~ ye2026world . Across these approaches, the ambition is the same. A person specifies a physical goal and leaves the system to decide how to achieve it~ liu2023agentbench,chen2026show,li2026vision,li2026sponge,qian2025wristworld,robotics2026envisioning . We call the system making those decisions the agent and its capacity to choose and execute actions through a body its physical agency. The decisions an agent must make depend on the goal. To find a hidden object, it must decide where to look and what to move out of the way~ das2018embodied,danielczuk2019mechanical,huang2026era . To put that object through a narrow opening, it must also choose an orientation that fits. An agent may therefore find the right object and still fail to put it away. This leads us to the central question of our study. What range of physical goals can today's AI systems achieve autonomously? Organizing robot benchmarks around household activities~ li2023behavior,nasiriany2026robocasa365 obscures what success on each activity establishes about an agent. Consider a robot asked to deliver a cup. If the user names the cup and it is in plain sight, the robot can select it from its current view. If the user asks for the cup that has moved since the robot last visited the room, the robot must use an earlier observation to decide what to pick up. Both tasks count as cup delivery. Yet success on the first leaves the decisive requirement of the second entirely untested. To establish the range of an agent's physical abilities, we must vary what the agent has to work out for itself and verify that its actions bring about the requested outcome. We introduce WorldLeague, a benchmark of 60 simulated robot tasks organized by the physical demands that determine success. We evaluate VLMs, VLAs, and WAMs against shared goals and constraints. For each task, the robot's trajectory shows which goal requirements it satisfies and whether it completes the task. The tasks span three tracks, each defined by what the robot must do to achieve its goal. WorldSeek tests navigation and goal grounding as systems explore and gather evidence. WorldShape tests geometric reconfiguration and physical reasoning as systems change the scene. WorldShift tests temporal memory and constraint management as systems track a changing world and recover from disturbances. The three tracks span six capability dimensions (Sec.~ sec:world_challenges ). We group each task by its primary challenge, and a single task can draw on capabilities from several dimensions. To compare systems across these tasks, we instantiate each goal in a scene with specified objects, initial conditions, and constraints. Physical predicates check conditions such as stable placement or recovery after a disturbance. We inspect all 60 task--scene pairs, verify that reference runs meet the goals and constraints, and check the scoring conditions against the task specifications. Each system pursues its goal through physical interaction. For VLMs, our decision-preserving action abstraction draws on how sensorimotor mechanisms coordinate fine-grained human movement~ todorov2002optimal, wolpert2011principles, graybiel2008habits . The interface executes motions, and the agent chooses the targets, action parameters, sequences, and responses to feedback that shape the outcome. We adapt a motion interface~ chen2026show to implement this abstraction on R1~ li2023behavior . VLA and WAM policies use their native interfaces under shared task goals, constraints, and physical scoring rules. We score the resulting trajectory for progress toward individual requirements and for physical success, which requires satisfying the full goal and all task constraints. A Physical Agency Profile reports Interactive Score for progress and physical success rate for complete goal achievement in each capability dimension. For VLMs, terminal question answering (QA) provides an auxiliary measure of scene understanding, outcome recognition, and memory within the same episodes. Among the 13 evaluated embodied AI systems, Claude Fable 5.2 earns the highest overall Interactive Score, 28.58 out of 100, and achieves physical success on 13 of its 60 tasks. Fable leads in navigation, goal grounding, geometric reconfiguration, and temporal memory, while GPT-6.1-Sol and GPT-6-Astra lead in constraint management. The trajectory analysis also identifies goal requirements that remain unmet after systems make physical progress. Of 347 VLM episodes with full terminal QA credit, 249 (71.8 ) receive an Interactive Score of zero. These results show that goal-relevant understanding and successful intermediate actions can coexist with unmet physical goals. Turning demonstrated capabilities into desired physical outcomes is central to Embodied AI, Physical AI, and Agentic AI, which share the ambition of building systems that can pursue human goals through their own actions in the world. WorldLeague turns this ambition into a common experiment. A person specifies the desired outcome, an agent determines how to pursue it through a body, and the evaluation verifies what it achieves in the physical environment. Evaluating systems against common goals and physical success criteria allows advances in perception, reasoning, and control to be assessed in terms of what they enable these systems to accomplish~ wang2026practical . Our broader aim is to make autonomous goal achievement a shared measure of progress for AI systems that act in the world. We make three contributions to the evaluation of physical agency in embodied AI systems. We test physical agency by goal achievement on tasks with different capability combinations. We build and validate WorldLeague, a suite of 60 tasks that measures progress and physical success across six capability dimensions using shared goals and scoring rules. We compare the capability profiles of 13 systems and identify goal requirements that remain unmet in episodes with correct answers or partial physical progress. Related Work sec:related_work The Demands of Physical Goals BEHAVIOR-1K~ li2023behavior takes everyday household activities as the unit of evaluation. Within a single activity, what a robot must decide can change as it acts~ liu2023reflect . In RoboQuest~ renhang2026roboquest , a robot uses trial impressions to decide how to stamp the requested pattern. MeMoREval~ wang2026should makes a later request depend on what the system encountered earlier, while RobotAgentBench~ mao2026robotagentbench introduces disturbances that require an agent to revise an ongoing manipulation. WorldLeague organizes goals by the primary challenge they pose. Finding a specified object and fitting it through a narrow opening both require identifying the object, but the second goal also requires reasoning about orientation and clearance. Grouping tasks this way lets us trace how success varies across exploration, physical transformation, and adaptation. Action Abstraction for Embodied AI Systems An action interface determines which decisions the agent makes~ yang2025embodiedbench . SayCan~ ahn2022can uses a skill's feasibility to guide selection, and Code as Policies~ liang2023code lets a model compose robot actions in a program. Inner Monologue~ huang2022inner feeds execution outcomes back into planning. Show-Harness~ chen2026show translates agent-selected commands through an embodiment-specific interpreter, and HumanCLAW~ siyao2026humanclaw uses the separation between action selection and motor execution to study how VLMs direct a body. WorldHarness adapts Show-Harness to preserve the VLM's decisions throughout a task. To place an object, the VLM chooses where to grasp, how far to move, and when to release. The controller executes the motion and returns feedback that the VLM can use to correct its next move. VLA and world-action policies pursue the same goals through their native interfaces. Measuring Physical Goal Achievement ESI-Bench~ closesesi lets systems move and manipulate objects to gather evidence for a spatial answer. Once the physical outcome is fixed, terminal QA probes the VLM's understanding of the scene and its actions. title: Generalizing Agentic Robotics via Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
summary: Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. In large language model (LLM) post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) has been used to consolidate domain specialists into a single generalist. Yet whether MOPD can build a generalist planner for agentic robotics, how well it performs, and how it compares with other consolidation methods remain unexplored. In this paper, we systematically study these questions: we introduce Robo-MOPD, which trains a single student on closed-loop rollouts in simulation under token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists, and compare it with weight merging, off-policy specialist supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-domain online RL. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9% and 44.8% success (58.9% average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on LIBERO-10.
full_text: Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9 and 44.8 success (58.9 average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on . Introduction sec:intro Building general-purpose robots has long been a central goal, and agentic robotics has recently emerged as a promising path toward it~ codeaspolicies,capx,harnessvla . In this paradigm, a multimodal planner interprets the instruction, decomposes the task, and acts by calling tools: callable functions that either perceive the scene (e.g., segmenting an object or locating it in 3D) or invoke a frozen low-level executor, such as a motion primitive or a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. After each call, the tool returns feedback from the environment, such as the execution status and updated camera views. This loop closely resembles how recent coding agents work. Because low-level executors handle embodiment-specific control, the planner only reasons and calls tools rather than directly outputting motor commands. As with coding agents, achieving general capability then comes down to obtaining a capable planner. However, most existing planners are proprietary models prompted through APIs~ capx,openrua,harnessvla , whose per-call cost and latency accumulate over long closed-loop episodes and rule out on-device deployment. To remove this dependence, recent post-training methods~ agenticroborl,guava,captain train open-weight models with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL). Each resulting planner is trained for a single domain, i.e., one robot environment together with its executors and tools. Because tools differ across domains in names, arguments, and feedback formats, every domain requires its own planner, and serving domains means deploying planners (Figure~ fig:teaser a). This raises a natural question: A natural approach is to consolidate specialist planners across domains into a single generalist planner. Large language model (LLM) post-training offers four common consolidation methods: weight merging~ modelsoups,taskarithmetic,mopd , off-policy specialist SFT~ mopd,openmopd,kdrl , multi-domain online RL~ nemotroncascade2,mopd,openmopd , and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD)~ mimov2flash,nemotroncascade2,mopd,openmopd . Agentic robotics, however, differs fundamentally from the language and software domains where these methods were developed, so conclusions drawn there do not transfer directly. First, domains differ in robot embodiment, camera views, and low-level tools. Second, the planner acts over dozens of turns from multi-view camera images, repeatedly recovering when stochastic physical execution slips or fails. Third, a physical task often fails because a single step selects the wrong tool or a slightly inaccurate spatial parameter, yet the episode outcome reveals only success or failure, not where the error occurred. Under these conditions, it remains unclear how these consolidation methods should be adapted to agentic robotics and which of them actually work. To answer this question, we compare the four methods on the same Qwen3.5-9B backbone~ qwen35 , with the three training-based methods starting from a shared cross-domain SFT initialization under a matched consolidation rollout budget. To include MOPD in this comparison, we adapt it to agentic robotics as Robo-MOPD (Figure~ fig:overview ). In Robo-MOPD, the generalist student runs closed-loop rollouts in simulation, and the matching frozen specialist scores each token of the student's reasoning and tool call via token-level reverse KL, correcting errors such as a wrong tool or an inaccurate coordinate at the step where they occur. This same scoring scheme works across all robots because, even when embodiments and tools differ, every turn shares the same format: camera images and tool feedback go in, and reasoning plus a tool call come out. Across all training-based methods, we drop prior-turn reasoning from the context~ stateopd , subsample a random subset of turns per episode~ agenticroborl , and balance the loss across episode lengths~ minillm,mopd,kdrl and domains~ openmopd to keep training efficient and balanced over long, multi-view episodes (Section~ sec:method ). All low-level executors~ pi05,rldx remain frozen throughout. At test time, a single generalist planner operates robots across all domains without any specialist. We evaluate on tabletop LIBERO-PRO~ libero,liberopro and mobile-kitchen RoboCasa365~ robocasa,robocasa365 and obtain three findings. Robo-MOPD reaches 72.9 on LIBERO-PRO and 44.8 on RoboCasa365, the only method to surpass both 9B specialists, achieving a 58.9 average while all baseline methods fall below the specialists' 56.9 (Figure~ fig:teaser b,c and Table~ tab:main-consolidation ). On the long-horizon LIBERO-10 suite, neither off-policy SFT nor online RL improves over the shared SFT initialization, while Robo-MOPD leads online RL by 13.0 percentage points (Figure~ fig:liberopro-suites ). On LIBERO-PRO, budget-exhaustion failures drop from 31.6 under online RL to 20.3 , while voluntary finish() calls on unsolved episodes rise from 2.6 to 6.8 : on hard tasks, Robo-MOPD stops voluntarily after failed attempts rather than repeating actions until the 100-turn limit like the baselines (Section~ sec:exp-analysis and Figure~ fig:suppl-turn-timeout ). Our contributions are as follows: Systematic comparison. We present the first systematic comparison of four consolidation methods for agentic robot planners: weight merging, off-policy specialist SFT, multi-domain online RL, and MOPD. Robo-MOPD. To our knowledge, we are the first to bring MOPD to agentic robotics, adapting it to closed-loop multimodal planning so that a single generalist planner spans incompatible robot domains toward general-purpose robots. Findings and performance. Consolidation works best when it combines on-policy rollouts with token-level supervision, and its advantage is largest on long-horizon tasks. A single 9B generalist planner surpasses both 9B domain specialists. Related Work sec:related Agentic Robot Harnesses. In agentic robotics, a domain's tool interface and closed-loop execution wrapper is commonly referred to as a robot harness. Language and vision-language models guide robots by sequencing learned skills~ saycan , generating control programs~ codeaspolicies , specifying spatial or keypoint constraints~ voxposer,rekep , or steering motor policies in hierarchies~ hirobot . Recent agentic systems invoke VLA skills or analytic primitives in execution loops~ agenticrobot,harnessvla,physicalagency,vlasastools,pyrua , synthesize control code~ capx , expose modular perception and workspace interfaces~ spark,openrua,unirobotagent , or couple code skills with video and action generation~ aw0 . Other harnesses add spatial measurement~ roboharnessk1 , action rehearsal~ worldactionagent , safe motion routing~ safeharness , task memories~ baton,roboharness , video keyframes~ rvicl , or distilled playbooks~ rhd . Related systems build reusable skill libraries from exploration~ aspire,rats,racap , evolve harnesses online~ dynaharness,roborsi , or optimize primitives before deployment~ rho . Rather than expanding external tools, memories, or skill libraries around a fixed model, we keep each harness and its executors fixed and consolidate planner weights across domains. Post-Training Robot Planners. RL improves embodied planners for spatial reasoning, visual state modeling, and mobile manipulation~ embodiedr,vagen,real . Agent RL systems decouple rollout execution or asynchronous optimization from policy updates~ agentlightning,sao , though joint RL across coding harnesses adapts to interface conventions rather than transferring skills~ multiharnessrl . Within robot harnesses, recent methods fine-tune compact students on teacher or recovery trajectories~ guava,roboharnessk1,worldactionagent , internalize validated interaction logs into an embodied planner~ sensenovaroborsi , or apply group relative policy optimization~ deepseekmath over code and primitive interfaces~ capx,pyrua,guava . CaPtain~ captain trains a 4B planner to write control code over perception and motion primitives via SFT and streaming multi-turn RL~ sao with a physical critic over privileged simulator state. AgenticRoboRL~ agenticroborl pairs a serving proxy with harness adapters to run demonstration SFT without external memories and multi-turn outcome RL across fixed VLA and code harnesses. These methods train one specialist per harness or domain, whereas Robo-MOPD consolidates frozen specialists across harnesses, embodiments, and task suites into one generalist planner. On-Policy Distillation and Specialist Consolidation. Building on interactive imitation learning~ dagger , on-policy distillation trains a student on its own rollouts under dense token divergence supervision~ minillm,gkd,thinkingmachinesopd,rethinkingopd . Recent studies gate teacher guidance on failed rollouts where outcome RL~ dapo lacks positive signal~ kdrl,rstg , fuse bounded distillation advantages with RL~ safopd , or supervise multi-turn text agents under one teacher~ turnopd,memopd,stateopd . Across multiple domains, parameter merging combines weights or task vectors~ modelsoups,taskarithmetic , whereas MOPD routes student rollouts to matching specialists for token supervision in language domains~ mimov2flash,mopd,openmopd,nemotroncascade2 . In robotics, scaling end-to-end VLA policies~ openvla,pi0,pi05,rlinfvla across robots requires large cross-embodiment datasets~ openvla,pi0,xvla , and fine-tuned policies can forget prior skills on new tasks or embodiments~ xvla,vlaopd . Recent work adapts or merges VLAs via task-routed masked adapters~ mergevla , embodiment-specific soft prompts~ xvla , dual-teacher distillation~ dualvla , offline specialist or residual RL rollouts~ rldg,pld , or single-teacher on-policy distillation~ vlaopd,wamopd . Without test-time routing, direct VLA weight merging collapses~ mergevla , and concurrent multi-teacher flow distillation~ flowvlamopd across distinct continuous action spaces still yields consolidated policies that trail individual specialists. Whereas language MOPD shares one text interface and VLA consolidation updates low-level action generators, Robo-MOPD keeps perception tools, motion primitives, and VLA controllers~ pi05,rldx frozen and consolidates high-level planners across distinct harnesses. title: EmboEagle: An Efficient Agentic Embodied Framework for Long-horizon Robotic Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon robotic manipulation demands reliable execution across interdependent stages, yet standalone World-Action Models (WAMs) suffer from compounding physical errors, while stateless Vision-Language Model (VLM) supervision incurs prohibitive chunkwise latency and lacks 3D spatial persistence. We present EmboEagle, a closed-loop agentic framework that unifies subtask-conditioned WAM control, latent-space adaptive supervision, and memory-guided geometric recovery. First, we adapt sequential WAMs via decoupled two-stage flow matching that preserves cross-stage visual history while calibrating truncated action supervision at subtask boundaries. Second, without an auxiliary vision encoder, we distill teacher intervention decisions into a lightweight routing gate driven solely by the WAM Action Expert's pre- and post-chunk latent transitions and subtask embeddings. Third, upon invocation, the VLM decouples diagnostic status from discrete routing actions and executes parameterized recovery primitives grounded in structured memory (initial references, active grasp bindings, and tool traces), followed by mandatory post-repair verification. Across RMBench and LIBERO-Mem, EmboEagle achieves 91.3\% and 90.6\% average success, surpassing the strongest baselines by 8.0 and 9.8 percentage points, while boosting real-world success over VoLoAgent under identical executor weights. Moreover, adaptive gating cuts VLM calls by 74.2\% versus chunkwise monitoring (91.3\% vs. 93.7\% success).
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Long-horizon robotic manipulation requires a robot to preserve task intent across changing object configurations and grasp states, deciding when a subtask completes, retaining spatial cues needed by subsequent stages, and correcting physical errors before they compound. World-Action Models (WAMs) establish a strong foundation for this execution layer by coupling visual dynamics prediction with continuous action generation. Recent advances extend this paradigm through history-conditioned control in Long-WAM~ huang2026longwam and episodic visual guidance in MaP-WAM~ map2026 . Nevertheless, turning a capable visuomotor executor into a reliable long-horizon agent raises a complementary control question: how should a system allocate high-level supervision and translate its decisions into physical corrections during an ongoing task? VLM-based orchestration bridges learned policies with explicit planning, monitoring, and manipulation tools~ volo2026,gu2026harnesswam , yet the timing of this supervision imposes a sharp efficiency--responsiveness trade-off. As contrasted in Figure~ fig:introduction (a--b), open-loop execution lacks error recovery, whereas querying a VLM after every action chunk repeatedly returns routine continuation commands and incurs unnecessary overhead; conversely, lengthening a fixed checking interval delays the detection of subtask completions, auxiliary tool opportunities, and failed grasps. While progress-based and event-driven triggers mitigate parts of this cost~ gu2026harnesswam , existing triggers often rely on heuristic rules or auxiliary visual processing. We instead investigate whether a lightweight predictor can use the executor's internal representations to anticipate a teacher's intervention decisions, including stage advancement, proactive assistance, and failure recovery. [18] r 0.65 Motivation of . (a) Open-loop WAM execution suffers from unrecoverable errors. (b) Fixed-interval VLM supervision incurs redundant overhead on routine chunks. (c) uses a lightweight gate to trigger VLM orchestration and geometric recovery only when needed. fig:introduction Beyond knowing when to intervene, effective recovery requires a persistent physical reference for what to restore. Returning a displaced object to an earlier location requires retaining that location after the object has moved, and placing a held object requires accounting for the spatial offset between its geometric anchor and the gripper. Because the live observation, the initial scene reference, and the active grasp record each supply distinct geometric evidence, structured memory is essential both for semantic interpretation and for synthesizing corrective trajectories. Moreover, once a corrective motion finishes, fresh observations must be reassessed before low-level policy control safely resumes. To address these challenges, we propose , an agentic framework that integrates subtask-conditioned WAM execution with adaptive VLM invocation and memory-guided geometric recovery (Figure~ fig:introduction (c)). Crucially, its design separates the decision to request supervision from the supervisory decision itself, uniting three tightly coupled components: ~ Starting from pretrained Long-WAM checkpoints, we perform decoupled two-stage flow-matching adaptation (Video DiT LoRA followed by full Action DiT fine-tuning) on subtask-conditioned demonstrations, preserving cross-stage visual history while truncating action supervision at subtask boundaries via a calibrated fixed-horizon loss. ~ Rather than duplicating visual encoding with an external perception network, we train a lightweight routing gate distilled from teacher decisions using the WAM Action Expert's pre- and post-chunk token transitions and subtask embeddings, keeping post-intervention verification outside optional gating. ~ When invoked, the VLM separates diagnostic status from discrete routing actions. Assist operations can establish gripper--object bindings for subsequent recovery or directly support execution. Recovery draws on these bindings, initial references, and recent tool feedback to select tool primitives, with immediate verification after each intervention. Our main contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=1em,itemsep=-0.1em] Closed-loop agentic architecture. We present , which unifies subtask-conditioned WAM execution, decoupled VLM task orchestration, and persistent geometric memory with mandatory post-repair verification. Latent-space adaptive VLM invocation. We formulate selective monitoring as teacher-decision distillation over WAM action-token transitions and subtask semantics, enabling lightweight runtime gating without an auxiliary vision backbone. Boundary-aware WAM adaptation and empirical validation. We develop a two-stage subtask adaptation scheme to adapt to the long-horizon settings. We validate our method alongside closed-loop evaluations on RMBench and LIBERO-Mem. Related Work World Action Models for Robotic Manipulation. World action models (WAMs) couple visual dynamics prediction with action generation to bring video pretraining into robot control. LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbotva jointly learns frame prediction and policy execution through an autoregressive diffusion framework, while DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero adapts a pretrained video diffusion backbone to joint video--action modeling. Further, Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam retains video co-training while omitting explicit future prediction at inference, reducing action-generation latency. Long-WAM~ huang2026longwam studies how autoregressive video pretraining supports the use of extended observation histories and combines causal world-action adaptation with efficient execution. MaP-WAM~ map2026 organizes historical observations into episodic records and generates language and visual plans from memory. Then it conditions action and progress prediction on those plans. These models provide predictive and temporal representations that support higher-level orchestration. Agentic Embodied Frameworks. Agentic embodied frameworks connect high-level reasoning to executable skills and use feedback to coordinate multi-stage tasks~ liu2023reflect,huang2022inner . SayCan~ ahn2022saycan grounds language-based skill selection in learned affordance estimates. VoLo~ volo2026 extends physical orchestration to interruptible learned policies, perception models, and manipulation primitives, allowing the controller to switch tools when execution requires correction. HarnessWAM~ gu2026harnesswam maintains scene beliefs and a task graph, constrains plans to the executor's capabilities, and combines outcome verification with local recovery. State maintenance provides another axis of design: HiMe~ hime2026 separates execution, working memory, and longer-term planning, whereas LAW~ law2026 couples planning, status assessment, and action evaluation with hierarchical visual memory. VLM supervision. The cost of VLM supervision motivates separating frequent observation from expensive reasoning~ gu2026safe . Checking every action chunk can repeat unchanged decisions, whereas fixed intervals cannot adapt to when transitions or failures occur. Existing systems use different signals to schedule deliberation. HarnessWAM~ gu2026harnesswam uses learned progress and completion cues to trigger its task manager. Spotter~ li2026spotter employs a local Qwen screener to flag potential errors for a VLM judge, with bounded asynchronous supervision and checks following repair. TUD~ yang2026tud triggers generalist reasoning from the cross-step dispersion of action re-predictions, using computations already performed by its dual-system architecture. Problem Definition sec:problem_definition We consider language-conditioned robotic manipulation in a partially observable environment, where accomplishing a global instruction requires completing a sequence of interdependent subtasks. At control step , the robot receives multi-view RGB observations and proprioceptive state , with calibrated depth available for geometric perception. Let denote the interaction history of observations, robot states, and executed actions up to ; early observations often establish object identities or spatial relations required later in the task~ map2026 . We assume access to a pretrained World-Action Model and target-task demonstrations annotated with subtask instructions from a supported vocabulary . Let denote the active subtask instruction, whose index may span multiple control chunks. Conditioned on its retained observation history , proprioception , and active instruction , the WAM policy generates an -step action chunk: where is a robot control action and is the chunk horizon. Executing long-horizon tasks purely in open loop leads to compounding errors and unrecoverable failures, whereas querying a Vision-Language Model (VLM) at every chunk boundary incurs substantial latency on routine motion. Our problem therefore requires coordinating low-level chunk execution with a selective VLM invocation decision and structured physical recovery: bypassing supervision ( ) during routine progress while invoking high-level orchestration ( ) at stage transitions or failures to reliably fulfill with minimal redundant VLM queries. Methodology Overview. Figure~ fig:framework presents the overall closed-loop workflow of . At runtime, a subtask-conditioned WAM executes chunkwise control while a structured memory anchors geometric invariants and a VLM orchestrates subtask transitions and physical recovery ( Section~ sec:framework ). To eliminate redundant supervision during routine execution, a lightweight routing gate distilled from teacher decisions dynamically schedules VLM invocations from internal WAM transitions ( Section~ sec:adaptive_invocation ). Finally, to support accurate stage execution and latent gating, we adapt the WAM through a boundary-aware two-stage flow-matching scheme ( Section~ sec:wam_adaptation ). The Framework of EmboEagle sec:framework High-level planning and structured state. organizes long-horizon execution through a hierarchical, tree-structured task plan rooted at the global goal , decomposing the task into an ordered sequence of active and remaining subtasks that can be dynamically pruned or regenerated upon replanning. Whenever high-level supervision is requested, the controller assembles a structured VLM state context: where aggregates initial, current, and recent historical visual observations, provides end-effector poses and gripper openings, and denotes the structured recovery memory detailed below. Chunkwise execution. During routine control, the adapted WAM policy predicts action chunks via Eq.~ eq:wam_interface (Section~ sec:wam_adaptation ), executed directly as joint or end-effector commands on simulated or real-world robotic arms. To preserve physical consistency when resuming policy execution, active grasp bindings maintained in automatically enforce gripper closure, while single-arm instructions keep the non-active arm stationary. Upon completing each chunk, the routing gate evaluates (Section~ sec:adaptive_invocation ): on , execution continues directly under ; on , the controller passes to the VLM and pauses policy control. Upon a subtask transition or tool intervention, the controller clears pending actions while retaining and continuously updating the visual history , allowing subsequent action predictions to incorporate the current subtask instruction and latest observations. title: VITA-WAM: Manifold-Aligned World-Action Modeling for Real-Time Robot Control
comment: Project page. http://ucd-dare.github.io/VITA-WAM. Equal Contributors: Boqi Zhao, Dechen Gao. Corresponding Author: Junshan Zhang
summary: World action model (WAM) is a promising paradigm for visuomotor control by jointly modeling world dynamics and actions. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large generative models and iterative sampling which incur substantial latency for action generation, limiting real-time deployment. In particular, there are two root causes of inefficiency in conventional flow matching or diffusion based action models in WAMs: 1) transporting uninformative Gaussian noise into precise actions necessitating multiple ODE steps, and 2) repeatedly injecting task context through expensive cross-attention modules. Our key insight is that jointly learning and aligning the source and action manifolds streamlines the transport between them, substantially accelerating action generation. Building on this insight, we introduce VITA-WAM, a WAM architecture with manifold-aligned flow-matching (VITA flow matching) that directly transports latent observation representations containing visual, language, and proprioceptive information into latent actions. More specifically, a flow latent alignment (FLA) mechanism is employed to facilitate manifold alignment between latent observation and action representations, enabling accurate generation with few ODE steps. The resulting architecture also eliminates costly attention for observation conditioning during repeated denoising steps. Notably, with a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and by 1.65 pp on LIBERO, achieving these gains through the FLA objective without distillation, while inferring at 55.67~ms latency, a $2.10\times$ speedup compared to FastWAM.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot learning by jointly modeling physical dynamics and robot actions zhu2025uwm, li2025uva, bi2026motus, ye2026dreamzero . Learning to predict future dynamics encourages representations that capture how the environment evolves, supporting physical understanding and policy generalization. Notably, existing WAMs often rely on large diffusion or flow matching based video and action models that require iterative sampling. The resulting latency during inference limits robots' ability to incorporate new observations and respond promptly to environmental changes for real-time control. A central challenge is therefore to reduce the computational cost of action generation while retaining the benefits of world modeling. Recent work has made attempts to address this challenge. Fast-WAM eliminates explicit future video generation at inference while retaining video co-training to learn representations that enhance action prediction yuan2026fastwam . Nevertheless, its action model uses conventional flow matching, with multiple ODE integration steps, repeating cross-attention conditioning on task observations at each step. Action generation still remains a computational bottleneck. Complementary approaches reduce the number of sampling steps through distillation or specialized few-step training objectives~ geng2025meanflow,ye2026dreamzero,akbari2026flashwam , which may incur costly training procedures or even degrade performance. A primary objective of this work is to overcome the inefficiency of action generation for WAMs, while maintaining the performance (e.g., success rate). Our earlier work, VITA flow matching~ vita-arxiv,gao2026vita , identified the sampling from uninformative Gaussian noise as a potential bottleneck to low-latency action generation. More specifically, conventional flow matching begins with a Gaussian prior as the source of the flow and progressively transforms it into actions, which is inherently inefficient for two reasons: 1) Complex Gaussian-to-action transport. Gaussian noise is uninformative and distant from the target action manifolds, necessitating multiple ODE steps for denoising into precise actions; 2) Heavy computational cost associated with cross-attention based conditioning. When starting from uninformative Gaussian sources, conventional flow-matching models must incorporate task contexts through heavy cross-attention based conditioning at each ODE step. VITA addresses these inefficiencies by jointly learning the source and target latent manifolds and directly modeling the flow from observation latents to action latents. To the best of our knowledge, VITA~ vita-arxiv is the first work to apply a non-Gaussian source to flow matching policies, and to develop learnable source and target latents for flow matching. VITA proposed two flow latent objectives, flow latent decoding (FLD) and flow latent consistency (FLC), to enable source--target co-adaptation while preventing latent collapse arising from the training--inference discrepancy, in the sense that during training the target latent is provided by an action encoder, whereas at inference the action latent is generated by solving the ODE using the learned velocity field. The resulting joint optimization promotes alignment between the source and target manifolds, simplifying their transport and facilitating accurate action generation with fewer ODE steps. Moreover, since the source is grounded by observations, VITA eliminates the need for repeated conditioning modules. Nevertheless, VITA studied FLD and FLC mainly through empirical studies, and is task-specific, constrained by a smaller-scale network of around 30M parameters without language conditioning. In this work, we develop VITA-WAM, scaling up VITA to a 6B WAM architecture, formalize flow latent objectives under a unified Flow Latent Alignment (FLA) mechanism, and establish a theoretic foundation for manifold alignment. A key challenge is to learn an informative flow source from visual, language, and proprioceptive representation while matching the dimensionality of latent actions, as required by flow matching. To address this, we develop a Q-Former-based source encoder to effectively extract and fuse multimodal observations into a compact, learnable source representation. The FLA mechanism, designed to minimize the reconstruction loss using ODE-generated latent actions, effectively boils down to the co-optimization of flow matching, and the source and target manifolds in VITA-WAM, thereby driving the source observations and target actions towards aligned manifolds. Our theoretic study shows that aligning the source and target latent representations reduces the coupling cost, facilitating simpler, less curved flow trajectories, and allowing the corresponding ODE to be solved accurately with fewer steps, thereby reducing inference latency, as illustrated in . From an optimization perspective, this joint learning shifts part of the action generation burden from the flow matching model to the source encoder, which learns an action-relevant initialization that simplifies the subsequent transport to latent actions. In essence, through FLA-enabled manifold alignment, VITA-WAM streamlines the flow between source latent and action latent, and speeds up the action generation process. We conducted comprehensive empirical evaluations across four real-world tasks using a Franka Research 3 robot arm, as well as on the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus simulation benchmarks. With a single ODE step, VITA-WAM outperforms 10-step FastWAM by 21.47 pp on LIBERO-Plus and 1.65 pp on LIBERO. On LIBERO-Plus, this improvement stems from FLA learning action-relevant representations that are invariant to visual perturbations, thereby improving robustness. With a single ODE step and repeated language and proprioception cross-attention removed, VITA-WAM achieves an inference latency of 55.67~ms, compared to 116.65~ms for 10-step FastWAM and 62.32~ms for 1-step FastWAM. We emphasize that these results are achieved without distillation. Our contributions are: 1) VITA-WAM: A highly efficient WAM architecture. We introduce VITA-WAM, a novel world-action model for visuomotor control that substantially reduces action-generation latency. By jointly optimizing the source and target manifold representations with flow matching, VITA-WAM begins generation from an informative, learnable source and avoids repeated attention to multi-modal observations during denoising. In particular, VITA-WAM learns manifold-aligned source and target latent representations for flow matching, simplifying transport and enabling low-latency action generation for real-time robot control. 2) Flow Latent Alignment (FLA). We formalize FLA that enables VITA flow learning, and provide theoretic studies to demonstrate that FLA enforces the source and target manifold alignment of flow matching, thus simplifying the transport from the source to the target and reducing the ODE steps needed. The VITA flow using FLA is a general flow matching method that can be applied to the WAM or VLA architecture. 3) State-of-the-art success rates and efficiency. We conduct empirical studies on both real-world and simulation tasks. With a single ODE step, VITA-WAM achieves higher success rates than 10-step FastWAM while providing an inference speedup.

title: SilentWAM: Planning in the Masked State of a Diffusion World Model
summary: World-action models learn from future prediction, but accessing their future representations directly at test time can require costly frame generation. Methods that generate future frames before planning incur additional forward passes, while future co-training methods omit explicit future predictions at inference. We introduce \method, a planner that reads the hidden states of masked future tokens without decoding future frames. We pretrain MMaDA-Parallel-M on driving video using frame-level masked world modeling, which predicts a masked suffix of future frames and explicitly includes inputs with all future frames masked. Learned planning queries attend to these masked positions and the observed context, and a continuous head predicts the trajectory in the same forward pass. With a single front camera, \method reaches 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with an end-to-end latency of 60.3\,ms.

Introduction sec:intro End-to-end driving models predict a trajectory directly from sensor input~ hu2023uniad,jiang2023vad,liao2025diffusiondrive . Much of the difficulty is anticipating how the scene will develop, such as whether an adjacent car will cut in or the lead vehicle will brake. World models learn such dynamics from unlabeled driving video by predicting future observations~ hu2023gaia1,gao2024vista , and world-action models (WAMs) train a single network to predict both future observations and actions~ zhao2025pwm,li2026drivevlaw0,zhao2026simwam . For onboard deployment, the planner needs access to these predictions, and producing them must fit the inference-time budget. Current WAMs handle these two requirements differently ( ). Imagine-then-act models~ zhao2025pwm,zhang2025epona,yao2026discretewam first generate future frames and then plan from them ( a). This gives the planner access to a predicted future, but requires additional generation steps. Future co-training models~ li2025law,li2026drivevlaw0,zhao2026simwam,yuan2026fastwam predict the future only during training and discard it at test time ( b), allowing single-pass planning without explicit future predictions. ForeDrive~ wang2026foredrive and RIFT~ zhang2026rift keep a predicted future at test time without generating frames, using a separately trained latent predictor and learned anticipation tokens, respectively. We study whether a planner can reuse the world model's future representations without decoding frames or adding a separate future predictor. Autoregressive and masked-diffusion world models expose future predictions in different ways. The autoregressive world models considered here~ hu2023gaia1,zhao2025pwm,zhang2025epona predict future frames sequentially, conditioning each prediction on preceding frames. Accessing their multi-frame predictions therefore requires a rollout. Masked diffusion models~ nie2025llada,yang2025mmada are trained differently: arbitrary subsets of tokens are masked and predicted from the visible ones. We explicitly train on the case in which all future frames are masked. The hidden state at each masked future position is trained to support prediction of the corresponding token~ ou2025absorbing , for example whether a neighboring car will occupy that image region a second later. We refer to these hidden states as the masked future state. A planner that attends to them can use the predicted future within the same forward pass that produces the trajectory, while the future frames themselves are never decoded ( c), hence the name . Masked diffusion has been used in driving before~ li2025reflectdrive,ma2025dvlmad,xu2025wamdiff,zhang2026fastddrive , but as a decoder for actions and text, on vision-language backbones that read the camera image without being able to generate it ( ). Our approach uses an image-generative backbone to learn representations at masked future positions. We therefore build on MMaDA-Parallel-M~ tian2025mmadaparallel , an 8B masked diffusion model that generates text and images as tokens of one vocabulary, with bidirectional attention over the whole sequence. To our knowledge, is the first to plan from the masked future state of a unified image-text masked diffusion model, reading the predicted future in one pass instead of decoding it. We pretrain it on driving video with frame-level masked world modeling, which masks a suffix of future frames and predicts it from the observed ones ( ). Its fully masked case uses the same future-token configuration as planning. For planning, learned queries attend to the masked future state together with the current frame, the ego state and the navigation command, and a continuous head regresses the waypoints ( ), followed by a short post-training stage with simulator rewards ( ). We evaluate on NAVSIM v1, NAVSIM v2, and nuScenes using only the front camera ( ). In summary, our contributions are as follows. We show that the masked future state of a masked diffusion world model can serve as the input of a planner, which then uses the predicted future in one forward pass without generating frames or adding a separate predictor. We introduce frame-level masked world modeling, a pretraining objective that explicitly trains on fully masked futures and predicts multiple future frames from the observed context. We report 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with one camera at 60.3\,ms per plan. In ablations, retaining the masked future lowers the nuScenes collision rate from 0.18 to 0.06 . Decoding future frames adds generation steps for only a marginal improvement in NAVSIM PDMS. Related Work sec:related End-to-end planning. Modular end-to-end planners pass the scene through intermediate representations such as BEV maps, tracked agents and motion forecasts before planning~ hu2022stp3,hu2023uniad,jiang2023vad , and TransFuser~ chitta2023transfuser fuses camera and LiDAR features. Generative planners produce multimodal trajectories with diffusion or flow matching~ liao2025diffusiondrive,xing2025goalflow , and vision-language-action models plan with a pretrained multimodal backbone~ zhou2025autovla,li2026drivevlaw0 . Planners that receive the ego state can reach low open-loop errors from the vehicle's own motion alone~ li2024egostatus , a form of the copycat problem in imitation from observation histories~ wen2020copycat . Closed-loop reward optimization has recently been added on top of imitation~ zou2025diffusiondrivev2,zhou2025autovla . uses a single front camera, reads the plan from learned queries with a continuous head, and adapts the reward optimization of DiffusionDriveV2~ zou2025diffusiondrivev2 to this deterministic head for post-training. World models for planning. Driving world models were first built to generate scenes~ hu2023gaia1,wang2024drivedreamer,gao2024vista or to forecast occupancy~ zheng2024occworld,yang2025driveoccworld . Several planners forecast compact BEV or latent states with a small module and use them at test time: WoTE~ li2025wote rolls out future BEV states to score candidate trajectories, SeerDrive~ zhang2025seerdrive feeds the predicted BEV back to the planner, and World4Drive~ zheng2025world4drive scores latent futures of candidate intentions. These states are supervised with BEV semantic maps or with pseudo-labels from vision foundation models, so the resulting future representations are shaped by the chosen labels or teacher features. World-action models instead learn the dynamics from the observations themselves, and use them to plan in three ways. Imagine-then-act models generate the future before acting: PWM~ zhao2025pwm forecasts frames one at a time with a block-causal mask and then predicts the trajectory, Epona~ zhang2025epona rolls out an autoregressive diffusion model, and Discrete-WAM~ yao2026discretewam generates frames frame by frame while editing action tokens in parallel. Future co-training models predict the future only as a training signal and drop it at test time, predicting latent features~ li2025law or images~ li2026drivevlaw0 , or co-training a video expert whose future tokens are hidden from the action expert~ zhao2026simwam,yuan2026fastwam . A third group keeps a predicted future at test time without a full rollout: ForeDrive~ wang2026foredrive predicts latent futures with a separate predictor and injects them into the planner, and RIFT~ zhang2026rift fills the future positions with learned anticipation tokens in one pass. reuses the world model's masked future positions, without a separate future predictor or additional anticipation tokens. Masked diffusion models. Masked diffusion models corrupt discrete data by replacing tokens with a mask and learn to recover them~ austin2021d3pm,sahoo2024mdlm,shi2024md4 ; MaskGIT~ chang2022maskgit applies the idea to image tokens. At scale, LLaDA~ nie2025llada is competitive with autoregressive language models of the same size, and LLaDA-V~ you2025lladav adds a continuous vision encoder for image understanding. Unified models also generate images as discrete tokens: Show-o~ xie2025showo generates text autoregressively and predicts masked tokens within each image, while MMaDA~ yang2025mmada and MMaDA-Parallel~ tian2025mmadaparallel apply masked diffusion with bidirectional attention to text and images in one vocabulary. In driving, masked diffusion decodes the plan: ReflectDrive~ li2025reflectdrive generates trajectory tokens from an action codebook and inpaints unsafe ones, ReflectDrive-2~ wang2026reflectdrive2 learns to edit its own trajectory tokens with reinforcement learning, dVLM-AD~ ma2025dvlmad decodes structured reasoning and the trajectory together, Fast-dDrive~ zhang2026fastddrive decodes them in causally ordered blocks for speed, and WAM-Diff~ xu2025wamdiff adds a mixture of experts and policy optimization. ReflectDrive, dVLM-AD and WAM-Diff build on LLaDA-V, and Fast-dDrive converts an autoregressive vision-language model to block diffusion; all of these models read the camera through a continuous vision encoder, can describe an image but not generate one, and do not model the future. Discrete-WAM~ yao2026discretewam tokenizes both images and actions and edits action tokens in parallel, but generates future frames frame by frame. Copilot4D~ zhang2024copilot4d learns a discrete diffusion world model, but on LiDAR tokens, and forecasts future point clouds by unmasking them rather than planning from the masked state. All of them use masked diffusion as a decoder that unmasks tokens over several steps. We use MMaDA-Parallel-M because bidirectional masked diffusion supports joint prediction of multiple future frames. The planner reads their masked states in one pass rather than iteratively unmasking them. title: Urban State Representation for Autonomous Mobility: A Survey of Multimodal Perception, Architectures, Datasets, and Benchmarks
comment: Accepted to the UrbanState Workshop at WACV 2027. 8 pages + references + 5-page supplementary appendix. Code and data: https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation
summary: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.

Introduction sec:intro Autonomous mobility in cities depends on a model of the world that is accurate, current, and actionable. The sensing needed to build such a model is now abundant. A single autonomous test vehicle carries multiple cameras, LiDARs and radars~ caesar2020nuscenes,sun2020waymo . Instrumented intersections stream roadside camera and LiDAR data~ yu2022dairv2x,zimmer2024tumtraf . Drones capture naturalistic trajectories from above~ krajewski2018highd,zhu2022visdrone . Loop detectors and phones record city-scale mobility~ li2018dcrnn,zheng2010geolife . The representations learned from this data, however, remain fragmented. Perception builds BEV or occupancy features for one ego vehicle~ li2022bevformer,tian2023occ3d ; cooperative perception fuses features across a few agents~ xu2022v2xvit,hu2022where2comm ; neural rendering reconstructs scenes for simulation~ tancik2022blocknerf,yan2024streetgaussians ; and urban computing learns from traces and maps with little contact with sensor-level perception~ zheng2014urbancomputing,zhang2024ufmsurvey . Each community has its own datasets, metrics, and vocabulary, even though all describe the same streets at the same moments. and positioning. Strong surveys cover individual pieces: BEV perception~ li2024bevsurvey , occupancy~ xu2025occsurvey , collaborative and V2X perception~ han2023collabsurvey,huang2025v2xcp , end-to-end driving~ chen2024e2esurvey , multimodal LLMs for driving~ cui2024mllmsurvey , Gaussian splatting~ chen2024gssurvey , driving world models~ feng2025wmsurvey,tu2026dwmsurvey , and urban foundation models~ zhang2024ufmsurvey . Closest to our framing, Hu ~ hu2026maead review shared world models maintained across vehicles and infrastructure; we extend the shared-state view to aerial platforms and mobility traces, connect it to urban computing, and propose a protocol to measure sharing. As shows, none spans every sensing platform and the full chain from sensing to evaluation. methodology. This is a structured narrative survey rather than a systematic review. We focus on 2017--2026 work, plus earlier foundational datasets and methods, at vision, learning, robotics, transportation, and data-mining venues (CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, WACV, NeurIPS, ICLR, ICRA, CoRL, ITSC, KDD) plus influential preprints, seeded by the surveys in and expanded by citation search and by searching these venues for each family and platform ( , BEV, occupancy, V2X, HD map, Gaussian splatting, world model, cross-view geo-localization, traffic forecasting). We include works that propose or evaluate a representation for urban perception, prediction, planning, or simulation, or release urban data or protocols, and exclude work outside road mobility; per line of work we cite the first or most adopted method and its current representative. All entries were checked against official records; the supplementary material details the protocol. . (1)~A formal, layered definition of the Urban State Representation ( ) with five desiderata ( ). Problem Formulation: the Urban State sec:formulation Let be the set of sensing platforms active in a region . Platforms include ego vehicles, roadside units, aerial sensors, and trace providers. Each platform produces observations of modality in its own frame, with pose (or a 2D geolocation for traces), latency , and bandwidth budget . We define the Urban State Representation as a latent field over space and time, where is a platform-specific encoder that maps observations into a shared georeferenced frame and is an update (fusion and temporal) operator. A task reads a prediction and, ideally, an uncertainty . Planning and world models add an action-conditioned transition . cases. specializes to familiar settings. With a single ego platform and a BEV grid, it is BEV perception~ li2022bevformer . With several vehicles and intermediate feature sharing, it is collaborative perception~ xu2022v2xvit . With an optimization over posed images, it is neural reconstruction~ kerbl20233dgs . With a learned generative , it is a driving world model~ hu2023gaia1 . With aggregating loop-detector or map-matched GNSS readings and a road-graph signal, it is traffic-state estimation~ li2018dcrnn,newson2009mapmatching . and benefits of USR. USR is primarily a conceptual lens that organizes existing work (Secs.~3--8), not a new method; the desiderata and USR-5 describe what a system maintaining such a state would need, as targets rather than claims about existing systems. The unified view brings four benefits. (i)~Comparability: works from separate communities are compared by which term of they change; cooperative perception and traffic-state estimation are both choices of and . (ii)~Gap finding: placing all platforms in one state exposes gaps no single community sees, , no dataset pairs infrastructure with aerial views or traces ( ). (iii)~Reuse: a state written once and read by many heads amortizes computation (D2), and a persistent static layer need not be re-estimated each frame (D3). (iv)~Measurability: it defines what ``shared'' means and so what to measure ( ). Unlike digital twins, single-agent world models, or shared V2X world models~ hu2026maead , USR separates layers by update rate and admits aerial and trace writers. state. Urban content changes at very different rates, so we decompose the state into three layers, The static layer (road geometry, lane topology, buildings) changes over months and is best estimated by aggregating trips, aerial imagery, and maps~ liao2023maptr,tancik2022blocknerf . The semi-static layer (parked vehicles, work zones, signal plans, congestion) changes over minutes to days and is observed well by traces and infrastructure~ li2018dcrnn . The dynamic layer (moving agents, signal states) changes within seconds and needs low-latency on-board and V2X sensing~ caesar2020nuscenes,yu2022dairv2x . Layering makes explicit which platform should write which layer, and at what rate. Each layer favors different representations ( , column L), and layers interact both ways: the static layer gives priors and a frame for dynamic observations, as in map-conditioned forecasting and planning~ shi2022mtr,jiang2023vad , and accumulated dynamic observations update slower layers, as in map-change detection~ lambert2021tbv . heterogeneous platforms. The shared frame is map-anchored (ENU or UTM), not ego-centric. Integration follows in four steps: (1)~register observations into it with , using cross-view matching for aerial images~ zhu2021vigor and map matching for traces~ newson2009mapmatching ; (2)~synchronize by compensating latency , since latency and pose errors become feature misalignment, a major failure mode of cooperative fusion~ xu2022v2xvit,huang2025v2xcp ; (3)~route each platform to the layer matching its rate; and (4)~fuse with , weighting by confidence and staleness within ~ hu2022where2comm . Steps (1)--(2) are mature in V2X perception; (3)--(4) across aerial and trace platforms remain open. . The platforms are complementary along three axes: viewpoint (ego, elevated, overhead), spatial and temporal density, and latency. title: SpatialDuet: Bayesian task routing between a metric expert and a geometry expert for spatial intelligence
summary: Embodied assistants and wearable devices need 3D spatial reasoning, and their limited hardware restricts them to small vision-language models (VLMs). Small spatial VLMs acquire different abilities from their training: a model trained on large spatial question sets estimates object and room sizes well, whereas a model with a 3D geometry encoder is better at relative directions and absolute distances. Instead of training a single model for all spatial tasks, as published methods do, we build one system that uses each frozen model for the tasks it handles best. We propose SpatialDuet, which pairs a metric expert with a geometry expert under a Bayesian task router. The metric expert is a data-driven spatial VLM run with three training-free modules: training-aligned sampling, metric-aware minimum Bayes risk decoding and per-type metric calibration. The geometry expert is a VLM with a 3D geometry encoder. For each question type, the router estimates from labelled development questions how likely each expert is to be better, and pools their answers with that probability as weight, in log space for numeric answers and over the option distributions for multiple-choice answers. Extensive experiments on four spatial benchmarks covering video and single images validate SpatialDuet; it outperforms the best published small VLMs by 3.17% on VSI-Bench and, excluding a model trained on CV-Bench-style data, by 1.44% on CV-Bench, without training any model weight.

Introduction sec:intro Embodied assistants and wearable devices need visual-spatial intelligence~ yang2025thinking : the ability to tell where objects are, how large they are and how they relate in 3D. Because they run on limited hardware, they rely on small vision-language models (VLMs). Open video VLMs have become strong on spatial benchmarks such as VSI-Bench~ yang2025thinking along three lines of work. The first fine-tunes on large spatial question sets, as in Cambrian-S~ yang2026cambrians . The second gives the model 3D geometry, through an added geometry encoder or 3D supervision: VLM-3R~ fan2026vlm3r , VG-LLM~ zheng2025vgllm , Spatial-MLLM~ wu2025spatialmllm , 3DRS~ huang2025threedrs and SpatialStack~ zhang2026spatialstack . The third trains spatial reasoning, often with reinforcement learning: ViLaSR~ wu2025vilasr , SpatialLadder~ li2026spatialladder , 3DThinker~ chen2026thinkwith3d , EagleVision~ wan2026eaglevision , EgoMind~ chen2026egomind and Object-Centric 3D Rollout~ tang2026oc3d . Each of these methods trains one model to cover every spatial task. The first two lines produce models with different abilities. On the VSI-Bench test split, Cambrian-S-3B, trained on a large spatial question set, scores 67.56 on object size against 61.71 for SpatialStack-4B, which stacks the features of a VGGT geometry encoder~ wang2025vggt into its language model. On relative direction the order reverses: 70.54 for SpatialStack-4B against 62.58 for Cambrian-S-3B (Table~ tab:pertype ). Choosing, for every question, the better answer of the two experts of Section~ sec:system would score 74.32 , against 61.74 for the better of the two. Two obstacles stand between a single model and this potential. First, the data-driven model is not run the way it was trained and scored: its official evaluation feeds fewer frames than its training, decodes numeric answers greedily, and leaves a per-type scale bias (it overestimates room area by about 20 ). Second, a system must decide, without the ground truth, which model to trust for each kind of question. We propose , a training-free system that assigns spatial tasks to two frozen experts according to their abilities (Fig.~ fig:method ). The metric expert (expert A) is Cambrian-S-3B run with three modules that align its inference with its training and with the benchmark's metric. Training-aligned sampling (TAS) feeds the 128 uniformly sampled frames of its last training stage. Metric-aware minimum Bayes risk decoding (M-MBR) returns the numeric answer that the model's own samples support most under the benchmark's metric. Per-type metric calibration (PMC) removes the scale bias of each numeric question type. The geometry expert (expert B) is SpatialStack-4B, whose geometry encoder supplies 3D cues for relations and directions. The Bayesian task router (BTR) decides, for each question type, how much to rely on each expert. It estimates the accuracy gap between the experts on labelled development questions, shrinks noisy estimates toward the gap of the type's ability group, and turns the result into the probability that expert B is better. The two answers are pooled with this probability as weight, in log space for numeric answers and over the option distributions for multiple-choice answers. A type with a clear winner follows that expert, and a type with a small or uncertain gap mixes both, in line with the classic result that a weighted combination of two predictors can be more accurate than the better one~ bates1969combination . We evaluate \ on VSI-Bench, its debiased version, VSTI-Bench~ fan2026vlm3r and CV-Bench~ tong2024cambrian1 , which cover video and single images. Our contributions are the following. We identify three mismatches between how a data-driven spatial VLM is trained or scored and how it is run, and remove them with three training-free modules (TAS, M-MBR and PMC). Together they raise Cambrian-S-3B from 57.41 to 61.74 on the VSI-Bench test split (Section~ sec:metric ). We propose the Bayesian task router, which assigns each spatial question type to the expert whose abilities suit it, using a hierarchical empirical-Bayes estimate of the per-type accuracy gap and format-aware pooling of numeric and multiple-choice answers. Adding the geometry expert through the router raises the score to 64.28 , 6.87 above Cambrian-S-3B and 2.54 above the stronger expert (Section~ sec:router ). \ outperforms the best published small VLMs by 3.17 on VSI-Bench and, excluding a model trained on CV-Bench-style data, by 1.44 on CV-Bench. It also beats the stronger expert on the camera questions of VSTI-Bench, and no model weight is trained (Section~ sec:results ). Related work sec:related Spatial video VLMs Video multimodal large language models~ openai2024gpt4o,team2024gemini15,chen2024internvl,zhang2024llavavideo,bai2025qwen25vl remain weak at spatial questions over indoor scenes~ yang2025thinking . The spatial models reviewed in Section~ sec:intro narrow this gap by changing the weights of one model: with more spatial training data, with geometry encoders or 3D supervision, or with reasoning trained by reinforcement learning. Each reports a single model per benchmark score, and none assigns tasks across models. Our two experts come from the first two lines: Cambrian-S is trained on a large spatial question set, and SpatialStack stacks VGGT geometry features into the layers of its language model. Recent preprints describe training-free add-ons that give a VLM access to detectors, depth or reconstruction tools~ mou2026visra,izhac2026spacemcp,cho2026spatialclaw,du2026graft,glantz2026seeing . \ is training-free as well, and its second source of answers is another spatial VLM. Forecast combination, opinion pools and stacking bates1969combination showed that two forecasts, combined with weights chosen from their error variances and covariance, can beat both. granger1984improved cast the weights as a regression, but estimated weights often do worse than the simple average, a finding that stock2004combination documented and that smith2009simple explained through the estimation error of the weights. For probability distributions, linear and logarithmic opinion pools have different properties~ genest1986combining . In machine learning stacked generalization~ wolpert1992stacked trains a combiner on held-out predictions, and ensembles in general combine outputs by averaging or voting~ dietterich2000ensemble . The Bayesian task router addresses the estimation problem that these works describe by shrinking per-type estimates toward their ability group. Mixtures of experts, model routing and selective prediction Mixtures of experts~ jacobs1991adaptive learn a gate that sends each input to the experts best suited to it, and sparsely gated layers~ shazeer2017outrageously made this practical inside large networks. A related line routes whole queries between separately trained language models, either to save cost~ chen2024frugalgpt,ding2024hybrid or to pick the best model from preference data~ ong2025routellm . Selective prediction lets a model abstain when it is unsure~ chow1970optimum,geifman2017selective , and learning to defer sends an input to another decision maker~ madras2018predict,mozannar2020consistent . The Bayesian task router is a gate over question types: it is estimated in closed form from labelled development questions instead of being trained with the experts. Minimum Bayes risk decoding~ kumar2004minimum and post-hoc calibration~ platt1999probabilistic,guo2017calibration are the sources of two modules of the metric expert. Preliminaries sec:prelim Problem formulation A spatial question about an input , a video or a single image, has a type from a fixed set given by the benchmark, such as object size or relative direction. Its answer is numeric or a choice among options. A numeric answer with ground truth is scored by mean relative accuracy (MRA)~ yang2025thinking , with , and a multiple-choice answer by exact match. We use each benchmark's official score, which on VSI-Bench is the macro average over types. We are given two frozen pretrained VLMs and a labelled development split; no model weight is trained. Baseline sec:baseline Our baseline is ~ yang2026cambrians , which combines a SigLIP2 encoder~ tschannen2025siglip2 , a connector and the Qwen2.5-3B language model~ qwen2025qwen25 and is trained on a large spatial question set. With its official evaluation it scores 57.41 on the VSI-Bench test split. We find four limitations and propose one solution for each. L1: frame mismatch. The official evaluation takes one frame per second and resamples to 128 frames only when more remain. On the 288 VSI-Bench videos this gives a median of 82 frames (range 22--128), whereas the last training stage of Cambrian-S uses 128 uniformly sampled frames. We propose training-aligned sampling (TAS), which feeds the 128 training frames and raises the score by 1.70 on the test split (Section~ sec:ablation ). L2: greedy numeric decoding. The greedy answer to a numeric question is often not the value that the model's own samples agree on. In the example of Fig.~ fig:panels b the greedy answer is 160\,cm, the value best supported by 16 samples is 145\,cm, and the ground truth is 113\,cm. We propose metric-aware minimum Bayes risk decoding (M-MBR), which returns the value that the samples support most under the benchmark's metric and adds 1.05 . L3: per-type scale bias. Numeric answers carry a bias that depends on the question type; room area is overestimated by about 20 on the development split (Fig.~ fig:panels c). We propose per-type metric calibration (PMC), which fits one scale per numeric type on the development split and adds 1.57 . L4: weak relational reasoning. Without 3D geometry input, \ scores 62.58 on relative direction and 40.24 on absolute distance, against 70.54 and 47.10 for , which has a VGGT geometry encoder (Table~ tab:pertype ). We add a geometry expert through the Bayesian task router, which assigns these types to it and adds 2.54 over the metric expert. The \ system sec:system Overview Fig.~ fig:method shows the system. Given an input and a question of type , each frozen expert returns an answer . For multiple-choice questions it also returns a probability over the option letters , taken from the first-step distribution and renormalised over the valid options. title: Seeking in Space: Benchmarking Purposeful Active Exploration of Vision-Language Models for Spatial Reasoning
summary: Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision-language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95% of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence.
