Right: (a) Score when each model explores on its own, and when the same model is shown the ideal route. (b) Group-mean score as the views come from different sources. (c) Score by task. (d) How often each model answers and how often answers are correct. fig:teaser ] Humans explore unfamiliar spaces with purpose, deciding where to look until they have gathered the evidence a spatial question requires. However, can vision–language models (VLMs), which reason increasingly well over curated images and videos, also seek in space when the evidence is not handed to them? We present ActSpace-Bench, a benchmark of 994 questions across 234 exploration episodes in 72 real-scanned indoor scenes, where a model starts from a single view, navigates real captured frames, and must gather evidence before answering. To assess whether such exploration is purposeful, we introduce a controlled evaluation protocol that fixes each model as the reasoner and compares its own exploration against a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, separating evidence seeking from spatial reasoning. Every question is verified to require exploration and answered from 3D annotations, masked-evidence questions test whether models know when to abstain, and over 95 of sampled questions are confirmed correct by human verification. Evaluations of 23 proprietary, open-weight, and spatially specialized VLMs reveal that the strongest models do seek evidence with purpose but lose much of it to limited memory, whereas weaker and specialized models explore no better than a random walk or fail to reason over the evidence they are given, pointing to memory and evidence-grounded reasoning as the next targets for active spatial intelligence. Introduction sec:intro Human spatial understanding is acquired through exploration rather than from a fixed set of views~ yang2025thinking,yang2026mmsibenchbenchmarkmultiimagespatial . Faced with a spatial question in an unfamiliar environment, people move, turn, and gather the views that the question requires, then stop once the evidence is sufficient. Perception in this sense is an active process, in which what to observe is chosen in service of the task~ wu2024v,liu2025aligning,wang2025actiview . Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly deployed where the same demand arises, as the reasoning core of embodied agents and wearable assistants~ majumdar2024openeqa,kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0,team2025gemini,yang2025egolife . In such settings no one selects the informative views in advance, and a model must decide for itself where to look and when it has seen enough before it can reason about the space~ ren2024explore,yang20253d . Spatial reasoning has become a central target in evaluating VLMs~ cai2025holistic , and benchmarks have grown from single images~ chen2024spatialvlm,cheng2024spatialrgpt to multiple views~ yang2026mmsibenchbenchmarkmultiimagespatial,wang2026mindcubespatialmentalmodeling,yeh2026seeing,li2025viewspatialbenchevaluatingmultiperspectivespatial and egocentric videos~ yang2025thinking . They have exposed a large gap to human performance, yet share one design choice. The observations are fixed before the model is queried, selected by annotators or recorded by a human who has already walked through the scene. Such benchmarks measure how well a model reasons over evidence it is handed, and leave out how that evidence is obtained. A failure cannot be attributed to missing the evidence or misusing it, and a success says little about whether the model could have found the evidence on its own. We therefore introduce , a benchmark that returns this choice to the model. In each episode a model is placed at one view of a real indoor scan~ baruch2021arkitscenes,yeshwanth2023scannet++ , moves among the captured frames within a limited number of steps while retaining only its most recent views, and answers when it judges the evidence sufficient or reports that the question cannot be determined. Existing active benchmarks~ majumdar2024openeqa,ren2024explore,jiang2025beyond,sakamoto2026e3vs,hong2026esibenchembodiedspatialintelligence mostly rely on rendered or simulated scenes and report the active score alone or against a random policy only (Table~ tab:comparison ), which leaves finding and reasoning entangled. We instead pose every question under two matched references, a random walk of the same length and an oracle route through the required evidence. The gap to the random walk shows whether the model explores with purpose, and the gap to the oracle route shows how much score better exploration would add. When the random walk is restricted to the same recent views, the strongest models outperform it by 12-26 points. Most of this lead disappears once the walk may keep everything it has seen, because evidence found earlier but no longer in view is largely lost. Weaker models do no better than the random walk in either case, and spatially specialized and small open models answer incorrectly even along the oracle route, where the evidence is directly given to them. Our core contributions are three-fold: We formulate active spatial reasoning as a problem of seeking evidence, and propose an evaluation protocol that measures whether active exploration is purposeful. By pairing each question with a same-budget random walk and an oracle route, the protocol turns a single active score into separate estimates of exploration and reasoning ability. We build , comprising 994 questions over 72 real indoor scenes and five spatial tasks. Every question is verified to require exploration beyond the starting view, and every answer is derived from 3D annotations. We provide a diagnosis that locates, for each model, where score is lost among finding, remembering, and reasoning. It identifies memory of gathered evidence and reasoning over it as the main targets for future models. Related Work sec:related Spatial Intelligence in VLMs. Benchmarks for spatial intelligence have expanded along the form of their input. Early ones are single-image and emphasize local metric cues such as depth and distance, , SpatialVLM~ chen2024spatialvlm and SpatialRGPT~ cheng2024spatialrgpt . Multi-view benchmarks require fusing several images into one layout, including MMSI-Bench~ yang2026mmsibenchbenchmarkmultiimagespatial , MindCube~ wang2026mindcubespatialmentalmodeling , All-Angles Bench~ yeh2026seeing , and ViewSpatial-Bench~ li2025viewspatialbenchevaluatingmultiperspectivespatial . Video benchmarks extend this to egocentric recordings of whole scenes, as in VSI-Bench~ yang2025thinking , MMSI-Video-Bench~ lin2025mmsi , and DSI-Bench~ zhang2025dsi , and OST-Bench~ lin2026ost further feeds the frames online to stress memory. In parallel, models have been strengthened with geometry encoders~ fan2026vlm,wu2026spatial or large-scale spatial tuning~ cai2026scaling,yang2026visual,yang2026cambrian . In both lines the observations are chosen by an annotator or fixed by a recorded trajectory. keeps the task types and 3D-grounded answers of these benchmarks but lets the model decide what to observe. Active Perception and Embodied QA. A second line lets the model act before it answers. Within a single image, V ~ wu2024v and ActiView~ wang2025actiview study visual search through zooming and shifting the field of view. In 3D scenes, embodied QA benchmarks such as OpenEQA~ majumdar2024openeqa , EXPRESS-Bench~ jiang2025beyond , E3VS-Bench~ sakamoto2026e3vs , and ESI-Bench~ hong2026esibenchembodiedspatialintelligence require navigation in rendered or simulated environments, while methods such as Explore until Confident~ ren2024explore and 3D-Mem~ yang20253d improve exploration with semantic maps and scene memory. These works establish that active exploration is difficult, yet they seldom pair the active score with both a chance-level and an oracle reference, leaving exploration and reasoning entangled. provides both references on real captures and tests whether a model recognizes absent evidence. ActSpace-Bench sec:method Problem Formulation sec:formulation We model active spatial reasoning as answering questions about a scene while choosing what to observe. As shown in Figure~ fig:formulation , a scene is a view graph whose nodes are real captured frames and whose edges correspond to a set of movement actions . An episode begins at node with a question episode . At step , the agent holds observations , where each is the frame at node together with its pose relative to , and selects Exploration stops when the agent chooses to answer or after steps, and the model then answers all questions from the observations collected along its trajectory, Ground-truth answers come from 3D annotations. Each question is built so that the start view does not show all objects involved, while some path within steps does. This formulation separates collecting evidence ( ) from reasoning over it ( ). Let be the expected score of when its observations come from policy . In the active setting, itself acts as the policy . Keeping fixed, we replace its policy with a random walk under the same budget, or with the oracle route that observes all required objects in the fewest steps, and define A positive indicates purposeful exploration beyond chance coverage, and is the accuracy lost when the model has to collect the required evidence by itself. Task Taxonomy sec:taxonomy Answering spatial questions in an unfamiliar scene requires assembling a coherent spatial representation from egocentric views gathered at different places. Our taxonomy probes this representation along two complementary axes: Metric, what it encodes, and Directional, the reference frame in which it is queried (samples in Figure~ fig:cases ). On the metric axis, absolute distance (T1) requires recovering metric scale across views, whereas relative distance (T2) only requires ordering distances consistently, which separates failures of scale estimation from failures of relational structure. On the directional axis, the reference frame moves from the scene to the agent. Perspective taking (T3) queries an allocentric frame anchored at objects, which the agent must imagine occupying. Start-relative direction (T4) asks where a target lies relative to the agent's initial pose after it has moved, so a later observation must be transformed back into the starting frame. Passive benchmarks cannot pose this question, as their observer never moves. Multi-hop questions (T5) chain the two axes by filtering objects by direction before comparing distances, and test composed queries rather than isolated lookups. We further adapt the questions to the active setting in two ways. Instead of asking one question per exploration, we ask several questions about different objects after a single exploration, so the agent has to cover multiple targets. title: RMR-VLA: Recurrent Memory Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, RMR-VLA achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46% overall, 79.83% on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08%).
full_text: Long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation often requires acting on visual cues that have disappeared, such as an object indicated earlier or a target hidden under a moving cup. The key challenge is to maintain what past evidence means for the next action as the scene changes. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), an explicit reasoning step that connects memory to action inside a vision-language-action model (VLA), with no external reasoning model. At each update, the VLA first infers an event from visual evidence, then revises the task state and grounds a subgoal in the current scene to guide action generation. Carrying the state and subgoal across updates lets remembered identities and task progress determine the current target, doubling RoboMME success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence. Joint training lets one VLA both reason and act; because its memory decisions are text tokens with exact likelihoods, GRPO refines them from rollout rewards without making action generation stochastic. Among the compared methods, achieves the best results on RoboMME (66.46 overall, 79.83 on the Reference category) and LIBERO-Mem (90.08 ). Introduction sec:intro The visual evidence that determines a robot's next action can disappear before the robot is ready to act. Consider a red cube hidden under a cup that then trades places with another cup. Choosing which cup to lift requires linking red to the cup that now hides it. Similar demands arise when an indicated object loses its highlight or when a repeated manipulation returns the scene to a familiar configuration. In such long-horizon, history-dependent robotic manipulation~ robomme,liberomem , the next action depends on task information that the current image does not reveal. Memory-augmented vision-language-action models (VLAs) retain temporal context through sampled or compressed visual representations or through language records~ robomme,divide,dualstream,ltm,t2mem,notestoself,tacitvla,unimem , while agentic systems reason over history with external models~ ponderpounce,gamma,pal . When visual histories or latent memories feed action prediction directly, the policy must infer from the accumulated context how object associations and task progress have changed. Language records make spatial context, plans, and attempted or completed subtasks explicit~ notestoself,tacitvla , yet the policy must still resolve these entries against the changed scene. Both leave the policy to work out, while acting, what past information implies now; agentic systems reason about it explicitly, but in an external model. What must be carried across decisions is twofold: the task state, since an object association can stay relevant across many actions, and the operation under way, since its completion advances progress and changes the next target. We introduce Recurrent Memory Reasoning (RMR), which turns each memory update into explicit reasoning inside the VLA. At each update, its vision-language model (VLM) writes one reasoning trace: from observed evidence it infers an event, revises the task state, and grounds the next subgoal in it. The state and subgoal feed the next update, and the subgoal guides the next actions. In , the cups hiding red and blue swap while the robot presses a button; the trace records the swap and red's new location, and once the button is pressed, the VLM reasons that the next subgoal is to lift the cup now hiding red. Each update thus reasons out what past information implies now, before the robot acts. RMR reasons within the VLA, with no external reasoning model. We build on ~ pi05 , whose VLM already predicts a semantic subtask that conditions its action expert; in , this subtask becomes the subgoal reasoned out by the memory update. The central difficulty is that the VLM must serve two roles, writing the reasoning trace and encoding inputs for the action expert, and training them one after the other weakens one of them. We therefore train trace generation and action prediction jointly, then freeze the VLM and fine-tune the action expert. Since the deployed model reads the state it wrote itself, we refine the model by reinforcement learning (RL) on its own rollouts. Flow-based VLAs such as give no tractable action likelihood, so RL recasts their action generation as a stochastic process before applying RL~ pirl . makes its memory decisions in text with exact token likelihoods, so group relative policy optimization (GRPO)~ shao2024deepseekmath,guo2025deepseekr1 optimizes the reasoning trace directly while the action expert stays frozen. is strongest where earlier observations determine later targets, setting the best results among the compared methods on the RoboMME Reference tasks~ robomme (79.83 ) and on LIBERO-Mem~ liberomem (90.08 ). Across all RoboMME tasks, its 66.46 is the best result among the compared methods, including systems with an external reasoning model. Carrying the state and subgoal forward doubles success over an otherwise identical model without recurrence, and among the trace fields the maintained state brings the largest gain, doubling the correctness of subgoals that act on earlier cues. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*,nosep] Recurrent memory reasoning. Each memory update is an explicit reasoning chain from visual evidence through events and a maintained task state to a grounded subgoal, revising what changes and preserving what still holds. Memory reasoning and control in one VLA. The VLA's own VLM reasons out the subgoal for its action expert; joint training and action-expert fine-tuning preserve both roles, and GRPO optimizes the text trace directly. Performance and mechanism validation. The best RoboMME and LIBERO-Mem results among the compared methods, including systems with an external reasoning model, with controlled comparisons of recurrence, trace structure, training, and reward. Related Work sec:related Retaining and compressing visual history. Memory policies keep past observations through frame sampling~ robomme , token selection~ divide , feature memory banks~ fang2025sam2act,memoryvla , gated attention over cached tokens~ gmp , or, for long videos, adaptive memory management~ jin2026videomem,zhu2025memorize . Within each step, token pruning guided by semantic attention compresses a VLA's visual input for efficient manipulation~ ma2026safe . LTM- encodes visual transitions~ ltm and ActMem-VLA encodes executed actions~ actmem ; other policies store episodic tokens, fast weights, object slots, or recurrent and retrieved visual streams~ memoryvam,t2mem,slotvla,liberomem,dualstream . These representations supply temporal context for action prediction; turns it into an explicit task state and a grounded subgoal. Embodied reasoning before action. ECoT predicts plans, subtasks, motion descriptions, and spatial features before action prediction~ ecot , and predicts a semantic subtask for its action expert~ pi05 ; other policies keep language records of plans, subtasks, or events across steps~ notestoself,tacitvla,unimem . makes the subtask the result of recurrent memory reasoning: the current state resolves which target to act on, and the subgoal supplies it to control. Memory and planning with external models. GAMMA coordinates external memory and reasoning agents~ gamma , MemER retrieves keyframes for an external VLM that instructs a low-level policy~ sridhar2026memer , and HeLM and 2AM steer low-level action models with external commands, task memory, or 2D hints~ helm,twoam ; PAL and PonderPounce add planning or context models~ pal,ponderpounce . LoopVLA stores completed subtasks as event memory, segmented by online Qwen3-VL-4B subgoals~ zhu2026loopvla . learns memory reasoning and control in its shared VLM and action expert. Reasoning in multimodal models. Explicit reasoning also strengthens multimodal models beyond manipulation: AdaThinkV adapts its thinking for token-efficient video reasoning~ tian2026adathinkv , Context-CoT synthesizes high-quality reasoning to enhance context learning~ jin2026context , OP-CAD distills on-policy from clean audio for robust audio-visual reasoning~ shui2026op , and Ponder Press advances visual GUI agents toward general computer control~ wang2025ponder . Other multimodal models align disentangled audio semantics with visual features for audio-visual segmentation~ tian2026delayed or keep style aligned across generated images~ zhang2025alignedgen . brings explicit reasoning into the memory of a VLA and refines the resulting trace with GRPO. Recurrent Memory Reasoning sec:method maintains a current task state so that earlier visual cues continue to determine the robot's next target after they leave view ( ). At each update, the VLM interprets new evidence, revises this state, and grounds the next subgoal; the action expert executes the subgoal, and the resulting observations feed the next update. Recurrent Memory Interface sec:interface Let index memory updates, denote the task instruction, the current observation, comprising the camera views and the robot's proprioception, and the visual history, a bounded window of past frames, each pooled into a few visual tokens as in~ chen2024videollm,robomme (Appendix A). keeps the architecture, a VLM with parameters and an action expert with parameters ; we write for the VLM and for the full model. Each memory update consists of a write pass and an act pass. Write pass. The VLM reads these inputs together with the recurrent pair and generates the trace whose fields are the observation evidence , the typed event , the maintained state , and the grounded subgoal , produced as one autoregressive text output. Act pass. The full model then predicts a continuous action chunk by flow matching~ lipman2023flow,pi0 , conditioned on the subgoal just written: The VLM encodes these inputs for the action expert. The subgoal carries memory to control. The act pass conditions on the present inputs and , while the visual history and the maintained state remain in the write pass. Everything control needs from the past therefore reaches it through the subgoal. The subgoal resolves which object to act on, such as the cup that now hides red, and guides the action expert's execution. The recurrent pair carries the updated task information into the next write. Reasoning over the Current State sec:reasoning Each write must leave behind a state that is still true after the scene has changed and hand the action expert a target it can act on now. The trace does both with four fields written in the order in which they depend on one another ( ): the VLM commits to what it saw before it edits the state, and updates the state before it chooses a subgoal. The state changes only when the scene gives a reason. The observation evidence reports motion, contact, and completion cues. The typed event identifies a change such as covering, swapping, highlighting, or arrival at a target, with none when no such event occurs. The maintained state lists task progress and the image location of each task-relevant object under that object's identity. The VLM revises using both evidence and events: an event updates the affected identity--location associations or arrival count, completion evidence advances task progress, and unaffected entries carry over. Completion cues can therefore advance progress while is none. A cube that disappears under a cup stays in the state as red, at a location that follows its cup, and a cue shown once, such as the order of demonstrated placements, stays in the state after it has left the visual history. The subgoal turns the state into a target. The grounded subgoal resolves the instruction against the updated state, naming the operation, the image location of its target, and the condition that completes it. title: ContinuLoc: Continuous Pose Inference over Neural Fields for UAV Geo-Localization
summary:
Cross-view UAV geo-localization involves three design choices: how to represent the UAV observation, how to represent the geo-referenced map, and how to infer pose from their interaction. The dominant paradigm organizes the map as a discretized 2DoF candidate library, coupling map representation to pose inference and thus bounding spatial localization precision by candidate sampling resolution. We decouple map representation from pose inference by encoding the geo-referenced map as a continuously queryable semantic neural field, enabling localization to be formulated as explicit optimization over a continuous 4DoF pose space parameterized by 2D ground position, in-plane heading, and viewing scale. Pose hypotheses are evaluated on demand using global descriptors in a shared semantic feature space, bypassing the sampling bottleneck of retrieval. We learn 4DoF pose-sensitive visual representations under full 4DoF supervision provided by ContinuScenes, a multi-city benchmark with dense near-nadir UAV imagery and complete pose annotations. Inference proceeds hierarchically, progressing from broad pose-space coverage to adaptive concentration on high-compatibility regions. Experiments demonstrate substantial gains over representative localization paradigms under progressively stricter 4DoF accuracy criteria.
  Code is available at https://github.com/ZhouWeikun/ContinuLoc/

Inference proceeds hierarchically, progressing from broad pose-space coverage to adaptive concentration on high-compatibility regions. Experiments demonstrate substantial gains over representative localization paradigms under progressively stricter 4DoF accuracy criteria. Code is available at . Introduction Cross-view UAV geo-localization is often framed as a two-degree-of-freedom (2DoF) retrieval problem aimed at bridging severe appearance discrepancies between UAV observations and geo-referenced remote-sensing maps~ Dai2022VisionBasedUS,A2025,JointRepresentationLearningAnd2022,Hu2025QueryDrivenFL,AnObliqueRobustAbsolute2024,CrowdSourcedPicturesGeo2018,VL2024,Xu2024UAVVisLocAL . However, describing the task purely in terms of visual matching obscures its internal structure. Beyond learning discriminative visual representations, a localization system must also determine how reference-map evidence is represented and how the query pose is inferred from observation--map compatibility. This reveals three interdependent components: visual representation, map representation, and pose inference. How these components are organized jointly shapes the achievable localization accuracy, map storage requirements, and online inference cost. Viewed through this three-component perspective, the prevailing 2DoF retrieval paradigm~ Dai2022VisionBasedUS,A2025,JointRepresentationLearningAnd2022,Hu2025QueryDrivenFL,AnObliqueRobustAbsolute2024,CrowdSourcedPicturesGeo2018,VL2024,Xu2024UAVVisLocAL has primarily emphasized learning geographically discriminative visual representations. The geo-referenced map is typically organized as a discrete reference library, while pose inference reduces to one-step similarity-based candidate selection, restricting pose estimates to predefined hypotheses. For visual representation, the question is which pose cues should be preserved for localization. Under the typical near-nadir viewing setting~ Xu2024UAVVisLocAL , cross-view UAV localization can be viewed as placing a UAV observation into a geo-referenced remote-sensing map through geometric alignment. This setting can be parameterized by a task-specific 4D localization state, consisting of 2D ground position, in-plane heading, and viewing scale. The viewing scale captures the relative ground footprint of the UAV observation with respect to the reference map, from which flight altitude can be recovered given known camera intrinsics. This reveals a gap between the pose information available from observation--map alignment and what the prevailing 2DoF retrieval paradigm explicitly recovers. Although such alignment can constrain all four pose variables, 2DoF retrieval explicitly estimates only position. Moreover, position-only supervision encourages observations from the same location to have similar representations regardless of heading or viewing scale, potentially suppressing the cues needed to recover these two variables. In this work, we instead learn 4DoF pose-sensitive visual representations, enabled by ContinuScenes, a multi-city benchmark providing full 4DoF pose annotations. Here, we use the term 4DoF pose to describe planar similarity alignment, where viewing scale constitutes an alignment degree of freedom rather than a kinematic one~ Craig1986IntroductionTR . While 4DoF-aware visual representations preserve richer pose cues, recovering these variables also exposes a structural limitation of the retrieval paradigm. par:sampling_density_bottleneck Extending a discrete reference library to jointly cover position, heading, and viewing scale requires increasingly dense sampling, leading to rapidly growing map storage and indexing costs. The underlying issue is that the reference library simultaneously serves as a representation of map evidence and an enumeration of pose hypotheses, directly coupling inference resolution to the density of stored map evidence. From the three-component perspective, however, map representation need not be tied to the fixed set of pose hypotheses used for inference. Indeed, a dense retrieval library is generated from the same geo-referenced map under different pose hypotheses and thus contains substantial redundancy~ shannon1948mathematical . We exploit this redundancy by representing the geo-referenced map as a compact pose-conditioned map function~ mildenhall2021nerf, kolmogorov1965three that generates map descriptors on demand for arbitrary continuous pose hypotheses, rather than storing each sampled hypothesis independently. For a new scene, the field is fitted solely from its geo-referenced map, without retraining the visual representation model. This architectural decoupling, in turn, invites a rethinking of pose inference. Matching the visual representation against this pose-conditioned map function defines a continuously evaluable compatibility landscape over the pose space. Localization can thus be formulated as a global optimization problem over this landscape. However, high-compatibility regions occupy only a small fraction of the pose space, making them costly to identify reliably through uniform sampling alone. This gives pose inference the characteristic structure of a rare-event search problem~ Rubinstein1999TheCM,Botev2013CrossEntropyOptimization . Motivated by distribution-adaptation principles in stochastic optimization~ Ollivier2011InformationGeometricOA,Wierstra2014NaturalES , we develop a hierarchical pose inference scheme that exploits this sparsity by progressively concentrating sampling from broad pose-space exploration toward a small number of high-compatibility regions. Together, these designs enable pose inference to shift from one-step retrieval among fixed candidates to adaptive search over a continuous pose space, as shown in Figure~ fig:intro_stages_zurich . In this work, we introduce ContinuLoc, a framework that rethinks UAV geo-localization from a decoupled perspective. Our contributions are threefold: We propose a neural-field representation of geo-referenced maps that exploits redundancy in descriptors extracted from pose-conditioned reference crops, enabling compact storage and on-demand evaluation. We formulate pose inference as a rare-event search problem and propose a hierarchical inference scheme that exploits the sparsity of high-compatibility regions to adaptively concentrate computation, avoiding dense enumeration of pose hypotheses. We construct ContinuScenes, a multi-scene UAV geo-localization benchmark with complete scene-level reference maps and refined 4DoF annotations. Experiments demonstrate the benefits of continuous pose inference and its complementarity with geometric refinement. Related Work Discrete Reference Retrieval. Early cross-view localization benchmarks primarily formulate the task as center-aligned retrieval~ Cisneros2022ALTOAL,Dai2022VisionBasedUS or landmark classification~ Zheng2020University1652AM . Game4Loc~ Ji2024Game4LocAU extends this paradigm to unaligned UAV localization through retrieval over discretized satellite tiles, where finite reference sampling introduces a gap between the continuous true pose and the discrete candidate set, as also evidenced by DReSS~ xia2025cross . Local geometric matching~ AnObliqueRobustAbsolute2024,CrowdSourcedPicturesGeo2018,VL2024 can further refine retrieved poses beyond the reference resolution. However, such post-retrieval refinement depends on the correct region being retrieved and is typically restricted to a small top- shortlist due to computational cost~ Shen2024GIMLG,Ye2025ExploringTB . Thus, localization remains sensitive to discrete candidate coverage and initial retrieval recall. Grid-Based Template Matching. In the broader setting of 2D-map-based localization, some methods~ Sarlin2023OrienterNetVL,AirgeonetAMapGuided2024,VecmaplocnetVisionBasedUav2025,Chen2024F3LocFA rely on dense local feature maps to evaluate pose hypotheses over discretized 3DoF spaces, producing rotation-sensitive score distributions suitable for sequential probabilistic localization~ Arulampalam2002ATO,Jonschkowski2017EndtoEndLH . However, compared with the global-vector similarity used in descriptor retrieval, dense template matching requires aggregating similarities across multiple local features, increasing per-hypothesis evaluation costs. Combined with enumerative pose evaluation, this exacerbates the sampling-density bottleneck discussed in the . Absolute Pose Regression. Beyond planar-map localization, research on 6DoF localization addressing full pose estimation in 3D environments~ Zhu2024LoDLoc,Dhaouadi2025OrthoLoCU6,cheng2026pilot,Dhaouadi2026OrthoTrack has extensively explored absolute pose regression (APR)~ NeuralRefinementForAbsolute2024,Kendall2017GeometricLF,Kendall2015PoseNetAC , which directly predicts continuous poses from visual observations by amortizing scene-specific inference into learned network parameters. While computationally efficient, embedding the appearance-to-coordinate mapping within the regressor can complicate transfer to unseen scenes. More fundamentally, standard point-regression models do not explicitly score alternative pose hypotheses, limiting their ability to assess prediction confidence. Neural Scene-Based Pose Alignment. Another line of 6DoF camera relocalization research builds on neural implicit map representations~ Mescheder2018OccupancyNL,mildenhall2021nerf,Park2019DeepSDFLC , which provide continuous alternatives to discrete scene storage. Existing methods typically recover poses through iterative alignment against rendered RGB or feature observations~ Lin2021BARFBN,Lin2024LearningNV,Lin2020iNeRFIN , or geometric refinement using rendered scene evidence~ GS2025,FromSparseToDense2025,TheUnreasonableEffectivenessOf2024 . Although these methods provide continuous scene access, inference remains predominantly local and often requires expensive per-hypothesis rendering or alignment. Table~ tab:localization_paradigms highlights the trade-offs among these localization paradigms in map representation and pose inference. ContinuScenes: Enabling 4DoF-Aware UAV Geo-Localization ContinuScenes_Benchmark To address the limitation of conventional 2D representation learning, we first construct ContinuScenes, as shown in Figure~ fig:ContinuScenes and Table~ tab:dataset_taxonomy , to provide the 4DoF supervision required for learning pose-sensitive visual representations. We collect UAV images and reference maps from two sources: the publicly released UAV-VisLoc~ Xu2024UAVVisLocAL dataset for the Chinese scenes, and orthophotos from swisstopo for the Swiss scenes. We derive refined 4DoF pose annotations from coarse sensor metadata by aligning each UAV image with its corresponding reference-map crop and extracting translation, heading, and viewing-scale corrections from the estimated 2D similarity transform. Standardized data splits and unified evaluation protocols are also provided for this continuous 4DoF localization tas

title: Can Multimodal Fusion MakeSense for Embodied Vision in Degraded Sensing?
summary: Embodied vision systems rely on complementary sensors to perceive and act as conditions change. Even models that accept arbitrary sensor subsets can exhibit negative fusion: adding a sensor increases prediction error. We propose MakeSense, a multimodal fusion framework that preserves sensor-specific evidence in private streams and combines information through shared bottleneck tokens. Training pairs full and subset views of the same degraded observations, penalizing higher error with more sensors. Where geometry permits, the distance readout uses range measurements alone, while the rest of the prediction draws on all available inputs. Paired tests across five datasets reveal helpful and harmful sensor additions. MakeSense reduces negative fusion on MM-Fi. With lightweight adapters and per-dataset training, the same design improves UAV localization on MMAUD, cooperative 3D detection on V2X-Real, few-shot pose transfer to RELI11D, and command prediction on Humanoid-Everyday, where a world model trained on the frozen core's outputs forecasts future fused states more accurately than a linear baseline at longer tested horizons. MakeSense supports embodied sensing across human activity, aerial systems, robotics, and autonomous driving.

Introduction Embodied vision systems combine sensors that measure different quantities in different formats, and the value of each sensor varies with the scene and the sensor's state. For instance, in poor light, RGB cues degrade while LiDAR and mmWave radar still provide geometric measurements~ yang2023mmfi . Sensor availability can also fluctuate due to changes in cooperating agents~ xiang2024v2xreal and delayed or missing proprioceptive measurements~ zhao2025humanoideveryday . Many recent models run on whichever sensors are present. X-Fi fuses features from the available sensors~ chen2025xfi , COMPASS completes missing sensors with a generator~ compass , and HEAL fuses a varying set of agents~ heal . FlexPose selects LiDAR, mmWave, or both per sample~ flexpose , while AWC balances learning across modalities~ awc . However, training on sensor subsets does not ensure that added sensors improve performance. A model that accepts arbitrary sensor subsets can still exhibit negative fusion: adding inputs increases prediction error. This raises a question: On the MM-Fi test frame in Fig.~ fig:why , adding RGB and mmWave to depth, LiDAR, and WiFi channel state information (CSI) raises pose error for X-Fi and COMPASS, while slightly lowering it for . Scores averaged across sensor subsets can hide these effects. (Fig.~ fig:overview ) encodes only the sensors present. Sensors keep private token streams, which interact only through eight shared bottleneck tokens, without a completion network. In training, we apply sensor-specific degradations and fuse two views of each sample: one with all available sensors and one with a random subset. In MM-Fi, RGB and WiFi CSI can provide pose cues without directly measuring target range. On Humanoid-Everyday, a world model uses the frozen fusion representation to forecast future fused states. Our contributions are: Paired protocol for negative fusion and degraded sensors. We quantify the harm of adding a sensor while holding the model, test samples, and existing inputs fixed. We measure how often and by how much error rises across all 75 single-sensor additions over 31 nonempty subsets in familiar and unseen environments. We also compare errors when retaining or dropping degraded sensors. Measurement-grounded multimodal fusion. combines cues from the available sensors while restricting the distance readout to range measurements where geometry permits. To generalize the design across tasks and sensor suites, we train models with the same fusion core and dataset-specific adapters and heads. Thorough evaluation across tasks, models, and sensors. We measure negative fusion across five datasets and multiple fusion models. Training with the range readout reduces the penalty of adding RGB and WiFi CSI on both MM-Fi splits. On MMAUD and Humanoid-Everyday, keeping degraded LiDAR and biased proprioception yields lower error than dropping them. is more accurate than every baseline. Fusion architectures control how complementary cues interact through bottleneck tokens, masked streams, or fixed-size latents~ nagrani2021mbt,recasens2023zorro,jaegle2022perceiverio . Applications span pose estimation~ chen2025xfi,fan2024mmdiff , detection in a shared bird's-eye view (BEV)~ attfuse,xu2022v2xvit,heal,bevfusion , UAV tracking~ mmudct,unlidar , and LiDAR motion capture~ li2022lidarcap,Yan_2024_CVPR . Yet joint training can underuse or overfit modalities and underperform the best unimodal model~ wang2020makes,peng2022ogmge,huang2022modality . With fixed training sensor sets, AWC balances learning and FlexPose selects inputs~ awc,flexpose . SimMLM penalizes regressions from added inputs and reports their pairwise frequency as the counterintuitive rate~ li2025simmlm . We retain signed error changes for each single-sensor addition and condition. Missing and degraded inputs. Missing inputs motivate subset training~ neverova2016moddrop,bachmann2022multimae , reconstruction or distillation~ ma2021smil,wei2023mmanet , feature separation~ wang2023shaspec , and adaptive Transformers or prompts~ ma2022robust,lee2023prompting . COMPASS aligns masked views to detached full-view targets and generates missing inputs with frozen encoders~ compass , while trains end to end on available inputs alone. Absence masks do not describe degradation. PTA distills from a noisy teacher~ pta , and driving methods address sensor failures~ ge2023metabev,wang2024unibev,park2025mome . Corruption benchmarks test detectors trained on clean data~ dong2023benchmarking , while we train and test with sensor-specific degradations. Even clean monocular RGB leaves absolute distance ambiguous~ moon2019camera . Camera--radar detectors position image features using radar range~ kim2023crn , and estimates target distance from available range measurements alone. Shared cores across sensors and tasks. HPT shares a Transformer trunk across robot embodiments with embodiment-specific stems and heads~ wang2024hpt , and AnySat shares one model across Earth-observation sensors and resolutions~ astruc2025anysat . Unlike these methods, which share one set of weights, shares the core design and training recipe, and a separate model with its own adapters and heads is trained on each dataset. Humanoid-Everyday evaluates action-generating policies such as Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), Diffusion Policy and 3D Diffusion Policy~ act,chi2023diffusionpolicy,dp3 , trained per task for closed-loop control. In contrast, we score offline command prediction. Predictive world models. World models can forecast future states in a latent space. Methods such as JEPA and V-JEPA~2~ ijepa,assran2025vjepa2 , DreamerV3~ hafner2025dreamerv3 , and MUVO~ bogdoll2025muvo form their latent states with their own encoders. MRSSM and AquaJEPA study latent prediction when sensor observations are missing~ tremblay2021multimodal,gazzaev2026aquajepa . We study whether an existing fusion representation supports forecasting by training predictors inspired by JEPA, DreamerV3, and DINO-WM~ zhou2025dinowm on the fused states produced by a frozen fusion model. title: World Models as Native Latent Action Models
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Project page: https://pawteam-eai.github.io/native-lam/
summary: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.

title: GlanceNav: Efficient Vision-and-Language Navigation with Streaming Memory and Counterfactual Rewind
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have become strong policies for vision-and-language navigation (VLN). However, most of them encode a sample of past frames again at every decision and are trained on isolated decisions, so computation is redundant and the usable history is short. They also learn from their own mistakes through outcome rewards that give one scalar to a whole episode. We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9% and 73.6% on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104 ms per step.

We ask whether a navigator can encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its mistakes. We present GlanceNav, a streaming navigator built on a hybrid MLLM. Its Gated DeltaNet layers carry a recurrent state through the whole episode, while its attention layers keep a short window of recent observations and a small bank of keyframes, selected by how much each frame changes the recurrent state. This constant-size memory keeps the cost per step fixed and allows training on whole episodes with the same memory as at inference. Because the entire memory can also be copied in constant time, we further propose Counterfactual Rewind (CoRe), a reinforcement learning stage that rewinds a drifting rollout to its closest approach to the goal, lets an expert correct a few actions, and credits decisions by the resulting change in outcome. Trained only on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits, with 1,000 instructions for reinforcement learning, a 4B GlanceNav reaches success rates of 71.9 and 73.6 on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen. On R2R-CE, it outperforms the strongest previous single-RGB method trained without external data by 9.1 points, while running at 104\,ms per step. Introduction sec:intro Vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE)~ anderson2018vision,krantz2020beyond,ku2020room asks an agent to follow a natural-language instruction through an unseen building, using only its egocentric observations. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) now power most strong VLN-CE agents~ zhang2024navid,zhang2024uni,cheng2024navila,wei2026streamvln,zeng2026janusvln . Many of them treat navigation as video question answering ( a): at every step, they sample a fixed number of past frames, typically eight, and encode them again together with the current view. This design has two problems. The first is the memory: each frame is processed once for every later decision that samples it, the policy cannot see what falls outside the sample, and every decision is trained as a separate sample. Streaming navigators avoid re-encoding by caching the key-value (KV) states of past observations~ wei2026streamvln,zheng2025efficient . A full cache, however, grows linearly with the episode, so these methods bound it with sliding windows and pruned or compressed memories. Bounding the cache fixes the cost but not the memory: eviction is final, and whatever leaves the cache is invisible to every later decision. The second problem is how the agent learns from its own mistakes. Beyond DAgger~ ross2011reduction , recent navigators are fine-tuned with outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) such as GRPO~ shao2024deepseekmath,zhang2026activevln , which gives one scalar to all of the roughly one hundred decisions of a rollout and learns mostly from instructions on which some rollouts succeed and others fail, which become rarer as the policy improves. We therefore ask: can a navigator encode each frame only once, at a constant cost per step, and still remember what matters and learn efficiently from its own mistakes? Hybrid MLLMs~ yang2025gated, hatamizadeh2026gated, qwen35blog remove the need to choose between cost and memory. Most of their layers are Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers, which fold every token into a fixed-size recurrent state, and only a few are softmax attention. The whole episode is therefore always summarized in the state. The summary is lossy, so the few attention layers still need exact tokens, but only as a complement. The memory question thus changes from which part of the history to keep to which few frames should also be kept exactly. ( b) answers this question with the state itself. Its attention layers see a window of the most recent observations and a small bank of older keyframes, selected by a state-change score: the relative change that a frame causes in the recurrent state of the GDN layer below. A frame that the state already predicts changes it little, whereas a frame with new content, such as a new room, changes it more and is kept. The score has no parameters. Two properties follow. The memory has a constant size: each frame is encoded once, and a step costs the same throughout an episode. It is also causal: keyframes are selected from the past only, so the memory of every step can be built inside one forward pass over an episode, and is trained on whole episodes with its test-time memory instead of on isolated decisions. The constant size also addresses the second problem: a snapshot of the agent's entire memory takes 136\,MiB and 1.4\,ms to copy, at any step, so a rollout can be rewound to any earlier decision. Our Counterfactual Rewind ( ) detects when a rollout starts to move away from the goal, restores the simulator and the agent's memory at the rollout's closest approach to the goal, lets a shortest-path expert redo a few actions, and lets the policy finish. The difference in outcome between this branch and the original rollout then credits the policy's continuation, and the expert's actions only when the branch did better. A drifting rollout thus yields a contrast between two outcomes from the same state, instead of one scalar for the whole episode. We train in three stages, using only the R2R-CE and RxR-CE training splits: episode-level supervised fine-tuning (SFT), DAgger, and on 1 , 000 instructions. With a 4B backbone, reaches 71.9 success rate (SR) on R2R-CE val-unseen and 73.6 on RxR-CE ( c, ). On R2R-CE, this is 9.1 points above the best previous single-RGB method trained without external data, and among all single-RGB methods that we compare with, only an 8B model trained with additional data scores higher. runs at 104\,ms per step, less than half the step time of a step-wise navigator with a backbone of the same size ( ). Our contributions are: [leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=2pt,parsep=0pt,topsep=3pt] We propose a constant-size streaming memory for hybrid MLLM navigators, which keeps keyframes selected by a parameter-free state-change score, and an episode-level training scheme that matches deployment and encodes fewer frames than step-wise training. We propose Counterfactual Rewind, an RL method that branches from a rollout's closest approach to the goal using an memory snapshot, and credits the expert's corrections and the policy's continuation by their counterfactual outcome. One pass over 1 , 000 instructions adds 8.2 SR to the DAgger-trained policy, against 3.1 for GRPO on the same instructions ( ). With a 4B backbone and no external training data, reaches 71.9 and 73.6 SR on R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen at a constant 104\,ms per step. Related Work sec:related Early VLN-CE agents rely on panoramas, depth and waypoint predictors~ krantz2020beyond,krantz2021waypoint,hong2022bridging,wang2023gridmm . Video MLLMs made navigation from a single RGB camera competitive~ zhang2024navid,zhang2024uni,cheng2024navila . Later work scales the training data~ zhang2026embodied,zhang2026qwen , or adds self-correction data~ yu2026correctnav , dual-system planners~ wei2026ground,xue2026omninav , geometry encoders~ zeng2026janusvln,zhang2026futurenav,pham2026adageovln , auxiliary objectives~ zhu2026textsc,dao2026stagevln,wang2026think , agentic decomposition~ xin2026agentvln or stereo input~ wang2026limits . Most of these methods build each decision from a resampled set of frames, and their best results use external data such as ScaleVLN~ wang2023scaling , VQA or web video. keeps one persistent stream and uses no external data. title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action
summary: Reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) models for autonomous driving use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide action generation, but incur substantial memory and computational costs. We study structured pruning for these models, focusing on preserving both scene understanding and trajectory prediction. Our analysis of Taylor importance in Alpamayo-1.5-10B shows that reasoning and trajectory objectives assign different importance to the same vision-language model (VLM) structures. In the action expert, MLP channels exhibit more stable importance rankings across denoising steps than query heads, and a small fraction of channels accounts for most of the measured importance. Based on these findings, we propose MoOP, which combines importance ranks from both objectives for VLM pruning and aggregates stepwise importance to select a fixed subset of expert MLP channels. At 24.0% total parameter reduction, VLM-only pruning with MoOP performs comparably to or slightly better than the strongest baselines in driving, while retaining 94.0% of the dense model's LingoQA score, far above all other methods. At a higher reduction of 30.0%, MoOP degrades much less than every other method, as it is the only one whose reasoning does not collapse. Removing 93.75% of expert MLP channels increases total parameter reduction to 39.4%, with nearly unchanged open-loop errors relative to VLM-only pruning and competitive closed-loop performance. The resulting model achieves a 1.37x end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6% lower peak memory than the dense model, without post-pruning fine-tuning.

Introduction sec:intro Reasoning vision--language--action~(VLA) models for autonomous driving~ nvidia2025alpamayo, zhou2025autovla, fu2025orion, yuan2026autodriver extend action prediction with explicit chain-of-thought~(CoT) reasoning~ wei2022chain to understand complex driving situations and explain driving decisions. Alpamayo~ nvidia2025alpamayo , for example, conditions a flow-based~ lipman2023flow action expert on context from its backbone, which includes Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning generated by a vision--language model (VLM). Incorporating CoC in action denoising process improves trajectory prediction and closed-loop driving over a trajectory-only baseline, particularly in challenging scenarios~ nvidia2025alpamayo . However, this procedure involves substantial computation: a large VLM generates CoC tokens autoregressively, and an action expert runs repeatedly to predict trajectories through iterative denoising. As autonomous driving requires continuous action updates under rapidly changing scene conditions, this computational bottleneck presents a critical challenge for real-time deployment~ li2026flashdrive . Structured model pruning offers a promising direction to reduce this cost by removing unnecessary parameters based on objective-driven importance scores~ ma2023llm, li2025trthepruner, muralidharan2024compact . However, applying structured pruning to reasoning VLA is particularly challenging. Unlike standard VLM, reasoning VLA leverages a shared VLM backbone for two different roles~(i.e., scene-level CoC reasoning and action expert conditioning), while the action expert operates under different mechanism~(i.e., iterative denoising steps). Deciding what to prune thus requires assessing structural importance across both training objectives and architectural components. To derive a tailored pruning strategy for reasoning VLA, we examine Alpamayo~ nvidia2025alpamayo , a representative VLA framework for autonomous driving that predicts trajectories along with CoC reasoning. Specifically, we assess the importance of structural units for both reasoning and action predictions using Taylor importance~ molchanov2017pruningconvolutionalneuralnetworks,Molchanov_2019_CVPR, lecun1989optimal, 298572 , which estimates the loss change induced by removing each unit. We further analyze the distribution of importance scores within the action expert across iterative denoising steps, accounting for its distinct operating mechanism from the autoregressive VLM backbone. Our analysis of the VLM backbone reveals that the parameters important for reasoning and those important for action generation are only partially aligned. Thus, pruning based solely on a single objective leads to either CoC collapse or a sharp decline in action prediction, as described in Figure~ fig:overview . These findings suggest that preserving both scene understanding and action generation requires accounting for both objectives during pruning, unlike existing single-objective pruning methods. For the action expert, parameter importance may vary across denoising steps. We find that the importance of attention heads shifts with the step, whereas MLP channel importance remains nearly constant. Moreover, while the importance score for Q-heads is broadly distributed, Figure~ fig:expert_cumulative discloses that the top 10 of MLP channels account for approximately 98.2 of the measured importance. Motivated by these findings, we propose Mixture-of-Objective Pruning (MoOP), which jointly considers the dual objectives and the distinct architectural characteristics of both VLA modules. For the VLM backbone, where the two objectives are only partially aligned, scores each unit by the maximum of its importance ranks under the two objectives and removes units critical to neither CoC reasoning nor trajectory generation. In the action expert, instead prunes dense MLP channels that contribute little to prediction across denoising steps. At a matched 24.0 total parameter reduction, matches or outperforms the compared methods on open- and closed-loop driving, and achieves the highest driving QA score by a large margin. At a higher reduction of 30.0 , the gap widens: is significantly better than all other methods in open-loop driving and the best in closed-loop driving. With additional MLP-channel pruning in the action expert, the model reaches 39.4 total parameter reduction, a end-to-end inference speedup and 36.6 lower peak memory without post-pruning fine-tuning, while retaining competitive driving performance. Our main contributions are as follows: We demonstrate that VLM pruning must simultaneously account for both reasoning and action generation to preserve scene understanding and driving capability in reasoning VLA models. We discover that a small subset of MLP channels in the action expert is sufficient to maintain robust action prediction quality. We propose , the only compared pruning method that preserves reasoning, which keeps it robust at higher pruning ratios where existing methods degrade sharply. Related Work sec:related Reasoning Vision--Language--Action Models for Autonomous Driving. Driving VLAs connect scene understanding and language reasoning with action prediction. DriveVLM~ DBLP:conf/corl/TianGLLWZZJLZ24 integrates scene analysis with hierarchical planning, while ORION~ fu2025orion conditions a generative planner on an LLM-generated planning token. AutoVLA~ zhou2025autovla unifies reasoning and discrete actions within an autoregressive model. Alpamayo~ nvidia2025alpamayo generates Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning and conditions a separate action expert on the VLM context to predict continuous trajectories. We study how to prune this architecture while preserving its contributions to reasoning and trajectory prediction. Pruning Language and Vision-Language Models. Language-model pruning methods estimate importance through gradients or weight–activation statistics, as in LLM-Pruner~ ma2023llm and Wanda~ sun2024simple , and optimize layerwise sparsity allocation, as in Týr-the-Pruner~ li2025trthepruner . For VLMs, SlimVLM~ wen2026slimvlm accounts for visual-token redundancy and module sensitivity. Reasoning-aware approaches further adapt compression to the generation process: RAC~ lucas2026reasoning reconstructs activations from model-generated CoT~ wei2022chain traces, while MuCRASP~ dutta2026mucrasp considers reasoning-critical transitions and cross-modal alignment. Our work examines a shared VLM that supports both textual reasoning and continuous action generation, combining importance measured under the two objectives. VLA Compression. VLA compression has explored structural pruning, quantization, and inference acceleration. For robotic manipulation, EfficientVLA~ yang2025efficientvla combines layer pruning, token selection, and action-head caching; CLP~ nguyen2026finetuning removes redundant VLM and action-head layers before fine-tuning; and QVLA~ xu2026qvla allocates channelwise precision using action sensitivity. In autonomous driving, Depth-Wise Probing and Pruning~ babu2026depth removes ORION decoder layers based on changes in the planning token, while FlashDrive~ li2026flashdrive accelerates Alpamayo through caching and speculative decoding. We combine CoC- and trajectory-based VLM pruning with action-expert MLP pruning guided by importance stability and concentration across denoising steps, without post-pruning fine-tuning. Given multimodal input which consists of multi-camera images , ego history , and a text prompt , the VLM autoregressively generates a Chain--of--Causation (CoC) that links a driving decision to its causal factors. The VLM thus processes one sequence of images, ego-history and prompt text tokens followed by CoC tokens. In each layer of the action expert, action tokens attend jointly to their own keys and values and to the full key--value (KV) cache of VLM layer . Conditioned on , the expert denoises Gaussian noise in steps into acceleration and curvature values, converted into a future ego trajectory. Training objectives. The VLM is trained with cross-entropy (CE) on a ground-truth CoC , and the action expert with flow matching (FM)~ lipman2023flow on a normalized ground-truth action , using with , and target velocity : Structured Pruning and Taylor Importance sec:taylor_importance Structured pruning. Structured pruning reduces model size by removing computational units with low estimated importance, together with their parameters~ ma2023llm, li2025trthepruner, muralidharan2024compact . title: Prompt-Consistent Cross-View Object Geo-Localization
summary: Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL) aims to locate an object indicated by a click point in a ground or drone query image within a satellite reference image. Through a quantitative prompt-sensitivity evaluation, we find that existing CVOGL methods suffer from a prompt-disobeying overfitting problem: when the click point is moved or removed, their predictions barely respond, indicating that the models rely on spurious feature correlations rather than genuinely following the prompt semantics. We trace this behavior to the limited scale of the benchmark dataset, which contains only 4,343 prompt-object pairs per task, so that the models simply memorize the object associated with each scene instead of learning the true prompt-to-object correspondence. To address this, we propose two plug-and-play components. First, we construct the CVOGL-MO dataset by expanding the existing training and test sets with diverse multi-object annotations, mitigating the memorization that induces shortcut learning. Second, we propose the Cross-View Co-Scene Multi-Object Contrastive Loss (CVMCL), which enforces distinct feature representations for different click points within the same scene, compelling the model to follow prompt instructions. We further design a prompt-sensitivity evaluation protocol with prediction-shift metrics, providing the first quantitative measurement of prompt-following capability for CVOGL. Both components are architecture-agnostic and can be integrated into existing methods without any architectural modification. Experiments on three representative backbones show that our components substantially improve prompt-following accuracy on the new multi-object test sets and markedly increase prompt sensitivity. Our dataset and code will be publicly released at https://github.com/Sunny-Fresher/CVOGL-MO.

Cross-view object geo-localization (CVOGL), object detection, prompt understanding, contrastive learning, dataset expansion, benchmark evaluation. Introduction ROSS-VIEW object geo-localization (CVOGL) is a pivotal task in computer vision and remote sensing, with extensive real-world applications spanning smart city management ref2, ref3, ref4 , disaster monitoring ref5, ref6 , and drone navigation ref7, ref8, ref9 . The core goal of CVOGL is to pinpoint the geographic location of a specific object indicated by a point prompt in a query image (ground-view or drone-view) within a high-resolution satellite reference image ref1 . Its development provides critical technical support for geospatial intelligence and autonomous systems ref10, ref11 , attracting sustained research attention. In recent years, research on cross-view geo-localization has advanced rapidly, with cross-view image geo-localization (CVIGL) methods achieving notable success in addressing view gap challenges via metric learning and geometry-based strategies. These methods achieve global geographic localization for the entire reference scene by framing cross-view geo-localization as an image retrieval paradigm. However, with the growing demand for fine-grained and high-precision localization, image-level geo-localization can no longer meet such requirements. Therefore, CVOGL approaches have emerged to tackle the more demanding object-level localization task, moving beyond the image-level localization capability of CVIGL. State-of-the-art CVOGL methods, including VAGeo ref15 , OCGNet ref12 , and HALO ref14 , have effectively improved the accuracy of CVOGL and laid a foundation for subsequent research on prompt-guided object geo-localization. However, despite the promising performance of these state-of-the-art methods, we find that they suffer from an overfitting problem that fails to truly follow point prompt instructions in essence. Specifically, these detection frameworks rely on spurious correlations in the training data rather than accurately understanding the semantic intent of the point prompt to localize the target object. This issue leads to the model making correct predictions in benchmark scenarios but failing to generalize to those scenes where prompts move to other places. This phenomenon is clearly illustrated in Fig.~ fig1 . Figure (a)(b) shows the ground-view query images. When the click point is relocated from the green-marked house to the red-marked road, the model still predicts the house initially indicated by the green point and fails to adapt to the updated prompt. A similar phenomenon can be observed in the drone-view query images in Figure (c)(d): the predicted bounding box remains anchored to the object specified by the original click, even after the click position is moved. This observation suggests that the model learns spurious feature correlations instead of faithfully following the semantic instruction of the click prompt. Beyond this qualitative observation, we quantitatively confirm this behavior. Completely removing the click prompt at test time changes the accuracy of existing models by about 1 percentage point on the new multi-object G S test set (Table~ tab:prompt_cond_new ), and their predicted boxes remain almost unmoved when the click is shifted to a different object (Table~ tab:prompt_shift ). This prompt-independence serves as direct evidence that existing models largely disregard the prompt and instead rely on rote memorization of the object annotated in each scene. We identify that the root cause of this overfitting problem lies in the limited scale of the existing CVOGL benchmark dataset, which contains only 4,343 prompt-object pairs per task. With such scarce training data, the models are prone to overfit the training scenes: they simply memorize the location of the object annotated in each scene and associate it with any click point, rather than learning the true semantic correspondence between the point prompt and the indicated target. Consequently, when the click point is moved to a different object or removed entirely, the models still output the memorized object, and their predictions barely respond to the prompt change. Notably, existing CVOGL methods have focused predominantly on optimizing feature aggregation and prompt embedding mechanisms, while the critical issue of data scarcity and its resulting overfitting has not been explicitly studied. To achieve prompt-consistent cross-view object geo-localization, we propose two complementary and plug-and-play components. First, we construct the CVOGL-MO dataset by re-annotating the training set of the benchmark CVOGL dataset with diverse multi-object annotations. The re-annotated dataset provides multiple annotated objects per scene, effectively enlarging the training data and ensuring that the model can learn the true click-to-object correspondence rather than memorizing a single fixed answer for each scene, thus avoiding ``cheating'' during training. Second, to further prevent the model from taking shortcuts ref45 , we propose the Cross-View Co-Scene Multi-Object Contrastive Loss (CVMCL), a lightweight auxiliary loss that enhances the model's ability to align prompt semantics with target objects, effectively constraining the model to focus on the true intent of the prompts. Furthermore, we construct new multi-object test sets where multiple objects are annotated per scene, enabling a more rigorous evaluation of prompt-following capability beyond the limitations of the original single-object test set. Importantly, both components are architecture-agnostic and can be directly integrated into any existing CVOGL model without modifying its backbone, fusion modules, or detection heads. The main contributions of this work are as follows. We identify and characterize the prompt-disobeying overfitting problem in existing CVOGL methods, and propose the first quantitative prompt-sensitivity evaluation protocol for CVOGL, with prediction-shift metrics (SelfIoU, TSR and PCS) that measure whether models genuinely follow click prompts. We re-annotate the training set of the benchmark dataset, constructing a more diverse prompt-target pair dataset (CVOGL-MO), which mitigates the memorization issue induced by data scarcity. We propose the Cross-View Co-Scene Multi-Object Contrastive Loss (CVMCL) to constrain the model to follow prompt instructions, preventing the model from ``cheating'' by relying on spurious correlations. We conduct extensive experiments on the standard CVOGL benchmark and the newly constructed multi-object test sets, verifying that our dataset and loss improve the prompt-following capability of existing methods without any architectural modification. Related Work Cross-View Image Geo-Localization CVIGL, a pivotal task in image-level geo-localization, aims to pinpoint the geographic position of the camera that captures a ground-view query image. This goal is accomplished by establishing correspondences between the query image and the most relevant reference image ref17, ref18, ref19, ref20 , or alternatively, the most matching position within a reference image ref21, ref22, ref23 . Owing to its broad utility in fields such as autonomous navigation, aerial reconnaissance, and environmental management, CVIGL has emerged as a prominent research topic at the intersection of computer vision and geographic information science. Existing research on CVIGL can be divided into two primary categories: metric learning-based methods and geometry-based methods ref1 . For metric learning-based methods ref24, ref25, ref26, ref27, ref28, ref29, ref30, ref31, ref32, ref33 , the primary focus lies in learning features that are invariant to changes in viewpoint, with little consideration given to geometric structures. Recent advancements in this area have involved the integration of self-distillation techniques, multi-scale feature reasoning ref34 , and multi-scale attention mechanisms ref35 . These enhancements facilitate improved cross-view matching by enabling hierarchical feature interaction and self-supervised guidance. Furthermore, metric learning-based methods have been adapted to UAV-to-satellite geo-localization scenarios ref36 , shedding light on the domain shift induced by differences in altitude and scale. Additionally, diffusion-based architectures have been employed to tackle extreme environmental variations ref37 , thereby broadening the scope of application for this class of methods. On the other hand, geometry-based methods ref20, ref38, ref39, ref40, ref41, ref42 aim to narrow the viewpoint gap between ground-view and aerial-view images explicitly through the utilization of geometric constraints, such as orientation data, which in turn enables precise camera geo-localization. These methods underscore the critical role of geometric information in addressing the cross-view discrepancy, a major bottleneck in CVIGL research. While substantial advancements have been made in camera-level localization using existing CVIGL techniques, notable limitations remain. In particular, current CVIGL methods are confined to camera-level localization and are unable to achieve precise object-level localization ref1 . In other words, these approaches can only estimate the approximate location of the query image relative to the reference image, which fails to satisfy the demands of object-level geo-localization tasks. title: AsyncMixVLA: Runtime Asynchronous Robot Policy Switching for Adaptation to Dynamic Environments
comment: Manuscript prepared for the DAC 2027 Research Track (IEEE conference format)
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions, enabling general-purpose robotic control. However, environmental perturbations, such as objects moving during execution, can undermine their reliability. Different policies exhibit complementary failures under mid-rollout perturbations, motivating selective switching between policies for recovery. Such switching can stall the robot during inference of the newly invoked policy or, if performed asynchronously, act on stale observations. We present AsyncMixVLA, an adaptive inference framework for proactive, asynchronous switching across heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned trigger balances recovery potential against intervention harm to selectively escalate to a higher-compute policy. AsyncMixVLA overlaps its inference with committed outgoing actions and aligns its context to the anticipated takeover state. On LIBERO-Long with mid-rollout perturbations, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed task success from 69.5% to 77.1% over the lightweight policy. It achieves 84.9% overall success, comparable to 84.5% for synchronous switching, while reducing median exposed handoff latency from 226.5 ms to 0.1 ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1% success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3% for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate.
