Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1 success across three unseen perturbation families, compared with 71.3 for the stronger constituent policy in aggregate. VLA models, Physical AI, asynchronous inference, policy switching, model routing, robustness Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, enabling a single policy to perform diverse manipulation tasks~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0 . However, strong nominal performance does not guarantee reliable execution under deployment shifts: VLA policies remain sensitive to changes in adjoining environment~ fei2025liberoplus . Mid-task perturbations are particularly challenging because they can invalidate the state on which ongoing actions were generated. Robust deployment therefore requires both effective recovery and timely delivery of corrective actions. As shown in Fig.~ fig:motivation_fig , heterogeneous VLA policies can exhibit complementary failure modes, motivating selective switching rather than continuous use of a single policy, or switching to a compressed version of the same policy. Table~ tab:model_complementarity confirms this empirically: VLA-Adapter~ wang2025vlaadapter recovers substantially more OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025oft failures than the same-family OFT-Exit16 (Early exit song2025ceedvla applied to OpenVLA-OFT) variant. We therefore use VLA-Adapter as the default policy and selectively invoke OpenVLA-OFT for recovery. Policy switching, however, introduces a systems challenge. A synchronous handoff exposes incoming-policy inference latency directly to robot control; in our evaluation, the median exposed wait is 226.5~ms, equivalent to more than four nominal 50-ms control intervals at 20~Hz. Launching OFT asynchronously can hide this computation behind remaining committed Adapter actions, but the robot continues moving during inference, making the launch-time context stale at takeover. Heterogeneous switching must therefore determine both when to intervene and how to transfer control without blocking or context misalignment. We present AsyncMixVLA, a runtime framework for proactive, asynchronous switching between heterogeneous VLA policies. A learned intervention trigger selectively escalates from VLA-Adapter to OpenVLA-OFT. Once accepted, the remaining Adapter actions form a committed-action bridge that executes while OFT preparation proceeds asynchronously. AsyncMixVLA then aligns the incoming policy's proprioceptive and visual context to the anticipated takeover state using controller-calibrated state roll-forward and an action-consistent visual-token residual. When the environment changes mid-execution, the runtime must decide whether another policy is more likely to complete the task from the current trajectory and, if so, prepare that policy for the state it will inherit. Unlike prior asynchronous VLA execution methods that primarily maintain temporal consistency within a single deployed policy ~ black2025rtc,tang2025vlash,wei2026f2fap , AsyncMixVLA couples selective transfer between independently trained policies with asynchronous, context-aligned handoff. Our contributions are: Complementarity-driven heterogeneous switching. We characterize complementary failures of independently trained VLA policies and introduce a learned rescue-versus-harm trigger for selective escalation. Proactive asynchronous handoff with context alignment. We overlap incoming-policy inference with committed outgoing actions and align proprioceptive and visual context to the anticipated takeover state. End-to-end robustness, responsiveness, and generalization. Across 238 LIBERO-Long episodes, AsyncMixVLA improves perturbed success from 69.5 to 77.1 over VLA-Adapter, achieves 84.9 overall success versus 84.5 for synchronous switching, and reduces median handoff latency from 226.5~ms to 0.1~ms. Without retraining or recalibration, it achieves 75.1 success across 289 episodes spanning three unseen perturbation families, showing generalization to unseen perturbations. Related Work sec:related_work robustness and efficient inference. Robustness studies such as LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus and RobustVLA~ guo2025robustvla document VLA sensitivity to environmental and observation perturbations. Efficient inference reduces policy cost through compact backbones~ wang2025vlaadapter,shukor2025smolvla , layer/token pruning and feature caching~ yang2025efficientvla,jiang2025lightvla,xu2025vlacache , parallel action decoding~ kim2025oft , and adaptive early exit~ song2025ceedvla . AsyncMixVLA complements these optimizations by addressing when to invoke a higher-compute policy during execution. It exploits complementary outcomes across independently trained policies while retaining lightweight inference when escalation is unnecessary. policy routing. RoboRouter~ chen2026roborouter selects policies for tasks using semantic representations and accumulated execution experience. Pan et al.~ pan2024switching perform event-based transitions between VLA and diffusion controllers for language-guided positioning and dexterous grasping. These works establish precedents for heterogeneous selection and switching during execution. AsyncMixVLA focuses on intervention under disturbances: learned rescue-versus-harm utility decides whether to transfer control from the current state, and asynchronous handoff reduces the transfer's exposed cost. policy execution. Action chunking~ zhao2023act amortizes inference but delays incorporation of new observations; asynchronous execution~ shukor2025smolvla overlaps prediction with ongoing control. Real-time chunking (RTC)~ black2025rtc preserves committed actions through inpainting to maintain chunk continuity. VLASH~ tang2025vlash conditions predictions on rolled-forward robot states and incorporates temporal offsets during fine-tuning. F2F-AP~ wei2026f2fap uses predicted object flow to anticipate observations and a contrastive objective to align visual features. These methods address temporal consistency for a deployed policy. AsyncMixVLA shares their need to account for motion during inference, while addressing selective handoff between independently trained controllers. Its incoming policy is conditioned on the context expected after the outgoing policy's committed actions. Visual alignment is trained through action consistency: the frozen incoming policy's outputs under predicted and true handoff contexts are matched, rather than directly matching visual features. AsyncMixVLA thus combines intervention-utility routing, preparation during committed outgoing actions, and alignment to the incoming controller's anticipated takeover context. title: Entangle: Scaling Human-Video In-Context World-Action Models across Unseen Tasks and Contexts
summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools.
full_text: [ enhanced, breakable, colback=labblue!10, colframe=labblue!35, boxrule=0.5pt, arc=6pt, left=10pt, right=10pt, top=2pt, bottom=2pt ] Executing an unseen task. The input context (top) shows a human using a brush (1) to sweep a plastic block (2) into a dustpan (3), a task absent from training. Task-OOD (middle): conditioned on this context, the robot executes the unseen task with the same objects. Context-OOD (bottom): the robot executes the same interaction with objects that differ from those in the input context, using a banana (1) to sweep a wooden block (2) into a cardboard box (3); dashed outlines mark substituted objects. fig:teaser Introduction sec:intro In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without updating model parameters~ brown2020language . In robotic manipulation, language instructions often underspecify multi-step order, spatial constraints, and fine-grained motion, whereas a single human demonstration video directly shows how a task should be performed~ jain2024vid2robot,fu2025icrt,vosylius2025instant,sridhar2025ricl,zhang2026understanding . World-action models (WAMs)~ ye2026world,zhang2026native,zhou2026zerowam,motubrain2026,vidarc2025 , which jointly model future visual dynamics and robot control within a shared generative backbone, offer a natural foundation for such video-conditioned policies: given a single human demonstration video as context, a WAM can predict future visual states and executable actions for unseen manipulation tasks without parameter updates. However, scaling human-video ICL on WAMs faces two core challenges. First, human and robot videos are typically paired only at the task level. Whether collected independently or synthesized from an edited initial frame via text-to-video generation~ zhou2026zerowam,bao2024vidu , task-level pairs share a high-level goal but diverge in motion paths, contact timing, and execution speed. Without temporal alignment between the human video and ground-truth robot actions, the model cannot localize which segment of the demonstration corresponds to a target action chunk, reducing the video prompt to a coarse task label. Second, even when paired trajectories are aligned, standard action-prediction losses supervise each trajectory in isolation and leave room for shortcuts: when a task admits multiple valid executions (e.g., different manipulation orders or obstacle-avoidance paths), a policy can lower its loss by inferring the task identity or relying on the initial scene layout rather than tracking the specific progression shown in the demonstration. To address these challenges, we present , an in-context world-action model that maps a single human demonstration video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. First, to scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human demonstrations via reference-conditioned video-to-video (V2V) generation, supplemented by real paired recordings (Fig.~ fig:paired_dataset_overview ). Unlike first-frame editing followed by text-driven generation, V2V translation preserves the camera viewpoint, object interactions, and timing of the source robot trajectory, so each generated human video remains temporally aligned with the recorded ground-truth actions. Second, we encode the human demonstration and current robot observations in a shared video-action backbone and concatenate their tokens along the temporal axis (Fig.~ fig:model_architecture ). For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task InfoNCE contrastive objective~ oord2018representation inspired by negative-aware fine-tuning~ zheng2026diffusionnft : by pulling predicted actions toward the video-paired trajectory while repelling other trajectories of the same task, it prevents task-identity shortcuts and forces the policy to follow the demonstrated motion. We evaluate on an Astribot S1 robot and the RoboTwin benchmark~ mu2025robotwin,chen2025robotwin2 . Without task-specific fine-tuning, improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on Astribot S1, and achieves a 69.5 average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM~ zhou2026zerowam by 22.6 percentage points. More surprisingly, although our training pairs are strictly scene-aligned, goes beyond unseen tasks with the same objects (Fig.~ fig:teaser , middle): it transfers the demonstrated behavior across rearranged layouts and substituted tools, such as using a banana to sweep a wooden block into a cardboard box from a brush-and-dustpan demonstration (Fig.~ fig:teaser , top and bottom). Our main contributions are as follows: Scalable temporally aligned data: we turn recorded robot trajectories into temporally matched human demonstrations with reference-conditioned video-to-video generation, so alignment scales with the robot-video corpus without human reenactment. In-context WAM training: we concatenate demonstration and robot-video tokens along time, train on variable-length windows, and add an intra-task loss that removes the task-identity shortcut. Data scaling and cross-scene transfer: unseen-task scores grow monotonically with aligned data; scene-aligned training transfers to new layouts and tools. Related Work sec:related_work In-Context Learning for Robotic Manipulation In-context learning enables a frozen robot policy to infer a task from deployment demonstrations, such as sensorimotor trajectories in ICRT~ fu2025icrt , demonstration graphs in Instant Policy~ vosylius2025instant , or retrieved segments in RICL~ sridhar2025ricl , extending one-shot policies based on task embeddings~ duan2017oneshot,james2018tecnets , frame attention~ dasari2021transformers,mandi2022mosaic , or skill priors~ yu2019composition,xu2023xskill,zhu2026humanprompt . To leverage human videos, prior works learn visual features~ pmlr-v205-nair23a , latent actions~ ye2025lapa , or play plans~ pmlr-v229-wang23a , co-train on egocentric data in EgoMimic~ kareer2025egomimic , retrieve play segments in RHyME~ kedia2025one and MimicDroid~ shah2026mimicdroid , or condition deployment on a single human video via video retrieval in ViP~ chanesane2023vip , language grounding in BC-Z~ pmlr-v164-jang22a , and cross-attention in Vid2Robot~ jain2024vid2robot . However, reducing a demonstration to a task identifier limits policies to recalling training behaviors~ pan2023disentangling , whereas generalizing to unseen procedures and novel object uses requires tracking how the interaction unfolds, as explored through subgoal or trace prediction~ goswami2026osvi,qian2026synthicl,son2026seetraceact , temporal alignment~ sermanet2018tcn,dwibedi2019tcc,zakka2022xirl,chen2026host , intra-task keyframe separation in JEDI~ liang2026jedi , layout shifts in SimpleICL~ li2026simpleicl , and functional substitutions in The Imitator Game~ zhou2026imitatorgame . uses a single human video to specify the procedure within a world-action model, generalizing across unseen procedures (Task-OOD) and altered scenes or tools (Context-OOD). World-Action Models World-action models jointly predict future observations and actions~ wu2024gr1,li2025unified,zhu2025unified,bi2026motus,motubrain2026 , extending visual foresight~ finn2017foresight , action recovery from visual plans~ du2023learning,ko2024avdc,liang2024dreamitate , predictive representations for control~ tian2025seer,hu2025vpp,zheng2025flare , and video generators adapted for policy learning~ shen2026videovla,ye2026world,li2026causal,vidar2025,vidarc2025 or rollout synthesis~ jang2025dreamgen . Recent WAMs further incorporate context and demonstrations: ICWM~ wang2026context infers system properties from self-interaction, WATCH~ watch2026 pretrains on task-paired human videos, LingBot-VA 2.0~ zhang2026native and WorldScape Policy 2.0~ su2026worldscape accept demonstration prompts, and Zero-WAM~ zhou2026zerowam generates task-matched human clips while predicting temporally spaced future chunks to encourage prompt usage. However, conditioning on a demonstration alone does not ensure that predicted actions follow the demonstrated execution over task-level cues; addresses this by combining temporally aligned training with intra-task action contrast~ oord2018representation to distinguish different executions of the same task. Test-Time Training Meta-imitation adapts policy parameters from a demonstration~ finn2017oneshot,yu2018one , while test-time training adapts models or fast weights to test inputs~ sun2020test,hansen2021policy,sun2025learning . WAM-TTT~ feng2026wam updates fast weights from human videos before rollout, and RoboTTT~ jiang2026robottt updates them as the robot's visuomotor history grows. keeps its weights fixed at deployment, conditioning each prediction directly on the human demonstration and current robot observation. Motion Retargeting and Paired Data Motion retargeting transfers object-relative motions~ heppert2024ditto,zhu2024orion or human hand trajectories~ li2024okami,park2025demodiffusion,qin2022dexmv to a robot; BEHAVE~ bhatnagar2022behave records human--object contact, and CORE4D~ liu2025core4d retargets two-person rearrangement motions to new object shapes. Robot training data can also come from paired human--robot recordings~ sharma2018mime,fang2024rh20t,human2robot2025 or synthesizing robot demonstrations from human footage~ lepert2025phantom,egoengine2026,lee2026robotryon,chen2025vivla , whereas Gen2Act~ pmlr-v305-bharadhwaj25a generates a human video from an initial image and task description. uses the full robot recording as a motion reference, verifies the generated human video for temporal and interaction agreement with the source, and combines these clips with synchronized human reenactments so each sampled demonstration window pairs directly with the recorded robot actions. Ent-Dataset Construction sec:paired_dataset Dataset Overview and Strict Pairing sec:strict_pairing Each training example in the Ent-Dataset pairs a human demonstration video with a recorded robot trajectory containing camera observations, proprioceptive states, and actions (Fig.~ fig:paired_dataset_overview (c)). As summarized in Fig.~ fig:paired_dataset_overview (b), the dataset contains 21.3k pairs split across disjoint robot episodes for training and validation, comprising 5.3k real pairs from Astribot S1 (Ent-Real) and 16.0k synthetic pairs from Astribot and AgiBot (Ent-Syn). To supervise fine-grained action prediction from human video, each target action chunk requires a localized visual reference in the demonstration. When human and robot videos are paired only by task label or synthesized from an edited initial frame~ zhou2026zerowam , subsequent motion paths and contact timing remain unaligned with the ground-truth robot actions. To provide unambiguous supervision, we enforce strict pairing: using the recorded robot trajectory as an anchor, the paired human video matches (i) the camera viewpoint and scene layout, (ii) the manipulated objects and sequence of interaction events (e.g., reaching, grasping, transporting, and releasing), and (iii) the timing of each event. This alignment requires the policy to track visual progression instead of relying on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts; we ablate strict pairing in Table~ tab:real_robot_main and evaluate cross-scene transfer at deployment in Section~ sec:context_ood_evaluation . Ent-Real sec:real_paired_data We construct real pairs by having humans reenact recorded Astribot S1 trajectories in the same workspace under a viewpoint matched to the robot's head camera. During recording, demonstrators watch the source robot video playback and perform the manipulation in synchrony, matching the object interactions, motion paths, and execution tempo. title: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
summary: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.
full_text: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments Ahad Jawaid, Alexander Swerdlow, and Yu Xiang Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data. Robot learning, action tokenization, autoregressive policies, vision-language-action models, robot manipulation Introduction Large language models minaee2024large have benefited from a simple scalable training recipe: convert text into a shared vocabulary of tokens, then train a single autoregressive model on a large corpus of tokens. A similar recipe may help scale robotic learning. Robot data, however, comes from many embodiments, often with different action spaces, control frequencies, and ranges of motion, and is collected in different ways: teleoperation on real robots, handheld grippers such as UMI chi2024umi , simulation, and recordings of human hands. A foundation robot policy that uses this recipe will likely need a tokenizer that can encode large and diverse sets of actions, ideally including those from embodiments it has not seen. The action tokenizer therefore plays an important role in training autoregressive robot policies, and its design can substantially affect policy performance, training efficiency, and inference speed pertsch2025fast . Early autoregressive policies discretized each action dimension into uniform bins~ pmlr-rt2-zitkovich23a, openvla2024 . Binning can be applied to most robots, but it tends to produce long token sequences that slow down inference. FAST~ pertsch2025fast compresses action chunks with a frequency-domain transform and byte pair encoding, yielding shorter sequences and faster training, and the released FAST+~ pertsch2025fast is trained on 1M robot trajectories such that it can work across embodiments. A growing line of work instead learns the tokenizer: a neural encoder, a quantizer~ lee2022rvq, mentzer2024fsq , and a decoder that reconstructs the action chunk~ wang2025vqvla, liu2026faster, liu2026oat, jawaid2026nac, dong2026actioncodec . These tokenizers can represent actions with fewer tokens than FAST~ pertsch2025fast , but most are trained on comparatively small datasets, so how they behave on the scale and diversity of data a foundation policy would require remains largely unexplored. In this work, we study action tokenization at scale. We assemble a corpus of 49k hours of action data from 156 datasets spanning real-world robots, universal manipulation interfaces (UMIs) chi2024umi , simulated robots, and human hand motion, and use it to train and evaluate action tokenizers. We also introduce the Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT) Website: . Tokenizer: . , a causal neural tokenizer that encodes action chunks into short token sequences using finite scalar quantization (FSQ)~ mentzer2024fsq at multiple temporal scales. Its causal decoder supports streaming: actions can be decoded as their tokens are generated, so the robot can begin executing while the policy is still predicting the rest of the chunk, and the policy can condition its next chunk on the actions still executing. We then pretrain vision-language-action models (VLAs) with NAT to test whether these results carry over to large pretrained policies, and compare acting through NAT tokens with acting through a flow-matching action head~ lipman2023flow, black2024pi0 . Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*, labelindent=1em] State-of-the-art neural action tokenization. NAT outperforms FAST~ pertsch2025fast and prior neural action tokenizers (OAT~ liu2026oat , ActionCodec~ dong2026actioncodec , and NAC~ jawaid2026nac ) in mean success on unseen robot embodiments. A universal streaming action tokenizer. We train NAT on 49k hours of actions from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. Its causal decoder supports immediate execution, and its time-ordered tokens let a policy condition its next chunk on the actions still executing without retraining. Human data for action tokenizers. Our experiments suggest that robot data may not be necessary to train an action tokenizer: a NAT trained only on human hand motion is nearly as effective as one trained on all sources. Pretraining vision-language-action models with NAT tokens. We show that NAT tokens can help pretrain vision-language-action models: further training a pretrained vision-language model on 1.8k hours of robot data through NAT tokens, before fine-tuning, raises mean success on four simulation benchmarks over fine-tuning the vision-language model directly. Flow action heads and action tokens. Acting through NAT tokens produces first actions sooner than acting through a flow-matching action head, and on some benchmarks matches its success: on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , the two are within the 95 intervals. Related Work Autoregressive Robot Policies Robot foundation models are commonly built by fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language model on robot data~ black2024pi0, black2025pi0.5, nvidia2025groot, fang2026molmoact2actionreasoningmodels . Since these backbones are autoregressive transformers~ vaswani2017attention , actions can be tokenized and predicted with next-token prediction; early work showed that even simple binning transfers web-scale knowledge to robot control~ pmlr-rt2-zitkovich23a, openvla2024 . Other models, such as ~ black2024pi0 and GR00T~ nvidia2025groot , instead decode actions with a flow-matching or diffusion head which showed improvements in inference latency. FAST~ pertsch2025fast showed that mid-training on discrete action tokens improves training efficiency and policy performance, and later work adopts this for models with a continuous action expert~ black2025pi0.5, driess2026knowledge, fang2026molmoact2actionreasoningmodels . Action Tokenizers Binning each action dimension~ pmlr-rt2-zitkovich23a, openvla2024 is simple but produces long token sequences that can make real-time inference impractical. FAST~ pertsch2025fast uses handcrafted frequency-based compression to produce much shorter sequences, improving training efficiency and policy performance, and its variant FAST+ pertsch2025fast , fitted on 1M real robot action sequences, tokenizes new action spaces zero-shot. Learned tokenizers compress actions further with vector-quantized autoencoders~ wang2025vqvla , and have been extended to multiple embodiments~ liu2026faster , aligned with language~ dong2026actioncodec , ordered so that partial token sequences can be decoded~ liu2026oat , and scaled to 2B action frames with vision-language alignment~ kang2026xtokenizermultimodalactiontokenizer . Most neural tokenizers have been trained on comparatively smaller datasets, so it remains largely unexplored how learned tokenizers behave when trained on large, heterogeneous action data spanning real robots, UMIs chi2024umi , simulation, and humans. Real-Time Execution Action chunking~ zhao-act, chi2025diffusion lets a policy predict several future actions per inference, but the robot must wait for each new chunk, and switching between independently sampled chunks can cause discontinuities. Many VLAs predict chunks with a diffusion or flow-matching action head~ black2024pi0, nvidia2025groot , which generates every action of a chunk in parallel over a fixed number of denoising steps; knowledge insulation~ driess2026knowledge trains such a head beside discrete action tokens, and consistency distillation~ prasad2024consistency reduces the number of denoising steps. Other work hides inference latency during execution: asynchronous inference~ shukor2025smolvla predicts the next chunk while the current one runs, bidirectional decoding~ liu2024bid selects among sampled chunks for coherence with the previous one, and real-time chunking~ black2026rtc inpaints the actions still executing into a flow policy's sampling so that consecutive chunks join smoothly. Autoregressive policies, in contrast, usually decode a chunk only after all of its tokens are generated~ pertsch2025fast . NAT's time-ordered tokens and causal decoder give them both properties: actions are executed as their tokens are generated, and executing actions are fixed as a token prefix. Preliminaries Action chunking. We consider policies that, given an observation (camera images, proprioception, and a task), predict a chunk of future actions , where is the action dimension. During execution, the robot executes the first actions of each chunk before querying the policy again. We refer to as the execution horizon~ black2026rtc . Action tokenization. Autoregressive policies that predict discrete tokens, the setting we study, require continuous action chunks to first be converted into a token sequence. A tokenizer maps an action chunk to a sequence of tokens, with , where is the tokenizer's vocabulary, and a detokenizer maps a token sequence back to an action chunk, . The policy only predicts in the token space, while the robot executes the continuous action reconstructed by . Existing tokenizers differ in how they construct this mapping. Binning~ pmlr-rt2-zitkovich23a, openvla2024 normalizes each action dimension to and assigns each value to one of uniform bins, giving one token per dimension per timestep ( ). FAST ~ pertsch2025fast applies the discrete cosine transform ahmed-dct to each action dimension, rounds the resulting coefficients, and compresses them with byte-pair encoding gage1994bpe . Neural tokenizers~ wang2025vqvla, liu2026faster, liu2026oat, jawaid2026nac, dong2026actioncodec instead learn the mapping: an encoder compresses the chunk into a short sequence of latent vectors, a quantizer~ lee2022rvq, mentzer2024fsq maps each latent to an entry of a discrete codebook, and a decoder reconstructs the chunk. Streaming. For most tokenizers, the detokenizer needs the complete token sequence before it can decode any action, so the robot must wait for the policy to generate all tokens. We call a tokenizer streaming if every prefix of the token sequence already determines a prefix of the action chunk, and those actions do not change as further tokens are generated. With a streaming tokenizer, the robot can begin executing a chunk while the policy is still generating it. Neural Action Tokenizer We introduce the Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a neural tokenizer whose decoder enables streaming. title: JEPA-Tuner: From Predictive Fine-Tuning to Asynchronous Execution of Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate sequences of actions from visual observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions. In embodied interaction, executing these actions influences subsequent observations and robot states, providing a natural predictive signal for policy learning. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not explicitly capture these action-conditioned temporal dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action predictor. We introduce JEPA-Tuner, a predictive fine-tuning framework that regularizes the VLA's native policy guidance through action-conditioned future prediction. During fine-tuning, a predictor in JEPA-Tuner learns to match guidance encoded from a future observation given the current guidance and committed actions. This objective encourages a cross-modal guidance adapter to capture how the scene and robot state evolve under those actions, while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance keeps the representation informative for control. In addition, when deploying the VLA model with asynchronous action-chunk inference, the pre-trained predictor will anticipate the guidance needed at the next chunk boundary. The policy can thus generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction or additional predictor training, enabling efficient and high-quality asynchronous execution. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World show that JEPA-Tuner improves task success under synchronous inference with better multi-modal guidance embeddings. For asynchronous control, JEPA-Tuner improves performance and smoothness across different latency settings on both LIBERO simulator and multi-size real robot demonstrations. The project website with video demos is at https://qujx.github.io/JEPA-Tuner-Website.

Introduction sec:introduction =0 Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual observations, language instructions, and proprioceptive states to generate robot action chunks~ openvla,pi0,pi05,smolvla . Many recent VLAs couple pretrained vision-language models (VLMs)~ qwen,paligemma with action experts through multimodal policy guidance (vision, language, robotic states, etc.). Structuring this multimodal guidance is important for both policy adaptation and asynchronous execution. When a robot executes an action on an object, it changes both the arm configuration and the object's position. Prior works used this relationship to anticipate input to a policy. For instance, VLASH~ vlash estimates future proprioceptive states using current states and committed actions, while FutureRTC~ futurertc predicts visual representations and proprioceptive states to correct a frozen VLA policy. These examples suggest that multimodal control signals are coupled through learnable predictive dependencies. However, standard action-supervised fine-tuning does not enforce these dependencies in the guidance consumed by the action expert. We therefore use the observations of executed actions as an additional training signal for the guidance that conditions the action expert. Specifically, we encourage action-conditioned predictive consistency by jointly training a predictor to predict future guidance and proprioception from the current guidance, and further align the policy on it. Action-conditioned prediction also offers a natural way to address inference latency in asynchronous control. As Fig.~ fig:rtc_challenges illustrates, the robot continues to move while the next chunk is computed, shifting execution toward later predictions conditioned on an earlier observation. Real-Time Chunking (RTC)~ rtc corrects the overlap with committed actions through inference-time inpainting, while training based method (e.g., T-RTC~ training_time_rtc , Legato~ legato ) learn smoothness during training to continue the committed trajectory. Although conditioning on the committed action prefix can smooth transitions between chunks, a strong bias toward continuing the previous trajectory can limit the action expert's ability to respond to state changes, reducing closed-loop task success under inference delay~ legato,soft_rtc . To capture action-conditioned dependencies in multimodal guidance and better balance trajectory smoothness with action accuracy during asynchronous inference, we introduce JEPA-Tuner, a fine-tuning framework inspired by joint-embedding predictive architectures for robot control~ jepa_vla,vla_jepa,slim . Specifically, a cross-modal adapter mixes visual, language, and state information at the VLA's native input prefix. Given the adapted guidance at step , the robot state, and the next demonstrated actions, a predictor estimates the future guidance and proprioceptive state at step . In VLA model finetuning, we further train the action expert to generate action chunks from both observed and predicted guidance, while jointly training the predictor to match the guidance encoded from the observation at . This joint objective encourages the predicted guidance to capture the future scene and state while retaining the information needed for action generation. During asynchronous inference, we reuse the same predictor with the actions committed before the handoff, allowing the expert to generate the next chunk in advance and execute it from its first action without overlap correction. Our main contributions are as follows: We identify action-conditioned temporal dependencies in multimodal guidance that standard action-supervised VLA fine-tuning ignored. Motivated by this observation, we propose JEPA-Tuner, which improves VLA fine-tuning by regularizing native multimodal guidance through future prediction while jointly training the action expert on both observed and predicted guidance. To address latency-induced conditioning mismatch during asynchronous control, we develop a predictive execution scheme that reuses the predictor learned by JEPA-Tuner during fine-tuning to anticipate guidance at the next chunk handoff. This enables each new chunk to directly execute from its first action with anticipated guidance without additional training or overlap correction. Experiments on LIBERO and Meta-World demonstrate improved VLA fine-tuning performance. Asynchronous evaluations further demonstrate a better trade-off between task success and action smoothness, both in simulation and on robot platforms of different scales, SO-101 and ALOHA, under standard and severe inference latency. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and generalist robot policies integrate visual observations and language instructions for robot control. RT-2~ rt2 represents actions as tokens, while OpenVLA~ openvla and Octo~ octo advance generalist policy pretraining and adaptation. OpenVLA-OFT~ openvla_oft studies efficient action decoding and fine-tuning. Recently, diffusion~ diffusion and flow matching~ flow_matching play an important role in generative modeling across multiple data modalities~ sdxl, gaga, p2flow . These frameworks also support continuous action generation: ~ pi0 introduces a flow-matching action expert, ~ pi05 extends this paradigm through heterogeneous co-training, and SmolVLA~ smolvla emphasizes compact, affordable action-chunk policies. Unless otherwise specified, we consider VLA policies that generate continuous action chunks using diffusion or flow matching. Predictive Learning for VLA Policies VLA-JEPA~ vla_jepa and JEPA-WAM~ JEPA-WAM impose temporal supervision through visual targets defined by pretrained V-JEPA encoders, while JEPA-VLA~ jepa_vla augments existing VLAs with pretrained video-predictive embeddings. WoG~ WoG learns compact future-observation conditions for action generation, and SLIM~ slim models action-conditioned transitions within its own learned observation-latent space. Their future-representation targets or transferred features are primarily visual, even when actions and proprioception provide conditioning. These formulations do not address the joint problem of shaping an existing VLA's native multimodal guidance and forecasting that guidance at execution boundaries under inference latency. JEPA-Tuner addresses this joint problem by learning action-conditioned predictive consistency within an existing VLA's native policy guidance space. As a plug-in fine-tuning framework, it couples future visual-guidance and proprioceptive-state prediction with action supervision, directly regularizing the temporal evolution of the conditioning consumed by the action expert. Crucially, the same learned predictor is reused to anticipate guidance at the next execution boundary, unifying downstream representation adaptation with latency-aware asynchronous control. Asynchronous Inference of VLA Models Asynchronous VLA methods seek continuous, temporally aligned control under inference latency. RTC~ rtc uses inference-time inpainting conditioned on committed actions, while Training-Time RTC~ training_time_rtc learns committed-prefix conditioning during training. Legato~ legato similarly learns continuation for flow-based policies. These methods promote temporal compatibility in action space. Another complementary strategy anticipates execution-time conditioning. VLASH~ vlash rolls proprioception forward while retaining earlier visual observations; EagleVLA~ eaglevla predicts future compressed VLM features; and FutureRTC~ futurertc forecasts visual latents and proprioceptive states for a frozen policy. Latent Bridge~ latent_bridge predicts conditioning-feature changes to reduce backbone invocations. However, these methods primarily exploit prediction for deployment, leaving underexplored whether action-conditioned predictive regularization of native multimodal guidance can improve VLA fine-tuning. JEPA-Tuner obtains two benefits from a single fine-tuning procedure: improved VLA finetuning performance through predictive guidance regularization and a predictor directly reusable for asynchronous control. The jointly learned predictor anticipates execution-boundary guidance, supporting prefix execution without a separate predictor-training stage or inference-time overlap correction. Standard receding-horizon execution uses the first actions and discards the remaining actions, termed the unexecuted suffix, before replanning from new observations. title: Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head for Tiny Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Real-time onboard robot control calls for a lightweight vision-language-action (VLA) model, yet shrinking the backbone leaves less capacity for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter alternative by iterating in latent space before committing to an action, but existing designs refine a single undifferentiated state that must simultaneously encode slowly evolving task context and rapidly changing motor commands. We propose the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which maintains two latent states updated at different frequencies: a low-level state that updates fast, grounded in action tokens and proprioception, and a high-level state that updates slowly, grounded in visual understanding and the instruction-informed low-level state. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3-4.3x smaller than those of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0% success rate on LIBERO and a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC->D, at the lowest latency among compared methods. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost.

Chain-of-thought decoding, dual-system architectures, and larger backbones can restore deliberation but reintroduce the latency and memory costs that motivated going small. The two states exchange information through nested reasoning cycles. Because all iteration occurs in the compact head after a single backbone pass, HR-AH adds hierarchical reasoning without increasing the backbone size. We show that this hierarchy improves performance over a parameter-matched single-state head, and that routing distinct modalities to each level yields further gains in both accuracy and inference cost. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models attach an action decoder to a pretrained vision-language backbone, bringing general-purpose robotic manipulation directly from raw images and natural-language commands within reach~ kim2024openvla, black2025pi0, kim2025oft . However, deploying these models onboard at control frequency demands a compact backbone. A growing line of tiny VLAs delivers this by shrinking the backbone to a fraction of the original scale~ wen2024tinyvla, belkhale2024minivla, shukor2025smolvla, wang2026vlaadapter , but a smaller backbone has less capacity available for deliberation at inference time. Chain-of-Thought decoding at 3--8.5B parameters~ zhao2025cot, zhong2026flowvla, huang2025thinkact, huang2026fast and dual-system designs that distribute modalities across large VLM subsystems~ zhang2024hirt, chen2025fastinslow can restore deliberation, but they reintroduce the very costs that a tiny backbone was chosen to avoid. Recurrent action heads offer a lighter path by iterating in latent space before committing to an action~ tur2026rdvla, shen2026loopvla . Latent iteration suits chunked continuous control well, since the objective is to refine a motor plan rather than to generate tokens sequentially. However, latent recurrence alone does not determine how computation should be organized. Within an action chunk, task-level context remains relatively steady while concrete motor commands must be jointly refined across timesteps. Refining them in a single recurrent state forces it to represent quantities that evolve at different rates, analogous to running a task planner at servo rate~ tur2026rdvla, shen2026loopvla . This raises a central question: can explicitly separating the two improve the effectiveness and efficiency of recurrent computation without increasing the backbone's computational burden? We introduce the Hierarchical Reasoning Action Head (HR-AH), which decouples the two processes into levels that correspond to naturally distinct inputs. The motor command draws on instruction-conditioned action queries and proprioception, while the task context draws on vision and the evolving instruction-informed motor plan. This arrangement, fast proprioception-driven feedback operating beneath slower vision-driven deliberation, reflects a well-established principle in sensorimotor control~ todorov2002optimal, merel2019hierarchical and in layered robot control architectures~ brooks1986subsumption . Unlike dual-system designs that distribute this hierarchy across two large VLM subsystems~ zhang2024hirt, chen2025fastinslow , HR-AH routes modalities to two states inside a single lightweight action head, keeping the entire model compact. To our knowledge, HR-AH is the first hierarchical recurrent action head for a tiny VLA. The two levels exchange information through nested reasoning cycles with top-down refinement. Because vision tokens are the larger input, confining them to the slower path amortizes their cost over multiple fast executor steps. The backbone is evaluated once per observation, and all iterative reasoning takes place in the lightweight head. visualizes how the resulting attention sharpens over reasoning steps compared to a single-state baseline. The contributions of this paper are as follows: Hierarchical recurrent computation for tiny VLAs. HR-AH separates visual-context update from motor-command refinement through high- and low-level latent states, providing an explicit hierarchical structure for iterative action refinement entirely within the action head. Modality-specific routing for efficient reasoning. We route vision tokens to the high-level planner and action tokens with proprioception to the low-level executor, concentrating expensive visual attention in the slower reasoning pathway. Combined with adaptive halting, this routing allows inference depth to vary with task difficulty while keeping per-step cost low. Strong results with a compact head. With a 22.5M-parameter head, 3--4.3 smaller than the heads of RD-VLA and VLA-Adapter on the same backbone, HR-AH reaches 97.0 on LIBERO, a 4.40 average chain length on CALVIN ABC D, and 78.8 on a real Kinova Gen3 Lite robot, at the lowest latency among compared methods. Ablations show that hierarchical state separation accounts for most of the gain over a parameter-matched single-state baseline, while modality-specific routing contributes a further 3.4 points and reduces the number of reasoning steps required. Related Work sec:related Vision-language-action models. VLAs adapt pretrained vision-language models to robot control. They differ chiefly in how actions are decoded, e.g., whether by autoregressive discretization~ kim2024openvla , compressed action tokens~ pertsch2025fast , diffusion~ chi2023diffusionpolicy , flow matching~ black2025pi0 , or parallel decoding with regression~ kim2025oft . A complementary line shrinks the backbone for practical deployment~ wen2024tinyvla, belkhale2024minivla, shukor2025smolvla . Most relevant is VLA-Adapter~ wang2026vlaadapter , which trains a feed-forward policy over a tiny backbone by injecting per-layer VLM features through Bridge Attention. Its 97M-parameter head is purely feed-forward, with no provision for iterative refinement. We operate in the same tiny-VLA setting but show that a compact hierarchical recurrent head can surpass feed-forward decoding in both accuracy and efficiency. Iterative computation for action prediction. A growing body of work allocates variable computation per action. Early-exit methods adapt how much of the backbone runs at each step~ yue2024deervla , and dual-system designs split slow reasoning and fast control into distinct models or modules~ shi2025hirobot, nvidia2025groot, bu2024robodual, zhang2024hirt , with Fast-in-Slow~ chen2025fastinslow distributing modalities across two subsystems that share a 7B VLM at a 1:4 update ratio. UniFS~ sun2026unifs schedules backbone layer groups at decreasing update frequencies, LoopVLA~ shen2026loopvla repeatedly applies a shared transformer block to the multimodal tokens, and PredVLA~ sawada2026predvla is a sub-million-parameter multi-timescale recurrent policy with no VLM backbone. These approaches organize computation at different frequencies across backbone components or outside the action head. Recurrence inside the action head has been explored, but only with a single state. For example, RD-VLA~ tur2026rdvla places a single weight-tied recurrent core and shows that success scales with test-time iterations. Such a head uses the same recurrent representation to integrate visual context and refine motor commands at every iteration, rather than assigning these operations distinct update frequencies. No existing design combines multi-level hierarchy with iterative recurrence inside the action head. We close this gap with two latent states, updated at different frequencies after a single backbone pass, whose modality-routed inputs let scene context and motor commands be updated in separate but interacting streams. We show this design outperforms a parameter-matched single-state recurrent head with access to the same visual context, and competes with much larger architectures on standard benchmarks. Recursive reasoning models. Adaptive and weight-tied recurrent computation was explored early by adaptive computation time~ graves2016act and Universal Transformers~ dehghani2019universal , and has resurfaced as recurrent-depth language models~ geiping2025huginn and looped transformers for 3D vision~ burzio2026dejaview . HRM~ wang2025hrm couples a slow high-level and a fast low-level recurrent module on symbolic puzzles. Its high-level module observes only the low-level module's output, so both levels are ultimately grounded in the same representation despite differing in update frequency. Subsequent analyses find that this hierarchy adds little on these tasks~ arcprize2025hrm, ge2025hrmmisconceptions, rodrigues2026dissecting , and TRM~ jolicoeur2025trm outperforms it with a single tiny network trained by backpropagating through the recursion. Embodied control hints at a different outcome, as PredVLA reports that removing the temporal hierarchy from its predictive recurrent architecture lowers success substantially~ sawada2026predvla . Our hierarchy routes distinct modalities to each level, so the timescale separation arises naturally from the distinct input modalities. We ablate against a parameter-matched single-state head that sees the full context from the backbone and a variant that preserves both states and their update rates but feeds them identical inputs. Hierarchy accounts for the larger gain, while modality-specific routing contributes a further improvement in both accuracy and inference cost. Multi-layer VLM features for control. Which backbone depth best conditions an action head remains unsettled. GR00T~N1 conditions on a middle layer~ nvidia2025groot , SmolVLA discards the upper half of the backbone~ shukor2025smolvla , and FLOWER prunes layers and fuses intermediate tokens~ reuss2025flower . VLA-Adapter matches each policy block to one VLM layer~ wang2026vlaadapter and LIRA widens this to a local window of layers~ zhang2026lira , while ABot-M0 reports that, after large-scale robot pretraining, final-layer features alone suffice~ yang2026abotm0 . Our head reads both token groups from a deep backbone layer and additionally supplies the planner with gated vision features from the embedding layer. This retains both high-level semantic features and fine-grained spatial detail while extracting all representations once per observation. title: Detecting Is Not Choosing: What a World Model Needs to Keep a VLA Policy Safe
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Accepted at the CoRL 2026 Workshop "Do Robots Need World Models?". OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=oIzsAcOuYl
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Since they are stochastic, one remedy is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that a world model predicts is safe. We ask what such a model must do. In simulation, a lookahead safety filter with the simulator as an exact world model raises the safety rate of three VLA policies on LIBERO and of pi0.5 on LIBERO-Plus by 11.5 to 25.7 points. It also helps pi0.5 on three RoboCasa tasks. Learned critics trained on one policy's data detect dangerous states (pooled AUROC up to 0.864) but rank candidates at one state close to chance (within-decision AUROC 0.551-0.560), and the learned dynamics and video models we test do no better. When the simulator's state is perturbed, selection degrades long before detection. In the loop, a median position error of 3.18 mm removes 70% of the gain on LIBERO-Spatial, partly because the error also corrupts the displacement check. On LIBERO-10 the loss is smaller, and the intervals overlap. The median does not predict the cost: a pixel reader with a 0.56 mm median error keeps 6.5 points less of the gain than Gaussian error of a similar median. A world model for safety should thus be judged by within-state ranking, and its state must be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, not only in the median.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies complete most benchmark tasks but often violate safety constraints. Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) policies now complete most tasks in standard manipulation benchmarks, but often unsafely. On LIBERO-10, succeeds in of our episodes, yet only are free of violations such as pushing a non-target object, excessive contact force or tilting a carried object (Table~ tab:guard ). Because the policies are stochastic, a simple remedy at test time is to sample several candidate action chunks and execute one that is predicted to be safe. This requires a world model. The question is what kind of model, and how accurate it must be. Two families of approaches could make this prediction. Implicit approaches learn a critic or value function that scores candidates directly~ nakamoto2024steering,kwok2025robomonkey,sun2026prevla . Explicit approaches predict the future and evaluate it, as in latent safety filters~ nakamura2025generalizing,seo2025uncertainty , Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos and learned predictive models combined with a geometric shield~ zhong2026calibrated . Both are usually judged in closed loop or by how well they separate safe from unsafe states pooled over a dataset. RoboMonkey's offline comparisons at one state use the demonstrated action, not safety, as the reference~ kwok2025robomonkey . A safety filter needs something narrower: at a single state, it must tell which of the policy's own candidates is safe. We study this question with the most accurate world model available, the simulator itself. A lookahead safety filter rolls the policy's candidates forward from an exact copy of the simulator state and executes the one with the fewest predicted violations. For these candidates and this rule, no model can predict better, although another rule might be safer. Against it we place learned critics, dynamics and video models, and state estimators, and degrade the simulator's state by known amounts. With the exact model, the filter raises safety in all policy--benchmark pairs ( to points on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus), for largely via fallbacks. The learned critics we train detect dangerous states no better than a critic that never sees the candidate, and within a state they rank candidates near chance, as do the explicit models we test. Selection degrades with state error long before detection, and real estimators lose more than their median error predicts. Our answer to the workshop's question: such a filter needs a world model that ranks actions at one state, and among the models and data we tested only the exact simulator does. Its state must also be accurate in the tail and on handled objects, where the median error says little. The test is therefore within-state ranking rather than pooled AUROC, and simulator labels make it cheap. Setup and method sec:method A VLA policy maps images, proprioception and an instruction to a chunk of actions (0.5\,s). The robot executes five and then queries the policy again at the next decision. random seeds give candidate chunks. The first, the nominal chunk, is what the policy would execute alone. We test ~ black2025pi05 , ~ pertsch2025fast and SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-10~ liu2023libero (SmolVLA on LIBERO-Spatial only), and on LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus and three RoboCasa tasks~ nasiriany2024robocasa , all in MuJoCo via robosuite~ zhu2020robosuite . Constraints and thresholds follow SafeVLA-Bench~ fan2026safevlabench , except for tilt on LIBERO-10. An episode is unsafe if a non-target object other than the task's receptacle moves more than 5\,mm or a contact force exceeds 200\,N. It is also unsafe if the arm collides with itself or a carried object tilts more than ( on LIBERO-10). The safety rate is the share of safe episodes. The lookahead safety filter uses the simulator as its world model. At each decision it saves the simulator state, runs the nominal chunk for steps and restores the state exactly. If no constraint was violated, the robot executes the nominal chunk. Otherwise the filter simulates the other candidates and executes the one with the fewest predicted violations. At an infeasible decision, where all candidates are unsafe, it also tries two short fallback motions, a lift and a lift away from the nearest non-target object, and runs one if it predicts fewer violations. With , the filter departs from the nominal chunk at of decisions on LIBERO-Spatial and on LIBERO-10. Against it we test learned models of two kinds. An implicit model, a learned safety critic, predicts the probability that a candidate violates a constraint within steps. We train six critics on simulator labels of all 16 candidates at decisions. Five see the candidate with privileged object poses, policy features or images, and one sees only the state. An explicit model predicts the future, on which the constraints are checked. We test a learned dynamics model, a latent world model on DINOv2 features~ oquab2024dinov2 in the style of DINO-WM~ zhou2025dinowm , and Cosmos Policy's video predictions~ kim2026cosmos . title: Ego2Wrist: Bootstrapping Wrist-View Synthesis from Egocentric Video
comment: 27 pages (13 main + 14 appendix), 9 figures, 20 tables. Project page: https://adonis-galaxy.github.io/Ego2Wrist/
summary: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.

Introduction sec:intro Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation~ zhao2023learning,khazatsky2024droid,chi2024universal . However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging, as the camera setup is cumbersome and can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale~ grauman2022ego4d,grauman2024egoexo4d,buildai2025egocentric10k . Synthesizing wrist views from these videos could therefore transform scalable real-world human demonstrations into action-centric data for robot policy training. Paired recordings of head and wrist cameras were rare until 2026, when several datasets released about a thousand hours of synchronized head and wrist video of people performing manipulation tasks~ lightwheel2026egosuite,zhou2026touchanything,humaid2026egoviz,lyu2026humantouch,chen2026spark0 . This makes it possible to learn the mapping from a head video to both wrist videos directly (head-to-wrist synthesis, ). Head-to-wrist synthesis presents two key challenges beyond conventional novel-view synthesis. First, wrist cameras move with the forearms, but their trajectories cannot be directly inferred from head views. Existing methods either require known target camera trajectories~ fu2026plenoptic or estimate them from static views~ qian2025wristworld , neither of which is readily available for egocentric human videos. Even with estimated wrist poses, depth-based reprojection provides only marginal improvements ( ). We therefore train a video diffusion model that jointly generates both wrist views alongside the clean head view in a shared latent panel, allowing attention to establish cross-view relationships without explicit geometric modeling. Second, in-the-wild egocentric videos lack wrist-view ground truth, making reference-based evaluation impossible. To address this, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), a ground-truth-free metric that measures whether generated wrist views are consistent with the corresponding hand regions in the input head view. Beyond evaluation, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement using in-the-wild human egocentric videos without wrist-view ground truth. Specifically, we synthesize wrist views for egocentric video windows and select the top 30 based on HCC scores for further training alongside paired data. We iteratively repeat this process with the updated model, progressively improving generation quality through self-generated training data. In summary, our contributions are: We introduce , which synthesizes both wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Evaluated on four datasets, generates wrist views consistent with the input head video and outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander~ song2026worldwander , reducing LPIPS by 28 and achieving human preference. We propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), a ground-truth-free metric for evaluating generated wrist views. HCC agrees with human judgments comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS and provides a practical criterion for selecting synthetic training data. We demonstrate recursive self-improvement using in-the-wild human egocentric videos. By iteratively generating and selecting wrist views with HCC, progressively improves over three rounds of self-training. HCC-based selection also outperforms random selection, demonstrating the potential to scale wrist-view training data from real-world human demonstrations. Related Work sec:related Cross-view video synthesis. Exocentric-to-egocentric methods render the first-person view of a person seen by third-person cameras, from several exocentric views~ liu2024exo2egov , with future prediction~ xu2025egoexogen , by point-cloud reprojection~ park2026egoworld , or by adapting pretrained video diffusion models~ kang2026egox,mahdi2025exo2egosyn ; WorldWander~ song2026worldwander translates in both directions with in-context conditioning. None of these works targets a wrist camera. For robots, WristWorld~ qian2025wristworld generates one wrist view from two static third-person views through a predicted wrist pose, WARPED~ freeman2026warped renders a robot wrist view from egocentric human video with Gaussian splatting, and PlenopticDreamer~ fu2026plenoptic re-renders a head-camera video into both gripper views given their camera trajectories. OpenLongTail~ liu2026openlongtail completes the surround cameras of a driving rig from the front view, and camera-controlled video models~ vanhoorick2024generative,bai2025recammaster,yu2025trajectorycrafter,ren2025gen3c likewise follow a given camera path. We generate both wrist views of a person from a moving head camera, and the wrist poses are not given at inference. Camera-controllable video generation. Camera poses condition video generation directly~ wang2024motionctrl or as per-pixel Pl\"ucker embeddings~ he2025cameractrl,sitzmann2021light , also in video diffusion transformers~ bahmani2025vd3d,bahmani2025ac3d . Most of this work assumes a pinhole camera; AKiRa~ wang2025akira , UCPE~ zhang2026unified and CRePE~ jin2026crepe use ray-based representations that include lens distortion. Our ray condition specifies the lens and mount of a target wrist camera, and our virtual-camera augmentation, close to that of AKiRa, lets one model serve wrist lenses from circular fisheye to rectilinear. Evaluating generated video without ground truth. FVD~ unterthiner2018towards compares distributions of videos, VBench~ huang2024vbench and WorldScore~ duan2025worldscore score predefined dimensions, CrashTwin~ chen2026physics tests whether generated multi-agent dynamics obey physical laws, and VideoScore~ he2024videoscore and WorldModelBench~ li2025worldmodelbench train vision-language models on human ratings. LPIPS~ zhang2018unreasonable agrees well with human similarity judgments but needs a reference. MEt3R~ asim2025met3r measures multi-view consistency without a reference by warping one view into another with DUSt3R~ wang2024dust3r ; dense matchers such as MASt3R~ leroy2024grounding , DINO features~ caron2021emerging,oquab2024dinov2,simeoni2025dinov3 and CLIP~ radford2021learning also relate views. HCC asks a narrower question, whether a generated wrist view shows the content of the head view around the same-side hand, and we compare it with MASt3R, CLIP and MEt3R. Learning manipulation from human and synthetic video. A hand-centric camera improves training efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization~ hsu2022vision , and ALOHA~ zhao2023learning , DROID~ khazatsky2024droid and UMI~ chi2024universal record wrist cameras. Human egocentric video is easier to collect at scale~ grauman2022ego4d,grauman2024egoexo4d,buildai2025egocentric10k , sometimes together with touch~ li2026touchscale , and it is used to pretrain representations~ nair2023r3m and to learn manipulation with 3D hand tracking~ kareer2025egomimic,hoque2026egodex . Phantom~ lepert2025phantom , Masquerade~ lepert2025masquerade and DexUMI~ xu2025dexumi replace the human arm or hand by a robot within the recorded view, whereas we synthesize views that were not recorded. Video generation also supplies robot data, for planning~ du2023learning , as an interactive simulator~ yang2024learning , as synthetic training videos~ jang2025dreamgen , and with tactile conditioning~ zeng2026dtwm . Self-training methods keep the model samples that pass a reward or a verifier and fine-tune on them~ zelikman2022star,gulcehre2023reinforced,singh2024beyond,dong2023raft , and large image-text datasets are filtered with a learned score~ gadre2023datacomp ; HCC plays this role for synthesized wrist views. Training a generative model on its own samples can degrade it unless enough real data enters every round~ shumailov2024ai,alemohammad2024self,bertrand2024stability ; our loop keeps the full real stream in every round and adds the bootstrapped windows at about one in four. Method sec:method Problem setup sec:setup Given a head-camera video of frames and a one-line description of the task, we generate the two wrist-camera videos and of the same interval, each view at pixels. title: LMnOP: Pruning 3D Gaussian Splatting via Leave-Many-Out Importance
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting renders photorealistic views in real time. However, a single scene often needs millions of Gaussians, so these models are costly to store and render. Pruning reduces this cost by keeping a subset of the Gaussians. A common score is the leave-one-out importance, which is the loss increase when a Gaussian alone is removed. At high pruning ratios, many Gaussians are removed together, so Gaussians that are redundant alone but essential together are lost. We present LMnOP (Leave-Many-Out Pruning), which estimates the importance of each Gaussian under the removal of the other Gaussians. This leave-many-out importance is the average loss increase when a Gaussian is removed while the others are also removed at random. We compute the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form, and approximate the importance from them without sampling removal patterns. We refine each Gaussian's probability of remaining with its importance and prune once at the end. Without fine-tuning, LMnOP achieves the best results in 16 of 18 metrics on three datasets at 90% and 99% removal. It improves SSIM and LPIPS over GaussianPOP in all 13 scenes.
