Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023 represents a scene with 3D Gaussians and renders photorealistic views in real time. This combination of quality and speed has quickly made 3DGS a common choice for representing 3D scenes. However, a single scene often requires millions of Gaussians, so the model is expensive to store and render, especially on devices with limited memory. Several directions have been explored to reduce this cost. One direction reduces the bits needed for each Gaussian through quantization and coding~ compact3dgs,eagles,mesongs . This lowers storage but leaves the number of Gaussians, and thus the rendering cost, unchanged. Another direction creates fewer Gaussians during training~ minisplatting , but this requires training the model again. Pruning instead keeps only the Gaussians of a trained model that are actually needed. It reduces both storage and rendering cost, and it can be combined with compression. The more Gaussians we remove, the larger the savings, and the more it matters which Gaussians we keep. To decide which Gaussians to keep, most pruning methods give each Gaussian an importance score and keep those with the highest scores. The scores take different forms, such as accumulated blending weights~ lightgaussian,minisplatting , sensitivity to parameter changes~ pup , and the image error caused by removing a single Gaussian~ gaussianpop . Despite their differences, each of these scores is computed while the rest of the model remains in place. The most direct form of this idea is the loss increase when one Gaussian alone is removed. We call this quantity its leave-one-out importance. In GaussianPOP~ gaussianpop , it is computed exactly for the squared error. Such a score is accurate when only a few Gaussians are removed, because the rest of the model then barely changes. However, when far more Gaussians must be removed, most of them are removed together rather than one at a time. Consider a region that several Gaussians cover together. If any one of them is removed, the others still fill the region, so the leave-one-out importance of each is low. Removing all of them leaves a hole, as (a) shows. Such Gaussians are redundant alone but essential together, yet their leave-one-out importance is as low as that of truly unnecessary Gaussians. Iterative pruning reduces this problem by removing Gaussians over several stages and scoring the remaining ones again after each stage~ gaussianpop . We investigate whether the effect of removing the other Gaussians can instead be incorporated into the importance itself, before any Gaussian is removed. A Gaussian should be evaluated in the situation that pruning actually creates, where many of the other Gaussians are removed as well. Following this principle, we present LMnOP, which scores each Gaussian by its leave-many-out (LMO) importance ( (b)). This importance is the average loss increase when the Gaussian is removed while the other Gaussians are also removed at random, each according to its keep probability. When every keep probability is one, LMO importance reduces to leave-one-out importance. The keep probabilities should reflect which Gaussians will remain, but this is not known in advance. We therefore refine them with the importance over several steps, so that each Gaussian is evaluated in a situation close to the final selection. No Gaussian is removed during these steps, so the selection can still change. One final pruning step then keeps the Gaussians with the highest importance. Computing LMO importance is the main difficulty. It is an average over all removal patterns, and rendering each pattern would be prohibitively expensive. We introduce - rendering, which computes the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form. From these two statistics, we compute the importance of all Gaussians without sampling removal patterns. The importance is exact for the squared error and approximate for the loss that we use. Our contributions are as follows: We define LMO importance to evaluate each Gaussian while the other Gaussians are also removed at random. We refine the keep probabilities with this importance and prune once at the end. We introduce - rendering, which computes the exact mean and variance of each pixel's color under random removal in closed form. With these exact statistics, we approximate the importance of all Gaussians without sampling removal patterns. Without fine-tuning, LMnOP achieves the best results in 16 of 18 metrics across three datasets at 90 and 99 removal. We also show that it keeps Gaussians whose importance rises after pruning. Related work sec:related Compact 3DGS. 3DGS models~ kerbl2023 can be made compact in two complementary ways. One reduces the bits needed for each Gaussian, and the other reduces the number of Gaussians. Compact3DGS~ compact3dgs , EAGLES~ eagles , and MesonGS~ mesongs combine compact attribute representations with mechanisms that reduce model size. Mini-Splatting~ minisplatting instead creates fewer Gaussians during training. Pruning a trained model is the most direct way to reduce the number of Gaussians, and it can be combined with attribute compression. Its result, however, depends entirely on which Gaussians are judged important. Importance-based pruning. Most pruning methods assign a score to each Gaussian and keep the highest-scoring ones. LightGaussian~ lightgaussian and Mini-Splatting measure how much each Gaussian contributes to rendering. PUP 3D-GS~ pup approximates the sensitivity of the loss to second order. GaussianPOP~ gaussianpop analytically computes the error caused by removing a single Gaussian. Trimming~ trim uses gradient information, and RAP~ rap predicts importance from Gaussian attributes and neighborhood statistics. Other methods learn masks instead of computing scores~ compact3dgs,maskgaussian , but they must optimize the model again. MaskGaussian, for example, samples probabilistic masks during optimization and keeps gradients for masked Gaussians. The scores above differ in form, but each of them is computed while the rest of the model is present. As a result, they reflect what a Gaussian contributes alone, not what happens when many Gaussians are removed together. Interaction-aware pruning. What happens when Gaussians are removed together depends on how they interact, since removing one changes the transmittance of every Gaussian behind it. The same issue arises in network pruning, where Optimal Brain Surgeon~ obs and its combinatorial extension~ cbs account for interactions between weights. Within 3DGS, prior work handles the interaction in three ways. REFINE~ refine approximates the importance without rendering, under the assumption that the Gaussians are independent. The rendering guarantee of coresets~ coreset relies on assumptions of validity and log-transmittance stability. GaussianPOP repeats scoring over multiple pruning stages, so that later scores reflect earlier removals. Concurrent work, SplatQ~ splatq , models the effect of removing pairs of Gaussians within spatial blocks and solves a quadratic selection problem. The interaction is thus assumed away, captured only across pruning stages, or modeled only between pairs within blocks. We instead score each Gaussian by its LMO importance. It averages over the random removal of all the other Gaussians. The interactions among all Gaussians on each ray are thus taken into account in the importance itself, before any Gaussian is removed. The -th Gaussian has color and alpha , which is its opacity multiplied by its projected 2D Gaussian at the pixel. The pixel color is then where the transmittance is the fraction of light that reaches the -th Gaussian. Since a Gaussian appears at different depths on different rays, we write for a Gaussian in the model and for its position on the current ray. We write all equations for one color channel and assume a black background. Pruning objective sec:prelim_objective Pruning keeps of the Gaussians without changing their attributes. We describe which Gaussians are kept with a binary mask , where keeps Gaussian and removes it. In , this amounts to replacing each with , so a removed Gaussian contributes nothing. To measure the damage of pruning, we compare the images rendered with to reference images. A reference image is the render of the original model from a training view, and is its color at a pixel. The reference images stay fixed throughout pruning. The pruning loss averages this comparison over all pixels and views, using an L1 term and a D-SSIM term. The pruning problem is There are far too many possible masks to search directly, so most methods instead score each Gaussian and keep the highest-scoring ones. A common score is the leave-one-out importance, which is the loss increase when only Gaussian is removed from the original model. Method sec:method Leave-many-out importance sec:lmo Leave-one-out importance is measured while all the other Gaussians remain. We instead evaluate each Gaussian while the other Gaussians are also removed at random. We treat each as an independent random variable that equals with probability . A large value means that keeping Gaussian reduces the expected loss. When all the other Gaussians remain, the LMO importance equals the leave-one-out importance. The simplest choice of keep probabilities is for every Gaussian, but important Gaussians are more likely to remain than the others. title: Thermal-Guided Low-Light UAV Image Enhancement: A Reliability-Aware Guidance Network and a Unified Benchmark
summary: Thermal-guided low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is promising for nighttime unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) perception because thermal imagery remains informative under severe visible degradation. However, the degraded visible image serves as both the alignment reference and the enhancement target, making thermal guidance uncertain in its spatial correspondence and local utility under low illumination, sensor differences, and UAV motion. Misaligned or unsuitable thermal cues may introduce artifacts, while spatially varying degradation requires region-specific restoration rather than uniform enhancement. To address these challenges, we propose a Reliability-Aware Multi-Strategy Guidance Network (RMGNet) for thermal-guided UAV LLIE under weak optical-thermal alignment. Its Reliability-Aware Guidance Calibration Module (RAGCM) performs coarse-to-fine displacement estimation and jointly evaluates the reliability of aligned thermal guidance and the usability of degraded visible evidence. Based on calibrated guidance, degradation, and reliability cues, the Multi-Strategy Enhancement Routing Module (MSERM) generates candidates for detail preservation, highlight-protected relighting, and thermal compensation, then spatially routes their contributions. We further construct the UAV weakly aligned Optical-Thermal dataset (UWOT), the largest UAV-oriented benchmark to date for weakly aligned optical-thermal low-light enhancement, containing 5,000 triplets. Extensive experiments show that RMGNet outperforms representative single-modal and multimodal state-of-the-art methods in enhancement quality while retaining competitive computational efficiency and greater robustness to practical cross-modal misalignment. The dataset and code will be publicly available at https://github.com/mmic-lcl/Datasets-and-benchmark-code.

Low-light image enhancement UAV remote sensing Weak cross-modal alignment Confidence-aware thermal guidance Region-adaptive restoration UAV optical-thermal benchmark Introduction Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) support nighttime surveillance, infrastructure inspection, search and rescue, and navigation. However, limited illumination, sensor noise, and platform motion degrade visible images through low contrast, color distortion, blur, and detail loss xu2022snr,darkir . These degradations impair visual quality and obscure the structural and semantic cues required by downstream perception, particularly for small objects and narrow boundaries. Reliable low-light image enhancement (LLIE) is therefore important for nighttime UAV vision Retinexformer . Visible-only LLIE methods have made substantial progress in illumination adjustment, noise suppression, color recovery, and joint degradation modeling Chen2018Retinex,xu2022snr,Retinexformer,hvi,darkir . Nevertheless, their effectiveness remains constrained by the information retained in the visible observation. In severely underexposed UAV imagery, object boundaries and small structures may be weakly represented or obscured by noise. Their restoration then relies heavily on learned image priors, and multiple plausible reconstructions may be compatible with the same degraded input wang2022llflow,VIIS . Complementary observations can provide additional evidence for constraining these ambiguous structures. Thermal imagery is less dependent on visible illumination and can provide complementary contours when visible observations are severely degraded cao2023deep,wang2025thermal . However, differences in sensor geometry, spatial resolution, and field of view, together with parallax and platform motion, can introduce residual spatial discrepancies between UAV visible and thermal images chen2024oafa . Here, weak alignment refers to scene-level correspondence accompanied by local spatial discrepancies. Transferring displaced thermal structures into the visible image may produce shifted boundaries, duplicated contours, or blurred details. Low-light degradation further weakens the visible structures used to estimate correspondence, particularly in regions where auxiliary information is most needed. The first challenge is therefore to establish locally reliable optical–thermal correspondence and assess the reliability of thermal guidance under degraded visible observations. Spatial correspondence alone does not determine the usefulness of thermal guidance. Thermal responses do not directly encode visible brightness or texture, and their relevance to visible-image restoration varies across the scene. Where visible details remain usable, large corrections may be unnecessary; where illumination is insufficient but structures remain discernible, luminance recovery is needed; where visible structures are weak, thermal cues may support restoration if their correspondence is reliable. Thermal guidance should also be attenuated where cross-modal responses are inconsistent. Fig.~ fig:motivation illustrates over-enhancement, loss of fine structure, and spatially uneven restoration, highlighting the need to accommodate different local conditions. The second challenge is therefore to adapt restoration to the remaining visible evidence, the degree of degradation, and the estimated reliability of thermal guidance. Existing thermal-guided enhancement methods demonstrate the value of complementary thermal observations for restoring degraded visible images cao2023deep,wang2025thermal,jha2025rt . For weakly aligned UAV imagery, exploiting this complementarity requires joint consideration of spatial correspondence, the remaining visible evidence, and local restoration needs. This motivates coupling correspondence and reliability estimation with region-adaptive restoration. Evaluating these requirements also calls for suitable data. Existing benchmarks support visible-only enhancement lolv2,u3d , optical–thermal fusion and perception roadscene,m3fd , or thermal-guided enhancement with normal-light references wang2025thermal . Dedicated benchmarks for examining low-light UAV restoration in the presence of residual optical–thermal misalignment remain limited. To address these challenges, we propose the Reliability-Aware Multi-Strategy Guidance Network (RMGNet) for thermal-guided restoration of low-light UAV imagery under weak cross-modal alignment. The framework jointly considers the spatial reliability of thermal guidance and the usability of the remaining visible evidence. The Reliability-Aware Guidance Calibration Module (RAGCM) uses visible and thermal structural cues to estimate local correspondence, evidence reliability, and spatial routing weights. Guided by these estimates, the Multi-Strategy Enhancement Routing Module (MSERM) combines detail preservation, highlight-protected relighting, and thermal-assisted compensation according to local restoration needs. The enhanced RGB image is produced in the coordinate system of the visible input. To support evaluation, we construct the UAV weakly aligned Optical-Thermal dataset (UWOT), comprising 5,000 low-light RGB, thermal, and normal-light reference triplets. UWOT combines UAV-acquired observations and DroneVehicle-derived samples, including both real nighttime and synthetically degraded low-light images. The main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose RMGNet, a thermal-guided framework for low-light UAV image enhancement that jointly considers uncertain cross-modal correspondence and spatially varying visible evidence to adapt thermal guidance to local restoration needs. We design RAGCM to perform structural-prior-guided coarse-to-fine alignment and estimate both thermal guidance reliability and visible evidence usability, supporting reliable cross-modal information transfer under residual misalignment. We introduce MSERM to adaptively combine detail preservation, highlight-protected relighting, and thermal compensation through spatial routing, addressing diverse local restoration requirements based on reliability and degradation cues. We construct UWOT with 5,000 low-light visible, thermal, and normal-light reference triplets. By combining real nighttime observations with synthetically degraded samples, UWOT supports UAV image enhancement research under residual optical-thermal misalignment. Related Work sec:related_work In this section, we review related studies on visible-image enhancement, thermal-guided restoration, and cross-modal correspondence in UAV imagery. Particular attention is given to the observations available to each method, the restoration or interpretation objectives, and the correspondence and reference conditions provided by existing benchmarks. Low-Light Visible Image Enhancement subsec:visible_llie Low-Light visible image enhancement addresses several interacting degradations, including insufficient illumination, noise, color distortion, and blur. Beyond enhancement of processed RGB images, chen2018sid investigate extreme low-light imaging directly in the RAW domain, learning a mapping from short-exposure observations to long-exposure references. Retinex-based approaches separate illumination adjustment from reflectance estimation Chen2018Retinex , while Retinexformer incorporates illumination information into learned restoration Retinexformer . SNR-aware enhancement adapts processing to local signal quality, accounting for spatial differences in noise and usable image content xu2022snr . Other methods address complementary aspects: HVI-CIDNet separates color and intensity representations hvi , DarkIR jointly addresses low illumination and blur darkir , and MambaLLIE models global and local image dependencies MambaLLIE . Zero-DCE formulates low-light enhancement as image-specific curve estimation and learns pixel-wise enhancement curves without reference images, providing an alternative to paired-supervision-based restoration guo2020zerodce . These developments provide useful foundations for restoring degraded UAV visible imagery. UAV-oriented enhancement research further considers the acquisition and processing conditions of aerial imagery. u3d introduce a benchmark and framework for ultra-high-resolution UAV low-light enhancement, addressing nonuniform illumination, limited paired data, and deployment constraints. Such work highlights the importance of evaluating enhancement under aerial imaging conditions. For image interpretation, the visibility of small objects and the continuity of fine structures are also relevant considerations. Visible-only methods, however, must estimate these structures from the degraded RGB observation and learned priors. When the observation contains little usable structural evidence, complementary sensing modalities offer an additional source of information. title: Quantization for Action, Execution for Deployment: Joint Precision and Execution Selection for World Action Models
summary: World action models guide robots by predicting the effects of actions or generating commands from observations. A model may compare hundreds of candidate futures before acting, repeatedly reading weights that must fit in device memory. Post-training quantization reduces the number of bits used to store pretrained weights, but a smaller model is not necessarily a deployable one: temporary tensors can exceed graphics processing unit (GPU) memory limits, while even small prediction errors can change the selected action. This creates two coupled challenges: identifying bit assignments that preserve task performance and determining which of them meet real execution constraints, without exhausting costly task trials. We present PTQ4WAM, a framework for choosing layer-wise bit assignments and execution routes under memory, latency and task-evaluation budgets. Calibration measurements guide candidate proposals, optionally with a language model agent. We profile full-model routes on the GPU before spending task trials on feasible assignments. Fusing group rescaling and reading visual history in place can make an otherwise infeasible assignment deployable. Across 15 workloads from four model families, the median task score is 99.2% of the corresponding 32-bit floating-point (FP32) score. On fixed GPU replays, the median speedup over FP32 is 2.36 times and the median reduction in peak allocated memory is 71.5%. The code will be released soon.

Introduction sec:introduction A robot choosing its next move can predict where several actions would take it, then execute the one that brings it closest to its goal. DINO-WM and LeWorldModel (LeWM) make these predictions in a learned visual feature space~ zhou2025dinowm,maes2026leworldmodel . V-JEPA~2-AC plans with a predictor built on pretrained video features~ assran2025vjepa2 . Fast-WAM uses video and action supervision to generate commands directly~ yuan2026fastwam . These world action models (WAMs) must fit alongside the observations and intermediate features they process. A predictive planner also uses the same weights repeatedly. In one physical robot setup, V-JEPA~2-AC uses a 300M-parameter predictor and compares 800 action candidates in each of ten refinements. Choosing one action takes 16 seconds on an RTX~4090~ assran2025vjepa2 . An onboard controller must meet a memory budget as well as a deadline for choosing its next action. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers a way to shrink a pretrained WAM without collecting new robot interactions for retraining. Fewer bits per weight reduce the size of the saved model and the data its operators must read on each call. With a fixed storage budget, keeping more bits in one set of layers leaves fewer for the rest. With only a few task evaluations, how can we find an assignment that preserves control performance and runs within the device limits? alignment. Consider two candidate trajectories whose predicted endpoints lie at nearly the same distance from the goal. A small feature error can swap their order and change the action. A larger shift that moves both predictions together can leave the decision intact. This makes average reconstruction error an unreliable guide to which layers need more bits. Action sensitivity and rollout feedback already guide quantization in recent WAMs~ wang2026steerquant,zhou2026quantwams,akbari2026qwam . To choose a whole model, we need to know how its precision choices work together when the original planner or controller acts. cost. Representative inputs used for calibration can reveal numerical errors in many layers in a single pass. Testing a complete assignment for control success can require running the controller from many initial states until each trial ends. Each action can change the observation used for the next decision. Testing every way to distribute bits would spend most of the preparation time running the task. With a limited budget, we must carefully decide which assignments are actually worth running on the task. feasibility. Assignments of the same saved size can differ in whether they fit during prediction. A quantized layer may write a temporary result before rescaling it. Attention over past observations may first copy the history into a new tensor. The peak depends on which of these tensors coexist with the rest of the model. An individual kernel's speed or the size of the weight file cannot tell us whether the complete call will finish within both the memory and time limits. A trial spent on an infeasible model leaves one fewer chance to test a model the device could use. PTQ4WAM first measures which bit assignments the device can run, then uses limited task evaluations to choose the best-performing model and its GPU implementation. Reading history in place, for example, can qualify a model that exceeds the memory limit when its history is copied. The map can then enter the task comparison in Figure~ fig:workflow (a). Each assignment is tested and saved with the GPU kernels that meet the device's memory and time limits. Calibration-guided proposals. We can use a large language model (LLM) agent with model structure and calibration measurements to propose a small set of assignments. A deterministic generator checks them before the planner or controller spends time scoring them. Low-memory execution. We rescale outputs inside the low-bit operator and read past visual features directly from their existing buffers. We time a full call and measure its memory to find the routes that meet both limits. Removing a buffer saves little at the model level if a different operator sets the peak. title: RigidAnchor: Cross-View Geo-Localization for UAV via Iterative Planar Rigid Alignment
summary: A UAV that flies without GNSS has to estimate its absolute position and heading without any external signal. Most existing methods for UAV-to-satellite cross-view geo-localization (U-S CVGL) treat the task as image retrieval: they compress the UAV image and each satellite tile into separate descriptors, rank the tiles by their similarity, and return the center of the best tile. The output can therefore only lie on a pre-defined grid, its accuracy is limited by the tile size, and no heading is produced. Regressing the pose in a single pass removes the grid, but it leaves no chance to correct the estimate afterwards. We observe that satellite tiles are not independent samples. They are laid on the map at a fixed spacing, scale and orientation, so neighboring tiles join into one continuous satellite block with a consistent metric, and a nadir UAV view of that block differs from it by a planar rigid transform only, i.e. a 2D translation plus an in-plane rotation. We therefore reformulate U-S CVGL as solving for this transform between two images of different sizes. Position and heading then become parts of one geometric quantity, and the accuracy is no longer limited by the tile grid. We propose RigidAnchor, which solves the transform iteratively. The network encodes the two images and builds a multi-level correlation pyramid between them. At each iteration, it indexes the pyramid with every aerial cell carried through the current estimate, pools the descriptors of all cells into one hidden state, and lets two decoupled heads predict a translation increment and a rotation increment, the latter being composed rather than added. On Bearing-UAV-90K, the cross-view mean errors are 78.6% lower in position and 69.7% lower in heading than Bearing-UAV, and HSR@15 increases by 19.06 points. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/RigidAnchor.
full_text: Introduction A UAV that flies without a global navigation satellite system (GNSS) has to estimate its absolute position and heading without any external signal~ fragoso2021seasonally, li2025geovins . Its nadir-view camera sees the ground from above, and the geo-referenced satellite imagery that is now available for most of the world covers the same ground. The UAV view can therefore serve as an observation and the satellite image as its reference. If we register one onto the other, we can read the UAV position and heading in the map frame directly. This gives a low-cost alternative to GNSS that does not drift over time, and the task is known as UAV-to-satellite cross-view geo-localization (U-S CVGL)~ zheng2020university, durgam2024cross . U-S CVGL is useful in beyond-visual-line-of-sight inspection, target designation and terminal guidance, where the output serves as a navigation state~ liu2026beyond and as the reference for payload pointing. Most existing methods treat U-S CVGL as image retrieval. They compress the UAV image and each satellite tile into separate feature descriptors, rank the tiles by their similarity, and take the center of the best-matching tile as the position estimate, as in NetVLAD~ arandjelovic2018netvlad , University-1652~ zheng2020university and scene-graph-based encoding-and-matching networks~ duan2024scene . Retrieval therefore turns a continuous localization problem into tile-level ranking. The output can only lie on a pre-defined regular grid, the error is limited by the tile size, and no heading is produced. fig: overview fig: overview fig: overview A second group of methods adds fine matching or direct regression to retrieval, so that the result is no longer tied to a tile center. OS-FPI~ chen2024os extracts both inputs with a single-stream network and regresses a response map, which an offset prediction then refines. The second stage of GRiM-Net~ hu2026grim detects keypoints on the candidate tiles, matches them in both directions and estimates a weighted homography. Bearing-UAV~ liu2026beyond goes further: it gives up the tile-center assumption and regresses the UAV position and heading together from the global and local structure of neighboring tiles. Satellite tiles are not independent samples. They cover the map on a regular grid, with fixed spacing, scale and orientation, so any set of neighboring tiles forms one continuous satellite block, which covers a single geo-referenced plane with a consistent metric. A nadir UAV view observes a local part of that plane. Once the two are brought to the same ground sampling distance, the relation between them is exactly a planar rigid transform, i.e. a 2D translation plus an in-plane rotation, and not a set of independent similarity scores. Existing methods either compare the UAV image with each tile separately~ arandjelovic2018netvlad, yin2023isimloc or match points inside one candidate tile~ wang2023fine, tang2025r2ploc, hu2026grim . Both choices ignore the regularity between tiles and the global rigidity of the observed scene. If the problem is instead formulated as planar rigid transform estimation, position and orientation can be solved continuously across tiles, and the tile grid no longer limits the accuracy. We therefore recast U-S CVGL, for the first time, as solving the planar rigid transform between two images of different sizes. Instead of scoring the UAV image against neighboring tiles one by one, we design a network that regresses the transform of the UAV image with respect to the satellite block stitched from those tiles, i.e. a 2D translation and an in-plane rotation. The network first encodes the UAV image and the satellite block into coarse features, then builds a multi-level correlation pyramid between them, and indexes the pyramid iteratively with the current estimate. At each iteration, it solves the update globally from the indexed correlation and the previous transform, and emits the rigid transform increment of that iteration in a decoupled form. Fig.~ fig: overview shows the whole pipeline. The study offers the following contributions: We propose RigidAnchor, which formulates U-S CVGL as solving the planar rigid transform between a UAV image and a satellite block of different sizes. This formulation puts position and heading into one geometric quantity, and it brings the accuracy below the tile level. We build a multi-level correlation pyramid between the UAV image and the satellite block, and index it dynamically at each iteration. This handles the large displacement between the initial and the ground-truth position. We solve the position and orientation update of each iteration globally and emit the rigid transform increment in a decoupled form. This improves inference efficiency. On Bearing-UAV-90K~ liu2026beyond , in the cross-view setting, RigidAnchor reduces the mean localization error of Bearing-UAV by and its mean heading error by . Related Work Retrieval-Based CVGL Methods Cross-view geo-localization was first studied between ground panoramas and aerial imagery. CVUSA~ workman2015wide established the wide-area protocol with aerial reference imagery, CVM-Net~ hu2018cvm learned a shared embedding with a two-branch network, SAFA~ shi2019spatial introduced spatial-aware feature aggregation, and CVACT~ liu2019lending added orientation priors, so that the descriptor becomes sensitive to the relative camera azimuth. These works fixed the retrieve-and-rank paradigm: the query and every reference image are mapped to a compact descriptor, and the most similar reference gives the position. The UAV case later received its own benchmarks and descriptors. University-1652~ zheng2020university provides a multi-view, multi-source benchmark that covers UAV, satellite and ground images, together with the Recall@K protocol. LPN~ wang2022each shows that local patterns, rather than one global vector, carry the discriminative signal. TransGeo~ zhu2022transgeo replaces the CNN backbone with a transformer to model long-range dependencies. DenseUAV~ dai2024vision moves the evaluation to low-altitude urban flight with a denser gallery, SUES-200~ zhu2023sues varies the flight altitude and the scene type, and UAV-VisLoc~ xu2024uav extends coverage to a larger geographic span. Later work improves the representation, the training signal or the evaluation protocol. MCCG~ shen2024mccg combines a ConvNeXt backbone with multiple classifiers, Sample4Geo~ deuser2023sample4geo shows that hard negative sampling matters greatly, VIGOR~ zhu2021vigor supplies a benchmark in which the query and the reference do not overlap one-to-one, and GeoDTR~ zhang2023cross, zhang2024geodtr disentangles the geometric layout from the appearance. PFIRNet~ kang2026pfirnet goes one step further and converts the top- retrieval responses into a probability field in coordinate space. In all of these methods the gallery is still a finite, uniformly sampled set of tiles, so the output is a tile index or a tile center, and the attainable resolution follows the sampling step rather than the network. Vision-Only Orientation Estimation Retrieval gives a position but no heading, while a navigation state needs both. Estimating the heading from images alone is therefore a problem of its own, since a magnetometer is disturbed by nearby structures and the yaw of an inertial unit drifts without bound. The most developed route treats the task as 3-DoF ground-to-satellite localization. Shi et al.~ shi2020where regress location and orientation together by matching a ground image against a polar-transformed satellite image. The extended journal version~ shi2023accurate refines the formulation and the training, and a geometry-guided cross-view transformer~ shi2023boosting further improves the accuracy of the estimated azimuth. SliceMatch~ lentsch2023slicematch aggregates the features into one ground descriptor and a set of pose-dependent aerial descriptors, so all candidate poses are compared at once and the pose is read from a single similarity volume. A second route obtains the heading from an explicitly estimated geometric transform. CAHomo~ wang2023fine warps the ground image onto the satellite plane and recovers the camera orientation from a point above the central axis of the warped image, so the azimuth comes from the homography instead of from a dedicated head. A third route regresses the heading together with the position, as Bearing-UAV~ liu2026beyond does from the structural features of neighboring tiles. Fine-Grained Localization Methods Fine-grained methods replace the tile index with a metric coordinate. A common recipe matches the two images with a detector-free matcher such as LoFTR~ sun2021loftr or a sparse one such as LightGlue~ lindenberger2023lightglue , and then solves a geometric transform from the resulting correspondences. OS-FPI~ chen2024os extracts UAV and satellite features in one stream, keeps the intermediate maps for fusion, and regresses a response map that an offset branch refines. R2PLoc~ tang2025r2ploc casts the task as region-to-point localization; it aligns multiscale semantics with a hierarchical aggregation module and enforces geometric consistency with a semantic-enhanced refinement matcher. GRiM-Net~ hu2026grim uses both granularities: it narrows the search by retrieval and then runs a keypoint-based homography estimation on the candidate patches. Bearing-UAV~ liu2026beyond skips the correspondence step and regresses position and heading from neighboring tiles, and PFIRNet~ kang2026pfirnet keeps the retrieval backbone but replaces the discrete readout with a continuous posterior. Proposed Method Problem Formulation sec:problem The network takes two images that observe the same ground area at the same ground sampling distance (GSD). We assume that the gimbal keeps the camera pointing to the nadir, so the aerial image is a square footprint of the ground plane, and that the camera is calibrated with a known focal length in pixels. Under the pinhole model, the GSD of the aerial image and the ground side length it covers follow from the height above ground and the focal length, where is the height above ground, the focal length in pixels, and the ground side length covered by the aerial image. The satellite map is provided at its own GSD , which is in practice coarser than . We resample it to the metric resolution of the aerial image by the factor so that one pixel of either image covers the same number of meters and no scale factor remains between them. Given the coarse position from the onboard navigation filter, we crop a satellite block from the resampled map. The block is centered at and covers on the ground, i.e. twice the side length of the aerial image. We define a frame for the aerial image, with its origin at the image center, to the right and towards the top of the image, i.e. along the nose. We define a frame for the block, with its origin at the block center, to the east and to the north. Both frames are right-handed, so they differ by a rigid transform only. The quantity to estimate is the planar rigid transform that maps to , where is the in-plane rotation and the translation. The translation is measured in units of : means a shift of to the east, and a shift of to the north. Because the navigation filter places within of the true position along each axis, the ground truth satisfies and . The range of is therefore a fixed unit square, while the block itself extends to and thus leaves a ring of context around the aerial footprint, which the correlation stage uses. The angle is the rotation about the upward axis, positive counter-clockwise, so means that the top of the aerial image, i.e. the nose, points west of north. Since and denote the same rotation, we let the network regress the cosine and the sine of the angle rather than the angle itself, and recover at inference. title: AdvMTO: Multimodal and Temporal Adversarial Object Attacks via 2D Gaussian Splatting for BEV-Based 3D Object Detection
summary: Adversarial object attacks pose a threat to BEV-based 3D object detectors in autonomous driving. Existing attacks typically target a single modality, coordinate camera and LiDAR observations at the current timestamp, or model temporal persistence mainly in camera streams. Without a unified construction of current and historical observations, attacks can leave part of the detector's accumulated evidence unsuppressed, limiting their effectiveness. In this paper, we propose AdvMTO, a 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) framework for suppressing detection of persistent adversarial objects. Its oriented surfels encode appearance, geometry, and opacity in one object state, from which camera images and scanline LiDAR returns are generated. AdvMTO then constructs current and historical inputs through detector-native processing, regenerating LiDAR returns in each native source sweep for fusion detectors. We optimize bounded appearance perturbations for each detector, propagating gradients through historical BEV memory for temporal camera detectors. For fusion detectors, bounded geometry refinement along local normals further perturbs both sensing modalities. Experiments on nuScenes demonstrate effective suppression of traffic-cone detection across three BEV detectors. Temporal ablations further highlight the importance of detector-native history modeling for both attack construction and optimization.

Existing attacks typically target a single modality, coordinate camera and LiDAR observations at the current timestamp, or model temporal persistence mainly in camera streams. Without a unified construction of current and historical observations, attacks can leave part of the detector's accumulated evidence unsuppressed, limiting their effectiveness. In this paper, we propose AdvMTO, a 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) framework for suppressing detection of persistent adversarial objects. Its oriented surfels encode appearance, geometry, and opacity in one object state, from which camera images and scanline LiDAR returns are generated. AdvMTO then constructs current and historical inputs through detector-native processing, regenerating LiDAR returns in each native source sweep for fusion detectors. We optimize bounded appearance perturbations for each detector, propagating gradients through historical BEV memory for temporal camera detectors. For fusion detectors, bounded geometry refinement along local normals further perturbs both sensing modalities. Experiments on nuScenes demonstrate effective suppression of traffic-cone detection across three BEV detectors. Temporal ablations further highlight the importance of detector-native history modeling for both attack construction and optimization. Introduction Bird's-eye-view (BEV) representations provide a common spatial framework for 3D object detection in autonomous driving, supporting perception from camera images, LiDAR point clouds, or both philion2020lift,yin2021centerpoint,liu2023bevfusion,li2022bevformer . Although sensor fusion and temporal aggregation improve perception, they do not ensure robustness to adversarial objects zhu2023bevrobustness,cheng2024fusion . A persistent adversarial object can affect both current observations and the historical evidence accumulated as the vehicle moves. Evaluating such attacks therefore requires considering how the same object is observed across sensing modalities and over time. Existing object-level attacks span single-modal, multimodal, and temporal settings. Single-modal attacks modify surface appearance to deceive camera-based perception wang2022fca,suryanto2022dta or alter object geometry to suppress LiDAR-based detection tu2020physically . Multimodal attacks construct adversarial 3D objects that jointly affect camera and LiDAR perception abdelfattah2021adversarial,tu2022multisensor , with MSF-ADV coupling the two modalities through a deformable mesh cao2021lidaradvmulti . Temporal attacks seek consistent adversarial effects across views and consecutive frames zhu2023bevrobustness . SABER, for example, maintains a scene-fixed adversarial object across camera frames to disrupt the detection of other vehicles li2026saber . Existing multimodal object attacks typically coordinate camera and LiDAR observations at the current timestamp, while temporal object attacks mainly model persistence in camera streams. We therefore aim to suppress detection of persistent adversarial objects across sensing modalities and over time. For a persistent adversarial object, multimodal consistency must extend from the current frame to the detector's historical inputs. LiDAR returns depend on the acquisition geometry of each source sweep, while historical camera observations influence the current prediction through BEV memory. Historical observations can retain evidence of the object even when its current observation is perturbed, limiting attack effectiveness. The challenge is to construct consistent current and historical observations across sensing modalities and account for their accumulated influence during optimization. This requires an editable 3D object state from which both camera images and LiDAR returns can be generated. Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) uses volumetric primitives whose orientations do not directly define surface normals, whereas 2DGS uses oriented planar primitives with explicit local surface directions kerbl20233dgs,huang20242dgs . These planar primitives support camera rendering and scanline LiDAR return generation, while their local normals guide bounded geometry refinement. To this end, we propose AdvMTO, a 2DGS-based framework for suppressing detection of persistent adversarial objects. Its oriented surfels encode appearance, geometry, and opacity in one object state. Within each sequence, the object remains fixed in world coordinates while its observations follow the recorded sensor poses. For fusion detectors, AdvMTO regenerates object returns in every native LiDAR source sweep before temporal alignment, while temporal camera detectors process current and historical camera observations through their native temporal pathway. We optimize bounded appearance perturbations separately for each detector. For temporal camera detectors, gradients propagate through BEV-memory updates, allowing the current attack objective to guide appearance optimization across historical renderings. Bounded geometry refinement along local normals further perturbs both sensing modalities for fusion detectors. Our main contributions are: We introduce AdvMTO, a 2DGS framework that converts one editable object state into camera images and LiDAR returns, with local surface normals guiding bounded geometry refinement. We develop detector-native temporal construction and optimization. LiDAR returns are regenerated at each source pose for fusion detectors, while gradients propagate through BEV memory and historical renderings for temporal camera detectors. Temporal ablations show that LiDAR history construction changes both clean detectability and measured attack effectiveness, while backpropagation through BEV memory improves suppression over stop-gradient optimization under the same adversarial histories. Across three BEV detectors on nuScenes, 2DGS attacks also achieve larger relative reductions in traffic-cone target scores than 3DGS attacks. Related Work Adversarial Attacks on Autonomous-Driving Perception. Adversarial attacks on autonomous-driving perception differ in the sensor inputs and temporal relationships they manipulate. Camera-based attacks optimize surface camouflage under varying viewpoints and environmental conditions zhang2019camou,wang2022fca,suryanto2022dta . Further work considers visual naturalness and transferability wang2021das,suryanto2023active , and addresses conflicting texture gradients across viewpoints liang2025grac . Related physical attacks also target monocular and stereo depth estimation yamanaka2020depthpatch,cheng2022physicaldepth,zhao2026cheatingstereo . LiDAR attacks manipulate object geometry through adversarial 3D objects tu2020physically , or alter sensor returns through point injection and physical removal cao2019lidarattack,cao2023physicalremoval . Multi-sensor attacks, including MSF-ADV, construct adversarial objects that jointly affect camera and LiDAR perception cao2021lidaradvmulti,abdelfattah2021adversarial,tu2022multisensor , with further work targeting camera--LiDAR--radar fusion zhu2024malicious . Camera-only patches can also compromise camera--LiDAR fusion models cheng2024fusion . For BEV perception, Zhu et al.\ introduce spatially consistent and temporally universal patch attacks zhu2023bevrobustness . SABER places a scene-fixed adversarial object to disrupt the detection of other vehicles, accounting for perspective and occlusion across views and frames li2026saber . Temporal-misalignment attacks instead manipulate synchronization between sensor streams shahriar2026temporal . AdvMTO aims to suppress detection of the adversarial object itself. It generates camera and LiDAR observations from the same object state and incorporates historical observations through each detector's native input pathway. Object Representations and Multimodal Sensor Rendering. Object representations determine how appearance and geometry can be optimized and converted into sensor observations. MeshAdv uses differentiable rendering to optimize adversarial mesh geometry and texture xiao2019meshadv , while mesh-based multi-sensor attacks couple camera and LiDAR effects through an explicit object surface cao2021lidaradvmulti,abdelfattah2021adversarial . Neural representations provide alternative parameterizations for adversarial objects. Adv3D li2024adv3d adopts neural radiance fields (NeRF) mildenhall2020nerf for attacks on camera-based 3D detection. Building on 3DGS kerbl20233dgs , PGA, 3DGAA, and BiTAA study multi-view camouflage, appearance and geometry optimization, and joint attacks on object detection and depth estimation, respectively lou20253d,zhang2025dgaa,zhang2026bitaa . These attacks primarily target camera-based perception. Whereas 3DGS represents scenes with volumetric Gaussian primitives, 2DGS uses oriented planar Gaussian disks that explicitly encode local surface directions huang20242dgs , providing a surface-oriented basis for appearance rendering and geometry refinement. Sensor simulation models how scene geometry and appearance produce observations at different sensor poses. LiDARsim combines ray casting with learned correction for LiDAR simulation manivasagam2020lidarsim , while SurfelGAN synthesizes camera views from texture-mapped surfels yang2020surfelgan . UniSim and NeuRAD extend neural rendering to camera and LiDAR observations in dynamic driving scenes yang2023unisim,tonderski2024neurad . SplatAD further demonstrates real-time rendering of both modalities using 3DGS, accounting for sensor-specific effects such as rolling shutter and ray dropout hess2025splatad . These methods focus on scene reconstruction and sensor simulation. AdvMTO uses a surface-oriented 2DGS representation for bounded optimization of an adversarial object's appearance and geometry. Method Problem Formulation We study white-box evasion of an inserted object against a frozen BEV detector . Each detector uses one adversarial object state across observation records. Each record comprises a current sample, an object placement, and the history consumed by the detector. The object's world pose is fixed within that history and current sample but may vary between records. For record , let denote recorded sensor inputs and the target class and location. Appearance is optimized for all detectors, with geometry refinement for fusion detectors. Detector parameters, calibration, ego poses, and timestamps remain fixed. title: AirVT-15k: A Query-Diverse UAV Video-Text Dataset and Query-Adaptive Evidence Alignment Network for Retrieval
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle video-text retrieval (UAV-TVR) requires matching language to both scene context and subtle object changes. A harbor-layout query relies on global scene context, whereas a departing-vessel query requires local functional cues and motion states. Existing benchmarks provide diverse aerial descriptions but give limited attention to distinct evidence needs within the same video. We introduce AirVT-15k, a benchmark of 15,504 UAV videos and 155,040 captions, with ten complementary bilingual captions per video describing scenes, object states, and temporal changes. We also propose AirFocus-CST, which selects query-relevant frames and patches, encodes temporal feature differences, and combines coarse-to-fine interaction (CFI) with optimal-transport alignment (OTA). Average mean recall reaches 63.67% on AirVT-15k and 24.41% on CapERA, improving over the strongest baselines by 2.96 and 1.91 percentage points, respectively. The dataset and code are available at https://chenxi000233.github.io/AirVT-15k-site/.
full_text: Unmanned aerial vehicle video--text retrieval (UAV-TVR) requires matching language to both scene context and subtle object changes. A harbor-layout query relies on global scene context, whereas a departing-vessel query requires local functional cues and motion states. Existing benchmarks provide diverse aerial descriptions but give limited attention to distinct evidence needs within the same video. We introduce , a benchmark of 15,504 UAV videos and 155,040 captions, with ten complementary bilingual captions per video describing scenes, object states, and temporal changes. We also propose , which selects query-relevant frames and patches, encodes temporal feature differences, and combines coarse-to-fine interaction (CFI) with optimal-transport alignment (OTA). Average mean recall reaches 63.67 on and 24.41 on CapERA, improving over the strongest baselines by 2.96 and 1.91 percentage points, respectively. The dataset and code are available at . Introduction sec:intro UAV video--text retrieval supports traffic inspection, port monitoring, and disaster assessment. Queries about the same video can require different visual evidence. A harbor-layout query refers to docks and waterways; a departing-vessel query refers to the vessel's position relative to its berth and how that position changes over time (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). We describe these evidence types as global scene context, local functional cues, and motion states. Wide views, small objects, and subtle motion make their joint representation difficult. General video--text benchmarks such as MSR-VTT~ xu2016msrvtt cover diverse content, and aerial resources such as GeoChat~ kuckreja2024geochat support image-level understanding. UAV video benchmarks, including DVTMD~ zhao2025tcma , extend this setting to aerial video descriptions. Evaluating query-dependent evidence needs also requires captions that describe different aspects of the same clip. We introduce with 15,504 videos covering aerial scenes, object activities, and temporal changes. Each video has ten complementary bilingual captions, so queries can refer to its surroundings, local objects, or changes over time. Video-level data splits and bidirectional retrieval protocols define the training and evaluation setting. Retrieval methods address frame aggregation and cross-modal correspondence in different ways. CLIP4Clip~ luo2021clip4clip aggregates frame representations, X-Pool~ gorti2022xpool pools frames conditioned on text, and TCMA~ zhao2025tcma aligns sentences with frames and words with patches. UAV retrieval also requires distinguishing activities among videos with similar scenes and object appearances. We propose with two components: Query-Guided Multi-Evidence Modeling and Complementary Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Alignment. The first retains global scene context and combines query-guided temporal selection (TS), query-guided spatial refinement (SR), and temporal variation modeling (TV). TS and SR focus on relevant moments and local functional cues; TV encodes frame-feature changes associated with motion states. The second combines Coarse-to-Fine Interaction (CFI) on query-refined features with Optimal-Transport Alignment (OTA) on query-independent visual features. CFI checks sentence--frame, word--frame, and word--patch matches, while OTA jointly allocates word--patch correspondence weights across the video. Our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*,nosep] We introduce , a UAV video--text benchmark with 15,504 videos, ten complementary bilingual captions per video, and fixed bidirectional retrieval protocols. The captions link each clip to queries about its scene, objects, and temporal changes. We propose to select query-relevant visual evidence, encode temporal variation, and combine CFI with OTA for fine-grained video--text matching. Evaluation on and CapERA shows that achieves the highest average mean recall among the compared methods. Component ablations quantify the gains from temporal selection, spatial refinement, temporal variation, and the two alignment modules. Related Work sec:related General Video--Text Benchmarks sec:related_benchmarks MSR-VTT~ xu2016msrvtt pairs web videos with captions, and ActivityNet Captions~ krishna2017dense associates descriptions with temporal segments. HowTo100M~ miech2019howto100m and MIL-NCE~ miech2020milnce extend video--text learning to large collections of narrated instructional videos. Recent data-centric approaches refine noisy video annotations and expand event-level descriptions to improve the quality and coverage of video--text supervision~ wang2025dataflywheel,bai2025asymmetry . Feint6K~ ma2024feint6k , MotionBench~ hong2025motionbench , and VideoComp~ kim2025videocomp examine cross-frame reasoning, motion understanding, and compositional temporal alignment, respectively. For UAV-TVR, we pair aerial environments with captions that distinguish scene descriptions from object activities within the same clip. Aerial and UAV Vision--Language Benchmarks sec:related_aerial GeoChat~ kuckreja2024geochat and AerialVG~ liu2025aerialvg address aerial image understanding and visual grounding. For aerial videos, CapERA~ bashmal2023capera expands human captions through paraphrasing and back-translation. DVTMD~ zhao2025tcma provides five complementary descriptions per video from the ERA source, and USRD and UMCRD~ huang2026msam support drone video--text retrieval. extends this setting with videos spanning scenes, applications, and events, paired with ten captions describing different aspects of each clip. Section~ sec:dataset describes the collection, annotation, and evaluation protocols. Video--Text Retrieval sec:related_retrieval Video--language pretraining learns joint representations through temporal and multimodal encoding, global--local alignment, and image--video training~ gabeur2020mmt,wang2021t2vlad,bain2021frozen . Contrastive pretraining and adaptation of image--text models extend these representations to video--language tasks~ xu2021videoclip,wang2023allinone,xue2023clipvip . Building on Contrastive Language--Image Pre-training (CLIP)~ radford2021clip , retrieval models combine frame aggregation, multi-grained correspondence, and text-conditioned pooling~ luo2021clip4clip,ma2022xclip,gorti2022xpool . Hierarchical, token-level, and intra-modality contrastive objectives improve cross-modal alignment~ liu2021hit,yang2021taco,zolfaghari2021crossclr . Token clustering and spatiotemporal token selection reduce visual redundancy~ zhao2022centerclip,liu2022ts2net . Local association and coarse-to-fine alignment connect representations at different granularities~ ge2022bridgeformer,wang2023ucoa , while distillation transfers matching knowledge to retrieval encoders~ croitoru2021teachtext,gao2021clip2tv . Recent fine-grained models emphasize less salient discriminative objects, global--local interactions, token-wise matching, and context-aware text--frame relationships~ zheng2025lsdo,bian2026davrl,reddy2025videocolbert,chen2026eaglenet . Recent retrieval models explore pseudo-query interaction, bidirectional likelihood estimation, and generative--contrastive training~ lan2025hybridtower,ko2025blim,gupta2026ville . Auxiliary captions, scene elements, and speech provide additional semantic cues~ jang2026corecaption,le2025bima,zhao2026save ; drone-specific methods use text-conditioned alignment and adaptive semantic mining~ zhao2025tcma,huang2026msam . Partially relevant retrieval further matches queries to video moments through multi-scale similarities and diffusion-guided contextual registers~ chen2026prvr,li2026imagine . Temporal difference modeling. For action recognition, dynamic images~ bilen2016dynamicimage summarize temporal evolution by rank pooling, while Representation Flow~ piergiovanni2019representationflow and MotionSqueeze~ kwon2020motionsqueeze learn flow or inter-frame correspondence. STM~ jiang2019stm and TEA~ li2020tea encode feature-level motion, and TDN~ wang2021tdn models short- and long-range temporal differences. For video--text retrieval, CLIP2Video~ fang2021clip2video introduces a temporal difference block. combines differences of frozen frame features with query-refined local evidence, then computes correspondence on visual features before and after query refinement. The AirVT-15k Benchmark sec:dataset contains UAV videos of ports, airports, urban roads, waterways, and other aerial environments (Fig.~ fig:airvt_overview ). The collection covers traffic monitoring, infrastructure inspection, and area observation, with events such as moving, entering and leaving, crossing, and docking. Complementary captions describe the surroundings and the objects' activities and states, allowing the same clip to answer different queries. Data Collection and Curation sec:dataset_collection We collect videos from our UAV recordings and public online sources. We record footage with a DJI Mavic 3 equipped with a three-axis mechanically stabilized camera, primarily at and 30 fps with H.265 encoding. Flight altitudes range from approximately 20--120 m, with most footage captured at 30--80 m. Nadir, oblique, tracking, and orbiting views cover roads, built-up areas, farmland, rivers, and construction sites. Public videos from video-sharing websites, open datasets, and project pages extend geographic, viewpoint, and semantic coverage. Long recordings are segmented using shot boundaries and semantic continuity into approximately 15--30 s clips, with temporal overlap when needed to preserve complete events. We remove corrupted, low-resolution, severely blurred or shaky clips, prolonged static footage, and clips dominated by subtitles or editing effects. Deduplication combines file information and keyframe perceptual hashes for coarse screening, sampled-frame visual similarity for finer comparison, and manual review to remove duplicate clips. Annotation sec:dataset_construction For each video, we randomly sample 8--32 frames according to its duration and present them chronologically at their original resolution. ChatGPT-6 generates ten English--Chinese caption pairs using a structured prompt. The caption templates guide descriptions toward complementary aspects of the visible scene and object activity. Each template applies to content present in the sampled frames; additional captions describe other observable details. Caption pairs must preserve bilingual semantic consistency and ground objects, actions, directions, counts, and causal statements in visual evidence. Automated checks flag event-level semantic repetition among captions. Flagged samples undergo manual review, and captions are regenerated when problems are identified according to the annotation quality-control rules. Dataset Statistics and Analysis sec:dataset_statistics Figure~ fig:caption_complementarity shows how captions describe different content within a clip. Scene descriptions identify the surrounding environment, while activity descriptions follow object states and changes across chronological frames. The captions pair the scene context needed to interpret an activity with the changes that distinguish it. Figure~ fig:dataset_distributions (a,b) reports scene and event distributions derived from the captions. Waterways, urban areas, and roads are the largest scene categories, and moving objects dominate the event distribution. Entering and leaving, crossing, and docking describe more specific activities. The distributions are multi-label: a clip can belong to several scene and event categories. Figure~ fig:dataset_distributions (c) reports the distribution of video duration. title: NNS-GS: Non-Local Neural Scattering for Relightable Gaussian Splatting
summary: Creating relightable 3D assets of translucent objects is challenging because changing the illumination at one surface location can affect the appearance elsewhere through subsurface scattering. Existing Gaussian-based scattering models typically predict scattering from local features, making this dependence difficult to capture. We present Non-Local Neural Scattering for Gaussian Splatting (NNS-GS), which learns non-local scattering together with geometry-guided local reflection. The scattering module learns how illumination from light-visible surface regions in light space contributes to the shading point in view space, conditioned on regional diffuse responses and spatial relationships. The reflection module supplies these diffuse responses and uses additional geometric guidance to better capture specular highlights and sharp shadow boundaries. To reduce component mixing and support controllable scattering appearance, anchor-based progressive training establishes the diffuse-scattering base before introducing specular reflection and supervises the components separately. Under calibrated point lighting, NNS-GS improves mean PSNR over existing methods by 2.47 dB and 0.81 dB on the synthetic and real translucent scenes, respectively. Additional synthetic comparisons further show that NNS-GS better matches the reference when adjusting scattering attenuation.

Under calibrated point lighting, NNS-GS improves mean PSNR over existing methods by 2.47 dB and 0.81 dB on the synthetic and real translucent scenes, respectively. Additional synthetic comparisons further show that NNS-GS better matches the reference when adjusting scattering attenuation. Introduction sec:intro Creating relightable 3D translucent objects is important for realistic rendering in games, virtual reality, and product visualization. This task is challenging because subsurface scattering (SSS) allows light entering one surface region to scatter within the object and emerge elsewhere~ jensen2001subsurface . Predicting appearance under new lighting, therefore, requires accounting for illumination across the surface and its transport through the object, beyond the local lighting conditions at each point. Existing relighting methods based on neural scene representations, including neural radiance fields (NeRFs)~ mildenhall2020nerf and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussians , separate geometry, materials, and illumination to enable physically based relighting~ srinivasan2021nerv,zhang2021nerfactor,jin2023tensoir,gao2024r3dg,liang2024gsir,bi2024gs3,gu2025irgs or learn lighting-dependent appearance to reproduce complex material responses~ gao2020dnl,zeng2023nrhints,kuang2024olat,fan2025rng . These methods do not explicitly model SSS and can miss the soft illumination of translucent objects. SSS-GS~ dihlmann2024sssgs and SSD-GS~ zheng2026ssdgs model SSS within Gaussian representations using a learned scattering residual and a dipole-based formulation, respectively. However, their scattering modules evaluate per-Gaussian inputs without explicitly aggregating information from other surface locations. This limits their ability to accurately reproduce transmission effects under new lighting. In this paper, we present Non-Local Neural Scattering for Gaussian Splatting (NNS-GS), a novel framework built on a non-local neural scattering representation that couples surface illumination with relative geometry. To capture non-local scattering, we use the diffuse responses in light space as illumination cues at other surface locations with their 3D distances, allowing the model to learn how illumination across the surface contributes to local scattered appearance in view space. Alongside scattering, local surface reflection introduces sharp highlights and shadow boundaries, whose rapid angular and spatial variations can be difficult to reproduce. Therefore, our proposed geometry-guided neural reflection module introduces additional geometric cues to guide the prediction of these details: learned local frames provide directional context for highlight modeling, while light-space depth differences provide occlusion-related cues for refining shadow boundaries. During training, the flexible specular branch can absorb appearance already explained by diffuse reflection and scattering. Such mixing can compromise editing even when reconstruction quality remains high. We therefore introduce anchor-based progressive training, which anchors the diffuse–scattering base to its pre-specular estimate and supervises the specular branch with the positive residual relative to that anchor. On the translucent-material dataset, NNS-GS improves mean PSNR over existing methods by 2.47 dB on synthetic scenes and 0.81 dB on real scenes, supporting controlled scattering appearance adjustment and rendering performance at about 60 FPS. Overall, our main contributions are: a novel Gaussian framework (NNS-GS) that achieves more faithful relighting of translucent objects and supports plausible adjustments to scattering appearance, a dual-space non-local neural scattering model that learns how illumination at multiple surface locations jointly contributes to local scattered appearance, and a geometry-guided neural reflection model that uses additional geometric cues to enhance fine highlight detail and refine cast shadow boundaries. Related Work sec:related_work 3D Representations and Relighting NeRF~ mildenhall2020nerf represents scenes as continuous fields, while 3DGS~ kerbl2023gaussians uses explicit Gaussian primitives for efficient rendering. Both support high-quality reconstruction and novel-view synthesis, but their original formulations capture appearance under observed lighting rather than separate material and illumination. Relighting methods based on NeRF and related neural fields address this limitation by separating reflectance from illumination~ boss2021nerd,zhang2021nerfactor,zhang2021physg , modeling visibility and indirect light~ srinivasan2021nerv,jin2023tensoir , or learning how appearance varies with lighting from captured images~ zeng2023nrhints . Recent work uses physical constraints to better separate material properties from lighting~ wu2025pbrnerf and time-resolved measurements to distinguish direct from indirect light~ malik2025propagating . With 3DGS, relighting approaches extend explicit scene representations with material properties and shading models for relighting~ jiang2024gaussianshader,liang2024gsir,gao2024r3dg . Subsequent advances improve geometry and reflectance estimation~ sun2025svgir,zhu2025sdfgs , account for visibility and indirect illumination~ chen2025gigs,gu2025irgs , and reduce material--lighting ambiguity through cross-environment observations and stronger lighting or material priors~ li2025recap,du2025gsid,zhang2026irhgp,langsteiner2026matspray . For calibrated point-light capture, GS and related methods provide flexible directional appearance models~ bi2024gs3,kuang2024olat , while RNG~ fan2025rng learns neural reflectance from latent Gaussian features. Together, these methods establish effective reconstruction and relighting frameworks, predominantly for surface reflection from opaque materials. Subsurface Scattering SSS contributes to the soft appearance of translucent materials. It connects the appearance of a surface point to light entering the object at other locations. The bidirectional surface scattering reflectance distribution function (BSSRDF) describes this spatial relationship, while diffusion models enable efficient evaluation~ jensen2001subsurface,frisvad2014directional . Classical real-time approaches approximate the contribution of surrounding illumination through texture-space diffusion~ deon2007skin , screen-space and separable filtering~ jimenez2009screenspace,jimenez2015separable , light-space gathering~ dachsbacher2003translucent , and image-space irradiance splatting~ shah2009imagespace,chen2012multiresolution . Despite their different representations, these methods share the principle of aggregating illumination over a surface region rather than evaluating only a local response. Recent work learns compact scattering representations~ tg2024neuralsss and incorporates translucent appearance into Gaussian reconstruction~ dihlmann2024sssgs,zheng2026ssdgs,araneda2026diamondsss . SSS-GS~ dihlmann2024sssgs and SSD-GS~ zheng2026ssdgs extend Gaussian appearance with learned scattering responses and diffusion-based modeling, respectively. Building on light-space aggregation, our framework learns light-transport relationships between regional illumination and local appearance, capturing non-local scattering within the Gaussian representation for translucent effects. This supports accurate reconstruction and appearance adjustment of translucent objects. title: ViDiHand2: Unifying Video Diffusion Priors and Hand Geometry for 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild

summary: Learning robot manipulation from egocentric human videos requires accurate metric 3D hand motion. Recent methods leverage pretrained video diffusion model (VDM) priors to recover occluded hands directly from full-frame videos, but their appearance-based depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, a geometry-driven framework that reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into fine-grained geometric constraint solving. Specifically, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting, which recover metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joints and the metric structure of MANO hands, while leveraging temporal observations across the clip. Since the lifting relies on these 2D joints, to improve robustness under occlusion and image truncation, we further develop Confidence-Gated Fusion to adaptively combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions according to localization confidence. Finally, we enhance the VDM backbone to better capture spatial-temporal representations and produce the per-frame 2D joint and MANO predictions that both steps rely on. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets demonstrate that ViDiHand2 consistently outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82x compared with the best baseline on each metric, while running at 57 FPS. The code is available at https://github.com/NTUYWANG103/ViDiHand.
