Introduction sec:intro Human videos offer a scalable source of training data for robot manipulation~ kareer2025egomimic,yang2025egovla,luo2025beingh0,zheng2026egoscale and egocentric world models~ wang2026hand2world,yu2025egosim,tu2025playerone . Accurate metric 3D hand motion is essential for extracting high-quality supervision from these videos. Egocentric hand motion reconstruction aims to recover the 3D joint positions of both hands in camera coordinates. Detect-then-reconstruct methods~ pavlakos2024hamer,potamias2025wilor,zhang2025hawor first localize hands and then estimate their 3D poses from image crops. Within this paradigm, single-frame approaches lack temporal consistency, while motion-prior-based methods model temporal coherence but remain vulnerable to localization and tracking failures under occlusion. The current state-of-the-art methods ~ wang2026vidihand and ~ liu2026aceegohand instead adapt pretrained video diffusion models (VDMs) to reconstruct hands directly from full-frame videos, eliminating the need for explicit hand detection and enabling recovery of occluded hand motion. However, both methods exhibit substantial errors in recovering metric 3D hand trajectories from in-the-wild videos~ genrobot2026genhumanego , particularly in depth estimation and spatial localization, as shows. A key limitation is that directly regressing metric depth from appearance requires learning a complex mapping that is highly sensitive to focal length and generalizes poorly to unseen cameras~ yin2023metric3d,piccinelli2024unidepth , as illustrated in . Moreover, occlusion and hand truncation at image boundaries weaken the visual cues for hand localization, while coarse tokenization in both methods limits the preservation of fine-grained spatial details. Addressing these challenges further calls for richer spatial-temporal representations from VDMs and more consistent hand trajectory prediction over time. In this work, we propose , which reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into geometric constraint solving. Our key insight is that metric depth can be recovered by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joint predictions and the metric structure of MANO hands~ romero2017mano , both of which are more reliable than directly regressed depth. To realize this idea, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting ( ), which places each joint along its camera ray and constrains its depth using MANO joint distances. Unlike prior methods~ iqbal2018latent25d,sarandi2021metrabs,valassakis2024handdgp that recover metric scale through bone-length fitting or 2D–3D alignment, our approach exploits fine-grained constraints across multiple joints. We further introduce Clip-Level Ray Fitting to jointly estimate depth across a video clip, leveraging temporal observations to constrain frames with unreliable joints. Accurate joint localization is essential for maintaining reliable geometric constraints, particularly under occlusion and truncation. In , we introduce the Joint-Heatmap Refiner to recover fine-grained joint positions using heat maps at eight times the resolution of the VDM token grid. To further handle ambiguous visual evidence, Confidence-Gated Fusion adaptively combines the refined 2D predictions with the fitted MANO hand, assigning greater weight to MANO estimates when joint localization is uncertain. We further enhance the VDM-based architecture with improved feature aggregation and temporal modeling in . The Multi-Level Latent Encoder aggregates features across all adapted VDM blocks to exploit multi-level representations. The Hand Latent Decoder decodes each latent frame into its video frames, while Autoregressive Rollout Adaptation lets each chunk attend to the previous one. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of . We consistently outperform existing methods on every metric. On in-the-wild data, reduces absolute joint error by over 40 compared with the strongest baseline. On in-domain benchmarks, it lowers the absolute and 2D joint errors of by 20 and 31 . Our contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] We identify a key limitation of existing VDM-based hand reconstruction methods: direct depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. To address this, we reformulate depth estimation as fine-grained geometric constraint solving, recovering metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned joint predictions and MANO hand structure. To support reliable geometric reconstruction, we introduce fine-grained joint localization and confidence-gated fusion for handling occlusion and truncation, along with multi-level feature aggregation and autoregressive rollout for stronger spatial-temporal modeling. We conduct extensive experiments on seven public datasets against 18 baselines. title: GSDet: Gaussian Splatting for Oriented Object Detection
summary: Oriented object detection has advanced with the development of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformers. However, modern detectors still rely on predefined object candidates, such as anchors in CNN-based methods or queries in transformer-based methods, which struggle to capture spatial information effectively. To address the limitations, we propose GSDet, a novel framework that formulates oriented object detection as Gaussian splatting. Specifically, our approach performs detection within a 3D feature space constructed from image features, where 3D Gaussians are employed to represent oriented objects. These 3D Gaussians are projected onto the image plane to form 2D Gaussians, which are then transformed into oriented boxes. Furthermore, we optimize the mean, anisotropic covariance, and confidence scores of these randomly initialized 3D Gaussians, using a decoder that incorporates 3D Gaussian sampling. Moreover, our method exhibits flexibility, enabling adaptive control and a dynamic number of Gaussians during inference. Experiments on 3 datasets indicate that GSDet achieves AP$_{50}$ gains of 0.7\% on DIOR-R, 0.3\% on DOTA-v1.0, and 0.55\% on DOTA-v1.5 when evaluated with adaptive control and outperforms mainstream detectors.

However, modern detectors still rely on predefined object candidates, such as anchors in CNN-based methods or queries in transformer-based methods, which struggle to capture spatial information effectively. To address the limitations, we propose GSDet, a novel framework that formulates oriented object detection as Gaussian splatting. Specifically, our approach performs detection within a 3D feature space constructed from image features, where 3D Gaussians are employed to represent oriented objects. These 3D Gaussians are projected onto the image plane to form 2D Gaussians, which are then transformed into oriented boxes. Furthermore, we optimize the mean, anisotropic covariance, and confidence scores of these randomly initialized 3D Gaussians, using a decoder that incorporates 3D Gaussian sampling. Moreover, our method exhibits flexibility, enabling adaptive control and a dynamic number of Gaussians during inference. Experiments on 3 datasets indicate that GSDet achieves AP gains of 0.7 on DIOR-R, 0.3 on DOTA-v1.0, and 0.55 on DOTA-v1.5 when evaluated with adaptive control and outperforms mainstream detectors. Code link . Introduction Oriented object detection aims to identify and locate objects with arbitrary orientations in images~ GauCho,orientedrcnn . Unlike objects in horizontal object detection, oriented objects often appear in various scales, aspect ratios, and orientations, which significantly increases the difficulty of accurate detection~ dior,dotav1.0 . These challenges necessitate the development of techniques that can effectively localize and classify oriented objects regardless of their complexity. Over the years, oriented object detection has evolved significantly, driven by advancements in both CNN-based~ orientedrcnn,s2anet and transformer-based~ arsdetr methods. CNN-based object detectors can be broadly categorized into one-stage and two-stage detectors. One-stage detectors~ s2anet predict object categories and bounding boxes directly from the feature map in a single pass, utilizing dense object candidates like anchors to cover potential object locations. In contrast, two-stage detectors~ orientedrcnn first generate region proposals using a region proposal network and then refine these proposals to produce the final results. Recently, transformer-based methods~ arsdetr have gained traction in this field, which treat object detection as a set prediction problem and use a set of learnable queries from the encoder to directly predict the final bounding boxes and class labels. Although CNN-based and transformer-based methods have demonstrated promising performance, they still rely on manually designed object candidates, such as anchors, region proposals, and queries. Moreover, these candidates, which represent potential objects, struggle to effectively capture spatial information of objects. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework that directly detects oriented objects from random 3D Gaussians. The random initialization does not involve learnable neuron parameters. Regarding spatial information, a 3D feature space is constructed from image features. Within this space, the 3D Gaussians are optimized to represent oriented objects and can be projected onto the image plane to form 2D Gaussians, which are then transformed into oriented boxes. This Gaussian-to-box method eliminates the need for prior anchors, proposals, or queries, which simplifies the generation of object candidates and establishes a streamlined pipeline. Our method is inspired by Gaussian splatting (GS), as illustrated in Figure~ teaser . The philosophy of Gaussian-to-box paradigm is analogous to the Gaussian-to-image process in Gaussian splatting~ gsrender , where a scene is represented by 3D Gaussians and high-quality rendering is achieved by projecting these 3D Gaussians onto the 2D image space. Gaussian splatting has demonstrated significant advancements in 3D scene representation tasks. However, to the best of our knowledge, no prior work has successfully applied Gaussian splatting to oriented object detection. In this paper, we propose GSDet, a novel approach that formulates oriented object detection as Gaussian splatting. A 3D feature space is constructed by treating multi-scale feature maps from the encoder as supporting planes within a 3D coordinate system. In this space, 3D Gaussians serve as a flexible representation of objects and are initialized randomly, without relying on structure-of-motion (SFM) points. The Gaussian attributes, including the mean, anisotropic covariance, and confidence scores, are optimized using a decoder that incorporates 3D Gaussian sampling to extract spatial features. The predicted 3D Gaussians are projected onto the image plane to form 2D Gaussians, which are further transformed into predicted boxes via decomposition. Our GSDet exhibits remarkable flexibility during inference. Firstly, it allows for a dynamic number of initial 3D Gaussians as input. We can train the model with a certain number of Gaussians and then use a different number during inference. Secondly, GSDet enables iterative reuse of the decoder to refine the predicted Gaussians through adaptive control, allowing Gaussians to focus on foreground objects. Experiments on 3 datasets validate the effectiveness of GSDet. Its performance is further improved through the use of adaptive control and an increased number of Gaussians during inference. Contributions are summarized as follows: We propose a detector GSDet, which is the first work to formulate oriented object detection as Gaussian splatting to the best knowledge of our knowledge. We perform detection within a 3D feature space constructed from image features, where the designed 3D Gaussian sampling captures spatial information. Anisotropic 3D Gaussians are employed to represent oriented objects through their attributes. They are projected onto the image plane to form 2D Gaussians, which are then transformed into oriented boxes. Our Gaussian-to-box detection paradigm exhibits favorable properties, including adaptive control and dynamic Gaussians during inference, owing to the random initialization of 3D Gaussians. Related Work Oriented object detection. The mainstream methods in oriented object detection can be broadly categorized into CNN-based and transformer-based approaches. CNN-based methods, which have achieved significant success, are further divided into single-stage and two-stage methods. Two-stage methods~ roi_transformer,orientedrcnn utilize a region proposal network (RPN) to generate dense proposals, which are then refined by a region of interest (RoI) head. In contrast, single-stage methods~ sasm,dhrec bypass the need for region proposals and detect objects directly from dense anchors. To eliminate the need for dense anchor or proposal candidates, transformer-based methods establish a paradigm based on a set of queries~ arsdetr,emo2detr . These queries represent both the semantic and location information of objects, and are selected through the encoder~ deformabledetr . Mainstream transformer architectures consist of an encoder and a decoder, with attention mechanisms serving as their core. Self-attention in the decoder enables queries to interact with one another, while cross-attention integrates encoder features with queries. Unlike these methods, our approach is the first to predict oriented boxes directly from random Gaussians using Gaussian splatting, eliminating the need for pre-designed anchors, proposals, or learned queries, as illustrated in Figure~ teaserobject . Gaussian splatting has emerged as a significant technique in computer graphics, offering explicit scene representation and efficient rendering capabilities~ gsrender . It represents objects and surfaces as collections of Gaussians, allowing for high-quality image synthesis. This method has been explored in various applications, including scene reconstruction~ deformable3dgau,4dgausplat , SLAM~ gsslam,matsuki2024gaussian , and autonomous driving~ drivinggaussian,hugs , demonstrating its versatility and potential for real-time rendering. Despite the success of Gaussian splatting in these domains, there are no previous solutions that successfully adapt Gaussian splatting for oriented object detection. We believe that the slow progress of Gaussian splatting in oriented object detection is primarily due to the different optimization objectives, i.e., Gaussians and oriented boxes. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that adopts Gaussian splatting for oriented object detection. Method Oriented object detection identifies oriented boxes and class labels for objects in images. The core of our GSDet is to address oriented object detection through Gaussian splatting. title: GRAIN: Shared-Budget Complementary Re-observation for Object Detection
summary:
Re-running a frozen detector on enlarged image crops recovers small and crowded objects without retraining, yet every crop costs an extra detector call. Existing slicing and adaptive-cropping pipelines plan crops per image in isolation, even though inspection demand varies widely across an image collection. We present GRAIN, which unifies cross-image call allocation and bounded-output admission around cross-image comparable resolution-closure gains over boundary-safe crop interiors. Coarse hypotheses carry resolution deficits, crops close a geometric share of those deficits for hypotheses enclosed in their interior positive region, and multiplicative residuals discount covered evidence within a monotone submodular surrogate. Prefix sums and a global max-heap execute this collection-wide plan on CPU before crop inference, and Positive-Region Fusion aligns post-inference spatial admission with the planned interior support before class-balanced top-
  selection. Across 17 frozen detectors from five families on COCO, CrowdHuman, and VisDrone-DET, GRAIN beats call-matched tiling in 100 of 102 AP@100 settings and transfers to AI-TOD-v2. With RF-DETR-S on CrowdHuman, it nearly matches two-crop tiling using one eighth of the crop calls. At fixed budgets, the surrogate orders candidate plans with Spearman correlations of 0.95 to 0.99 while the sweep attains at least 98% of the exact surrogate optimum. Code will be publicly released.

title: A High-Resolution UAV Benchmark Dataset and Baseline Evaluation for Teak Crown Segmentation in Western Ghats Tropical Forests
summary: Accurate teak-tree segmentation from high-resolution drone imagery is critical for sustainable plantation management, yet lacks dedicated benchmarks. We introduce TeakTreeNet, a comprehensive dataset and evaluation protocol for binary teak-tree segmentation at native 2cm resolution. Four state-of-the-art architectures: U-Net, PSPNet, DeepLabV3, and SegFormer were rigorously benchmarked across scratch and ImageNet-pretrained settings with three-seed reproducibility. SegFormer establishes new SOTA performance with F1 0.938 +/- 0.002 (Teak), IoU 0.968 +/- 0.001 (Teak), and Accuracy 0.986 +/- 0.001, outperforming all pretrained CNNs. Domain-adaptive training suffices, as the scratch SegFormer outperforms ImageNet pretrained baselines, avoiding large-scale pretraining overhead. Comprehensive analysis reveals Transformer's superior boundary delineation for dense plantation scenarios. TeakTreeNet provides researchers with 6391 expertly annotated drone patches (224x224) and establishes reproducible evaluation protocols, enabling direct comparison of future methods. Our benchmark demonstrates SegFormer's optimal balance of accuracy, efficiency, and deployability for operational forestry monitoring of teak plantations for India's western tropical forests.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Teak Tree, Segmentation, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Transformer. Introduction Teak (Tectona grandis) is one of the most valuable tropical hardwood species, renowned for its strength, durability, and natural resistance to pests. Accurate mapping and continuous monitoring of forest tree species is recognized as critical for sustainable management fao2018state . Traditional ground surveys, while reliable, are time consuming, costly, and often cover only limited areas. In recent years, high-resolution drone imagery has transformed the way teak resources are assessed. Drones offer detailed spatial information, flexible and frequent data collection, and a cost-effective alternative to field surveys. Despite rapid progress in remote sensing and computer vision, publicly available benchmark datasets for tree crown delineation remain geographically limited, with less representation of Indian tropical forests and species-specific crown segmentation tasks. In particular, manually annotated Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) datasets covering spectral red, blue, green (RGB) channels that support reproducible training, validation, and model comparison for teak crown delineation are limited in open data repositories. However, widely used resources such as the National Ecological Observation Network (NEON) Tree Evaluation benchmarks weinstein2021benchmark provide standardized evaluation datasets for tree crown detection/delineation in multiple types of forests in the United States. Although there are UAV benchmark datasets, they are typically collected in non-Indian settings and forest compositions troles2024bamforests , limiting direct transferability to structurally complex and species-rich forests of the Western Ghats. Several open and widely adopted frameworks have accelerated crown delineation research by providing pretrained models and reproducible baselines, notably DeepForest weinstein2020deepforest , which was designed to generalize crown delineation in RGB data via large-scale pretraining and fine-tuning. Recent tropical studies have demonstrated that deep learning can delineate tree crowns from aerial RGB imagery even in complex canopies, but performance remains sensitive to crown overlap, spatial resolution, and domain shift between regions duguay2026selvamask . In this context, this work introduces a benchmark UAV RGB orthomosaic data set from the tropical forests of the western Ghats, India, with curated teak crown annotations designed specifically for reproducible evaluation of teak crown segmentation in natural forest conditions. The objectives are: (1) to develop a high-resolution drone RGB benchmark that captures the radiometric and structural complexity of teak crowns in mixed tropical canopies; (2) investigates whether transfer learning through large-scale pre-training can enhance teak crown delineation performance, particularly under limited annotated data and complex canopy conditions; and (3) to provide a rigorous comparison of representative state-of-the-art crown segmentation models under a consistent training/validation protocol and standardized metrics. Accordingly, this study aims to establish robust baseline performance metrics, identify model-specific failure modes in teak crown delineation, and provide a standardized and regionally representative benchmark dataset for teak crown delineation. Study Area and Data Study Area The Shimoga forests, Karnataka, India, and were chosen for developing benchmark data for this study. These study sites were established as part of the NASA-ISRO-synthetic-aperture-radar (NISAR) mission to support the calibration and validation of the above-ground-biomass (AGB) product das2024towards . Tropical semi-evergreen and mixed deciduous forests vegetation dominated by teak plantations make it a significant site for this study. Larger plots of 1ha sizes were established based on Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) protocol duncanson2021aboveground on forest AGB mapping. In Shimoga, ten randomly located plots (and sub-plots with in each plot) were established. Each square sized 1 hectare plot was laid in N/S and E/W directions for the principal axes of the plot. The tree species names, tree height, tree girth, stem diameter at breast height, and geo-locations were measured at each plot. RGB imaging using Drone Aerial imagery of the forest canopy over Shimoga was acquired (March, 2022) using a DJI Zenmuse P1 photogrammetric sensor integrated with a DJI Matrice 300 RTK UAV. The Zenmuse P1 is a high-performance RGB camera featuring a 45-megapixel full-frame sensor ( mm). The system utilized the TimeSync 2.0 synchronization module to align the camera, flight controller, and RTK positioning at the microsecond level, ensuring centimeter-level absolute accuracy without the need for extensive ground control points (GCPs). Missions were conducted at a flight speed of 15 m/s with a 75 front and 55 side overlap, resulting in a measured Ground Sample Distance (GSD) of 2cm. These raw images are then processed using pix4D photogrammetric software to create a georeferenced orthomosaic map of each plot. Teak is characterized by a distinct set of biophysical and phenological features that facilitate its identification in high-resolution RGB images captured by drones, in contrast with many other tropical tree species. Its broad leaves with a rough texture, open crown structure, and gray fissured bark create distinctive canopy patterns that are clearly visible in the high resolution colour images. Phenologically, teak is semi-deciduous, undergoing a marked seasonal cycle characterized by reddish young leaves during leaf flush, dark green mature leaves, and yellowing and dropping leaves during the dry season palakit2019influence . In comparison, many other tropical hardwood trees such as Dipterocarps, Shorea robusta (Sal) and Mahogany (Swietenia) tend to be evergreen with smaller leaves and denser canopies, maintaining stable colors and making them less distinguishable in optical imagery. Therefore, teak’s combination of large leaf morphology, open canopy, visible bark, and seasonal color variation provides distinguishable spectral and textural signals in drone RGB data. Data Preparation and Methodology Data Preparation and Annotation The methodology begins with the data preprocessing phase, which establishes the foundation for analyzing the 2cm high-resolution images. Teak crown delineation was carried out through manual interpretation (based on in-situ observations) and digitization in QGIS software, with the objective of producing less ambiguous and representative labels. Independent experts manually delineate the tree crowns using QGIS annotation tool. For regions which frequently occur where teak branches heavily interlock with other trees or shadows obscure the edges, a consensus review is introduced to resolve the discrepancies, ensuring accurate and unified ground truth mask before the data is used to train the models. All annotations were created as a binary scheme (teak vs. background) by visually interpreting tree crowns in the imagery and outlining only canopy regions that could be attributed with high confidence. To capture realistic variability in crown appearance, teak was annotated across multiple landscape contexts, including plantation, teak occurring within natural forest matrices, and in deciduous forest patches. This sampling strategy was intentionally designed to incorporate heterogeneity in crown texture, background composition, thereby reducing overfitting to any single forest type and improving model generalization. The teak crowns were labeled as teak when the foliage condition supported unambiguous identification, including trees with young leaves and fully mature leaves. Moreover, crowns exhibiting moderate blurring primarily attributable to wind-induced motion blur were retained within the teak class when the crown boundary and overall teak signature remained interpretable. Teak canopies in senescence and leaf-off (canopy absent) conditions were excluded from the teak class due to annotation ambiguity during model training. These conditions may reduce separability from non-teak crowns or background, and therefore were left unlabeled. The following rules were applied to maintain label consistency and avoid artifacts in the training data. Large inter-tree gaps and internal canopy voids were not delineated as teak, and only contiguous canopy surfaces with clear crown area were included in the teak polygons. Shadowed regions were also discarded, as shadow may spectral and textural responses and can lead to mis-classification when trained as part of the teak-crown. To handle class imbalance, a common issue in crown mapping where non-teak or teak dominated training data were organized into image patches with an equal number of teak and background samples. This balance was implemented at the patch level to stabilize contributions from both classes. Models For teak and non‑teak segmentation, this study evaluates four widely used semantic segmentation architectures, U‑Net ronneberger2015u , PSPNet zhao2017pyramid , DeepLabV3 chen2017rethinking and one transformer based SegFormer xie2021segformer model, each using a ResNet‑34 he2016deep encoder initialized with ImageNet deng2009imagenet weights to balance representation quality and computational cost. In addition to this, we have trained each model from scratch. The U‑Net employs a symmetric upsampling path with skip connections to recover fine scale crown boundaries, PSPNet adds pyramid pooling to better capture multi scale context around tree clusters, and DeepLabV3 relies on atrous convolutions with spatial pyramid pooling to improve sensitivity to object scale. A final convolution followed by a sigmoid activation in each model produces per pixel probabilities for teak and non‑teak. Training Details For model training and validation, the processed UAV RGB images are first divided into smaller image patches of size pixels, using an overlap of 64 pixels to ensure that tree crowns near tile boundaries are well represented. In teak canopy detection from drone imagery, where trees often have a diameter of 5-15 meters (for age above 15 years) the patch size influences how well the model understands what a teak tree-canopy looks like compared to other green vegetation. title: WildAnySplat: Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting in the Wild
comment: Accepted to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 (Conference Papers). Project page: https://wildanysplat.github.io/ ; Supplementary material: https://wildanysplat.github.io/wildanysplat_supp.pdf
summary:
We present WildAnySplat, a feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that enables robust novel-view synthesis from in-the-wild multi-view images. Unlike controlled captures, real-world images often contain multi-view inconsistencies caused by transient occluders, illumination changes, and camera ISP, which degrade the quality of existing feed-forward reconstruction methods.
  To address this challenge, we introduce a student-teacher framework that learns transient-robust and appearance-consistent 3D representations. A teacher network operates on clean images, while a student processes the corresponding in-the-wild inputs. The teacher provides clean supervision to guide the student toward a consistent canonical representation. Since paired clean and in-the-wild data are scarce, we use a hybrid data strategy, combining real paired captures, synthetic augmentations, and pseudo-clean labels generated from optimization-based reconstructions, bridging the domain gap between synthetic and real-world data.
  We adopt a transformer architecture with dedicated DPT heads for camera pose, depth, and Gaussian prediction. We additionally predict per-view transient masks to reweight photometric supervision and suppress unreliable Gaussians. To account for cross-view appearance variation, we incorporate a bilateral grid module that models per-image color transformations and enables recovery of a canonical radiance representation.
  Experiments on challenging in-the-wild benchmarks show that WildAnySplat improves robustness to transient occlusions and appearance variation while retaining the fast inference of feed-forward Gaussian Splatting.

Project page: https://wildanysplat.github.io/ fig:teaser Introduction Feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods have recently made significant progress in enabling fast novel-view synthesis from multi-view images~ wang2025vggt,Jiang2025AnySplatF3 . In particular, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs has emerged as a powerful representation due to its rendering efficiency and high visual fidelity, and various follow-ups have adapted foundational 3D models to decode Gaussian primitives~ Jiang2025AnySplatF3, offthegrid . However, existing feed-forward approaches largely assume consistent multi-view observations, limiting their applicability to controlled capture settings. In contrast, real-world image collections, such as those found in internet photo datasets, exhibit substantial multi-view inconsistencies. These include transient occluders (e.g., pedestrians, vehicles), illumination changes across time, and camera-dependent color processing. Such effects violate the assumptions of multi-view consistency and lead to degraded geometry, color artifacts, and ghosting in reconstructed scenes. While optimization-based methods such as NeRF in the Wild~ martinbrualla2020nerfw and WildGaussians~ kulhanek2024wildgaussians address these challenges through per-scene fitting and explicit robustness mechanisms, they incur high computational cost and are unsuitable for real-time or large-scale deployment. Feed-forward approaches, on the other hand, remain brittle under these conditions due to their inability to disentangle transient and persistent scene components. In this work, we propose WildAnySplat, a feed-forward framework that explicitly models and mitigates multi-view inconsistencies in in-the-wild images. Our method builds upon the AnySplat architecture and introduces three key components. First, we predict per-frame transient masks that identify unreliable regions, which are used both to reweight training losses and to guide voxelization fusion of Gaussians. Second, we model per-image color transformations via learned bilateral grids, enabling recovery of a consistent canonical appearance across views. Third, we use a student--teacher training framework with hybrid supervision, where a teacher network operating on clean observations provides stable geometric supervision to a student trained on in-the-wild inputs. A central challenge in this setting is the absence of ground-truth supervision for clean, transient-free observations. To address this, we combine large-scale synthetic augmentation with pseudo supervision derived from optimization-based methods. Specifically, we generate synthetic transient artifacts and color perturbations during training, and further leverage outputs from methods such as WildGaussians to provide pseudo-clean images and uncertainty maps. This hybrid supervision strategy enables our model to generalize effectively to real-world in-the-wild data. Our results demonstrate that WildAnySplat achieves improved robustness relative to the AnySplat backbone and competitive performance among current feed-forward in-the-wild methods, with the largest quantitative gains occurring on dynamic RealX3D captures. Our contributions are: Unified handling of in-the-wild inconsistencies in feed-forward 3DGS. A student--teacher framework learns transient-robust and appearance-consistent canonical 3D representations from inconsistent multi-view images. Transient-aware Gaussian fusion via learned masks. Per-view transient masks enable robust photometric supervision and suppress unreliable Gaussians during voxel fusion. Spatially-varying appearance modeling with bilateral grids. Per-view bilateral grids model cross-view appearance variation, enabling recovery of a canonical appearance. Hybrid supervision with synthetic augmentation and pseudo labels. Combining transient and ISP augmentation with pseudo labels from optimization methods addresses limited paired supervision and the synthetic-to-real domain gap. Related Work Optimization-based Novel View Synthesis in the Wild Opt-imization-based methods have been the dominant approach for handling in-the-wild image collections due to their flexibility in modeling inconsistencies. NeRF in the Wild~ martinbrualla2020nerfw introduced per-image appearance embeddings to account for illumination and color variation across images, with transient regions handled by uncertainty estimation. Subsequent methods further improved reconstruction quality, efficiency, and sparse inputs~ mipnerf, zipnerf, refnerf, regnerf, nerfonthego, Lin2024VastGaussianV3 . Recent methods based on 3DGS explore similar approaches. Methods such as GS-W~ zhang2024GS-W , Wild-GS~ Xu2024WildGSRN , SWAG~ Dahmani2024SWAGSI , and WildGaussians~ kulhanek2024wildgaussians incorporate robust loss functions, visibility modeling, or uncertainty estimation to handle occlusions and inconsistent observations. SpotlessSplats~ sabourgoli2024spotlesssplats and DeGauss~ wang2025degauss explicitly address distractors by separating static and dynamic components or filtering transient artifacts during optimization. While these methods achieve strong performance, they rely on computationally expensive per-scene optimization and are therefore not suitable for real-time or large-scale applications. Feed-forward Novel View Synthesis Recent feed-forward approaches enable faster, generalizable reconstruction by learning mappings from input images to scene representations. Early works such as pixelNeRF~ yu2021pixelnerf and MVSNeRF~ mvsnerf learn generalizable radiance field predictors from sparse views. More recently, feed-forward approaches have been extended to 3DGS~ offthegrid, pf3plat, zhang2025FLARE, Tian2025UniForwardU3, wang2025volsplat, pixelsplat, mvsplat, mvsgaussian , enabling efficient inference with high rendering quality. Recent pose-free methods such as AnySplat~ Jiang2025AnySplatF3 and DA3~ depthanything3 demonstrate that transformer-based architectures can jointly predict camera poses, depths and Gaussian representations directly from multi-view inputs. Although somewhat robust to minor inconsistencies, these approaches still assume consistent multi-view observations and struggle with heavy occlusions and appearance variation. Feed-forward Novel View Synthesis in the Wild Several recent works extend feed-forward NVS methods to unconstrained settings. GenWildSplat~ gupta2026genwildsplat and Sparse-View 3DGS in the Wild~ Li2025SparseGSWS3 address the challenge of generalization to real-world image collections with varying capture conditions, but focus on sparse views. WildSplatter~ Fujimura_2026_WildSplatter introduces appearance control mechanisms for feed-forward 3DGS, while WildRayZer~ chen2026wildrayzer explores self-supervised learning for large-scale dynamic environments. Wild3A~ Li2025Wild3A further demonstrates fast feed-forward reconstruction in dynamic scenes. Despite this progress, existing methods typically address only subsets of the challenges present in in-the-wild data. Handling transient occluders and color inconsistencies are often treated independently, and supervision remains limited due to the lack of ground-truth clean observations. Notably, GenWildSplat uses a pretrained segmentation network~ yolov8 to predict transient masks, rather than detecting occluders that are truly multi-view inconsistent. WildRayZer predicts motion masks and masks input tokens prior to entering the reconstruction network, rather than learning unified, robust 3D reconstruction at the representational level. Our work differs from these approaches in three key aspects. First, our clean-teacher/in-the-wild-student training strategy maintains more robust reconstruction and pose estimation in the presence of inconsistent inputs. Second, we jointly model transient occluders and spatially-varying appearance from multi-view inputs via learned masks and bilateral grids, influencing both training and Gaussian fusion. Third, we introduce a hybrid supervision strategy that combines synthetic augmentation with pseudo ground-truth signals derived from optimization-based methods, bridging the gap between synthetic and real-world data. Appearance Modeling and Color Consistency Modeling appearance variation across views is critical for in-the-wild reconstruction. While optimization-based methods~ martinbrualla2020nerfw, kulhanek2024wildgaussians, wang2024bilateral typically learn per-image latent variables or affine color corrections jointly during reconstruction, recent work explores harmonizing images before or after reconstruction. PPISP~ ppisp uses a learned post-processing module for radiance field rendering that models common photometric variations, e.g. exposure, white-balance, CRF etc. Difix3D+~ wu2025difix3d enhances NVS renderings through single-step diffusion. alzayer2025generativemvr employ a diffusion-based relighting model to match images with illumination variations to a given reference image prior to NeRF reconstruction. Similarly, CHROMA~ shin2023chroma proposes feed-forward bilateral grid prediction for consistent multi-view appearance harmonization prior to scene-specific 3DGS. We build on this idea by integrating bilateral grid prediction into a fully feed-forward 3DGS framework, allowing us to recover canonical Gaussian colors while compensating for per-image appearance variation. title: WorldLatent: A Unified 4D Latent Space for World Perception and Generation
summary: Generative Pre-Training (GPT) represents a profound milestone in natural language processing, serving as the foundation for most of today's state-of-the-art large language models. By casting diverse understanding and generation problems into a shared token representation, GPT enables a single architecture and unified optimization loop to master heterogeneous tasks across massive corpora, giving rise to powerful foundation models for natural language. In contrast, 4D spatiotemporal vision lacks a common representational protocol: perception (such as depth and camera estimation) and generation are either handled by separate one-way pipelines or bolted together from unaligned single-modality spaces. In this work, we introduce WorldLatent, a framework that formulates a unified 4D latent space as a common protocol for both world perception and generation. Rather than relying on fragmented, task-specific models or stacked single-modality representations, our framework proposes a multimodal VAE architecture that compresses and fuses complex 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single structured latent representation. Within this formulation, perception and generation operate as complementary denoising processes over the same latent space, enabling one generative model to learn both capabilities simultaneously within a single training loop. Experiments across representative 4D benchmarks verify that our fused latent protocol achieves specialist-level zero-shot 4D perception, coherent 4D generation, and controllable editing from a single model. By demonstrating that diverse 4D tasks can be seamlessly unified under a shared representational protocol, our work provides a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence.

Introduction sec:intro The establishment of a unified task protocol in Generative Pre-Training (GPT)~ radford2019language, raffel2020exploring, brown2020language marked a transformative milestone in natural language processing. Rather than relying on specialized architectures and loss functions~ kim2014convolutional, sutskever2014sequence, seo2016bidirectional, devlin2019bert for text classification, machine translation, question answering, and open-ended synthesis, casting these diverse problems into a shared token representation enabled a single model to learn both understanding and generation within one optimization objective. Inspired by this success, we argue that achieving general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence in computer vision requires a similar unification: an intelligent visual system must not only perceive the 3D geometry and camera motion of a dynamic scene from video, but also imagine, synthesize, and edit coherent 4D worlds over time. Yet, in contrast to language modeling, 4D spatiotemporal vision still lacks such a common representational protocol. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser (a), contemporary 4D perception and video generation still rely on separate one-way pipelines or unaligned, stacked modality spaces. On the perception side, feed-forward geometric reconstructors~ wang2024dust3r, leroy2024grounding, zhang2025monst3r, wang2025continuous, wang2025vggt, lin2025depth and diffusion-based depth or pose estimators~ ke2024repurposing, hu2025depthcrafter, xu2025geometrycrafter, zhang2024cameras , including recent adaptations of video generators for geometry estimation~ jiang2025geo4d, sun2025unigeo , map videos to depth, point clouds, or camera trajectories, yet overwrite or omit RGB generation and cannot synthesize new visual worlds. On the generation side, large-scale video Diffusion Transformers (DiTs)~ brooks2024video, yang2025cogvideox, wan2025wan synthesize compelling imagery in 2D RGB latent spaces without explicit 3D grounding, geometry-guided generators~ ren2025gen3c, wu2026geometry inject external 3D caches or feature alignment unidirectionally while still decoding solely into 2D pixels. Even recent frameworks that jointly diffuse appearance and geometry within one backbone~ zhang2025world, zhu2025aether, kiruga2026ugg bypass multimodal tokenizer learning, heuristically passing geometric maps through frozen RGB Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and concatenating disjoint latents. Bridging these two paradigms properly is non-trivial: geometric estimation methods seek representations that capture high-level structural abstraction to infer scene geometry and camera motions, whereas video generation models rely on generative compression that preserves low-level photometric details for high-fidelity visual reconstruction. This tension between geometric abstraction and generative compression motivates learning a genuinely fused representation rather than stacking separate latents. In this work, we take a step toward scaling general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence by tackling the fundamental question: ``How can diverse knowledge of 4D world perception and generation be consolidated into a single generative model with a shared multi-task training loop?'' Inspired by task unification in large language models, we seek a shared 4D representational protocol across visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics to bridge these capabilities. To realize this protocol, we introduce (Figure~ fig:teaser (b)), a framework that establishes a unified 4D latent space as a shared spatiotemporal representation for world perception and generation. Rather than relying on one-way pipelines or stacking unaligned modality latents, parameterizes a dynamic scene jointly via RGB video, dense depth, and pixel-aligned camera ray maps. To reconcile geometric structure with high-fidelity appearance compression, we design a multimodal 4D Variational Autoencoder (VAE) that compresses and fuses these modalities into a single spatiotemporal latent grid at the same token resolution as standard video VAEs. Built upon this shared representation, unifies perception, generation, and controllable editing as complementary Any-to-4D denoising processes within a single generative model: (1) Any-to-4D Perception (RGB Full 4D Latent), which conditions on an uncalibrated monocular video and denoises the full 4D latent to recover depth, dynamic 3D point clouds, and camera trajectories, (2) Any-to-4D Generation (Text Full 4D Latent), which jointly denoises appearance, depth, and camera rays from noise to synthesize coherent videos paired with aligned 3D scene geometry and camera motion, and (3) Any-to-4D Editing and Rendering (Depth + Text Full 4D Latent), which conditions on 4D depth structure and text prompts to render or edit visual appearance with strict 3D geometric adherence. Because every capability operates over the same latents with identical input and output spaces, a generative backbone can be adapted into a general-purpose 4D world model within a single multi-task training loop across perception and generation. We instantiate and validate on a 14B-parameter generative model trained jointly across 4D perception, generation, and controllable editing. Evaluating across indoor, outdoor, and dynamic 4D benchmarks (MPI Sintel~ butler2012naturalistic , Bonn~ palazzolo2019refusion , and ScanNet~ dai2017scannet ) as well as text-to-4D and depth-guided synthesis, we show that our fused 4D latent representation enables joint multi-task denoising within a single model, delivering strong geometric estimation, faithful geometry-guided rendering, and coherent 4D generation over a shared input-and-output latent space. In summary, our main contributions are threefold: We propose , a unified 4D latent protocol for world perception and generation, employing a multimodal VAE to compress and fuse 4D visual appearance, geometry, and dynamics into a single shared latent space for diverse downstream 4D tasks. We formulate a unified Any-to-4D generative modeling paradigm that consolidates 4D perception, generation, and editing into a single model with a shared multi-task training loop over the representation. Across controlled ablations and a 14B-parameter unified model, we demonstrate that a single generative model trained on effectively supports dynamic 4D perception, 4D scene generation, and controllable neural rendering, establishing a scalable foundation for general-purpose 4D spatial intelligence. Feed-forward pointmap regressors~ wang2024dust3r, wang2025vggt, lin2025depth, leroy2024grounding predict 3D point clouds without structure-from-motion, with extensions to dynamic and streaming videos~ zhang2025monst3r, wang2025continuous . Meanwhile, monocular~ yang2024depth, chen2025video and diffusion~ ke2024repurposing, hu2025depthcrafter, shao2025learning depth models recover 2.5D depth without camera poses, and video-diffusion adaptations~ xu2025geometrycrafter, jiang2025geo4d, sun2025unigeo estimate multi-frame 3D/4D geometry. and 4D World Generation. Video DiTs~ brooks2024video, yang2025cogvideox, wan2025wan lack 3D grounding in RGB latents, causing static-camera bias or drift. Conditioned generators inject camera, depth, or 3D cache cues~ he2025cameractrl, zhang2023adding, esser2023structure, ren2025gen3c , or align features to geometric teachers~ wu2026geometry , unidirectionally without inferring 4D geometry, while dedicated 4D generators~ wu2025cat4d, bahmani20244d, ling2024align, xie2025sv4d, fang2025worldreel remain synthesis specialists. Although WVD~ zhang2025world and Aether~ zhu2025aether jointly diffuse appearance and geometry, WVD targets image-conditioned static scenes and Aether drops text conditioning on synthetic-only data, neither supports general-purpose multi-task learning across open-world 4D perception, generation, and editing under a unified representation protocol. Multi-Task Representation Protocols. Inspired by unified task protocols in NLP~ raffel2020exploring and multimodal vision~ lu2022unified, mizrahi20234m, bai2024sequential , recent works explore joint latent spaces: Orchid~ krishnan2025orchid encodes RGB, depth, and normals for static 2D images, requiring separate image-conditioned fine-tuning for perception, while MotionCrafter~ zhu2026motioncrafter learns a 4D geometry-and-motion VAE without visual synthesis. In 4D world modeling, joint frameworks~ zhang2025world, zhu2025aether, kiruga2026ugg heuristically stack frozen RGB-VAE and geometric channels, retaining cross-modal redundancy and rigid modality boundaries. Instead, WorldVAE fuses RGB video, depth, and camera rays into a single compact bottleneck at an RGB-only VAE's token count, enabling the unification of 4D perception, generation, and editing within one model and multi-task training. title: GenPA: Image Generators as Efficient Robot Policies
summary: Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks (99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving 1.7-3.4x speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe.

However, a representative line of work still treats future visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes are no longer generated at inference time. This paradigm organizes policy learning around the proxy task of predicting future visual states. We argue that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight 19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their combinations within a common policy architecture. At deployment, GenPA requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks ( success on LIBERO and on LIBERO-Plus) and real-world manipulation tasks. Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9\,ms per action chunk on a single H100 GPU, achieving -- speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines. Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of visual generation backbones for efficient robot control. Ablations across visual tasks and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe. Together, these results show that image generators can be directly adapted into strong, efficient robot policies without requiring future visual prediction. Introduction sec:introduction Recent advances in image generation pretraining have yielded strong instruction-following and visual understanding capabilities. Beyond synthesizing realistic images, these models can identify objects referred to in language, follow spatial constraints, and visualize instructed changes to a scene~ xiao2025omnigen,blackforestlabs2025fluxkontext,zhao2026qwenimage2 . As illustrated in Figure~ fig:genpa-overview (a), given a robot manipulation instruction and a corresponding editing request, an image generation system can depict the scene after task completion or sketch end-effector motion paths on the current image. These behaviors suggest that the spatial understanding and visual imagination capabilities acquired through generative pretraining may provide valuable priors for robot action learning. Pretrained image and video generation models have both been adapted for robot control. A representative line of work treats future visual prediction as the central link between generative pretraining and action learning, using generated visual subgoals to guide goal-conditioned policies~ black2023susie or decoding actions from predicted visual transitions through inverse dynamics~ li2026lingbotva . Several methods jointly predict future observations and actions within a shared generative model~ shen2025videovla,kim2026cosmospolicy,ye2026dreamzero . Recent approaches further reduce or bypass future visual generation at deployment while retaining future prediction as a co-training objective~ yuan2026fastwam,zhang2026imagewam,ye2026gigaworldpolicy . In the broader context of predictive policy learning, future supervision has also been extended to depth, 3D pointmaps, and semantic features~ zhang2025dreamvla,yan2026flexpi . Despite differences in architecture and deployment, these methods continue to organize policy learning around the proxy task of predicting the future. We argue that the control value of image generation pretraining need not be realized through the intermediate objective of future visual prediction: image generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Prior work demonstrates the value of features from frozen image generators for control~ shin2026orca . We instead adapt the backbone itself through action learning, with a lightweight adapter mapping its features to actions. Meanwhile, direct action learning need not discard the generator's visual output capabilities. Research on generative perception shows that depth estimation, surface normal prediction, and segmentation can be learned as image generation tasks~ gabeur2026visionbanana,han2026sensenovavision . Together with evidence that auxiliary depth and spatial supervision benefit policy learning~ li2025qdepth,tu2026sgvla , these findings motivate reusing the generator's native interface for current-scene perception co-training. Representing different targets through this common interface also enables a systematic investigation of which visual supervision benefits control, including comparisons with future prediction and combinations of visual tasks. Building on this perspective, we introduce GenPA (Generative Perception for Action), an end-to-end policy that fine-tunes the pretrained image generation backbone FLUX.2 klein Base 4B~ blackforestlabs2026flux2klein with a 19M-parameter action regression adapter by default. During training, action and perception objectives jointly update the backbone, with perception supervision reusing its native image-editing interface and generative objective. Deployment requires only a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or iterative action denoising. Figures~ fig:genpa-overview (b) and~ fig:genpa-architecture provide an overview and the detailed architecture, respectively. Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA achieves strong control performance on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. On real-world contact-rich manipulation, GenPA outperforms , Fast-WAM, and ImageWAM while demonstrating strong robustness to visual perturbations. Under compiled inference on a single H100 GPU, GenPA takes 20.9\,ms per action chunk, achieving -- speedups over the evaluated VLA and WAM baselines. Our ablations further show that direct action regression achieves better closed-loop control performance with lower inference latency than a flow-based action head in our main evaluations. Compared with direct depth regression, native flow-based depth supervision improves control robustness at a higher training cost. Our contributions are twofold. (i) We introduce GenPA, demonstrating that an image generation backbone can be directly adapted into a strong, efficient robot policy without a future visual prediction objective. Its native visual co-training interface supports diverse supervision targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling systematic comparisons of visual tasks and their combinations within a common policy architecture. (ii) Our controlled studies show that strong closed-loop control can be achieved with direct action regression, without iterative action denoising, and identify current-depth supervision as a simple, effective training recipe. Our latency analysis further reveals an architectural advantage of visual generation backbones for robot control: lightweight observation encoding and independent language encoding align computation with the different update frequencies of observations and instructions. title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ pmlr-v270-kim25c,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_ leverage pretrained vision-language models to learn general-purpose robot policies, and have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. These models rely on camera observations to perceive their surroundings and extract visual features to guide action generation. However, prior studies have shown that vision models are usually vulnerable to adversarial perturbations~ goodfellow2014explaining,brown2017adversarial,zhang2025adversarial . Such vulnerabilities pose significant safety risks to VLA models, as adversarial perturbations can corrupt visual representations and consequently lead to incorrect robot actions. More dangerously, recent studies have demonstrated that many adversarial attacks against VLA models can transfer across different robotic tasks~ wang2025exploring,xu2025model,lu2026robots,fu2026vla . As illustrated in Figure~ fig:motivation ~(a), an adversarial patch can simultaneously cause failures in different tasks, even when these tasks are unknown to the attacker. In practice, attackers can develop such transferable patches using publicly available pretrained VLA checkpoints and datasets. If a VLA model is fine-tuned from one of these checkpoints, it is also likely to be vulnerable to the same attack, even if the attacker has no access to its fine-tuned parameters or private training data. Thus, this transferability could pose significant safety threats to real-world VLA deployment, as attackers can target a wide range of downstream tasks without developing task-specific attacks. To better understand why adversarial attacks can transfer across different robotic tasks, we first conduct a visualization analysis to examine the VLA model's visual representations under attacks. Specifically, we analyze representative transferable attacks in Section~ sec:preliminary and identify two common mechanisms. (1) Some attacks broadly disrupt visual features, including the object and robot-related features to mislead the model's perception across different scenes and tasks~ fu2026vla . This mechanism is similar to universal adversarial attacks observed in general vision models~ zhang2020understanding,zhang2021data,kim2024doubly . (2) Other attacks target the perception towards the robot itself~ wang2025exploring,xu2025model,lu2026robots . Through explicitly or implicitly mimicking visual features associated with the robot, these attacks mislead the model's perception of the robot. Since accurate perception of the robot is important across different tasks, such attacks can also achieve cross-task transferability. Despite their different mechanisms, we found that both types of attacks share a common consequence: they distort the visual representation of the robot itself. This observation reveals an important opportunity for defense: While adversarial patches can mislead a VLA model's visual perception of the robot, they cannot alter the robot's actual physical state. In fact, robots continuously measure their own states through proprioceptive sensors, which provide information such as joint positions and orientations independently of camera observations. We can leverage this proprioception information to verify whether a VLA's visual perception of the robot is reliable. Therefore, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that detects adversarial attacks by checking the consistency between proprioceptive information and visual representations. First, we use the robot's proprioceptive state, together with its kinematic model and camera calibration, to determine where the robot should appear in the camera scene. We then analyze the VLA model's visual features to estimate where the model perceives the robot. As shown in Figure~ fig:motivation ~(b), these two estimates are consistent under benign conditions but diverge when attacks distort the robot's visual representation. By measuring this discrepancy, our framework can detect adversarial attacks without requiring any additional training or expensive inference. Upon detection, our framework also leverages this discrepancy to locate and resist the adversarial attacks. We conduct extensive experiments on OpenVLA~ pmlr-v270-kim25c and ~ black2024pi_0 across LIBERO~ liu2023libero task suites and various adversarial attacks. Results demonstrate that our framework can accurately detect various transferable attacks, outperforming existing detection baselines. Beyond detection, our framework effectively mitigates adversarial patches and significantly improves task success under attack. To further examine the robustness of our detection, we conduct two adaptive attacks by preserving robot-related visual features and minimizing the visual-proprio inconsistency score. We find that both strategies reduce attack effectiveness, supporting the reliability of the defense design. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify a shared mechanism of transferable adversarial attacks in VLA: these attacks compromise robot-related visual representations. This observation motivates leveraging trusted robot proprioception to verify the reliability of visual perception. We develop a principled, lightweight, and attack-agnostic defense framework that leverages visual-proprioceptive consistency checking to detect, localize, and mitigate adversarial attacks. Our approach requires no adversarial examples or additional model training and can be integrated into existing VLA models without modifying their parameters. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first work to leverage robot proprioceptive information for adversarial defense in VLA models. Extensive experiments across two VLA models and a broad range of attacks validate the effectiveness and generalizability of our defense. Evaluations under benign visual variations and adaptive attacks, together with real-robot experiments, further validate its reliability. Threat model and attack mechanism analysis sec:preliminary Threat Model. We focus on adversarial patch attacks~ wang2025exploring,xu2025model,lu2026robots,fu2026vla that can transfer across robotic tasks. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:motivation (a), a single adversarial patch can compromise multiple robotic tasks, even when these tasks are unknown to the attacker. Such attacks do not require access to target-task data or the victim model's fine-tuned parameters. Instead, the attacker optimizes an adversarial patch using a publicly accessible VLA model and source-task data collected from diverse robotic tasks. The same patch can then be directly transferred to victim models fine-tuned from the public VLA checkpoint on unseen downstream tasks. Such transferability poses a significant threat to real-world VLA deployment, as a single adversarial patch can compromise a wide range of robotic applications. As a representative example, the work~ wang2025exploring introduces the Untargeted Action Discrepancy Attack (UADA), which aims to mislead the VLA model into generating incorrect robot actions. title: AlpaSafe: Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection for Vision-Language-Action Models in Autonomous Driving
summary: Reasoning-based driving vision-language-action (VLA) models propose multiple candidate trajectories at each decision, yet only one is executed. Standard evaluation scores the best candidate, assuming an oracle selector that deployment lacks, and leaves the risk of the executed candidate unexamined. Existing online evaluators typically close this gap with a purpose-trained scene or world model, often rolling out each candidate through it at inference time. We introduce AlpaSafe, a risk-aware trajectory selector that reuses the scene representation a frozen driving VLA computes while proposing its candidates. AlpaSafe reads the last hidden token of the VLA's prompt prefill. A lightweight head, trained on the closed-loop simulation outcomes of the candidates, fuses this token with each candidate trajectory and predicts a relative score and collision/offroad logits. A fixed rule removes candidates dominated on the two risk logits and selects the highest-scoring candidate among those remaining, adding neither rollouts nor VLA training. Experiments on 525 AlpaSim scenes show that AlpaSafe outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41% and 6.10% to 4.93%. The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75 ms per decision.
