The selector has 1.7M parameters and takes 0.75\,ms per decision. Autonomous driving, closed-loop evaluation, risk-aware planning, trajectory selection, vision-language-action models Introduction sec:intro Reasoning-based vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used as end-to-end planners for autonomous driving~ tian2024drivevlm,hwang2024emma,alpamayo2025 . Given a scene and a driving prompt, these models can generate multiple plausible trajectory candidates rather than committing to a single future. This creates a trajectory selection problem, because only one candidate can be executed. Proposal-based driving systems therefore learn trajectory scorers or selectors to rank the generated candidates~ kirby2026drivor . Best-of- metrics such as minADE@ , however, select the best candidate in hindsight and thus mainly measure whether the generated set contains a good trajectory. At deployment, the system must instead determine which candidate is most likely to produce the best closed-loop outcome before any candidate is executed. Existing online trajectory evaluators commonly address this problem through explicit imagination. WoTE~ li2025wote , for example, conditions a BEV world model on each candidate, predicts candidate-specific future BEV states, and evaluates the trajectory from those imagined outcomes. This makes future consequences explicit, but it requires a purpose-trained world model and additional candidate-conditioned prediction at inference time. Yet a large reasoning-based VLA has already integrated the observed scene, driving intent, and interaction context while generating its candidate trajectories. It remains unknown whether the hidden representation produced during this process contains enough scene-specific information to evaluate the candidates without explicitly predicting their futures. To answer this question, we introduce ( ), a risk-aware trajectory selector for reasoning-based driving VLAs. captures the final-layer hidden states of the frozen VLA's prompt prefill during the same forward pass that generates the candidates and reads only the last token, a byproduct of generation that requires no additional VLA computation. A lightweight head then scores each candidate against this token and filters the candidates on predicted collision and offroad risk. To isolate selection quality, we hold the candidate pool and its official closed-loop outcome labels from the simulator fixed across methods, and learned-selector predictions are out of fold at the scene level. Matched ablations that replace the last token with a zero token or with the full prefill sequence test whether the reused representation matters, and uncertainty is reported with paired scene-bootstrap intervals. The selector has 1.7M parameters and runs its full selection path in 0.75\,ms per eight-candidate decision on one GPU, whereas one closed-loop candidate rollout in the same simulator takes about 111\,s. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose , a risk-aware trajectory selection framework for reasoning-based driving VLAs that reuses the last prompt-prefill hidden token of the frozen generator, captured in the same forward pass that produces the candidates, and requires neither VLA training nor inference-time rollouts. We design a risk-aware selector head, a lightweight action-conditioned module that scores each candidate trajectory with a relative outcome score and collision/offroad risk logits, removes the candidates dominated on the two risk logits, and selects the highest-scoring trajectory among those remaining. Experimental results on scenes demonstrate that outperforms Alpamayo's default first-sample rule and uniform random selection in selected regret and top-1 agreement, and reduces the collision-at-fault or offroad rate from 6.41 and 6.10 to 4.93 , at only 0.75\,ms per decision. Related Work sec:related Driving scenes often admit several valid maneuvers, motivating candidate-based formulations that preserve multiple plausible trajectories rather than regress a single averaged future~ chai2019multipath,phanminh2020covernet . End-to-end planners encode the current observation using BEV, vectorized, or object-level scene representations~ hu2023uniad,jiang2023vad,chen2024vadv2,renz2023plant , while driving foundation models combine vision-language features with generative trajectory decoders~ shao2024lmdrive,tian2024drivevlm,hwang2024emma,alpamayo2025 . Once multiple ego trajectories are generated, however, planning becomes a selection problem. One family of methods scores each candidate directly from its geometry and the current scene, without predicting a candidate-conditioned future at inference time. Early neural motion planners learn costs over sampled feasible trajectories~ zeng2019nmp ; subsequent approaches distill metric-specific teachers or learn generalized trajectory values and metric sub-scores~ li2024hydramdp,li2025gtrs,yao2026drivesuprim,kirby2026drivor,ang2026clover . TOAD further treats a learned scorer as the objective for test-time trajectory optimization~ xu2026toad . A central distinction among these methods is the scene evidence exposed to the scorer. DrivoR uses multi-camera register tokens shared by its generation and scoring decoders, while recent studies show that intermediate VLA states can support downstream driving decisions and trajectory refinement~ ling2026blue,babu2026planningtoken,yang2026lwdrive . adopts this representation-reuse setting, combining every candidate with a shared representation extracted from a frozen driving VLA and learning a per-trajectory score. A second family evaluates a candidate only after constructing evidence about its possible consequences. PDM rolls out kinematic proposals against simplified agent forecasts and ranks them using hand-designed rules~ dauner2023pdm . DTPP replaces this fixed evaluation with jointly learned ego-conditioned prediction and context-aware cost evaluation for tree-structured policy candidates~ huang2024dtpp . Several world-model methods construct richer candidate-conditioned futures: WoTE predicts dense future BEV states, SafeDrive represents safety-critical future entities in a sparse world, and World4Drive uses an intention-aware latent world model to support multimodal trajectory selection~ li2025wote,kim2026safedrive,zheng2025world4drive . Foundation-model approaches instead employ a generative VLM reward model or a VLA critic to evaluate and refine proposed trajectories~ chen2026drivereward,yang2026criticvla . The principal distinction is therefore whether selection requires constructing a candidate-conditioned future world at decision time, not whether future prediction is used as a training signal. WPT removes the inference-time cost by distilling world-model guidance into a lightweight policy and discarding the world model at deployment~ jiang2026wpt . uses consequence supervision to train a per-trajectory scorer and event-risk heads rather than the trajectory-generation policy: each candidate is evaluated directly against the frozen VLA scene representation, and no candidate-conditioned future world is predicted at inference time. Methodology sec:method gives an overview of : one forward pass of the frozen VLA yields both the candidate trajectories and the prefill hidden states, and the selector pairs the last token of those states with each candidate. Problem Setting sec:setting We work in , a high-fidelity closed-loop driving simulator in the tradition of public closed-loop benchmarks~ caesar2021nuplan,dauner2024navsim,jia2024bench2drive , whose official scene score aggregates safety, compliance, and progress into a single scalar per rollout. Each scene contributes three decision groups at staggered decision times. For each group, the frozen 10B-parameter generator , a reasoning VLM coupled to a trajectory decoder ( a), samples candidate trajectories from one prompt prefill. Every candidate is then executed in closed loop and receives its own official score, giving 24 scoring rollouts per scene. In our data the official score equals zero when collision-at-fault or offroad occurs and otherwise equals the simulator's progress score. Each rollout also carries separate collision-at-fault and offroad event labels. Given a group with candidates and scores , a selector commits to . We evaluate two primary quantities: selected regret, , the selected candidate's gap from the oracle outcome, for which lower is better, and tie-aware top-1 agreement, with , for which higher is better. Both are averaged over the groups of a scene and then equally over scenes (scene-macro mean). Same-Prefill Representation Extraction sec:capture A representation-reuse claim is confounded if the representation could come from a different forward pass than the candidates, for example a different context window, different preprocessing, or a silently re-run prefill. We eliminate this by construction. A capture hook inside the production predict() path records the final transformer layer's post-normalization hidden states of the prompt prefill, , during the same call that samples the candidates ( ); the prefill length is the same for every group. An exactly-one-prefill assertion makes a second prefill in the call fail the capture rather than silently substitute context. The scene vector used at deployment is the last row, . Capture-time SHA-256 hashes of both tensors establish bit-exact provenance, with verified for every group, and every downstream artifact, from training tables to locked predictions and analysis records, carries these hashes forward. Candidates and representation are therefore co-produced, and the closed-loop scores remain linked to the corresponding candidates. Risk-Aware Selector Head sec:head The head has 1 , 708 , 871 trainable parameters and scores each candidate independently; the frozen VLA receives no gradients ( ). title: SANA-Robot: Efficient World Action Model with Hybrid Memory
summary: World action models (WAMs) leverage the world knowledge of video generation models to improve action generation by aligning visual prediction with action prediction. However, their prediction overhead prevents real-time deployment on edge devices, and they usually lack an effective long-term memory. We introduce SANA-Robot, a 4.5B WAM with minute-level memory that runs in real time on edge devices, built on the following core designs: (1) hybrid memory at constant cost: our WAM relies on linear attention to maintain a global memory with a fixed-size state, and on sliding window softmax attention layers that propagate previous information, enabling high success rates on tasks requiring whole-episode memory while keeping an efficient and constant inference speed; (2) a unified model: by dynamically applying different noise levels to action and video tokens, SANA-Robot can serve not only as a policy but also as a world simulator; (3) a full-stack infrastructure for both memory training and inference, including efficient data packing and shuffling as well as memory-phase-based asynchronous execution. SANA-Robot achieves the best performance on the memory dimension of RoboDojo among models of medium size (about 5B) and the highest success rates on LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-Pro and LIBERO-Max. In real-world deployment, SANA-Robot takes 135 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090 with FP8 GEMMs and 115 ms with NVFP4 GEMMs, and achieves closed-loop, real-time asynchronous robot control at 30 Hz on edge devices, demonstrating both the efficiency and the effectiveness of SANA-Robot. Project page: https://nvlabs.github.io/Sana/Robot/

They now match or surpass vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ black2024pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 on manipulation benchmarks~ chen2026robodojo,chen2026robotwin2,fei2026liberoplus , which makes them a strong candidate for the low-level policy that must run stably and safely on edge devices. However, current WAMs cannot yet serve as such a policy, for two reasons. First, video prediction adds a large overhead. Besides the actions, each action chunk requires denoising the far more numerous video tokens over several steps. Without optimization, a single request of our 4.5B model takes about 0.6\,s on an RTX 5090, compared with less than 0.1\,s for ~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 , and a synchronous robot stands still during each request. Second, many manipulation tasks depend on information that is no longer visible, such as the number of completed steps or the position of an occluded object. Existing WAMs either act from the current observation alone~ wang2026openwam or keep only a few sparsely sampled past frames~ miao2026internw0delta,guo2026vpp2 , which miss most of the episode and add to the latency as the memory grows. Instead, we present , a 4.5B WAM trained from Sana-Video~2~ chen2026sana that runs in real time on edge devices with a fine-grained, minute-level memory. is a hybrid linear diffusion transformer. It stacks 8 blocks, each with three Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers~ yang2024gated followed by one softmax attention layer. A GDN layer compresses the past into a fixed-size recurrent state, so its cost does not grow with the context. A softmax layer attends to every token exactly, at a cost that grows with the context. This architecture matches the needs of a real-time policy with memory, and we build three core designs on it ( ). World Action Model. is pretrained as one model that plays three roles. As a forward dynamics model (FDM), it predicts the future video caused by given actions and serves as a world simulator for policy evaluation ( ). As a policy, it predicts the actions and the future video from the current observation and drives manipulation ( ). As an inverse dynamics model (IDM), it predicts the actions that explain a given video, which makes the video and the actions predicted by the policy more consistent. All three modes share one token sequence of multi-view video, proprioception and actions, and differ only in which tokens are clean conditions and which are noised targets. One network thus learns all three roles from the same data, 19.4K hours from 23 datasets of robots, handheld grippers, simulation and human video ( ). Memory at Constant Cost. Building on its hybrid architecture, we equip with a hybrid memory. Attention is causal across action chunks, so each chunk reads the past but never the future. The softmax layers attend to the first frame and to a sliding window over the last few chunks, through which information propagates chunk by chunk. The GDN layers absorb every past chunk into their fixed-size state and thus keep a memory of the whole episode. Both memory types cover the long range, at different granularities ( ). During autoregressive generation, writes each chunk into the memory once and keeps only the GDN state and a rolling KV cache over the sliding window. Every action chunk therefore has the same cost, while the memory spans up to about one minute on RoboDojo. -Stack Infrastructure. The memory changes both training and deployment, and we design the infrastructure of around it. For training, the memory must be learned on whole episodes, whose lengths vary widely. We propose multimodal sequence packing with task-balanced ordering , which trains on whole episodes without padding and with a stable task mix in every step ( ). Balanced and shuffled data loading further mixes many datasets in every step ( ). For deployment, we propose memory RTC for asynchronous execution, which hides the inference latency. title: $ζ_0$: A Framework for World Action Models with Joint Scene and Body Foresight in Humanoid Control
comment: 18 pages (including appendix), 10 figures, 12 tables. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/ ; Code & Data: https://github.com/chenyizhi123/Zeta0
summary: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present $ζ_0$, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, $ζ_0$ built on $Ψ_0$ and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3 and 85.0 , gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5 tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: . Introduction sec:introduction Humanoid interaction couples whole-body motion with changes in the surrounding scene. Pushing a box, for example, moves the object while the arms keep contact and the legs and torso support the motion. World Action Models couple action generation with anticipated future observations~ wu2024gr1,tian2025seer,hu2025vpp,zheng2025flare,yuan2026fastwam,li2026lingbotva . For a humanoid, the consequences of an action also include its own body motion, which egocentric images may capture only partially and measured joint trajectories record directly. We therefore ask a policy to foresee scene and body changes jointly. Demonstrations provide this foresight as supervision: each action is followed by recorded images and measured body states. At execution time, those futures have not yet occurred and must be predicted from causal inputs. A common approach fits future predictions to recorded observations or their latent representations~ ha2018world,hafner2023dreamerv3,zheng2025flare . Latent-distance supervision, however, does not directly reflect how a policy uses the prediction: nearby futures need not induce the same action, and equally sized errors can have different effects on behavior. We therefore also supervise prediction in action space, asking whether a predicted future induces the action that the recorded future would. We introduce , a framework that turns a vision-language-action policy into a World Action Model with joint scene-and-body foresight for humanoid control, illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser . During training, a future encoder summarizes subsequent visual features and measured body trajectories into a shared temporal latent representation, and a causal predictor learns to estimate it from inputs available at execution time. The representation, predictor, and action models are trained jointly; at deployment, the policy acts on the predicted future and current observations. To supervise prediction in action space, we introduce dual-response transfer. A teacher learns to generate actions conditioned on recorded futures, providing a reference action response, and we train the predictor so that predicted futures induce this response through two readers. The teacher term asks the prediction to carry the action-relevant information the teacher extracts from recorded futures; the executing-policy term asks for the same response from the reader used at deployment. We make three contributions: [leftmargin=*,nosep] Joint scene-and-body foresight framework: turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models. Dual-response transfer: a training objective that supervises causal prediction through the responses of a recorded-future teacher and the executing policy. Consistent gains in simulation and the real world: built on and raises mean success over each base by 18.8 and 9.0 points on seven HumanoidArena tasks and by 16.7 and 10.0 points on six real-world tasks. Related Work sec:related Whole-body humanoid learning. Whole-body humanoid learning studies coordinated locomotion, posture, and manipulation, with hierarchical control separating high-level decisions from low-level execution~ cao2026hiwet,chen2026hierkick . Tracking controllers such as ExBody, ExBody2, HOVER, and SONIC learn to execute reference motions or end-effector targets across the body~ cheng2024expressive,ji2024exbody2,he2025hover,luo2025sonic , and ASAP aligns simulated and real-world physics to learn agile whole-body skills~ he2025asap . Teleoperation systems collect coordinated demonstrations~ he2024omnih2o,ze2025twist , while HumanPlus and 3D diffusion policies connect visual observations to autonomous humanoid skills~ fu2024humanplus,ze2024humanoid . HumanoidBench evaluates locomotion and manipulation across simulated tasks~ sferrazza2024humanoidbench , and HumanoidArena emphasizes egocentric hierarchical whole-body learning~ wang2026humanoidarena . These directions provide motion-control interfaces and demonstration-based learning settings for humanoid interaction; builds on such an interface and asks how a high-level policy can anticipate the consequences of its own commands. Vision-language-action policies. Recent VLA work adapts pretrained vision-language representations to robot control using demonstration data~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,chen2026geoalign . Building on large-scale robot transformers~ brohan2023rt1 , generalist policies such as Octo and the series learn across tasks and embodiments~ octo2024,black2025pi0,pi2025pi05 . Action generation has developed alongside representation learning, with action chunking~ zhao2023act and diffusion- or flow-based generators~ chi2023diffusion,black2025pi0 providing interfaces for continuous robot commands. Receding-horizon execution refreshes the observation context between action chunks, combining multi-step generation with feedback during control~ chi2023diffusion . For humanoids, GR00T~N1, , and HuGe combine pretrained vision-language backbones with action generators~ bjorck2025gr00t,wei2026psi0,liu2026huge , and Kimodo-Policy learns kinematic action models for loco-manipulation~ wang2026kimodo . These policies provide foundations for studying how additional predictive information can condition action generation. World Action Models. World models learn how an environment responds to actions, either to learn behaviors by imagining latent trajectories~ ha2018world,hafner2020dreamer,hafner2023dreamerv3 or as generative and predictive models trained on large video corpora~ bruce2024genie,nvidia2025cosmos,assran2025vjepa2 . Text-guided video generation can serve directly as a policy~ du2023unipi , and frozen self-supervised visual features can serve as world-model states for planning~ zhou2024dinowm . In feature-space planning, candidate action sequences are optimized so that predicted future features approach those of a goal observation~ zhou2024dinowm . Predictive policies couple action learning with future visual prediction~ wu2024gr1,tian2025seer,hu2025vpp or jointly model future observations and actions~ li2025uva,zhu2025uwm . FLARE aligns policy features with future visual latents~ zheng2025flare , DIAL separates latent intent prediction from execution~ chen2026dial , and ARPS learns predictive states from future features and their changes~ gu2026arps . Being-M0.7 jointly models visual and motion futures, then trains an action expert on a frozen, robot-adapted prior~ yue2026being . Most of these methods represent the future by images or visual features and supervise prediction by reconstruction or latent distance. foresees the scene and measured body trajectories in one shared latent representation and supervises its causal prediction in action space, keeping the predictor coupled to action learning throughout training. Knowledge distillation matches a student's outputs to a teacher's and thereby updates the student's parameters~ hinton2015distilling . Action-space constraints provide another form of supervision: cross-view action consistency matches flow velocities across action-equivalent observations~ huang2026crossview . Dual-response transfer in Sec.~ sec:response also compares action responses, but it holds the readers' parameters fixed and updates the predictor only through the readers' input, the predicted future. title: More Than Picturing the Future: Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning for Generalizable Robot Manipulation
summary: Latent reasoning lets Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models deliberate at a fraction of the cost of explicit chain-of-thought, increasingly through visual foresight, which we show to be indispensable for predicting actions. Yet this paradigm is inherited from Vision-Language Models, where it serves understanding rather than action: each latent is aligned with an isolated future frame, often enriched with further modalities of that frame. We find that this binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes, so that it degrades sharply once the scene changes. We argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. We therefore propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which redirects visual latents from the whole frame to the interaction that the action must bring about. Semantic latents, following the stages of embodied chain-of-thought, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine: from the global scene, to the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination, to the robot state. Relative to the state-of-the-art latent VLA LaST$_0$, our method raises the mean success rate on SimplerEnv-WidowX from 37.5% to 55.2% in distribution and from 22.4% to 30.2% under out-of-distribution shifts, and on an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform from 60.8% to 90.8% in training scenes and from 6.7% to 37.5% under environmental changes.

Introduction sec:intro Building on pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs)~ alayrac2022flamingo, karamcheti2024prismatic , Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ zitkovich2023rt2, kim2024openvla, black2024pi0 inherit web-scale visual-semantic priors and translate visual observations and language instructions directly into robot actions. Yet such reactive policies lack explicit deliberation over subgoals and action consequences, which is indispensable for complex, long-horizon manipulation~ sun2025emmax, huang2026fastthinkact . To bridge this gap, recent VLAs incorporate Chain-of-Thought (CoT)~ wei2022chain reasoning, verbalizing sub-task plans~ zawalski2024ecot, sun2025emmax, huang2025thinkact, lin2025onetwovla or anticipating future observations~ zhao2025cotvla, zhang2025upvla, zhang2025dreamvla before acting, and thereby attain stronger generalization. Despite these gains, explicit reasoning suffers from two inherent drawbacks: 1) autoregressive decoding incurs prohibitive latency~ huang2026fastthinkact, bai2026laravla , and 2) discretizing reasoning into tokens imposes an information bottleneck~ liu2026last0, bai2026laravla , both acute in embodied settings that demand real-time, continuous control. These limitations have spurred a shift toward Latent Reasoning~ map2025latent , which unfolds reasoning in continuous hidden states~ xu2026thinkinguncertainty and endows compact latent tokens with task-relevant content, from verbalizable textual rationales in Heima~ shen2025heima to visual evidence such as trajectory maps in Mirage~ yang2025machine , regions of interest in LVR~ li2025lvr , 3D geometric priors in 3DThinker~ chen2025think , and perceptual maps in CoVT~ qin2025chain . A burgeoning body of work has brought this paradigm into VLAs~ huang2025thinkact, ma2025hybrid, tan2026lcdrive, liu2026last0, xie2026flare, huang2026fastthinkact, bai2026laravla, luo2026lastvla : Fast-ThinkAct~ huang2026fastthinkact distills lengthy textual reasoning into compact verbalizable latents, whereas LaST ~ liu2026last0 , LaRA-VLA~ bai2026laravla , and, in autonomous driving, LaST-VLA~ luo2026lastvla further ground their latents in future visual dynamics, 3D structure, and robot proprioception. Such grounding proves essential for embodied control: our oracle analysis reveals that, added to the current observation, ground-truth future visual evidence attains an action predictability Action predictability measures how accurately the actions can be predicted from the given features; details are in . of 0.678, against 0.616 for textual latents ( ). Visual latents thus constitute an indispensable component of latent reasoning in VLAs. In VLMs, latent visual reasoning serves to comprehend the image at hand: its latents encode the current input across diverse modalities, from RGB features~ yang2025machine, li2025lvr and 3D geometry~ chen2025think to segmentation and depth maps~ qin2025chain , and the reasoning culminates in a single answer rather than an action sequence. Latent VLAs, however, inherit this understanding-oriented paradigm largely intact: each latent is aligned with the features of an isolated future frame, and richer foresight is pursued by stacking further modalities of that same frame~ liu2026last0 . This raises a pivotal question: does a paradigm built to understand a frame suit a policy that must decide how to act? We find that it does not. Reproducing what a future frame looks like rewards the backbone for encoding the appearance of the scene, and each additional modality of the same frame supplies further supervision on appearance rather than on how to move. For example, when only the workspace background changes while the task remains the same, the backbone of LaST ~ liu2026last0 recognizes the task in only 2 of the observations ( ), mistaking a change of scene for a change of task. Bound to the appearance of its training scenes, the latent VLA overfits the training distribution: under the same kind of change on a real robot, it succeeds in only 6.7 of trials, against 37.5 for our method ( ). In this paper, we argue that visual latents for action should capture not what a future frame looks like, but how the scene evolves toward the goal. Textual reasoning unfolds step by step, with each step conditioned on its predecessors and the goal. Visual latents should likewise follow a logic of their own: within each future step, they should progress from the global scene to the interaction region and the robot state, , from coarse to fine; across steps, each should build on the one before, so that successive steps chain into a motion path. Such a derivation supervises what changes, where, and in which order, which transfers across scenes, rather than the appearance that distinguishes one training scene from another. Based on this insight, we propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which organizes latent reasoning as a logically structured derivation. Semantic latents, aligned with the semantic stages of embodied chain-of-thought~ zawalski2024ecot and trained under random textual prefix substitution, first establish what to accomplish and how. Conditioned on them, motion-oriented latents anticipate each future step from coarse to fine, zooming from the global scene into the interaction region spanned by the manipulated object and its destination before specifying the robot state. Without altering the inference procedure of latent reasoning, the policy thereby learns how to move rather than what the training scenes look like, and still recognizes the task in unseen scenes ( ). Our contributions are threefold: (1) We reveal that latent VLAs inherit an understanding-oriented paradigm of latent visual reasoning from VLMs, and show that aligning latents with isolated future frames and their modalities binds the policy to the appearance of its training scenes and impairs its generalization. (2) We propose Motion-Oriented Latent Reasoning, which organizes visual latents as a logically structured derivation, from coarse to fine within each step and chained across steps into a motion path, scaffolded by semantic latents. (3) Extensive experiments on SimplerEnv-WidowX, LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and an AgileX Piper dual-arm platform demonstrate that our method matches or improves in-distribution performance while substantially improving out-of-distribution generalization. Related Work sec:related in VLA models. Vision-Language-Action models adapt pretrained VLMs to robot control by mapping observations and instructions directly to actions~ zitkovich2023rt2, kim2024openvla, octo2024, black2024pi0, li2024cogact, qu2025spatialvla, intelligence2025pi05 . To equip such reactive policies with deliberation, a line of work interposes explicit reasoning before acting: textual approaches verbalize subtasks, motions, and grounded object locations as embodied chain-of-thought~ zawalski2024ecot, chen2025ecotlite, sun2025emmax, lin2025onetwovla , while visual approaches synthesize a subgoal image~ zhao2025cotvla, zhang2025upvla or forecast dynamic regions, depth, and semantics~ zhang2025dreamvla . Others condition the policy on motion through predicted point tracks~ wen2024atm, bharadhwaj2024track2act , object flow~ xu2024im2flow2act , or tracked visual traces~ zheng2025tracevla , improving generalization across objects, scenes, and embodiments and corroborating that motion transfers where appearance does not. In both lines, however, the intermediate representation is decoded or tracked at every control step, incurring substantial latency at inference. reasoning. In language models, the chain of thought is replaced by continuous thoughts~ haotraining , compressed into fewer latent steps~ tan2025colar , interleaved with discrete text tokens~ su2025tokenassorted , or condensed into verbalizable hidden tokens~ shen2025heima ; VLMs extend it to visual evidence, aligning latent tokens with image features~ yang2025machine , regions of interest~ li2025lvr , 3D geometry~ chen2025think , or segmentation and depth cues~ qin2025chain , although recent analyses question how effectively such latents are exploited~ li2026imagination, zhang2026unsilencing . title: Contact Harness: Enabling VLM Agents to Perform Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Agents built on pretrained VLMs have demonstrated zero-shot control of real robots, but vision alone is often insufficient for reliable contact-state assessment in contact-rich manipulation. Force and tactile feedback provide complementary information, but their semantic ambiguity makes them difficult for agents to use directly. These signals must be interpreted according to their physical meaning, together with task phase and visual evidence. We propose Contact Harness, which uses reusable, optimized skills to guide a VLM agent in assessing contact states from multimodal feedback and selecting subsequent actions. A compliant execution mechanism regulates in-contact motions using real-time force feedback. The framework requires no model fine-tuning, task demonstrations, or simulation training. We conduct zero-shot real-robot evaluations using GPT-6 Astra on Rokae and Franka robots. With a single prompt skill, Contact Harness achieves a full-insertion rate of 90.7% across 15 connector types, with further evaluations on a real PC under variations in lighting, background, and position. Across four additional contact-rich tasks, including whiteboard wiping, writing, peeling, and pivoting, Contact Harness achieves an average success rate of 100%. On six simulated tasks, Contact Harness reaches 96.7% success, compared with at most 68.3% for pretrained VLA baselines fine-tuned on task demonstrations, showing the potential of agent-based manipulation for contact-rich real-world deployment.
full_text: -1 Introduction sec:intro Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) can support robot manipulation by combining task reasoning with action generation. An agent harness connects a VLM to robot observations and control interfaces, forming a VLM agent that interacts with the physical environment. The VLM reasons over observations to determine the next action, while the harness coordinates execution and returns feedback to inform subsequent decisions~ li2026k1,liu2026guava,chen2026survey . Recent systems have demonstrated this approach across tasks such as pick-and-place and towel folding, without additional model training~ jia2026agp,zhang2026astra,chen2026showharness . Contact-rich manipulation, however, is challenging for agents that rely primarily on visual observations~ lee2019making,zhang2026astra,fu2026capx . In cable insertion, contact feedback helps identify misalignment and regulate forces that are difficult to assess visually~ spector2021insertionnet,dong2021tactile,xing2026contactdp . Wiping~ hou2025adaptive,xue2025reactive and writing require maintaining appropriate contact force during motion. In addition, occlusion and limited visual precision make vision alone insufficient for reliable contact assessment~ dong2021tactile,xing2026contactdp . Force and tactile feedback complement vision~ he2025foar,jones2025beyond,yu2025forcevla,huang2025tactile,chen2026implicitrdp,shan2026learning , but integrating them into VLM agents poses two challenges. First, reliable contact-state assessment requires interpreting what each signal reveals about the interaction. Increased force, for example, cannot distinguish intended contact from an unintended collision without task knowledge. Second, VLM agents typically receive execution feedback and issue new commands only after the current action or code segment finishes~ chen2026showharness,zhou2026gptgear,fu2026capx , limiting their ability to respond to contact changes during execution. Continuing a command after contact changes can produce excessive forces, particularly at high robot stiffness~ will1975guarded,hogan1985impedance . To address these challenges, we propose Contact Harness, which combines multimodal contact reasoning with compliant execution to improve task and scene understanding and force regulation, thereby increasing success rates in contact-rich manipulation. Our contributions are as follows. We introduce Contact Harness, which uses reusable textual skills to enable a frozen VLM agent to integrate visual, force, and tactile feedback for contact-state assessment and action generation without model fine-tuning. We develop a compliant execution mechanism that combines impedance control with contact-force constraints to regulate motion using real-time force feedback between successive agent decisions. We evaluate Contact Harness on two real robot arms, Rokae and Franka. With a single insertion prompt, it inserts 15 connector types at a 90.7 success rate over 150 trials, and it completes wiping, writing, peeling, and pivoting in all 40 trials. In simulation, it reaches 96.7 success on six tasks, compared with at most 68.3 for trained VLA policies, and ablations show that textual skills, force feedback, and compliant execution each contribute. Related work sec:related Classical hybrid force-position control and impedance control provide a foundation for contact regulation in robotics~ mason1981compliance,raibert1981hybrid,hogan1985impedance . We review related work on contact policy learning, planning and program generation with large language models, and VLM-based agent harnesses. Contact policy learning. Generalist vision-language-action models learn manipulation policies from large-scale robot demonstration data~ brohan2022rt,brohan2023rt, team2024octo, kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, black2025pi05, liu2025rdt, bjorck2025gr00t . For contact-rich tasks, models acquire contact skills from interaction data~ li2022seehearfeelsmart, chi2025diffusion, xue2026tube . Facet-0~ deng2026facet0 trains a foundation model for precise manipulation using large-scale manipulation data with synchronized force measurements. ContactDP~ xing2026contactdp integrates visual, force, and tactile feedback into a diffusion policy. Some approaches combine large language model reasoning with learned control policies. A neuro-symbolic assembly method~ li2026neurosymbolic uses a large language model to generate assembly sequences and combines search with an impedance control policy trained through reinforcement learning for insertion. CompliantVLA~ zhang2026compliantvla uses a VLM to adjust stiffness and damping, while a VLA fine-tuned on task-specific data generates motion. These methods rely on learned policies. Program generation, planning, and control with large language models. Large language models can generate task plans, control programs, or motion-planning objectives from language instructions~ Lin_2023,singh2022progprompt,huang2023instruct2act,rana2023sayplan,vemprala2024chatgpt,yu2023language,chen2024roboscript,huang2024rekep . SayCan~ ahn2022saycan plans sequences of skills based on language goals and skill feasibility, while VoxPoser~ huang2023voxposer generates 3D value maps to guide motion planning. Code as Policies~ liang2023cap , CaP-X~ fu2026capx , COAP~ hu2026coap , and Act-Observe-Rewrite~ kumar2026aor investigate how large language models generate and iteratively develop robot programs. These programs can support closed-loop execution through calls to perception tools, conditional logic, and feedback loops. For contact tasks, GenCHiP~ burns2024genchip generates compliant motion programs with termination conditions defined by force thresholds. LEMMo-Plan~ chen2024lemmo infers skill sequences and success conditions from multimodal demonstrations. Unfettered~ xie2025unfettered uses a VLM to infer desired forces, torques, and execution durations. CoRAL~ cicek2026coral uses a large language model to generate cost functions for model predictive control. These approaches translate model reasoning into skill calls, programs, parameters, or optimization objectives. VLM-based agent harnesses. An agent harness connects a model to observations and execution interfaces, coordinates command execution, and returns feedback for subsequent reasoning and action generation~ yao2022react . Some systems enable agents to generate motion commands directly or invoke primitive skills~ duan2024manipulate,lima2026agentic . Show-Harness~ chen2026showharness supports VLM-based robot control through semantic action interfaces and perception plugins. GPT-GEAR~ zhou2026gptgear evaluates GPT-6 Astra for direct closed-loop robot control, examining depth perception, in-context learning, and the use of tactile feedback for action correction. Robo-Harness K1~ li2026k1 provides callable perception tools for segmentation, depth measurement, and grasp candidate generation. Other methods use language or vision-language models to detect and explain manipulation failures~ liu2023reflect,duan2024aha . Hierarchical systems combine task-level agent decisions with learned policies for action generation~ shi2025hi,hu2026matters,galanti2026addressing . Harness VLA~ zhang2026harnessvla , SafeHarness~ xu2026safeharness , and BATON~ xu2026baton use agents to coordinate task execution and invoke VLAs for manipulation, separating task-level reasoning from low-level action generation. Beyond runtime execution, several methods use interaction experience to improve agents or manipulation policies. RPG~ wang2026rpg refines shared skills and system prompts through simulated practice. RoboFoundry~ liang2026robofoundry improves skills and context using execution experience. EmbodiRSI~ lang2026embodirsi investigates corrective data generation, while ENPIRE~ xiao2026enpire explores improvements to policy training procedures. In contrast to these methods, our work focuses on using a frozen VLM for contact-state assessment and action generation from multimodal feedback. Contact Harness uses reusable textual skills to guide the VLM in interpreting and integrating visual, force, and tactile information, while a compliant execution mechanism regulates motion using real-time force feedback throughout each action. The supplementary material compares related methods in terms of observation, action, and contact regulation. Contact Harness sec:method Overview sec:overview As shown in , Contact Harness connects a VLM to the robot through observation and command interfaces, textual skills, and a compliant execution mechanism. Textual skills guide the VLM's interpretation of multimodal feedback and its selection of motion commands, while compliant execution uses real-time force feedback to regulate motion within each command. Each task is specified by a skill that defines its goal, essential steps, completion criteria, and task-specific decision rules. At each iteration, the VLM requests observations, assesses the contact state, and generates a single command or a short batch of commands. Each command specifies a target displacement and an execution duration. The harness executes the commands under impedance control with contact-force constraints and returns the accepted reference poses and measured final poses. The VLM uses these results and newly requested observations to determine its next action. The interfaces and execution mechanism are shared across all tasks and robot platforms in our evaluation, while the textual skills combine a common contact-state assessment procedure with task-specific rules. Observation interface The observation interface returns the latest measurements from the sources requested by the VLM. The interface provides four complementary modalities: vision, force, tactile sensing, and proprioception. Wrist cameras and third-view cameras provide geometric cues, such as alignment error and insertion depth, but cannot directly measure contact forces. The six-axis external wrist wrench provides evidence of contact and indicates the magnitude and direction of loading, but cannot uniquely identify the contact source or location. When available, tactile sensors on both gripper fingers jointly estimate the bending load at the grasped object's tip. This signal provides an additional cue for rotational corrections, complementing the end-effector wrench estimated from joint-level signals~ 1570247,8059840 . Proprioception provides the end-effector pose and joint angles. Discrepancies between the measured pose and the accepted reference pose help identify motion blocked by contact. Textual skills for contact-state assessment sec:text_skill For each task, the VLM receives a system prompt and a task skill. Although the VLM can independently reason through many operating details and task requirements, the prompts make these explicit to reduce ambiguity. This guidance is intended to reduce the reasoning effort required to determine task procedures and how to operate the system, allowing the agent to focus on selecting effective actions. Functionally, the system prompt describes the harness architecture and the VLM's interaction with the robot. It introduces the commands for acquiring observations and executing motions, explains how to handle exceptions, and establishes operating rules shared across tasks. The task skill prompt specifies the task goal and procedure, the robot settings required for that task, and practical considerations at each stage. Together, they provide the operational context needed to use the interfaces and carry out the task. Conceptually, these prompts guide contact-state assessment through three questions: has contact occurred, is it at the intended location, and is it proceeding as expected? The first two require interpreting force estimates alongside visual evidence, because inaccurate force estimates can mislead the assessment and force information alone cannot distinguish intended contact from unintended collisions. title: A ROS2 based Human-In-The-Loop Framework for UAV Search and Rescue Operations
comment: 30 pages, 10 figures, Submitted to and under review in "International Journal of Intelligent Systems" of Wiley
summary: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.
full_text: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates this migration to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89 confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations, a critical factor for UAVs that enables situational awareness during SAR operations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7 across all scenarios and distances. The framework further demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15 ), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We further implement the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation and evaluate them on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80 accuracy, depth keeps 77 at a visibility of 10~m where RGB drops to 24 , and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91 in simulation and 99 on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation provides a structured pathway for SAR-UAV platforms transitioning from ROS1, ensuring seamless integration of human intent. This work bridges critical gaps in human-robot collaboration, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning, thus advancing mission-critical ROS2 deployments in SAR operations. Introduction sec:intro Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have become a game changer in search-and-rescue (SAR) operations de_alcantara_andrade_autonomous_2019 . Their ability to quickly provide aerial surveillance in disaster zones, collapsed buildings, and remote terrain is unparalleled. However, while autonomous UAVs perform exceptionally well in controlled environments, their reliance on pre-programmed flight paths and sensor-based navigation can limit their flexibility in dynamic SAR scenarios liu_real-time_2021 . In these real-world situations, conditions are constantly changing -- shifting debris, victims may be hidden from view, and new obstacles can appear without warning. This is where human judgement becomes more valuable than rigid, pre-programmed algorithms. For example, a firefighter controlling a UAV inside a smoke-filled building may need to override the system quickly, but traditional joystick interfaces can struggle to provide the precision required in high-stress moments. The Need for Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) Systems HITL systems aim to combine human expertise with machine autonomy, but current solutions often come with challenges such as high latency and operator overload cacace_control_2016 . As user interaction plays a critical role in operational efficiency, voice commands, while intuitive, tend to be unreliable in noisy environments, and touchscreen interfaces pull the operator’s attention away from more critical responsibilities at the worst possible moment. Gesture-based control offers a promising alternative, allowing human operators to interact with UAVs through simple, natural hand gestures---such as halt or move left---which require minimal training yoo_motion_2022 . This provides a more seamless, intuitive connection between the operator and the UAV, enabling faster, more effective responses when it matters most. The ROS2 Imperative for SAR Robotics Robot Operating System (ROS) quigley_ros_2009 is an open-source framework for building robotics applications more efficiently. It is a middleware, a set of tools, libraries, and conventions that simplify communication between hardware and software components in a robot or a drone. In ROS, topics act as communication channels for nodes, allowing the broadcast of information that multiple other nodes can receive. A node is an executable that communicates with other nodes via ROS by publishing or subscribing to topics. ROS has two versions: ROS1 and ROS2 macenski_robot_2022 . While ROS1 laid the foundation for robotic communication with its publisher-subscriber model, its real-time performance, security, and scalability limitations make it less ideal for mission-critical SAR operations. Referring to Fig.~ fig:ros2 , ROS2, however, addresses these challenges head-on with several important features ramezani_human-centric_2024, faessler_autonomous_2016,kratky_autonomous_2021,probine_shared_2021,jarecki_mixed_2024,djeradi_toward_2021 : Secure, Priority-Based Communication: By integrating the Data Distribution Service (DDS), ROS2 ensures secure, low-latency transmission of gesture commands. Deterministic Execution: With thread-safe executors and lock-free memory management and real-time optimisations, ROS2 ensures high reliability, especially in real-time tasks like obstacle avoidance and path planning, even in complex and dynamic environments. High-Fidelity Simulation Support: ROS2's integration with Gazebo allows for thorough testing in simulated SAR environments, ensuring optimal UAV performance before deployment. Improved Build System and Scalability: Introduced a more modern and flexible build system and tooling ecosystem, such as ``ament'' and ``colcon''. Modular Architecture: The flexible middleware and language-agnostic communication in ROS2 make it an ideal framework for seamlessly integrating components, such as a YOLOv11-based gesture recognition module (in Python). Cross-Platform and Embedded Support: The supported platforms for ROS2 are Ubuntu, Debian, Windows, Mac OS, etc. Also, Micro-ROS extends ROS2 to microcontrollers, enabling lightweight embedded applications. These advancements make ROS2 the ideal framework bonci_robot_2023,pandey_autonomous_2025 for developing next-generation HITL systems for SAR UAVs, where real-time responsiveness and security are critical. Contributions This paper introduces a ROS2-based framework using Gazebo simulator, PX4 Autopilot and YOLOv11 algorithm that integrates gesture-driven control for SAR UAVs. The following are the main contributions of this paper: ROS2 Migration Support: We propose a modular, hardware-agnostic algorithmic framework to simplify the transition from ROS1 to ROS2 for SAR-UAV developers. The framework outlines the integration of gesture recognition nodes, PX4-compatible flight control, providing a clear conceptual basis for implementation and field deployment. Unified Vision-Based Gesture Pipeline for UAV Control: We design a unified pipeline that combines RGB and depth data to estimate human pose, calculate distance, and classify pointing gestures using YOLOv11, enabling intuitive HITL UAV guidance in complex SAR missions. Robustness in Cluttered and Degraded Environments: We deploy a YOLOv11 model on RGB and depth data to detect directional gestures, which enhances recognition accuracy in cluttered environments. Furthermore, we quantify the framework's resilience in degraded visual conditions, demonstrating a 46.7 average improvement in detection confidence under fog compared to RGB-only baselines, ensuring operational viability where conventional vision fails. Mission Efficiency Validation: Through Gazebo simulations with PX4 autopilot, we demonstrate that the framework's direct gesture-to-command mapping minimises computational overhead, which is critical for time-sensitive SAR operations. Extended Evaluation on Datasets: We implement the modified YOLOv11 (YOLOv11- ) and the depth-weighted pose estimation, and test them together with Algorithm~ alg:algo on a fixed simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in two fog models (Section~ sec:ext_eval ). As the framework is modular, its perception model, gesture rules and UAV commands can be exchanged for other UAV tasks and evaluated on other datasets in the same way. Related Works sec:lit_sec Human-UAV Interaction Human-UAV interaction lygouras_unsupervised_2019 has evolved from basic static gestures in controlled settings to more sophisticated multimodal systems designed for dynamic environments. Andrade et al. de_alcantara_andrade_autonomous_2019 planned the paths of cooperative SAR UAVs in real time without operator input, and Yoo et al. yoo_motion_2022 controlled a UAV in real time with hand gestures, combining a thumb-mounted IMU with a camera. While effective at reducing latency, such vision-based gesture approaches relied heavily on RGB cameras, making them vulnerable to occlusion and varying lighting conditions. Liu et al. liu_real-time_2021 extended this concept by integrating deep learning for gesture recognition in rescue missions. However, because they relied on 2D skeletal tracking, they were prone to perspective distortions, particularly in high-altitude UAV operations where perception accuracy is critical. Further advancements were made by Cacace et al. cacace_control_2016 , who introduced multimodal interaction for controlling multiple UAVs. Although this method expanded control capabilities, it lacked depth-sensing technology, limiting its effectiveness in cluttered SAR environments. To overcome these limitations, our framework combines depth cameras with RGB data, which significantly enhances robustness against occlusion, lighting variations, and limited situational awareness. By incorporating 3D spatial information, our system demonstrates strong performance in dynamic SAR environments, surpassing approaches that rely exclusively on RGB-based recognition de_alcantara_andrade_autonomous_2019, liu_real-time_2021, cacace_control_2016 . ROS2 for Human-UAV Interaction ROS1 has long been the dominant middleware for UAV applications due to its flexibility and community-driven adoption. However, its architecture lacks real-time determinism and struggles with mission-critical responsiveness. Sampedro et al. sampedro_fully-autonomous_2019 deployed a fully autonomous indoor SAR UAV and tested it in Gazebo with PX4 SITL and in real flights, but it executes its missions without human intervention. Similarly, McConkey et al. mcconkey_semi-autonomous_2023 introduced a low-cost semi-autonomous ArduPilot UAV for wilderness SAR operations, but its video is transferred manually after the flight for human detection with YOLOv3, so the operator cannot act on detections during the mission. Recent efforts to transition UAV control to ROS2 have focused on improving human interaction reliability. Ramezani et al. ramezani_human-centric_2024 emphasised trajectory planning optimised for human comfort but treated autonomy and human input as independent processes rather than a collaborative system. Our work builds on these advancements by leveraging ROS2's DDS middleware to ensure deterministic communication and secure human-UAV interaction. By prioritising gesture commands with sub- latency, we keep the operator in the loop during the mission, which the systems above do not support sampedro_fully-autonomous_2019, mcconkey_semi-autonomous_2023, ramezani_human-centric_2024 . This approach lets the operator redirect the UAV with a gesture at any time, ensuring UAV efficiency in time-sensitive SAR missions. In recent years, significant research has centred on classification methods for human activity and gesture recognition in UAV-based search and rescue (SAR) operations

title: HIVE-Bench: Evaluating Patch-Level Visual Representations for Egocentric Robot Manipulation
summary: Pretrained vision is a common start for robot learning, but most comparisons still score one pooled vector from a third-person image. Bimanual policies instead read dense patch tokens from cameras on the robot. We introduce HIVE-Bench: one shared flow-matching policy reads 20 encoders from seven families on 24 egocentric bimanual tasks, across adaptation, task sharing, and sweeps of data, model size, and layer. Keeping the patches matters. Averaging each view to one token removes most of the success, adaptation helps every pair we test, and one shared policy keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The same tokens are then scored with statistics, state and object readouts, published vision scores, and an inverse-dynamics readout. That readout of the commanded motion is one of the strongest measurements available before a policy is trained. Recognition, depth, and correspondence do not transfer reliably. Fine-tuning can improve the action readout even when other measurements move the other way, and no statistic is stable enough to replace a rollout before any deployment.

HIVE-Bench. Twenty pretrained encoders from seven families compete through one shared patch-conditioned policy on egocentric bimanual tasks, across data and model scales, training regimes, and adaptation. fig:teaser Introduction sec:m-intro Robot manipulation policies increasingly reuse pretrained visual encoders instead of learning vision from scratch, which transfers poorly across objects, robots, and viewpoints~ r3m,cortex,mcr,parisi,generalizationgap . The candidates come from very different signals, including self-supervision, language alignment, 3D reconstruction, robot data, and vision--language models~ mae,dinov2,clip,spa,qwen3 . Choosing among them still means training and rolling out a policy. A benchmark with a shared policy can reveal which representations transfer, and whether inexpensive measurements explain their successes and failures across different training conditions. Earlier evaluations often read a pooled third-person feature and relate scene reconstruction to control~ cortex,hucontrol,datasets,burns,theia,mcr,structure . Bimanual policies do not use that interface. They attend to dense patch tokens, which keep the local detail that separates nearby grasps~ openvla,pi0,patchpolicy,afa , and they see through head and wrist cameras that move with the robot and are often occluded~ act,mobilealoha,robotwin,umi . We therefore ask how encoders compare when one policy reads their patch tokens from onboard cameras, and which properties of those tokens track the resulting success. We introduce HIVE-Bench (Figure~ fig:teaser ), to our knowledge the first comprehensive benchmark of patch-level representations for egocentric bimanual manipulation that jointly studies control and diagnostic correlations across training regimes. A flow-matching action head~ dit,gr00t reads 20 encoders from seven families on two egocentric bimanual suites~ robocasa,robotwin . We train it frozen and fine-tuned, on one task and on a shared suite, and we sweep data, model size, and the extracted layer, because a ranking from a single regime is easy to over-read. The same tokens are then scored in several ways: token statistics, state and object readouts, published vision benchmarks, and an inverse-dynamics readout (IDM) that recovers the commanded motion. Those runs support three simple conclusions. Keeping the patch tokens, rather than averaging each view into one, accounts for most of the success of the encoders we compare this way. Fine-tuning improves every encoder we adapt, and one policy shared across tasks keeps most of the success of separate policies at a fraction of the updates. The measurements are the second half of the study. Several of them correlate with success somewhere, but none is stable enough to prove which encoder a robot should use. IDM is among the strongest readouts, especially on RoboTwin, yet even its ranking misses the best encoder and fails to predict gains from adaptation. Our goal is to map these relationships and their limits; finding measurements that improve on IDM remains an open research problem. Our contributions are: An egocentric patch-level benchmark: one shared policy reads the dense patch tokens, not a pooled vector, of 20 encoders from onboard cameras on two bimanual suites under one shared update budget, through documented token interfaces (Section~ sec:m-design ). Evaluation from many angles: single-task and multi-task training, frozen and fine-tuned encoders, demonstration and model-size scaling, extraction layers, pooling, and optional robot state, with the action head and optimizer held fixed (Section~ sec:m-results ). A study of what tracks success, and where it stops: token statistics, action and state readouts, and published vision scores, compared across suites, task sharing, and adaptation, with the cases where a frozen ranking fails to predict improvement kept separate from the cases where it holds, and with IDM among the strongest metrics (Sections~ sec:m-diag and~ sec:m-disc ). ﻿ Related Work sec:m-related Pretrained representations for control. Global embeddings made pretrained vision easy to reuse in control~ parisi,r3m,cortex . Later encoders learn from robot data or distill several teachers~ voltron,spa,theia,radiov25,radio,aem,afro . Evaluations have compared adaptation, downstream learners, data, and objectives~ cortex,hucontrol,datasets,explorepretrain , usually from one pooled third-person feature and a separately trained policy. Newer studies keep more spatial input, but still differ in embodiment, task sharing, and what they measure (Table~ tab:m-coverage ). Spatial policy interfaces and egocentric bimanual manipulation. ALOHA, ACT, Mobile ALOHA, UMI, DexMimicGen, and GR00T advanced bimanual skills with onboard views, dexterous hands, and humanoids~ act,mobilealoha,umi,dexmimicgen,gr00t,dqnet,mmabc . Policies differ in how much spatial detail they keep, from TokenLearner compression in RT-1 to dense pretrained tokens in Patch Policy~ rt1,octo,patchpolicy , and VLA systems and world-action models integrate vision with action prediction~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05,dreamzero,fastwam,liang2026univep . HIVE-Bench holds the action head fixed, so only the encoder and its token interface change between two compared policies. Diagnosing representation quality. Proposed proxies include segmentation ability~ burns , objectness~ slotmim , manipulation relevance~ mcr , token-norm entropy~ theia , attention allocation~ ver , effective rank~ rankme , physical structure~ spa,structure , temporal progression~ temporaltrap , and action recoverability from world-model latents~ semanticwm . Each measures one aspect under its own policy. We measure token statistics, state and action readouts~ spatialprobe , and published vision scores under one patch-level policy, across task sharing, scale, and adaptation, and test which associations survive a change of setting. The environments that supply the tasks and the policy that reads them are introduced separately below. Appendix~ sec:design gives the implementation and the training recipe. Environments and protocols sec:m-bench We use 12 RoboCasa-GR1 kitchen tasks, performed by a humanoid whose 29-D action adds difficulty~ robocasa,gr00t,dexac , and 12 domain-randomized RoboTwin~2.0 tasks, performed by two arms with grippers~ robotwin,robonvs (Figure~ fig:m-simulation ; Table~ tab:app-tasks ). RoboCasa covers object transfer and cabinet, drawer, and microwave interactions. RoboTwin covers tool use, handover, placement, and articulated objects under randomized clutter, lighting, and textures. The suites differ in robot, action, cameras, tasks, and data at once, so differences between them are observational. Default policies see only the current images. One ablation adds robot state (Section~ sec:m-inputs ). Multi-task training (MT) fits one language-conditioned policy to the twelve tasks of a suite. Single-task training (ST) fits a separate policy to each RoboCasa task. The closed-loop comparison covers 20 frozen encoders under MT, 17 of them under ST, and five fine-tuned encoders on RoboCasa ST and on RoboTwin MT (Table~ tab:m-bench ). Further controls vary the number of demonstrations, the checkpoint size, the extraction layer, mean pooling, the state input, and the learned queries of the action head. Every configuration in the main comparison is trained with one seed and evaluated with three evaluation seeds of 50 rollouts per task. A suite score is the mean of the twelve task scores, and its deviation propagates the per-task evaluation deviations. A three-seed RoboCasa MT study, including its stability analysis, is reported in Appendix~ sec:results-seeds . Encoders and the token interface sec:m-encoders The 20 encoders span seven families (Table~ tab:encoder_families ): a supervised ViT~ vit ; the self-supervised MAE, DINOv2, DINOv3, and V-JEPA~2.1~ mae,dinov2,dinov3,vjepa21 ; the geometry-oriented SPA, VGGT- , and LingBot-Vision~ spa,vggtomega,lingbot ; the vision--language CLIP, SigLIP, SigLIP2, and InternViT~ clip,siglip,siglip2,internvl ; the robot-oriented VC-1 and Voltron~ cortex,voltron ; the multi-teacher Theia, RADIOv2.5, and C-RADIOv4~ theia,radiov25,radio ; and three VLMs, Qwen3-VL and its derivatives DepthVLM and Xiaomi-Robotics-1~ qwen3,depthvlm,xiaomi . Table~ tab:suite lists sizes and token counts. Appendix~ app:encoders documents checkpoints and preprocessing. The policy reads every patch token of every view. Class and register tokens are removed, and there is no extra feature normalization at the policy interface. Views are stored at , giving 196 or 256 tokens per view for patch size 16 or 14. V-JEPA~2.1 resizes to 384 pixels and produces 576 tokens, and each VLM contributes 64 final-layer image tokens. Those VLM states do not depend on the instruction, and we do not use Xiaomi-Robotics-1's action head. Two interfaces mix views before the policy reads them: VGGT- receives RoboTwin's three views as one input, and a VLM's image tokens of later views can attend to earlier ones. We therefore compare an encoder under a documented extraction interface, not in isolation (Appendix~ app:encoders ). title: WeaveVLA: 3D Relational Grounding for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained vision-language representations for instruction-conditioned robot control, yet their understanding of task-relevant 3D relations and how these relations evolve during manipulation remains largely implicit. To address this challenge, we introduce \textbf{WeaveVLA}, a framework that enhances VLA action generation by explicitly modeling task-relevant relative 3D relations and maintaining relational context across observations. WeaveVLA employs a task-conditioned sparse graph neural network to encode relative 3D relations among objects, the gripper, and nearby references. Pair-specific recurrent edge states integrate geometric evidence across observations to maintain evolving spatial context. A learned-query readout summarizes the updated graph representations into compact relational tokens, which condition the action expert alongside the original vision-language context. An auxiliary geometry reconstruction objective further encourages spatial structure preservation. We instantiate WeaveVLA on StarVLA-GR00T and $π_{0.5}$, achieving over 98\% average success on LIBERO with both backbones. On LIBERO-Plus, WeaveVLA improves success from 74.9\% to 82.0\% and from 85.7\% to 87.8\%, respectively, with additional improvements on CALVIN D$\rightarrow$D. On three real-world tasks, the StarVLA-GR00T-based variant improves average success from 55.6\% to 70.0\% under standard conditions and from 33.3\% to 53.3\% under OOD perturbations, surpassing the $π_{0.5}$ baseline in both settings.
